Ambulatory anaesthesia and NORA

A1 Multifactorial aspiration risk in the GLP-1 RA era: the role of prolonged air insufflation and airway management

F. Scialanga1, C.T. Caputo1, F. Sbaraglia1, G. Rizzatti2, C. Memoli1, E. Console1, M. Lucente1, F. Maiellare1, R. Braccini1, B. Barone1

1Department of Emergency, Anesthesiology and Intensive Care Sciences, Fondazione Policlinico Agostino Gemelli, Rome, Italy; 2Department of Medical and Surgical Sciences, Fondazione Policlinico Agostino Gemelli, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: F. Scialanga

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A1

Background

Aspiration pneumonia is a significant complication in anaesthesiology, associated with increased perioperative morbidity. Despite adherence to standard preoperative fasting guidelines1, aspiration risk is not completely abolished, particularly in patients with impaired gastric emptying. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA), increasingly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, are known to delay gastric emptying and may increase residual gastric volume.2 During deep sedation for endoscopic procedures, the lack of airway protection—even when advanced oxygenation strategies such as high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO/THRIVE) are used—may further increase the risk of aspiration. Additionally, air insufflation during endoscopy can significantly raise intragastric pressure; when this exceeds the lower oesophageal sphincter barrier pressure, it promotes regurgitation.

Case report

We report the case of a 49-year-old woman (BMI 30 kg/m2) with a history of arterial hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral semaglutide (Rybelsus), scheduled for endoscopic repair of a rectovaginal fistula. The patient had no respiratory symptoms at admission and had fasted from midnight; however, she had taken her last dose of oral semaglutide the day before the procedure. Deep sedation was maintained with continuous propofol infusion at 1.0 mcg/ml (effect site concentration, Eleveld model) combined with Optiflow/THRIVE support. During the procedure, performed in the left lateral position, it was necessary to increase the propofol infusion up to 2.5 mcg/ml. The procedure lasted approximately two hours. During emergence, the patient regurgitated gastric contents and was transferred to the recovery room for postoperative monitoring. She was dyspneic, with an oxygen saturation of 84% on room air, confirmed by arterial blood gas analysis. A chest X-ray revealed inflammatory changes in the left lung. Given the patient’s clinical condition, she was admitted to the intensive care unit. In the following days, she was treated with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (2.2 g three times daily) and supported with high-flow nasal oxygen, which was gradually weaned. The patient was discharged home after 7 days, with complete clinical and radiological resolution of the aspiration pneumonia.

Ethical compliance

Since this study is a case report, formal approval from the Ethics Committee ‘Lazio Area 3’, to which our hospital refers, was not required. However, written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report.

Conclusion

This report highlights several critical considerations about the origin of this adverse event and could lead to a severe warning. The prolonged and complex nature of the procedure necessitated significant gastrointestinal air insufflation, a factor that likely contributed to the regurgitation of enteric contents during emergence from sedation. On the other hand, the patient’s GLP-1 RA therapy—a class known to delay gastric emptying—suggests a full stomach condition may have been present from the early stages of the procedure. Current preoperative fasting guidelines for these patients remain poorly defined due to limited clinical evidence.3 Furthermore, the use of HFNC could theoretically mask silent micro-aspiration events by maintaining optimal SpO-2 levels, thereby delaying timely clinical intervention. These factors underscore the need for advanced airway management in lengthy endoscopic procedures, as standard fasting times may not guarantee patient safety. Anaesthesiologists should maintain a lower threshold for endotracheal intubation in patients on GLP-1 RA therapy to ensure safer airway protection. Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A2 Intranasal dexmedetomidine for pediatric procedural sedation: an observational study on efficacy and predictive factors of success

R. Messina1, C. Gerratana1, M. Vadala’1, R. Bruno1, V.F. Tripodi1, A.T. Mazzeo1, I. Russo Menna2

1Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Human Pathology Department, University of Messina, Italy; 2Anesthesia Department, Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) School of Medicine, Richmond, VA, USA

Correspondence: C. Gerratana

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A2

Background

Intranasal dexmedetomidine is an emerging and significant option for pediatric procedural sedation, offering a non-invasive approach characterized by both sedative and anxiolytic properties [1,2]. Despite its increasing off-label use in clinical settings, remain poorly defined regarding the optimal dosing strategies and the identification of patient subgroups that might benefit from combination therapy with other agents like midazolam [3]. This pilot study evaluates the clinical efficacy of intranasal dexmedetomidine at a standardized dose of 3 mcg/kg in a population of pediatric patients undergoing magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), aiming to identify predictive factors for sedation success. The primary objectives are: (1) to evaluate the efficacy of 3 mcg/kg intranasal dexmedetomidine; (2) to identify specific predictive factors for sedation failure that require rescue interventions such as sevoflurane or midazolam; and (3) to determine whether patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) or high levels of agitation at arrival require a pre-emptive combined sedation strategy.

Materials and Methods

This prospective observational pilot study was conducted on 14 pediatric patients, aged 2–11 years undergoing sedated MRI at the University Hospital G. Martino. All participants, after obtaining informed consent, received an initial dose of intranasal dexmedetomidine at 3 mcg/kg via nebulization. After 20 minutes, non-adequately sedated patients received a supplemental dose of 1 mcg/kg. If sedation remained insufficient after the supplement, midazolam was administered as rescue therapy at a dose of 0.2 mg/kg intranasally or orally. Patients requiring sevoflurane to complete the procedure were recorded as sedation failures and analyzed separately to identify risk factors. Primary outcomes focused on the success rate of dexmedetomidine monotherapy, the necessity for supplemental doses, the addition of midazolam, and failures requiring inhalational anesthesia. ASD and behavioral agitation at arrival were specifically recorded as potential predictive factors for failure of sedation. Standard monitoring during sedation included ECG, SpO2 and blood pressure.

Results

Of the 14 patients analyzed (mean age 5.7 ± 2.9 years), 6 (42.9%) achieved adequate sedation using the dexmedetomidine protocol alone, which included the initial 3 mcg/kg dose and the possible 1 mcg/kg supplement. Notably, all 6 patients were calm upon arrival. Two patients (14.3%) required the addition of 0.2 mg/kg midazolam in addition to the supplemental dexmedetomidine to reach the required level of sedation. 5 patients (35.7%) experienced complete sedation failure, necessitating the use of sevoflurane. Analysis revealed that all these failures occurred in patients diagnosed with ASD or those exhibiting significant agitation at arrival, confirming these conditions as strong predictors of monotherapy failure. The overall success rate, including patients who required midazolam but avoided sevoflurane, was 57.1%.

No common adverse events were observed in the monitored patients. All patients maintained spontaneous ventilation and did not require intravenous cannulation.

Discussion and Conclusions

The results of this study are largely consistent with existing literature identifying 3 mcg/kg as an optimal starting dose for pediatric sedation. Pharmacokinetic studies demonstrate that this dose maintains plasma concentrations safely below the toxicity threshold of 1000 pg/mL [1]. In contrast, a 4 mcg/kg dose can cause up to 50% of patients to exceed this limit. Our 42.9% success rate for monotherapy in calm patients is lower than the 60–90% reported in some studies. The literature strongly supports the use of 1 mcg/kg supplemental doses of dexmedetomidine as rescue therapy.

The high failure rate in patients with ASD or agitation aligns with evidence suggesting these patients benefit more from a combined dexmedetomidine-midazolam approach. Studies by Li et al. and recent meta-analyses confirm that such combinations significantly increase success rates in children with autism compared to monotherapy [3]. Our study confirms that the behavioural state at arrival is a clinically relevant predictor that should guide the selection of the sedation strategy. Regarding safety, common adverse events included mild bradycardia (2.3–11.5%) and desaturation (reported in ~40% of monitoring studies), though these rarely required clinical intervention. Karlsson et al. demonstrated a 93% success rate at 4 mcg/kg for MRIs with minimal adverse events, supporting this direction [4]. In conclusion, 3 mcg/kg is effective for calm patients, but for those with ASD or agitation, an initial combined strategy with midazolam is recommended [5]. Future studies will evaluate the effects of using a 4 mcg/kg dose of dexmedetomidine in pediatric patients undergoing MRI.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A3 High-flow nasal cannula and remimazolam sedation in frail patients undergoing gastrointestinal endoscopy: a preliminary observational experience

S. Ferraioli, D. Gaetano, D. Pignata, S. Brunetti, O. Ayoub, M.B. Passavanti, M.C. Pace, V. Pota, F. Coppolino, P. Sansone

University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: S. Ferraioli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A3

Background

Providing safe sedation for gastrointestinal endoscopy in high-risk patients remains challenging, particularly in non-operating room anesthesia (NORA) settings, where respiratory complications may rapidly compromise procedural safety. Remimazolam, an ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine, has emerged as a promising sedative due to its favorable hemodynamic and respiratory profile. In frail patients, systematic use of High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) may improve oxygenation and reduce peri-procedural respiratory events. This preliminary observational study evaluated the feasibility and safety of a sedation strategy combining remimazolam and HFNC in high-risk patients undergoing gastrointestinal endoscopy.

Materials and Methods

We enrolled forty-one adult patients with ASA physical status III scheduled for gastroscopy, colonoscopy or combined procedures after informed consent. 13 patients were older than 65 years, 18 had cardiovascular disease, 7 had chronic pulmonary disease, 15 were active or former smokers, 9 had class I obesity (BMI >30), and 1 had class II obesity (BMI >35). Sedation was induced with remimazolam 5 mg followed by 2.5 mg boluses, up to a cumulative dose of 20 mg. Due to the elevated respiratory risk, HFNC was routinely applied throughout the procedures at 40 L/min, FiO2 50% at a temperature of 31 °C. Supplemental propofol boluses (20–30 mg) and fentanyl 50 mcg were administered when clinically required.

Results

Remimazolam alone provided adequate sedation in 16 procedures lasting up to 20 minutes. In the remaining 25 cases, additional propofol was required, mainly during longer or technically demanding procedures, including combined procedures, polypectomy, biopsy sampling and procedures performed by less experienced operators. Fentanyl was administered in 10 patients, while flumazenil 0.5 mg was used in 9 cases to facilitate recovery. All procedures were successfully completed in the NORA setting with rapid recovery; most patients were awake, cooperative and hemodynamically stable within 20 minutes. Only one adverse event occurred: a 78-year-old woman with cardiovascular disease developed severe bradycardia, hypotension and mild desaturation requiring atropine, HFNC flow escalation and temporary interruption of the procedure. No further complications were observed.

Conclusions

The combination of remimazolam and HFNC appears to be a feasible and effective sedation strategy for high-risk patients undergoing gastrointestinal endoscopy in NORA settings. HFNC may represent a valuable adjunctive respiratory support tool, contributing to procedural safety, maintenance of adequate oxygenation throughout the procedure and rapid recovery.

The study is currently under review by the local Ethics Committee.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

General anesthesia and perioperative medicine

A4 I-TAP block as an opioid-sparing analgesic strategy in robotic hysterectomy: a case report

O.P. Volino, A. Palma, M. Loreto, M. Brita, F. Salvato, F. Russo, A. De Simone, E. Va Fai Rad, C. Sala, P. Vasta, M. Mainini, S. Perna, M. Pisanti, R. Villani

A.O.R.N. Antonio Cardarelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: O.P. Volino

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A4

Body

Robot-assisted gynecological surgery currently represents one of the most widely adopted minimally invasive approaches for the treatment of both benign and malignant uterine diseases. Despite its lower invasiveness compared with open surgery, postoperative pain following robotic hysterectomy may still be clinically significant, particularly during the first 24 postoperative hours, due to abdominal wall trauma related to trocar insertion, peritoneal stretching, and surgical manipulation. In this setting, ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia techniques have gained increasing interest as part of multimodal perioperative analgesic protocols.

We describe the case of a 58-year-old woman, classified as ASA physical status II, scheduled for robotic total hysterectomy with bilateral adnexectomy for benign gynecological disease. Her medical history was significant for well-controlled arterial hypertension and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. The patient reported allergies to amoxicillin and ketoprofen. Body weight was 84 kg, height 160 cm, with a body mass index (BMI) of 32 kg/m².

During the preoperative anesthesiology assessment, considering the presence of moderate obesity, the need to minimize perioperative opioid consumption, and the risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting, a multimodal analgesic strategy based on a preoperative I-TAP block was planned. The I-TAP technique consisted of a bilateral transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block combined with bilateral ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric nerve block under ultrasound guidance.

The patient was monitored according to standard ASA recommendations and underwent balanced general anesthesia. Before anesthetic induction, all regional blocks were performed under sterile conditions using a high-frequency ultrasound probe.

General anesthesia was induced with propofol, fentanyl, and rocuronium, followed by uncomplicated orotracheal intubation. Anesthesia maintenance was achieved with sevoflurane inhalation and titrated boluses of short-acting opioids. The robotic surgical procedure lasted approximately 170 minutes and was completed without relevant intraoperative hemodynamic or respiratory complications.

The bilateral TAP block was performed within the fascial plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. For each side, a mixture of ropivacaine 0.375%, mepivacaine 0.5%, and dexamethasone 0.02% was administered, with a total volume of 20 mL per side. Subsequently, bilateral ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric nerve blocks were performed using the same anesthetic mixture with a total volume of 10 mL per side.

At the end of surgery, the patient was extubated in the operating room and transferred to the recovery unit awake, cooperative, and hemodynamically stable. Initial postoperative pain assessment demonstrated complete absence of pain, with a Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) score of 0 both at rest and during mild mobilization.

The postoperative analgesic protocol included rescue therapy with intravenous paracetamol 1000 mg on demand. However, during subsequent clinical evaluations performed at 12 and 24 hours after surgery, the patient continued to report an NRS score of 0 without requiring any rescue analgesia or supplemental opioid administration. No episodes of postoperative nausea and vomiting, excessive sedation, or block-related complications were observed.

This case highlights the potential role of the I-TAP block as an advanced analgesic technique in minimally invasive gynecological surgery. The TAP block provides analgesia to the anterolateral abdominal wall through blockade of the anterior branches of thoracolumbar nerves from T6 to L1, whereas the ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric block offers more selective coverage of the lower abdominal dermatomes frequently involved in suprapubic trocar insertion sites.

Over the last decade, several studies have investigated the efficacy of TAP block in laparoscopic and robotic hysterectomy, demonstrating reductions in early postoperative pain and opioid consumption, although results remain somewhat heterogeneous. Similarly, the literature regarding ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric nerve blocks has reported significant reductions in postoperative pain and analgesic requirements in lower abdominal surgery.

The combination of these two techniques, referred to as the I-TAP approach, may provide broader and more effective analgesic coverage compared with TAP block alone, particularly in patients undergoing lower abdominal surgical procedures. Recent evidence suggests that combining TAP and ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric blocks may improve postoperative analgesia quality and patient satisfaction.

Another relevant aspect of the present case is the use of dexamethasone as a perineural adjuvant. Several studies have demonstrated that dexamethasone combined with local anesthetics in peripheral nerve blocks significantly prolongs postoperative analgesia duration and reduces opioid consumption. In our patient, the complete absence of pain up to 24 hours after surgery may also have been facilitated by the synergistic effect of ropivacaine, mepivacaine, and dexamethasone.

In conclusion, this case report suggests that ultrasound-guided I-TAP block may represent an effective and safe analgesic strategy in major robotic gynecological surgery. The combination of TAP block and ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric nerve block provided excellent postoperative pain control with complete absence of rescue analgesic requirements during the first 24 postoperative hours. Although further prospective randomized studies are required to establish the true clinical benefit of this combined technique, the I-TAP block appears promising as part of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols and opioid-sparing strategies in minimally invasive gynecological surgery. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying clinical data.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A5 Exploring the role of transthoracic echocardiography and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin i in perioperative risk stratification for non-cardiac surgery

E. Verrigni, E. Sassanelli, A. Tarallo Matarrese, A. Fogagnolo, M. Verri, C.A. Volta, G. Scaramuzzo, S. Spadaro

Department of Translational Medicine, University of Ferrara, Italy

Correspondence: E. Verrigni

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A5

Background

The 2022 European Society of Cardiology guidelines broadened recommendations for preoperative transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery. However, the extent to which preoperative TTE contributes to postoperative functional risk stratification remains uncertain. In parallel, growing evidence supports the prognostic value of cardiac biomarkers, particularly high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI), in the perioperative setting. In this exploratory study, we sought to investigate potential associations between preoperative TTE use, hs-cTnI levels, and postoperative functional outcomes in patients at high cardiovascular risk undergoing non-cardiac surgery.

Materials and methods

We conducted a prospective observational study including 75 high cardiovascular risk patients undergoing elective non-cardiac surgery. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Patients were categorized according to preoperative TTE exposure (TTE vs no TTE) and hs-cTnI levels (elevated vs normal). Baseline clinical characteristics included age, ASA III–IV status, Clinical Frailty Score, and Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI). Functional outcomes were assessed at 30-day follow-up using the 12-item World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0), along with disability-free survival (DFS) in patients with available follow-up data. Clinically significant disability was defined as WHODAS 2.0 > or equal to 25%. Continuous variables were expressed as median [IQR] and compared using the Mann–Whitney U test, while categorical variables were compared using Fisher’s exact test. Given the exploratory design, analyses were intended to identify potential signals rather than establish causality.

Results

Patients undergoing preoperative TTE appeared to have greater baseline vulnerability, with a higher prevalence of ASA III–IV status (94.0% vs 72.0%, p=0.013) and higher Clinical Frailty Score (4 [3–5] vs 3 [2–4], p=0.026), while age and RCRI were comparable between groups. These patients also showed higher WHODAS 30-day scores compared with the no-TTE group (16.7 [8.3–26.6] vs 7.3 [2.1–15.1], p=0.016), although median values remained below the threshold for clinically significant disability. No significant differences in 30-day DFS were observed between groups (52.0% vs 76.0%, p=0.356).

In contrast, elevated preoperative hs-cTnI was associated with a profile suggestive of increased perioperative risk, including higher Clinical Frailty Score (5 [4–5] vs 3 [3–4], p=0.006) and higher RCRI (1 [1–3] vs 1 [0–1], p=0.039). Elevated hs-cTnI levels were associated with higher WHODAS 30-day scores (31.3 [27.1–52.1] vs 12.5 [4.2–20.8], p=0.039), exceeding the threshold for clinically significant disability, and with reduced 30-day DFS (20.0% vs 77.2%, p=0.018) (Figure 1). These findings highlight a potential signal linking hs-cTnI elevation to adverse postoperative functional outcomes.

Conclusions

In this exploratory analysis, preoperative TTE use appeared to reflect underlying patient frailty and perioperative vulnerability rather than independently identifying patients at risk of clinically significant postoperative disability. Conversely, elevated preoperative hs-cTnI was consistently associated with worse postoperative functional outcomes and reduced disability-free survival, suggesting a potential role as an early marker of perioperative risk. These findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and warrant confirmation in larger, adequately powered studies. Further research is needed to clarify whether integrating TTE findings into perioperative decision-making or combining imaging with biomarker-based strategies may improve patient outcomes.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A6 The no-tests program in elective preoperative assessment: an observational study on clinical impact, feasibility, and healthcare costs

M. Ursitti, M. Viggiano, A. d’Amore, M. Luchini, R. Spina

Local Health Authority (ASL) Toscana Centro, Empoli, Italy

Correspondence: M. Ursitti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A6

Background

Routine preoperative laboratory testing in low-risk surgical patients remains widely practiced despite strong international evidence and guidelines discouraging its use. Evidence-based recommendations suggest that, in ASA I–II patients undergoing low- to intermediate-complexity elective surgery, clinical assessment alone is generally sufficient for perioperative risk stratification. This study evaluates the safety, feasibility, and economic impact of a “No-Tests” program implemented in a real-world preoperative setting.

Methods

A retrospective observational single-centre study was conducted on patients enrolled in the “No-Tests” program between May 2023 and August 2025 at San Giuseppe Hospital (Empoli, ASL Toscana Centro). Inclusion criteria were ASA physical status I–II, age 3–60 years, and elective low- to medium-complexity surgery. Patients with clinical or anamnestic findings requiring further investigation were excluded. A total of 1030 patients were included.

The primary endpoint was the incidence of intraoperative and postoperative complications within 30 days. Secondary endpoints included length of hospital stay, organizational feasibility, and cost analysis. A matched comparative analysis was performed in patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy (80 cases vs 160 controls). Data were collected using structured electronic records and Microsoft Excel and analysed using STATA 17.0.

Results

The study population had a mean age of 37.2 ± 17.5 years, with a slight female predominance (53.5%) and a majority of ASA I patients (58%). General surgery and otorhinolaryngology were the most represented surgical specialties, and both general and loco-regional anaesthetic techniques were included.

Overall, 26 complications were recorded (2.5%). Most events were surgical (58%), followed by anaesthetic (33%) and medical complications (10%), none of which were considered predictable based on preoperative clinical assessment or routine testing.

In the comparative analysis, complication rates were 6.2% in the “No-Tests” group and 10.6% in controls, without statistically significant differences (p = 0.268). ASA-stratified analysis confirmed no significant differences between groups. No association was found between comorbidities and complication rates.

Mean hospital stay was 1.10 ± 0.6 days in the “No-Tests” group versus 1.3 ± 1.3 days in controls (p = 0.149). The economic analysis showed a total estimated saving between €11,330 and €14,420, excluding indirect organizational benefits.

Discussion

The implementation of a clinically guided preoperative assessment program safely reduced unnecessary testing without increasing perioperative risk. The observed complication rate is consistent with published data for low-risk surgical populations. Importantly, no complication was considered preventable through routine laboratory or ECG testing, reinforcing the limited clinical value of indiscriminate preoperative investigations in ASA I–II patients. The comparative analysis further supports the safety and feasibility of the “No-Tests” approach in laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

Conclusion

A selective, clinically driven preoperative assessment without routine laboratory testing in ASA I–II patients undergoing low- to medium-risk elective surgery appears safe, feasible, and cost-effective. It was not associated with increased perioperative complications or prolonged hospital stay, while providing measurable economic and organizational benefits. These findings further support current international recommendations discouraging routine preoperative testing in clinically stable low-risk surgical patients.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A7 A multimodal anaesthesiologist approach to diep surgery: a report based on experience

A. Petrecca, F.V. Tessitore, L. Correale, A. Marra, N. Logrieco

Department of Neurosciences, Reproductive and Odontostomatological Sciences, University of Naples Federico II, Italy

Correspondence: F.V. Tessitore

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A7

Background

Breast reconstruction is an essential part of breast cancer treatment. Breast reconstruction using the DIEP (Deep Inferior Epigastric Perforator) flap is considered the gold standard for post-mastectomy treatment.1 Although ERAS (Enhanced Recovery after Surgery) protocols are well-established for breast reconstruction surgery,2, specific literature on comprehensive anaesthetic management remains limited. We treated 7 different patients undergoing diep flap reconstruction with a multimodal approach which included both spinal anaesthesia, ESP (erector spinae plane) block continuous, balanced general anaesthesia and advanced hemodynamic monitoring, motor block monitoring, and depth of sedation monitoring.

Material and methods

This is a pilot study conducted according to the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee of University of Naples “Federico II” (IRB protocol number 307/21). Informed consent was obtained from all subjects involved in the study.

We had 7 different female patients (average age of 49 years old), all gone under a previous mastectomy for breast cancer, undergoing DIEP flap operation. All the patients provided explicit informed consent. All of them received continuous bilateral/omolateral ultrasound-guided ESP block at D3-D4, with an initial single injection of ropivacaine, dexmedetomidine, and dexamethasone (doses based on each patient), followed by an elastomeric infusion pump with ropivacaine and dexmedetomidine connected to the ESP catheter for 48 hours at 8 mL/h. Moreover, spinal anaesthesia at L3-L4/l4-L5 was performed with a single shot of Ropivacaine, morphine, ketamine, atropine and dexmedetomidine. Balanced anaesthesia was maintained with desflurane (MAC 0.3–0.5) following induction with low dosage of sufentanil and propofol. The EV-1000, Conox, and TOF were used for monitoring.

Results

Patients reported exceptional pain control, with a Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) score of 0 upon awakening and through the first 24 hours. At 36–48 hours, the average NRS remained very low (1–2) All patients achieved an Aldrete score of 10 and a Bromage score of 0 immediately upon awakening. Hemodynamic stability, with management of fluids and/or vasoactive agents, was managed via the EV-1000 platform (Goal-Directed Therapy) to obtain MAP (Mean Arterial Pressure) of 65 mmHg. Depth of anaesthesia was tracked using CONOX (target range 50–70), and neuromuscular blockade was monitored via TOF (deep block). Three patients required re-operation due to venous thrombosis. In these cases, the indwelling ESP catheters provided sufficient analgesia to perform flap rescue attempts on awake patients. Two of this patients needed of a great dorsal flap, performed under general anaesthesia due to the patient’s position. ESP block catheters were used in these cases to ensure analgesia during the operations and in postoperative period. In each case, the NRS score upon awakening remained at 0.

Conclusions

The implementation of a multimodal anaesthetic plan, specifically the combination of continuous ESP blocks and spinal anaesthesia, provides superior perioperative stability and excellent postoperative pain management for DIEP flap surgery. Reducing the dosage of drugs used during the operation (low MAC and low doses of intravenous opioids used only for intubation), allow to optimise haemodynamic stability and improve postoperative recovery. Furthermore, the use of regional anaesthesia at both the donor site (spinal) and the recipient site (ESP) appears to promote vasodilation, thereby reducing post-operative complications related to arterial blood flow. The limitations of this study are the small sample size, a follow-up period of less than 72 hours, and the absence of a control group.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A8 Perioperative ultrasound monitoring for the diagnosis of diaphragmatic dysfunction after cytoreductive surgery with diaphragmatic debulking in ovarian cancer (Ovadia study)

M. Sanguigni1, G. Spinazzola1, L. Frassanito1,2,3,4, S. Empler1, F. Chiusolo2, S. Spadaro3, T. Michi1, S. Postorino1, G. Podagrosi1, G. Draisci1,2,3,4, T. Bove1,2,3,4, M. Antonelli1,2,3,4

1Agostino Gemelli IRCCS University Polyclinic Foundation, Rome, Italy; 2Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, IRCCS, Rome, Italy; 3Department of Translational Medicine, University Hospital, University of Ferrara, Italy; 4Catholic University of Sacre Heart, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: M. Sanguigni

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A8

Background

Postoperative diaphragmatic dysfunction (PDD) is increasingly recognized as a contributor to postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) after major abdominal surgery. In advanced ovarian cancer, cytoreductive surgery frequently requires diaphragmatic peritoneal debulking or resection to achieve complete cytoreduction; however, the impact of these procedures on postoperative diaphragmatic function has not been adequately investigated. This prospective observational study aimed to evaluate perioperative ultrasound-assessed changes in diaphragmatic contractility in patients undergoing cytoreductive surgery with diaphragmatic debulking for ovarian malignancy and to explore their association with PPCs.

Methods

This single-center prospective observational study was conducted at Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli IRCCS, Rome, Italy. Consecutive patients undergoing primary or interval cytoreductive surgery for FIGO stage I–IV ovarian cancer between August and December 2025 were enrolled. Diaphragmatic ultrasound was performed preoperatively, 2 hours after extubation, on postoperative day 1 (POD1), and postoperative day 4 (POD4). Ultrasound assessment included diaphragmatic excursion, diaphragmatic slope, and diaphragmatic thickening fraction (TF). Lung ultrasound score (LUS), respiratory rate, and dyspnea assessed by Borg scale were also recorded. The primary endpoint was perioperative change in diaphragmatic contractility. Secondary endpoints included PPCs, postoperative oxygen requirements, ICU admission, and hospital length of stay. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify predictors of PPCs.

Results

Seventy-eight patients completed the study protocol. Mean age was 59.1 ± 12.2 years, and 88% had FIGO stage III–IV disease. A significant postoperative impairment in diaphragmatic function was observed. Diaphragmatic excursion significantly decreased at POD1 compared with baseline (18.43 ± 5.98 mm vs. 15.31 ± 4.76 mm; p = 0.02). Diaphragmatic slope was significantly reduced immediately after surgery (12.97 ± 4.27 vs. 15.26 ± 5.17 at baseline; p < 0.001), with recovery by POD4. Similarly, TF significantly decreased both at 2 hours postoperatively and on POD1 compared with baseline (48.96 ± 11.27% vs. 38.54 ± 12.19% and 40.01 ± 12.20%, respectively; both p < 0.01), returning toward baseline values by POD4 (Figure 1).

The worsening of respiratory function is associated with diaphragmatic dysfunction. Respiratory rate and Borg dyspnea scores increased significantly at all postoperative time points, while LUS score progressively worsened postoperatively (baseline 0.5 ± 1.49 vs. 6.38 ± 2.05 at POD1; p < 0.01), indicating loss of pulmonary aeration.

Overall, 34 patients (44%) developed PPCs, predominantly pleural effusion (79%) and pneumothorax (21%). Diaphragmatic dysfunction on POD1 was observed in 14% of patients, and more than half of these patients subsequently developed PPCs. Univariate analysis identified longer operative time, higher intraoperative crystalloid and colloid administration, ascites, postoperative oxygen requirement, lower TF values, and higher LUS scores as factors associated with PPCs (Table 1). Multivariable logistic regression demonstrated that preoperative ascites (OR 10.12, 95% CI 1.04–98.2; p = 0.046), prolonged surgical duration (OR 1.01, 95% CI 1.00–1.02; p = 0.007), intraoperative colloid administration (OR 1.01, 95% CI 1.00–1.01; p = 0.017), and lower postoperative TF (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.83–0.97; p = 0.007) were independently associated with PPCs. The predictive model demonstrated excellent discrimination (ROC-AUC 0.9182) and satisfactory calibration.

Conclusion

Patients undergoing cytoreductive surgery with diaphragmatic debulking for ovarian cancer experience a significant but transient postoperative reduction in diaphragmatic contractility, associated with impaired lung aeration and a high incidence of PPCs. Perioperative diaphragmatic ultrasound, particularly assessment of diaphragmatic thickening fraction, may represent a valuable noninvasive tool for early identification of patients at increased respiratory risk. Integration of diaphragmatic ultrasound parameters with conventional clinical risk assessment may improve perioperative stratification and support targeted preventive strategies in complex gynecologic oncology surgery.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A9 BEYOND-MAP trial: beyond treating numbers — a randomized trial of integrated flow- and depth-guided hemodynamic management in major non-cardiac surgery

G. Sciacca, P. Kouroupis, L. Tritapepe

A.O. San Camillo Forlanini, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: G. Sciacca

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A9

Background

Intraoperative hypotension remains one of the leading preventable drivers of postoperative organ injury, yet its management is still predominantly pressure-targeted and fails to account for the underlying physiological drivers of hypotension [1–3]. Reliance on mean arterial pressure (MAP) alone does not capture the complex interplay between cardiac output, vascular tone, and anesthetic depth, potentially leading to inappropriate and non-individualized therapeutic interventions [4,5].

Aim

To determine whether a physiology-driven, integrated hemodynamic strategy combining arterial pressure, flow-derived parameters, and anesthetic depth reduces postoperative organ dysfunction compared with standard MAP-guided care.

Innovation and Rationale

BEYOND-MAP introduces a paradigm shift from “treating numbers” to “treating physiology.” Current perioperative hemodynamic strategies have largely focused on either pressure or flow optimization, and only partially on anesthetic depth, without integrating these domains into a unified framework [6,7]. To our knowledge, no randomized controlled trial has evaluated an integrated pressure–flow–depth strategy. By combining these elements into a single algorithm, the study enables treatment and prevention of hypotension and provides targeted, individualized hemodynamic therapy for each patient.

This approach is expected to reduce intraoperative hypotension burden, optimize fluid and vasoactive drug administration, and translate into a clinically meaningful reduction in early postoperative organ injury.

Methods

BEYOND-MAP is a prospective, randomized, single-blind controlled trial enrolling 320 adult patients undergoing major non-cardiac surgery under general anesthesia with invasive arterial monitoring and with an expected surgical duration of at least 2 hours.

Patients are randomized 1:1 to:

Integrated strategy: algorithm-guided management incorporating MAP, cardiac index, stroke volume index, stroke volume variation, dynamic arterial elastance, contractility (dP/dt), and BIS-guided anesthetic depth

Integrated strategy: algorithm-guided management incorporating MAP, cardiac index, stroke volume index, stroke volume variation, dynamic arterial elastance, contractility (dP/dt), and BIS-guided anesthetic depth

Standard care: MAP-guided management (>65 mmHg), with advanced hemodynamic variables and depth monitoring blinded

Standard care: MAP-guided management (>65 mmHg), with advanced hemodynamic variables and depth monitoring blinded

Perioperative care is standardized across groups. The trial is powered to detect a clinically meaningful reduction in postoperative organ dysfunction.

Endpoints

The primary endpoint is a composite of myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery (MINS), acute kidney injury (AKI), or postoperative delirium within 72 hours.

The co-primary endpoint is intraoperative hypotension burden, quantified as the time-weighted average (TWA) of mean arterial pressure (MAP) below 65 mmHg throughout the intraoperative period.

Secondary endpoints include severe hypotension (MAP <55 mmHg), total vasopressor and inotropic dose, intraoperative fluid balance, length of hospital stay, and 30-day mortality.

Conclusions

By moving beyond MAP-based management, BEYOND-MAP challenges a long-standing paradigm in perioperative care. If confirmed, this integrated pressure–flow–depth approach could redefine perioperative hemodynamic management and establish a new standard of care in major non-cardiac surgery.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A10 Mechanical power outperforms tidal volume per ideal body weight in predicting postoperative pulmonary inflammatory injury during one-lung ventilation: a retrospective cohort study

G. Gazzé1, E. Scalia2, M. Covotta1, M. Di Folco1, J. Salvato1, D. Sammartini1, S. Orlando1, V. Ceccarelli2, G. Torregiani1

1Unit of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, IRCCS Regina Elena National Cancer Institute, Rome, Italy; 2Department of Anesthesiology, Critical Care and Pain Medicine, Sapienza University of Rome, Italy

Correspondence: E. Scalia

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A10

Introduction

One-lung ventilation (OLV) represents a critical phase in thoracic surgery, during which the entire minute ventilation is delivered to a single lung with a significantly reduced functional residual capacity. This physiological challenge exposes the dependent lung to disproportionate mechanical stress and strain, potentially triggering a localized inflammatory response. Current lung-protective strategies are largely anchored to the use of low tidal volumes normalized to ideal body weight (VT/IBW <= 6 mL/kg), a target derived from two-lung ventilation trials in ARDS [1]. The fundamental limitation of the VT/IBW approach lies in its reliance on IBW as a proxy for lung size. While IBW reflects predicted total lung capacity, it fails to account for the dynamic reduction in aerated lung volume during OLV. Factors such as surgical compression, atelectasis, and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction can significantly alter the functional volume of the ventilated lung. Mechanical power (MP), formulated by Gattinoni et al. [2], integrates tidal volume, respiratory rate, and pressures into a single energy metric.

This study aimed to evaluate the discriminative performance of MP compared to VT/IBW and driving pressure (DP) in predicting postoperative pulmonary inflammatory injury.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study using high-fidelity data from the VitalDB database (Seoul National University Hospital). From 944 cases, 380 patients were analyzed after high-fidelity compliance-based OLV detection. Informed consent for data collection and its use for research purposes was obtained from all patients as per institutional protocols.

MP was calculated using the simplified Gattinoni equation and expressed as the mean value over the stable OLV period, excluding the first 10 minutes to allow for stabilization.

The primary outcome was systemic inflammatory injury, defined as postoperative Day 1 C-reactive protein (CRP) > 5 mg/dL.

Statistical analysis utilized Firth’s penalized logistic regression adjusted for eleven confounders, bootstrap AUROC, restricted cubic splines (df=3), and decision curve analysis (DCA).

Results

Median age was 62 years; 91.1% of procedures were VATS. The primary outcome occurred in 54 patients (14.2%). MP demonstrated markedly superior discriminative ability (AUROC 0.672) compared with VT/IBW (AUROC 0.371; p < 0.001) and DP (AUROC 0.596; p = 0.052) (Figure 1 A). A striking finding was the ‘VT/IBW paradox’: VT/IBW exhibited a significant inverse association with the primary outcome (OR per SD: 0.61; p < 0.001). This suggests that VT/IBW systematically underestimates risk in shorter patients and overestimates it in taller ones.

Component analysis (Figure 1B) revealed that absolute VT (OR 1.61) and DP (OR 1.47) were the primary drivers of inflammation, while respiratory rate and PEEP were not independent predictors. The risk of inflammatory injury increased monotonically across MP tertiles (T1: 7.6% vs. T3: 24.1%; p < 0.001). In the multivariable model, each 1 J/min increase in MP was associated with a 43% increase in the odds of injury (OR 1.43, p = 0.014).

The restricted cubic spline (Figure 1 C) confirmed a linear-like dose-response relationship with a Youden-optimal cutoff at 5.80 J/min. Finally, DCA (Figure 1D) demonstrated that an MP-based strategy provides a positive net benefit (0.043) up to a threshold probability of 0.55.

Conclusions

VT/IBW is an inadequate and potentially misleading lung-protective target during OLV because it conceals the true risk of inflammatory injury. Mechanical power offers a superior, physiologically grounded metric for predicting postoperative complications. Priority intervention should focus on reducing absolute tidal volume to maintain MP below 5.80 J/min. These results support the implementation of MP-guided individualized ventilation protocols in thoracic surgery.

Keywords

One-lung ventilation; mechanical power; tidal volume; driving pressure; postoperative pulmonary complications; VitalDB.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A11 Multidisciplinary approach for anesthetic and surgical management of a rare progressive spinal chondrosarcoma in a young woman: a case report

D. Sammartini1, C. Bonarrigo1, G. Tola1, M. Covotta1, M. Di Folco1, G. Gazzè1, S. Orlando1, J. Salvato1, V. Ceccarelli2, E. Scalia2, G. Torregiani1

1Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Therapy, IRCCS Regina Elena National Cancer Institute, Rome, Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Therapy, Policlinico Umberto I, Sapienza University of Rome, Italy

Correspondence: D. Sammartini

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A11

Background

Spinal chondrosarcoma is an aggressive malignant bone tumor of the spinal column(1). It represents the second most common malignant tumor of the spine. The thoracic region is the most commonly involved site(2).

Diagnosis is achieved through CT scan and MRI, followed by histological confirmation via biopsy. Only a few cases have been reported in the literature, therefore therapeutic decisions can be complex. The treatment of choice is surgical, as chondrosarcoma shows limited sensitivity to conventional chemotherapy/radiotherapy(3)(4).

Case Report

We report the case of a 40 year old woman, 164 cm, 50 kg, with an unremarkable medical history, ASA 1, diagnosed with low grade G1 atypical chondrosarcoma extending from D7/D9.

The patient reports the onset, approximately five months earlier, of dysphagia associated with localized pain in the dorsal spine in the left paravertebral region, worsened by palpation and prolonged standing, without evident neurological deficits.

MRI and contrast-enhanced CT scan of the spine revealed the presence of a left paravertebral lesion measuring 54×48×49mm, involving vertebral bodies, laminae, pedicles, costal arches, and costovertebral joints at levels D7/D9, showing extensive contact with the posterior wall of the aorta (Fig. 1). Histological examination ultimately confirmed the definitive diagnosis.

The patient underwent surgical intervention with a combined thoracotomic/posterior median approach, consisting of left D7/D9 costovertebral resection, vertebral stabilization, massive bone grafting coming from a Musculoskeletal Tissue Bank fixed with compression screws, reconstruction of the thoracic wall with a Gore-Tex membrane. Three different surgical stages were required (thoracic, vascular, orthopedic), with a total duration of 8 hours and 40 minutes.

Surgery was performed under general (using a 37 Fr double-lumen tube) and locoregional anesthesia (Erector Spinae/Serratus Anterior Plane Block were performed, injecting 20 ml of Ropivacaine 0.5% for each regional block). At surgery procedure 3 units of packed red blood cells were available. Two peripheral venous catheters, one central venous catheter and one arterial line were placed. Hemodynamic management was guided by continuous monitoring of Electrocardiogram, Heart Rate (HR), Invasive Blood Pressure, Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP), Cardiac Index (CI), Stroke Volume Variation, Pulse Oximetry and Temperature by esophageal probe. During surgery, homeostatic balance was monitored by serial blood gas analysis. The hemodynamic parameters remained constant without needing vasopressor support with average values of CI 2.4 L/min/m2, MAP 80 mmHg, HR 72 bpm. Total volume repletion was 6500 ml (7 Physiological Solutions, 4 Rehydration Solutions, 2 Lactated Ringer); 5 units of packed red blood cells have been transfused. Initial postoperative pain was controlled by infusion pump at the speed of 0,8 mg/ml/h of morphine. At the end of surgery the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit for 48 hours.

The postoperative course, was uneventful, and the patient maintained full neurological function. However, an episode of anemia was noted; therefore, the patient was evaluated by the transfusion center and, following their recommendations, therapy with Ferric Carboxymaltose and Folic Acid was administered, resulting in complete resolution of the clinical condition. The hospital stay lasted 27 days.

Postoperative MRI confirmed complete tumor resection. Pain symptoms significantly improved, decreasing from a preoperative NRS of 7 to an NRS of 3 at three months after surgery, controlled with analgesic therapy: Lyrica 200 mg/day + Oxycontin 5 mg/day.

Conclusion

Chondrosarcoma requires highly specialized management in referral centers with multidisciplinary expertise. Treatment strategies must be individualized based on tumor characteristics and patient clinical conditions.

Surgery is the treatment of choice; however, spinal involvement represents a significant surgical and anesthesiological challenge, requiring advanced perioperative multidisciplinary planning, dedicated surgical teams, and optimized anesthetic management to ensure hemodynamic stability, control blood loss, enable intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, and prevent neurological and respiratory complications.

Advances in surgical techniques now allow less demolitive approaches, while chemotherapy and radiotherapy retain a limited, mainly palliative or complementary role in advanced or unresectable cases.

Informed consent to publish had been obtained.

A12 Single-port robotic partial nephrectomy: anesthetic considerations from a tertiary oncologic center

J. Salvato1, V. Ceccarelli1, M. Covotta1, S. Orlando1, D. Sammartini1, M. Di Folco1, G. Gazze1, E. Scalia2, G. Torregiani1

1Department of Anesthesia, intensive Care and Pain Therapy IRCCS Regina Elena National Cancer Center Institute, Rome, Italy; 2Department of Anestesiology, Critical Care and Pain Medicine Sapienza University of Rome, Italy

Correspondence: J. Salvato

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A12

Background

Among solid renal lesions, renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common, accounting for approximately 90% of all renal neoplasms [1]. According to the most recent guidelines of the European Association of Urology, partial nephrectomy represents the gold standard in the surgical treatment of localized RCC [1]. The robotic technique guarantees the same surgical radicality at the same time [2–3].

Over the past two decades, successive generations of the da Vinci robotic platform have been developed, all based on a multi-port (MP) design with a fixed laparoscopic camera [4]. On January 24, 2024, Intuitive announced that the da Vinci Single-Port (SP) Surgical System received CE mark approval for use in Europe. This study aimed to compare perioperative and respiratory parameters between single-port l (SP) and multi-port (MP) robot assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN).

Materials and methods

Clinical, surgical and respiratory data of two groups of patients treated with SP RAPN and MP RAPN between January 2023 and September 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. Baseline characteristics and perioperative variables were compared. Following induction of general anesthesia, we recorded intra-abdominal insufflation pressure (IAP) and Peak inspiratory pressure (PIP) at induction time and at 5, 30, and 60 minutes after surgical start. Data were compared using t-test and chi-square.

Results

Detailed results are presented in Table1. We analyzed respectively 30 patients treated with SP RAPN and 33 patients treated with MP RAPN. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups except for gender distribution (p= 0.02), RENAL score (p = 0.01), and cT stage (p = 0.01), with larger and more complex tumors in MP group (mean size 4.1 cm vs 2.8 cm, p = 0.02). showed a longer mean operative time (127 vs 93.7 min, p = 0.01) but shorter hospitalization (2.3 vs 3.0 days, p = 0.004), and significantly lower PIP at surgery timepoints (at 60 min 21.5 vs 24.; all p < 0.001). The PIP variation (Figure 1) in the SP group suggests better respiratory stability during the procedure. Mean IAP remained significantly lower and more stable in the SP group (10.1–10.4 mmHg) compared with the MP group (12.4–17.1mmHg, p<0.001), confirming reduced IAP variation and a better respiratory safety profile (Figure 2) These results are shown in Table1. These findings align with recent meta-analyses showing comparable major perioperative outcomes for SP systems [5] and improved anesthesiologic parameters [6].

Conclusions

SP approach for RAPN offers comparable surgical efficacy to the MP route, with distinct perioperative advantages. Despite a slightly longer operative time, SP is associated with significantly shorter hospital stay, reduced drain usage, and lower intraoperative abdominal insufflation and airway pressures, indicating a favorable respiratory safety profile and enhanced postoperative recovery. These findings support the SP access as a safe and effective alternative, particularly in smaller and low complexity selected cases, and in patients with respiratory comorbidities.

A13 Hypotension prediction index–guided hemodynamic management in severe aki during radical cystectomy: a case report

F. Pulice1, A. Lombardo1, A. Corea1, F. De Seta1, I. Pezzoli1, D. Russo1, M. Mura1, G. Stagliano1, F. Galeno1, M. Fanile2, A. Monardo1

1Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Ospedale Lamezia Terme, Lamezia Terme, Italy; 2Emergency Department, San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milan, Italy

Correspondence: F. Pulice

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A13

Background

Intraoperative hypotension, characterized by a mean arterial pressure (MAP) < 65 mmHg, is associated with acute kidney injury (AKI) and elevated mortality rates. The Hypotension Prediction Index (HPI), derived from arterial waveform analysis, facilitates early hemodynamic intervention [1].

Case Report

A 78-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with hematuria, severe anemia and weight loss. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed bilateral hydronephrosis and non-metastatic bladder cancer. Serum creatinine evidenced post-obstructive AKI. Patient was stabilized with hemodialysis and bilateral nephrostomies, with recovery of urine output. Due to persistent hematuria, radical cystectomy was scheduled.

Preoperative assessment revealed hypertension and renal impairment with glomerular filtration rate (GFR) < 9 mL/min. The HAS2 score indicated low perioperative cardiac risk. ASA III.

Perioperative analgesia was achieved with intrathecal morphine 180 µg combined with 5 mg of levobupivacaine 0.15%. General anesthesia was induced with fentanyl 100 µg, propofol 150 mg, rocuronium 70 mg and maintained with sevoflurane at 0.9–1.0 MAC. Standard monitoring included ECG, SpO2, non invasive blood pressure, capnography. Urine output could not be estimated due to bilateral nephrostomies and supine positioning. Advanced hemodynamic monitoring using HPI, stroke volume variation (SVV), cardiac index (CI) and systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI) was use to guide goal-directed therapy.

Four HPI-predicted hypotensive events [1] occurred intraoperatively (Table 1). The first two were associated with SVV >13% and treated with balanced crystalloid fluid challenges. The third was related to reduced systemic vascular resistance and managed with norepinephrine infusion at 0.15 µg/kg/min. A fourth episode, again associated with elevated SVV and estimated blood loss, revealed hemoglobin of 7 g/dL on arterial blood gas analysis, prompting transfusion of one unit of packed red blood cells instead of further fluid administration. No further hypotensive events occurred and MAP remained consistently above 65 mmHg (Fig. 1). Norepinephrine was discontinued intraoperatively after hemodynamic stabilization. A total of 2500 mL of balanced crystalloids and one unit of packed red blood cells were administered. A restrictive fluid strategy was adopted due to severe renal impairment and limited urine output assessment.

Conclusion

Postoperatively, the patient was transferred intubated to the intensive care unit for protected awakening. Renal function remained stable (creatinine 4.10 vs 3.90 mg/dL), with no complications during hospital stay. HPI-guided monitoring [2] is useful in the early detection and individualized management of intraoperative hypotension, enabling differentiation between hypovolemia, vasoplegia, and hemorrhage, and supporting hemodynamic stability in high-risk renal patients undergoing major surgery [3].

The authors would like to acknowledge all members of the study group for their collaboration and intellectual contribution to this work.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A14 Hemodynamic stability during suspension microlaryngoscopy: comparison between blended general anesthesia and tiva-tci

M.R. Pirolo, M. Perrella, A. di giovanni, A. Scalvenzi, L. Baiano, V. Maffei, V. Donatiello, A. Alfieri

AORN Cardarelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: M.R. Pirolo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A14

Background

Suspension microlaryngoscopy is a short but highly stimulating airway procedure requiring close cooperation between surgeon and anaesthesiologist, adequate depth of anaesthesia, airway protection, rapid recovery and cardiovascular stability. Since suspension laryngoscopy may induce clinically relevant haemodynamic changes, the choice of anaesthetic technique remains important, particularly in patients with cardiovascular risk or limited haemodynamic reserve [1]. However, the optimal anaesthetic strategy to blunt the pressor and chronotropic response to laryngeal suspension remains clinically relevant, especially in patients with cardiovascular risk or limited haemodynamic reserve [2]. This study compared the intraoperative haemodynamic profile of balanced volatile-based general anaesthesia versus propofol-remifentanil TCI in adults undergoing elective suspension microlaryngoscopy.

Materials and methods

We conducted an observational analytical study including 36 adult patients scheduled for elective suspension microlaryngoscopy. Patients were grouped according to the anaesthetic technique used: balanced general anaesthesia (AG group, n=22), with intravenous induction followed by sevoflurane/desflurane maintenance and intermittent opioid boluses; or total intravenous anaesthesia with TCI (TCI group, n=14), using propofol and remifentanil. In the TCI group, propofol was administered using the Schnider pharmacokinetic model, targeting the effect-site concentration and titrated to maintain a bispectral index between 40 and 60; remifentanil was administered using the Minto model and titrated according to haemodynamic response. All patients received standard monitoring, neuromuscular blockade and multimodal analgesic preloading. Haemodynamic targets were avoidance of mean arterial pressure below 65 mmHg and avoidance of systolic arterial pressure or mean arterial pressure variations greater than 20–25% from baseline. Systolic arterial pressure, diastolic arterial pressure and heart rate were recorded before induction, immediately after suspension laryngoscopy, five minutes after suspension for heart rate, and at emergence. Continuous variables were expressed as mean and standard deviation. Between-group baseline comparisons were performed using independent-sample tests, and haemodynamic trends were analysed using two-way mixed repeated-measures analysis of variance, with group as the between-subject factor and time as the within-subject factor. Post-hoc comparisons were performed when appropriate. A p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results

Baseline demographic and haemodynamic characteristics were comparable between groups (Table 1: Baseline characteristics and haemodynamic values according to anaesthetic technique). Mean age was 55 ± 16 years in the AG group and 58 ± 8 years in the TCI group. Baseline systolic arterial pressure was 137 ± 20 mmHg versus 145 ± 14 mmHg, baseline diastolic arterial pressure was 78 ± 13 mmHg versus 78 ± 11 mmHg, and baseline heart rate was 80 ± 14 bpm versus 78 ± 14 bpm in the AG and TCI groups, respectively. Repeated-measures analysis showed a significant group-by-time interaction for systolic arterial pressure, diastolic arterial pressure and heart rate. After suspension laryngoscopy, the AG group showed a marked hypertensive response, whereas the TCI group maintained a more stable pressure profile. Systolic arterial pressure at suspension was significantly higher in the AG group than in the TCI group (p<0.001). A similar pattern was observed for diastolic arterial pressure, with significantly higher values in the AG group at suspension (p=0.001). Heart rate also differed significantly after suspension, with a greater tachycardic response in the AG group (p=0.0026), and this difference persisted five minutes after suspension (p=0.035). At emergence, systolic pressure, diastolic pressure and heart rate no longer differed significantly between groups (Figure 1: Hemodynamic and heart rate trends during suspension microlaryngoscopy according to anesthetic technique). The need for antihypertensive rescue medication with urapidil was clinically more frequent in the AG group, consistent with the observed intraoperative pressure peaks.

Conclusions

In adults undergoing elective suspension microlaryngoscopy, propofol-remifentanil TCI was associated with superior attenuation of the haemodynamic response to laryngeal suspension compared with balanced volatile-based anaesthesia. The effect was most evident during the peak nociceptive phase, with lower systolic and diastolic pressure responses and a shorter sympathetic “tail” in heart rate. Although limited by its observational design and small sample size, this study supports TCI as a rational anaesthetic strategy for suspension microlaryngoscopy, particularly when abrupt hypertensive or tachycardic responses may be undesirable.

Consent to publish

All patients provided written informed consent for the anesthetic procedure and for the anonymous use of their clinical and perioperative data for scientific and publication purposes. All data were fully anonymized prior to analysis, in accordance with institutional policies and the Declaration of Helsinki.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A15 Telemedicine-based anesthesiology assessment in fast-track trauma surgery: a model of early perioperative stratification

C. Barneschi, S. Pieri

Local Health Authority of South-East Tuscany, Arezzo, Italy

Correspondence: S. Pieri

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A15

Introduction

Fast-track trauma pathways require organizational models capable of ensuring timely surgery, anesthetic safety, prescribing appropriateness, and sustainable resource utilization. In traditional anesthesiology pre-assessment models, preoperative evaluation of trauma patients may occur through heterogeneous pathways: hospital admission on the day before surgery, with potential inappropriate use of inpatient beds and healthcare resources; anesthesiology assessment on the day of surgery, with the risk of unrecognized clinical issues leading to delays or surgical postponements; or referral to conventional pre-hospitalization pathways, which are often already overloaded with high patient volumes.

In this context, telemedicine-based anesthesiology assessment may represent an innovative tool for early perioperative stratification, allowing anticipation of anesthetic evaluation, identification of higher-complexity patients, and optimization of perioperative planning and care setting allocation Fig. 1

Objective

To describe the implementation of a telemedicine-based preoperative anesthesiology assessment integrated into a fast-track trauma surgery pathway and to evaluate its potential impact on perioperative risk stratification, anesthetic planning, and organizational optimization of the surgical process.

Materials and Methods

Since January 2026, a dedicated organizational pathway for patients undergoing fast-track trauma surgery has been implemented at Arezzo Hospital, based on telemedicine anesthesiology assessment performed before hospital admission or operating room access.

Within the adopted organizational model, following Emergency Department evaluation and orthopedic-trauma assessment, patients are informed by the orthopedic surgeon, at the time of surgical indication, about the possibility—when appropriate clinical and organizational criteria are met—of entering a simplified perioperative pathway avoiding conventional pre-hospitalization. Informed consent for telemedicine assessment is obtained and documented within the orthopedic consultation report. Patients also receive an informational brochure containing operational instructions for accessing the digital platform and performing the telemedicine consultation.

The anesthesiology assessment is performed through the Tuscany Regional Telemedicine Platform, compliant with current regulations regarding data protection, traceability, and cybersecurity. Telemedicine consultation includes structured review of the available clinical documentation and evaluation of comorbidities, ongoing therapies, functional status, ASA classification, anesthetic risk, and the potential need for further diagnostic investigations or specialist consultations.

At the end of the telemedicine visit, anesthetic informed consent is obtained verbally and documented in the medical record. This consent is subsequently reconfirmed on the day of surgery by the attending anesthesiologist after direct clinical reassessment and confirmation of suitability for the anesthetic-surgical procedure.

Patients presenting clinical instability, significant anesthetic complexity, insufficient documentation, or the need for non-deferrable physical examination are referred to standard in-person anesthesiology evaluation and conventional perioperative pathways.

Results

The integration of telemedicine-based anesthesiology assessment into the fast-track trauma pathway enabled earlier anesthetic evaluation before hospital admission or operating room access. This facilitated earlier identification of higher-complexity patients and improved planning of the most appropriate perioperative care setting, reducing unnecessary preoperative hospital admissions.

The model also reduced the need for “last-minute” anesthesiology evaluations traditionally performed immediately before surgery, potentially decreasing delays, cancellations, or postponements related to previously undetected clinical issues.

Telemedicine integration improved the appropriateness of the preoperative pathway by avoiding systematic referral of trauma patients to conventional pre-hospitalization services and reserving these resources for genuinely complex cases. The availability of diagnostic tests already performed in the Emergency Department contributed to rationalization of additional investigations, tailoring them to the patient’s actual clinical risk and the planned surgical procedure.

From an organizational perspective, the pathway proved consistent with resource optimization, reduction of avoidable hospital access, and improved continuity between Emergency Department, Orthopedics-Traumatology, Anesthesiology, and Operating Room services. Furthermore, the preliminary availability of laboratory tests, imaging studies, and instrumental investigations already performed in the Emergency Department allowed anesthesiologists to conduct a more comprehensive and decision-oriented clinical assessment, facilitating early planning of anesthetic strategy, including potential indications for regional anesthesia techniques, perioperative analgesia, and postoperative pain management.

Conclusions

Telemedicine-based anesthesiology assessment integrated into fast-track trauma pathways may represent an innovative model of clinical triage, perioperative risk stratification, and anesthetic planning. Its value lies not only in remote healthcare delivery itself, but in its ability to anticipate anesthetic decision-making, differentiate perioperative pathways according to patient complexity, and reduce organizational inefficiencies.

The preliminary experience at Arezzo Hospital suggests that integration of telemedicine into anesthesiology workflows may contribute to a proactive, appropriate, and sustainable perioperative model, enhancing the role of anesthesiologists in the governance of trauma surgical pathways and in the personalization of anesthetic and analgesic strategies.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A16 Perioperative complications in major urological surgery: an exploratory analysis from the recover study

V. Bellini, M. Panizzi, L. Giani, S. Fedele, A. Ariosto, E. Bignami

Unit of Anesthesia and Intensive Care 2, Parma University Hospital, Italy

Correspondence: M. Panizzi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A16

Background

Postoperative complications (PC) after major surgery have incidence rates between 17% and 44% in high-risk patients [1]. In wards, vital signs are checked only every 4–6 hours, leaving intermediate-risk patients — ineligible for ICU admission yet too vulnerable for standard care — without adequate surveillance to detect early deterioration [2–4]. Wearable devices enabling continuous vital sign monitoring (CMWD) offer a practical solution for this intermediate-risk population [5]. The RECOVER study is a single-centre, non-randomised, non-pharmacological post-market device investigation designed to evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of CMWD (Portrait Mobile®, GE Healthcare) in detecting early PC in urology ward following major surgery under general anaesthesia.

Materials and methods

A preliminary analysis of RECOVER control arm dataset was conducted. Trial was approved by Ethical Committee AVEN. Informed consent was obtained for each enrolled patient. Retrospective analysis of three prospectively collected longitudinal datasets: intraoperative (N=60), Recovery Room (RR, N=62) and ward (N=49). An integrated dataset (N=47 patients with complete data across all three settings) was used for inferential analyses. Statistical methods included Fisher’s exact test (with Haldane–Anscombe correction), Mann–Whitney U test, Spearman’s rank correlation, Firth’s penalised logistic regression and Poisson regression. Multiple testing correction was applied using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure.

Results

Complication rates followed a U-shaped pattern across phases: 46.7% intraoperative, 29.0% RR, 63.3% ward (Fig. 1). In-hospital mortality was 0%; no ICU transfers occurred. The predominant intraoperative complication was hypotension (MAP <65 mmHg, 28.3%), while desaturation (SpO2 <92%) dominated in RR (14.5%). Ward complications were led by pain (20.4%), desaturation (18.4%) and infections (18.4%); 27.1% of patients required unplanned physician activation. Intraoperative MAP <65 mmHg was the only statistically robust predictor of ward complications (Firth OR=0.22, 95% CI 0.06–0.82, p=0.049), with a paradoxically protective effect interpreted as selection or management bias. Intraoperative oliguria showed a paradoxical trend towards shorter LOS (Poisson IRR=0.73, p=0.061). Ward complications trended towards longer LOS (+28%, IRR=1.28, p=0.060). After FDR correction, no binary predictor reached formal significance, highlighting the exploratory nature of the findings (Table 1). Inter-setting complication independence was observed (Spearman coefficient=0.004, p=0.980 for RR vs ward).

Conclusions

This exploratory analysis reveals a high and phase-specific burden of PC in major urological surgery. Despite are included medium risk surgery, the number of PC it’s quite high. Intraoperative haemodynamic instability emerges as a candidate predictor for postoperative outcomes but its paradoxical protective effect should be studied. These findings will be contextualized upon completion of the CMWD arm (target N=150), which is expected to provide real-time physiological data to close the monitoring gap in general ward settings enhancing acute pain services and predicting patients requiring continuous monitoring in surgical wards.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A17 Clinical and electroencephalographic effects of bolus remimazolam prior to propofol and remifentanil TCI induction in endoscopic urologic surgery

A. Recchia1, A. Palumbo1, G. Mincolelli1, M. Copetti1, A. Manuali1, L. Farina1, M. Rauseo2

1IRCCS Foundation Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza, San Giovanni Rotondo, Italy; 2University of Foggia, Department of Medical and Surgical Sciences, Foggia, Italy

Correspondence: A. Palumbo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A17

Background

Remimazolam is a novel ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine characterized by rapid onset and recovery, with potentially favorable hemodynamic and electroencephalographic effects during general anesthesia induction. However, its role as pre-induction sedation before target-controlled infusion (TCI) anesthesia has not been fully investigated. This study evaluated whether bolus remimazolam administered before propofol-remifentanil TCI induction could reduce hypnotic and opioid requirements and improve hemodynamic and EEG-related outcomes during endoscopic urologic surgery.

Materials and Methods

This retrospective single-center observational study included 40 patients undergoing endoscopic urologic surgery under general anesthesia. Written informed consent for general anesthesia and retrospective anonymized data collection was obtained from all patients. Patients with preoperative anxiety (VAS-A >60 mm) received intravenous remimazolam 0.125 mg/kg over one minute before induction (RPR group), while controls underwent standard induction with propofol-remifentanil TCI alone (PR group).

In both groups, anesthesia induction was performed using propofol TCI (Schnider model, initial effect-site concentration [Ce] 4 µg/mL) and remifentanil TCI (Minto model, initial Ce 3 ng/mL), with incremental adjustments according to clinical and instrumental monitoring.

Pharmacokinetic, electroencephalographic, hemodynamic, and respiratory parameters were collected during six predefined phases: loss of response to verbal stimulus (LOR, t1), loss of respiratory drive (t2), loss of consciousness with laryngeal mask airway placement (LOC, t3), completion of induction and start of surgery (t4), end of surgery (t5), and return of responsiveness (ROR, t6).

Collected variables included propofol and remifentanil effect-site concentrations and total drug consumption, BIS-derived EEG parameters (suppression time [ST], spectral edge frequency, and median frequency), mean arterial pressure, heart rate, and oxygen saturation.

Results

The RPR group showed significantly lower propofol effect-site concentrations at t1, t2, and t3 (p<0.001) and at t4 (p=0.037), with lower propofol consumption throughout induction (p<0.001) (Figure 1- Table 1). Remifentanil effect-site concentrations were also reduced at t1 and t2 (p<0.001), while remifentanil consumption was lower at t3 and t4 (p<0.001).

Patients receiving remimazolam showed shorter induction and recovery times, with faster achievement of loss of respiratory drive, LOC, and ROR (p<0.001). Suppression time was significantly shorter in the RPR group at t4, t5, and t6 (p=0.048, p=0.018, and p=0.030, respectively) (Figure 2- Table 2). Moreover, fewer hypotensive episodes were observed in the RPR group (p=0.002), without differences in bradycardia or oxygen desaturation.

Conclusions

Pre-induction sedation with bolus remimazolam before propofol-remifentanil TCI reduces hypnotic and opioid requirements, shortens induction and recovery times, decreases burst suppression duration, and improves hemodynamic stability during endoscopic urologic surgery.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.
