A18 Multimodal anesthetic management for minimally invasive McKeown esophagectomy: a case report

A. Palma, O.P. Volino, R. Di Nola, U. De Angelis, A. Scalvenzi, V. Maffei, A. Frangiosa

A.O.R.N. Antonio Cardarelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: A. Palma

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A18

Body

Esophagectomy is one of the most challenging procedures in thoracic and upper gastrointestinal surgery because of prolonged operative time, one-lung ventilation, pneumoperitoneum, and significant perioperative physiological stress. Modern perioperative management requires multimodal anesthetic strategies integrating advanced monitoring, protective ventilation, opioid-sparing analgesia, and hemodynamic optimization to improve surgical outcomes and postoperative recovery.

We report the case of a 59-year-old male patient, weighing 85 kg and measuring 177 cm in height (BMI 27.1 kg/m²), admitted for surgical treatment of middle-distal esophageal carcinoma after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. His medical history included bilateral retinal detachment, the patient was categorized as ASA III. The patient underwent minimally invasive total esophagectomy according to the McKeown technique with esophagogastroplasty and feeding jejunostomy performed through combined thoracoscopic and laparoscopic approaches. After arrival in the operating room, monitoring including electrocardiography, pulse oximetry, and non-invasive blood pressure measurement. Advanced multimodal monitoring was subsequently implemented with BIS monitoring for anesthetic depth assessment, TOF monitoring for neuromuscular blockade evaluation, NOL monitoring for intraoperative analgesic guidance, and continuous body temperature monitoring. Before induction of general anesthesia, a thoracic epidural catheter was inserted at the T7–T8 interspace under sterile conditions for perioperative and postoperative analgesia. General anesthesia was induced intravenously, and orotracheal intubation was performed using a 41 Fr Robertshaw double-lumen tube to allow selective right lung exclusion during the thoracoscopic phase. A 20G arterial catheter was then inserted into the right radial artery for continuous invasive blood pressure monitoring and serial arterial blood gas analyses. Anesthetic maintenance was achieved using inhaled sevoflurane titrated according to BIS values, which remained stable within the target range of 38–40. Continuous epidural infusion with ropivacaine 0.12% combined with sufentanil 0.18 mcg/mL was administered at a rate of 5 mL/h to ensure perioperative analgesia. The surgical procedure lasted approximately 8 hours. During the thoracoscopic phase, ventilatory parameters were adjusted to optimize one-lung ventilation and reduce the risk of ventilator-induced lung injury. During the laparoscopic abdominal phase, ventilation was adapted according to pneumoperitoneum-related physiological changes and surgical positioning. NOL monitoring remained constantly below 15, indicating adequate antinociceptive control, while TOF monitoring persistently showed complete neuromuscular blockade during the main surgical phases. Body temperature remained stable at approximately 36.5°C.

3 EGA were performed intraoperatively and demonstrated stable respiratory and metabolic parameters. Hemodynamic parameters remained stable during the entire procedure. Toward the end of surgery, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia was reinforced with intravenous paracetamol 1000 mg and ketorolac 30 mg. At the end of the surgery, the patient emerged from anesthesia without complications. Immediate postoperative assessment demonstrated optimal pain control, with a NRS and RASS score of 0. The patient was subsequently transferred to the ICU for postoperative monitoring. Postoperative analgesia was maintained through continuous thoracic epidural infusion with ropivacaine 0.1% administered at a rate of 5 mL/h. Pain assessments performed at 12, 24, 36, and 48 hours after surgery consistently demonstrated NRS 0, confirming excellent analgesic efficacy without the need for rescue opioid administration. The postoperative course was uneventful. On postoperative day 3, the patient was discharged from the ICU to the surgical ward, and after 10 days he was discharged home in stable clinical condition. Esophagectomy is associated with major perioperative physiological stress because of prolonged operative duration, thoracic manipulation, one-lung ventilation, and postoperative respiratory impairment. Consequently, anesthetic management plays a central role in perioperative safety and postoperative outcomes.

Thoracic epidural analgesia remains one of the cornerstones of enhanced recovery pathways in esophageal surgery. In this case, continuous epidural administration of ropivacaine and sufentanil provided excellent perioperative analgesia and allowed a completely opioid-sparing postoperative course during the first 48 hours. Effective epidural analgesia improves respiratory mechanics, facilitates coughing and mobilization, and may reduce pulmonary complications.

Advanced multimodal monitoring significantly contributed to anesthetic optimization. BIS-guided anesthetic titration allowed maintenance of adequate hypnotic depth while avoiding excessive anesthetic administration. NOL monitoring provided continuous assessment of nociceptive balance, ensuring effective analgesic control throughout prolonged surgery. TOF monitoring guaranteed optimal neuromuscular blockade management, particularly important during minimally invasive thoracic surgery where adequate surgical exposure depends on profound muscle relaxation.

Ventilatory management also represented a critical component of the anesthetic strategy. Protective one-lung ventilation during thoracoscopy and individualized ventilatory adjustments during laparoscopy were essential to preserve adequate gas exchange and minimize postoperative pulmonary complications. Serial arterial blood gas analyses confirmed effective respiratory management throughout all surgical phases.

This case highlights the importance of comprehensive multimodal anesthetic management in high-complexity esophageal surgery. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying clinical data.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A19 Influence of lateral decubitus and pneumoperitoneum on distribution of ventilation and respiratory mechanics during robotic partial nephrectomy: an exploratory electrical impedance tomography analysis from an ongoing randomized trial

R. Natoli1, E. Antonucci1, F. Mulazzani1, J. Colombo1, D. Pettenuzzo3,4, P. Dell’Oglio2, S. Tappero2, A. Caviglia2, F. Marrazzo5, M. Bulian3, T. Langer5, A. Galfano2, G. Monti1

1Department of Transplant Anesthesia and ICU, Grande Ospedale Metropolitano Niguarda, Milano, Italy; 2Department of Urology, Grande Ospedale Metropolitano Niguarda, Milano, Italy; 3School of Specialization in Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, University of Milano-Bicocca, Milano, Italy; 4Department of Anesthesia, ASST Rhodense, P.O. Garbagnate Milanese, Garbagnate Milanese, Italy; 5Department of Anesthesia and ICU 1, Grande Ospedale Metropolitano Niguarda, Milano, Italy

Correspondence: R. Natoli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A19

Background

Exposure to higher lung stress during surgery is an independent risk factor for postoperative pulmonary complications [1,2]. Robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy requires pneumoperitoneum and often lateral decubitus positioning, which may promote heterogeneous regional stress and strain through ventilation redistribution [3]. Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) enables continuous bedside assessment of regional ventilation and has demonstrated ventilation redistribution and altered recruitment dynamics during robotic abdominal surgery [4]. While Trendelenburg positioning has been associated with changes in ventilation distribution and respiratory mechanics, the impact of lateral decubitus during robotic renal surgery remains poorly investigated. This study evaluated the effects of supine versus lateral decubitus positioning on regional ventilation distribution, respiratory mechanics, and gas exchange during robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy. We hypothesized that lateral decubitus would induce greater redistribution of ventilation toward non-dependent lung regions and increased respiratory mechanical stress.

Methods

This prespecified physiologic study was nested within the K-3 trial, a single-centre, patient-blinded randomized clinical trial, including patients undergoing Da Vinci single-port robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy between August 2025 and April 2026. The trial has received ethical approval (CETL 3 n°5448) and is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT07234409.

A written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to study enrollment. Patients were randomized 1:1 to supine or lateral decubitus positioning. Ventilation was standardized using volume-controlled protective ventilation with tidal volume 6–8 ml/kg predicted body weight and PEEP 5 cmH2O; ventilatory adjustments were allowed according to clinical needs. Pneumoperitoneum pressure was maintained at 8 mmHg.

EIT measurements were performed at three predefined timepoints: after induction in supine position (T0), 60 minutes after pneumoperitoneum induction in the assigned position (T1), and after desufflation in neutral supine position before extubation (T end). Regional ventilation was assessed using tidal impedance variation (%TIV) and center of ventilation. The primary outcome was the fraction of ventilation distributed to dependent lung regions at the end of surgery. Secondary outcomes included temporal changes in EIT-derived indices, respiratory mechanics, gas exchange variables, and postoperative pulmonary complications up to postoperative day 7 or hospital discharge.

Results

Twenty-two patients were included, with 11 assigned to lateral decubitus and 11 to supine positioning. Patients in the lateral decubitus group had higher body mass index (27 vs 24 kg/m2, p=0.038), while no other baseline differences were observed. Baseline respiratory mechanics and ventilation distribution were comparable at T0 (Table 1). During pneumoperitoneum (T1), lateral decubitus patients showed a lower fraction of ventilation distributed to dependent lung regions compared with the supine group (20.9 ± 5.6 vs 27.9 ± 6.1%, p=0.02), with a significant group-by-time interaction (p=0.01). Lateral decubitus positioning was also associated with higher peak pressure (21.9 ± 3.3 vs 18.3 ± 1.7 cmH2O, p=0.01), plateau pressure (19.0 ± 4.9 vs 14.2 ± 1.7 cmH2O, p=0.01), driving pressure (12.5 ± 4.1 vs 8.8 ± 1.6 cmH2O, p=0.02), and lower respiratory system compliance (43.5 ± 15.7 vs 56.7 ± 13.6 mL/cmH2O, p=0.05). After desufflation and return to supine position, these differences were attenuated. No differences were observed in gas exchange, dead space fraction, or postoperative pulmonary complications (Table 2).

Conclusions

Lateral decubitus positioning during robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy promotes redistribution of ventilation away from dependent lung regions and increases respiratory mechanical stress during pneumoperitoneum compared with supine positioning. However, these physiologic changes were not associated with differences in short-term postoperative respiratory outcomes. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, as this is a preliminary analysis of an ongoing study.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A20 The “In LOVAE for BHyA” project: comparison of perioperative analgesic techniques for hysteroannessiectomy in adult cancer patients - a systematic review

G. Mastrandrea1, M.F. Zerni1, M. Mucci1, Z. Namiri1, S. Iacovelli1, C. Calabrò1, G. Rosato1, R. Cascione1, N. Vitolla1, M. Frascolla1, A. Lupo1, M. Lombardi2, R. De Nola1, A. Cazzolla1, A. Franchini1, R. Massafra1, G. Cormio1, P. Nardulli1, E. Nicoletti1, T. Vetruccio1

1IRCCS “Giovanni Paolo II” Cancer Institute, Bari, Italy; 2University of Bari Aldo Moro (UNIBA), Bari, Italy

Correspondence: G. Mastrandrea

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A20

Background

Hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy are common surgical procedures that are indicated in benign and oncological disease. This approach requires a multidisciplinary strategy and careful postoperative pain management by the care team. In order to compare the intravenous, intrathecal and epidural analgesia techniques, a systematic review will be conducted and used as a reference for the project In LOVAE for BHyA (In Laparoscopic/Open technique we Value the Analgesic Effectiveness for Bilateral HysteroAnnexectomy). It is a two-phase study, with a retrospective observational phase followed by a prospective phase, aimed at comparing the efficacy of single-shot intrathecal, epidural, and intravenous analgesia in cancer patients undergoing laparoscopic or open hysteroannexectomy. A key focus is placed on the timing of analgesic administration, using perioperative protocols with synchronous administration regardless of the technique.

Materials and methods

Following PRISMA and Cochrane Collaboration guidelines, a systematic review evaluated the effectiveness of perioperative pain management protocols following hysteroannessiectomy in adult cancer patients. After identifying the research question using the PICO system, the search was conducted from 2005 to 2025 in two databases (PubMed, Embase) by four researchers independently. Specifically, the literature was analysed combining the MeSH terms analgesia, hysterectomy, and pain measurement. Filters included full-text availability, adult population (greater than or equal to 18 years), and study design (Randomized Controlled Trial, systematic review, and meta-analysis). Furthermore, the literature was reviewed for validated analgesia efficacy assessment scales (NRS Numerical Rating Scale, VAS Visual Analogue Scale, VRS Verbal Rating Scale) and whether there was a possibility of evaluating the effectiveness of postoperative analgesia using artificial intelligence techniques.

Result

A total of 197 records were initially identified. We excluded 13 studies because they were present in duplicate, 41 studies because they concerned irrelevant comparison to PICO, 110 studies because they discussed about non pertinent topics to PICO, and 2 studies because they were retracted. A total of 166 studies were excluded. 31 studies were included. No studies compared the three techniques and in a specific way no studies reported comparative data regarding the timing of analgesia administration.

Conclusion

Literature data on the three techniques demonstrate their effectiveness in reducing postoperative pain following hystero-annesiectomy. For a direct comparison between the three techniques, it would be appropriate to develop standardized administration protocols that also specify the timing of drug injection. So the researchers expanded the list of systematic review articles with 68 articles specifically addressing validated analgesia protocols, bringing the total to 99 reference articles. The multidisciplinary team developed analgesia protocols with standardized administration times and will assess their effectiveness using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Verbal Rating Scale (VRS), pain scores, opioid consumption, Post Operative Nausea and Vomiting (PONV) incidence, and length of hospital stay (LOS).

The In LOVAE for BHyA study has been approved by the Ethics Committee.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A21 Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS): data review of pas cases successfully managed by a trained multidisciplinary team in our tertiary referral hospital

T. Palladino, P.S. Mariotti, A. Maglione, P. Ricciardi, P. Vaira

Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza Hospital, San Giovanni Rotondo, Italy

Correspondence: T. Palladino

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A21

Background

Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS), is frequently associated with severe obstetric haemorrhage, anaesthesia risks and high mortality. We present a data review of PAS cases successfully managed by a trained, comprehensive, multidisciplinary team in an Italian Tertiary referral hospital.

Methods

The analysis includes all PAS cases which have been managed between 2020 and 1 st semester of 2024 at Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza (CSS), city of San Giovanni Rotondo, Italy.

Results

During the study period, 19 women underwent Caesarean Section for PAS-related reasons. More than half women were preterm at time of delivery and almost 100% had almost one previous caesarean section (CS) in their obstetric history. Regarding Obstetric management during pregnancy, 66.7% were placenta praevia major cases. MRI was performed in 3 cases. Regarding Multidisciplinary management at time of delivery, almost half CS were performed in Hybrid Operating Room; more than half were conducted under Regional Anaesthesia and for all of them interventional radiologic procedures with preoperative placement of catheters were carried out; iliac arteries occlusion was necessary for half of them. Ureteral stents were placed in 2 cases. Peripartum Hysterectomy was performed in 4 cases and one third of them were admitted to the ICU. More than half newborns were admitted to the NICU. No maternal or neonatal deaths occurred.

Conclusions

CSS has developed an internal protocol for managing PAS cases. We presented our cases successfully managed by a trained, comprehensive, multidisciplinary team, composed of Gynaecologists, Obstetricians, Sonographers, Anaesthesiologists, Urologists and Interventional Radiologists. A careful antepartum diagnosis by ultrasound imaging is critical to get ready for surgery; surgical and anaesthetic skills are significant to reduce risk of injury; interventional radiologic technique is fundamental to minimise high risk of intraoperative haemorrhage. These skilled facilities are fundamental for optimal management of these increasingly frequent cases.

A22 High dosage of dexamethasone reduces post-operative nausea and vomiting in patients undergoing sleeve gastrectomy: evidences from the BAR-HYP prospective study

S. Malerba1, F. Salvo1, V. Contardi1, A. Raineri1, E. Gallo1, F. Bruno1, A. Cannone1, A. Risoli1, R. Tenio1, A. Aprile2, E. Travaglio2, A. Gattolin2, I. Blangetti1

1Anesthesia and Intensive Care Unit. Regina Montis Regalis Hospital, Mondovì (CN), Italy; 2General surgery Unit. Regina Montis Regalis Hospiral, Mondovì (CN), Italy

Correspondence: S. Malerba

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A22

Background

Post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is one of the most frequent and distressing complication for surgical patients, leading to an increase of anxiety, discomfort, and in some cases a prolonged hospital stay [1–4]. Therefore the pre-operative utilization of diagnostic tools like the Apfel score, is essential to identify high-risk patients and implement effective preventive strategies [5]. However, metabolic bariatric surgery and in particular Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy (LSG) represents a peculiar case because the very high risk of PONV is often underestimated by traditional scoring systems [2,6]. The aim of this study is to analyse risk factors and the role of preventive strategies in patients with severe obesity undergoing LSG.

Materials and methods

We conducted a sub-analysis of the BAR-HYP prospective observational study analysing 69 patients (F/M 49/20) with a mean age of 45±11 years and a mean BMI of 44±11 kg/m². At baseline, during the anesthesiological pre-operative evaluation, we collected data on smoking habits, comorbidities, and the Apfel score. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study (Table 1).

Anesthesiological management was done according to Enhanced Recovery After Surgery protocol [7]. At the discretion of the anesthesiologist in charge, patients received dexamethasone 4 mg or 8 mg with additional anti-emetics as required; post-operative analgesia was provided using paracetamol and NSAIDs with opioid reserved for rescue. The incidence of PONV and the severity of post-operative pain, documented with the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) were monitored during the day of surgery, the first night and the first post-operative morning. Data were obtained from patient self-reporting, nursing log and/or rescue therapy administration. Groups comparison was performed using parametric or non-parametric tests, as appropriate for data distribution. Endpoints were adjusted using multivariate regression models; a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results

Baseline characteristics are listed in Table 1. Overall PONV was reported in 57% of cases and was more frequent in females (67.3% vs. 30%, p<0.05). PONV was statistically more frequent on the day of surgery (49.3%), progressively decreasing during the night (20.9%) and on the first postoperative day (9.0%); corresponding NRS were 4.9 ± 2.8, 3.2 ± 2 and 2.2 ± 1.9. In 41% of patients was required rescue therapy for PONV, whereas rescue opioids were administered in 50.7%. After data correction, female gender was independently associated with an increased risk of PONV (OR 4.34, 95% CI 1.07 - 17.63; p=0.04, Table 2). The Apfel score showed no predictive value, nor did smoking status, age, BMI, or surgical duration. Among modifiable interventions, the administration of 4 mg versus 8 mg of dexamethasone increased the risk of PONV (OR 7.31, 95% CI 1.35–39.70; p=0.02) and was also associated with a significant increase in perceived pain during the first postoperative day (β NRS + 1.03, p=0.039, table 2). No other significant effects were observed for other anti-emetic agents (Table 2).

Conclusion

PONV is a frequent complication following LSG and is often not accurately predictable using the Apfel score; the procedure itself should be considered a major risk factor. The administration of a higher dose of dexamethasone was the only preventive measure that proved effective in reducing the incidence of PONV, while also decreasing perceived pain.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A23 Arterial elastance as a predictor of post-induction hypotension in high-risk hypertensive patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery

P. Farris1, L. Pistidda2, C. Doldi3, F. Saba1, V. Falchi2, L. Schiaffino1, P. Terragni2, A. Messina4, S. Magnoni2

1Sassari University Hospital, Italy; 2University of Sassari, Italy; 3University of Milan, Italy; 4Humanitas Research Hospital, Milano, Italy

Correspondence: P. Farris

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A23

Introduction

Perioperative hypotension is a common and harmful event in high-risk hypertensive patients undergoing major abdominal surgery under general anesthesia, with hypotension post anesthesia induction representing a key target for prevention and early intervention.

Materials and Methods

In this single-center analysis of patients from the HISTAP multicenter randomized trial (NCT05637606), 21 hypertensive high risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery, were monitored using Pressure Recording Analytical Method (PRAM) with continuous real-time hemodynamic data. The study was approved by the local ethical committee and conducted according to the principles of Helsinki declaration. Pre- and post-induction values were calculated as 5-minute averages before and after anesthesia induction, respectively; hypotension was defined as SAP <90 mmHg or > 20% decrease in MAP. The study aimed to identify pre-induction hemodynamic profiles predictive of post-induction hypotension.

Results

Following anesthesia induction, significant decreases were observed in MAP, SAP, DAP, dP/dt, and systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI). Overall, 57.1% of patients developed post-induction hypotension. Compared with non-hypotensive patients, those who became hypotensive exhibited significantly higher pre-induction arterial elastance (Ea) (1.59 ± 0.37 vs. 0.95 ± 0.23 mmHg/mL; p = 0.004) and higher SVRI (3333 ± 1393 vs. 2422 ± 1609 dyn s cm-5; p = 0.02), along with a lower cardiac index (CI) (2.73 ± 0.57 vs. 3.8 ± 1.32 L/min/m²; p = 0.03). ROC analysis showed that Ea was the strongest pre-induction predictor of post-induction hypotension (AUC = 0.92), with an optimal threshold of 1.16.

Conclusione

These findings support the value of preoperative continuous hemodynamic monitoring in high-risk patients and suggest that arterial elastance may serve as a robust and reliable marker for hypotension prediction and tailored anesthetic management. Larger studies are needed to confirm these data and its clinical applicability.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A24 Evaluating the influence of dexmedetomidine concentrations on patient state index, spectral edge frequency, and analgesia nociception index during propofol target-controlled infusion general anaesthesia: a prospective observational study

G. Girotto1, M. Kreuzer2, P. Zanatta3, M. Carron1, F. Linassi3

1Department of Medicine - DIMED, Section of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, University of Padova, Padova, Italy; 2Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, Klinikum rechts der Isar, Technical University of Munich, School of Med, Germany; 3Department of anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Ca’ Foncello Treviso Regional Hospital, Treviso, Italy

Correspondence: G. Girotto

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A24

Background

Dexdemetomedine is a selective alfa 2-receptor agonist [1] with sedative effect. In addition, it has an opioid-sparing effect [2,3] and can be used as an adjuvant during general anaesthesia [4]. The impact of varying dexdemetomedine effect-site concentrations (CeD) on the electroencephalogram (EEG) and derived indices remains unclear. This study investigates how different CeD levels (delivered throughout Dick model [5]) influence the power spectrum (as density spectral array, DSA), periodic and aperiodic FOOOF components and the processed parameters Patient State Index (PSi), spectral edge frequency (SEF95), and Analgesia Nociception Index (ANI) during stable propofol-remifentanil total intravenous anaesthesia with target-controlled infusion (TIVA-TCI; Eleveld model [6,7])), and the relationship between these values and preoperative pupillometry evaluation.

Methods

Subsequently CeD of 0.2, 0.1 and 0.05 ng/ml were administered for 20 minutes each during stable propofol-remifentanil concentrations (CeP-CeR) in 50 breast surgery patients. Pre-operative pupillometry was also performed. The PSi and SEF95, ANI trend data were extracted from the monitor every two seconds. EEG traces with 178 Hz sampling rate were recorded from the frontal Sedline electrodes. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. According to distribution, continuous variables were analysed using parametric tests (two-tailed t-test) and non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U) and medians were reported as 1 st and 3 st IQR. Categorical variables were analysed with Chi-square or Fisher’s exact test. Cohen’s d was used as effect size and a p-value < 0.05 was considered significant. Relative change in PSi, SEF95, ANI, FOOOF parameters (peak bandwidth, Centerfrequency, Power and Slope) and DSA features were quantified using AUC as effect size with bootstrapped confidence intervals [8]. Confidence intervals exclusive 0.5 indicated significance and AUC<0.3 or AUC>0.7 was considered clinically relevant [9]. Relationships between EEG changes, demographic variables, CeP and pupillometry were evaluated with Spearman correlations and linear regression.

Results

A total of 50 women undergoing breast oncologic surgery were enrolled (Table 1).

Baseline DSA showed the characteristic propofol delta-alpha oscillatory activity (Figure 1). With decreasing CeD, beta-band power decreased first, followed by reductions across all frequencies except theta and alpha (Figure 1).

Relative changes of PSi and SEF95 showed a significant decrease during all the CeD considered, with a trend into returning to basal values at the end of CeD 0.05 ng/ml period.

Relative changes of peak bandwidth and center frequency significantly decreased at all CeD levels, whereas peak power and spectral slope did not manifest a clear behaviour.

Relative ANI changes did not show a significant variation.

Relative changes in SEF95 from baseline to CeD 0.2 ng/ml were inversely correlated to preoperative pupil latency left (p<0.05). CeP LoR was directly correlated to CeP MA; CeP MA was inversely correlated to age, CeP LoR and CeP RoR.

Conclusion

Varying CeD during stable CeP affects PSi, SEF95, and the DSA, by decreasing the power in all frequencies except alpha. Decreasing in gamma, delta and theta power seem consistent with a decrease in CeD, but this probably reflects the long dexdemetomedine half-time rather than the Dick model estimated CeD. Our findings of reduced bandwidth and center frequency, without significant changes in aperiodic slope or total power, suggest that dexmedetomidine enhances the stability and synchronization of the anesthetic state without substantially increasing global cortical depression.

This prospective study was approved by the Ethical Committee of Treviso Regional Hospital, Italy (Approval No. 681/CE Marca) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT07259460).

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A25 Opioid-sparing anesthesia in pediatric adenotonsillectomy

S. Ruocco1, G. Montenero1, G. Sfregola1, S. Bufano1, M. Ciuffreda2, C. Piangatelli2, D. Galante1

1Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care and Pain Therapy Hospital G. Tatarella, Cerignola (Foggia), Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care and Pain Therapy, Fabriano (Ancona), Italy

Correspondence: G. Sfregola

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A25

Background

Opioid-sparing anesthesia (OSA) is increasingly adopted in pediatric surgery to reduce opioid-related adverse events, particularly in adenotonsillectomy, where children are at elevated risk of respiratory complications. This study aimed to assess current OSA practices across 19 hospitals and evaluate perioperative outcomes in children aged 3–10 undergoing adenotonsillectomy.

Materials and Methods

A multicenter, observational survey was conducted among anesthesiologists in 19 tertiary and secondary hospitals. Data were collected for at least 110 pediatric patients receiving adenotonsillectomy under OSA protocols. Variables included anesthetic techniques, use of non-opioid analgesics, adjuncts (dexmedetomidine, ketamine, regional blocks), intraoperative hemodynamic stability, postoperative pain scores, incidence of rescue opioid use, and adverse respiratory events.

Results and Discussion

A total of 118 children were included. Non-opioid multimodal analgesia was applied in 92% of cases, most commonly acetaminophen (89%), NSAIDs (76%), and dexmedetomidine (54%). Ketamine (low-dose) was used in 38% of hospitals, while bilateral glossopharyngeal or peritonsillar blocks were performed in 21%. Hemodynamic parameters remained stable in 95% of patients. Postoperative pain scores were acceptable (median FLACC 3 at 1 hour, 1 at 4 hours). Rescue opioid administration was required in only 17% of cases, primarily in centers not routinely using dexmedetomidine. Respiratory complications were minimal (3%), with no severe events reported. Overall, OSA practices were heterogeneous but demonstrated favorable analgesic efficacy and safety (Figure 1).

Conclusion

This multicenter survey confirms that opioid-sparing strategies are widely implemented in pediatric adenotonsillectomy and associated with adequate pain control, low need for rescue opioids, and minimal respiratory adverse events. Standardization of OSA protocols across institutions may further optimize perioperative outcomes.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A26 Incidence of difficult tracheal intubation and related complications in children with severe osas undergoing adenotonsillectomy

S. Ruocco1, G. Montenero1, G. Sfregola1, S. Bufano1, M. Ciuffreda2, C. Piangatelli2, D. Galante1

1Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Therapy, G. Tatarella Hospital, Cerignola (Foggia), Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Therapy Fabriano Hospital, Ancona, Italy

Correspondence: G. Sfregola

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A26

Background

Severe pediatric obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS) is frequently associated with airway anatomical alterations that may complicate tracheal intubation during adenotonsillectomy. The primary aim of this study was to assess the incidence of difficult tracheal intubation and peri-intubation complications in children with severe OSAS across multiple centers.

Materials and Methods

A prospective observational survey was conducted in 23 Italian hospitals over a 24-month period. Children aged 3–10 years with polysomnography-confirmed severe OSAS undergoing elective adenotonsillectomy were included. A total of 160 patients were analyzed. Data were collected through a standardized questionnaire completed by the attending anesthesiologist and included demographic characteristics, airway assessment, intubation technique, number of attempts, use of adjuncts, and occurrence of complications such as desaturation, laryngospasm, bronchospasm, airway trauma, and postoperative respiratory events. Difficult intubation was defined as >2 attempts or the need for advanced airway devices.

Results and Discussion

Difficult intubation occurred in 14% of cases, with the majority associated with Mallampati III–IV scores and increased tonsillar hypertrophy. Videolaryngoscopy was used in 27% of all intubations and in 78% of difficult cases, significantly reducing the number of attempts compared to direct laryngoscopy. Peri intubation desaturation (<92%) occurred in 19% of patients, while laryngospasm was observed in 6% and mild airway trauma in 4%. No severe complications such as bradycardia, cardiac arrest, or failed intubation requiring surgical airway were reported. Children with higher BMI percentiles showed an increased rate of both difficult intubation and desaturation episodes (Table 1 and Figure 1).

Conclusion

Children with severe OSAS represent a population at increased risk for difficult airway management and peri-intubation complications. Videolaryngoscopy demonstrated a protective effect by reducing the number of attempts and associated events. Standardized airway assessment and equipment readiness may enhance safety in this high-risk group. Further studies with larger cohorts are warranted to refine predictive factors and optimize management pathways.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A27 One, no one and one hundred thousand: multidimensional frailty in the surgical patient

A. Fortini1, T. Buzzigoli2, G. Pratesi2, G.L. Biancofiore2

1Azienda USL Toscana Nord Ovest, Nuovo Ospedale Apuano, Massa, Italy; 2Department of Anaesthesia and Transplant Intensive Care, Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria Pisana, Italy

Correspondence: A. Fortini

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A27

Background

A surgical patient is often approached as a single entity: one age, one diagnosis, one procedure. Yet hidden vulnerability may render the patient effectively invisible, as frailty frequently remains undetected by conventional assessment. When functional, nutritional, psychological, and biological domains are evaluated together, however, the same patient may reveal a multitude of distinct perioperative risk profiles. Frailty is characterized by reduced physiological reserve and diminished resilience to surgical stress [1–3]. Several frailty-related domains are potentially modifiable through prehabilitation strategies targeting physical activity, nutrition, psychological wellbeing, and clinical optimization [4]. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of multidimensional frailty and identify actionable vulnerability domains in surgical patients evaluated in a preoperative clinic.

Materials and methods

We conducted a prospective observational study with retrospective analysis, including adult patients scheduled for elective surgery at the preoperative assessment clinic of the Anaesthesia and Transplant Intensive Care Unit, Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria Pisana. Patients voluntarily completed an anonymous structured paper questionnaire, either independently or with caregiver support. Multidimensional vulnerability was assessed using validated screening tools and perioperative variables [3,5,6]. Seven domains were evaluated: reduced functional capacity, assessed using the Duke Activity Status Index (DASI <= 34); clinical frailty, assessed using the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS >= 4); nutritional risk, assessed using the Patient-Generated Subjective Global Assessment Short Form (PG-SGA >= 4); anxiety and depression, assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS-A/D >= 8); significant pain; and preoperative anaemia, defined as haemoglobin <13 g/dL in men and <12 g/dL in women [7]. Patients were classified as robust (0–1 altered domains), pre-frail (2–3 altered domains), or frail (>= 4 altered domains).

Results

Overall, 128 patients were included; the median age was 73 years (interquartile range 63–78), and 51.6% were male. The most frequently altered domains were nutritional risk (53.1%), preoperative anaemia (51.6%), reduced functional capacity (46.9%), and clinically significant anxiety (46.9%) (Figure 1). Pain, depression, and clinical frailty affected approximately one-third of patients. Women more frequently presented with nutritional risk, anxiety, and pain, whereas anaemia and reduced functional capacity were more common among men (Figure 2). Vulnerability increased with age but was not confined to older patients: approximately one-third of patients younger than 75 years already exhibited >= 4 altered domains (Figure 3). Overall, 69.5% of patients had at least two altered domains, and 38.3% met the definition of multidimensional frailty (Figure 4).

Conclusions

Multidimensional frailty is common, actionable, and frequently overlooked before surgery. Systematic screening should not be restricted to older patients, as it may identify individuals who could benefit from targeted support without limiting access to care. Transforming preoperative waiting time into an opportunity for value-based preparation may facilitate personalized prehabilitation, improve shared decision-making, and promote more equitable, patient-centred perioperative care (Figure 5).

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A28 Bias before the algorithm: gender disparities in perioperative ai research leadership

V. Bellini, S. Fedele, T. Domenichetti, G. Maspero, E.G. Bignami

University of Parma – Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, Italy

Correspondence: T. Domenichetti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A28

Background

Artificial intelligence (AI) is being rapidly integrated into perioperative medicine, supporting clinical decision-making, risk prediction, and workflow optimization (1,2). However, its epistemic foundations remain largely unexamined. Because AI systems reflect the structure of the scientific communities that develop them (3), inequities in academic leadership may translate into algorithmic bias (4). Gender distribution in leadership within AI-driven perioperative research has not been systematically evaluated.

Methods

A five-year PubMed-based bibliometric analysis of AI applications in perioperative medicine was performed using combinations of terms related to AI (“artificial intelligence”, “machine learning”, “deep learning”), perioperative care (“perioperative”, “intraoperative”, “postoperative”), anesthesiology, and predictive modeling. After screening, 238 studies with standardized research methodologies were retained.

Author gender was inferred using name-based classification. Ambiguous names were manually verified through institutional or professional profiles; when no clear identification was possible (n = 11), gender was assigned probabilistically based on country-specific distributions.

Gender distribution was analyzed across authorship positions, pairings, geographic origin, and study design. Derived metrics included leadership drop-off ratio, odds ratios (ORs) for female senior authorship, and pairing asymmetry indices. Statistical comparisons were performed using Chi-square tests (p < 0.05).

Results

Across 238 studies, women represented 28.2% of first authors, 34.5% of second authors, but only 23.1% of last authors. This downward shift in representation occurred despite increasing interdisciplinary collaboration in AI research. Overall, women had lower odds of last authorship (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.51–1.16, p=0.19).

Authorship structures were heavily male-dominated: 57.1% of studies were male–male pairing, while only 8.0% showed female–female leadership. Female first authors were more frequently paired with male senior authors than vice versa (19.7% vs 15.1%), yielding a pairing asymmetry ratio of 1.31 (Figure 1).

Female senior authorship varied significantly across study designs (χ² = 8.9, p = 0.03). Clinical trials showed markedly higher female leadership (28.1% vs 13.4% in observational studies) and increased odds of female last authorship (OR 2.51, 95% CI 1.01–6.23, p=0.009).

Geographically, research output was concentrated in China (29.4%) and the United States (25.2%), other regions contributed marginally. Interestingly, female leadership patterns remained consistently limited in high-output countries (Table 1).

Conclusion

Despite being framed as neutral, AI-driven perioperative research reflects persistent gender inequities. Scientific leadership remains predominantly male, with women underrepresented in senior authorship positions. This mirrors the well described “leaky pipeline” observed in academic medicine (5,6). As AI increasingly shapes clinical decision-making, these imbalances raise concerns that future algorithms may be developed within inequitable academic structures. Without targeted intervention, AI expansion in perioperative medicine risks reinforcing, and potentially amplifying, existing disparities in scientific leadership and in the design of clinical intelligence systems themselves.

Consent to publish

Informed consent was not required in accordance with applicable institutional and ethical guidelines

A29 Impact of the clinical setting on central venous access devices in a tertiary-level pediatric intensive care unit: a prospective observational study

V. Bartolucci1, M. Shaich Yusef2, M. Pagano1, P. Rufini3, D. Colosimo3, E. La Rosa3, C. Greco3, Z. Ricci3

1University of Florence, Italy; 2University of Bari, Italy; 3Meyer University Hospital – IRCCS, Florence, Italy

Correspondence: V. Bartolucci

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A29

Introduction

The use of central venous catheters (CVCs) is essential in critically ill pediatric patients, but it is not without risks. Although the advent of ultrasound-guided techniques and insertion bundles (such as the ISAC-Ped protocol) has drastically reduced complications, there is a lack of prospective Italian studies comparing the incidence of adverse events across different in-hospital settings.

Objective

To describe the epidemiology of CVCs placed at Meyer Hospital and to compare complications between devices inserted in the Operating Room (OR) and in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU).

Methods

A single-center, prospective observational study conducted between October 2025 and May 2026. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee, which waived the requirement for patient informed consent due to the nature of the study.. The study included 100 patients (median age 4.81 years) who underwent short-term CVC placement, with subsequent follow-up for up to 30 days.

Results

A total of 87 catheters were analyzed (60.9% CICC, 17.2% FICC, 11.5% PORT, 10.3% PICC). Most were inserted in the OR (80.5%) compared to the PICU (18.4%). The median duration was 9 days. The incidence of the most serious complications was 17.2%. Comparison between settings revealed differences in risk profiles: CVCs inserted in TIP had a significantly higher rate of infectious complications (11.76 vs. 0 events/1000 days; p=0.037). In contrast, in the SO setting, a higher tendency toward mechanical complications was observed (13.27 vs. 5.88 events/1000 days).

Conclusions

The placement setting influences the type of complications. While the SO setting shows greater susceptibility to mechanical events, the TIP setting remains burdened by a higher risk of infection, likely related to the greater clinical complexity of patients and the prevalence of femoral access (FICC) in that setting.

A30 Prehabilitation interventions for major oncological surgery. a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

G. Aviani Fulvio1, N. Sella1,2, T. Pettenuzzo1,2, A. De Cassai1,2, A. Zambianchi1, P. Dissegna1, I. Paiusco1, G. Spoverato3,4, A. Boscolo1,2

1Department of Medicine - DIMED, Section of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Care, University of Padova, Italy; 2Institute of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care - Padova University Hospital, Italy; 3Department of Surgical, Oncological and Gastroenterological Sciences - DISCOG, University of Padova, Italy; 4Oncological and Colorectal Surgery Unit - University of Padova, Italy

Correspondence: G. Aviani Fulvio

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A30

Background

At present, cancer remains a predominant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Despite considerable therapeutic progress, a significant number of patients undergo curative surgical treatment with coexisting modifiable preoperative risk factors, such as poor physical, nutritional, and psychological statuses [1,2]. These factors can negatively impact surgical outcomes increasing the likelihood of postoperative complications and prolonged hospital stays [1]. Growing evidence indicates that prehabilitation, especially when multimodal, can enhance physiological reserve and reduce postoperative morbidity after major surgery [3,4]. The rationale for combining various interventions stems from their synergistic effects; addressing concurrently multiple aspects of patient health may be beneficial especially in oncological patients, whose functional impairment is often multifactorial [5].

Nonetheless, to date, the efficacy of prehabilitation in the oncologic population still remains uncertain.

This study aimed to identify and evaluate the effects of prehabilitation on postoperative complications in adult patients undergoing elective oncologic surgery for malignant neoplasms.

Materials and methods

We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The Central, Medline, Embase, and Scopus databases were searched from inception to September 9, 2025. Studies were selected based on the following PICOS criteria: (P) adults undergoing elective major oncologic surgery; (I) prehabilitation interventions (physical exercise, nutritional support, and psychological preparation); (C) standard perioperative care; (O) postoperative complications within 30 days or prior to discharge, defined by the Clavien–Dindo classification; (S) RCTs only.

Results

Eighty-one RCTs (8,145 patients) were included. Figure 1 illustrates the study selection process. Included studies covered various oncologic procedures, primarily abdominal (68%), thoracic (18%), and head and neck (6%) surgeries. In the network meta-analysis (Figure 2A-B), both isolated nutrition (OR 0.39; 95% CI 0.23–0.68) and combined prehabilitation (nutrition, exercise, and psychological support; OR 0.19; 95% CI 0.08–0.46) significantly reduced the number of patients with complications compared to usual care (low-certainty evidence). Isolated nutrition also decreased the overall number of complications (OR 0.61; 95% CI 0.41–0.90; low-certainty evidence). Furthermore, nutrition (−1.59 days; 95% CI −2.38 to −0.80) and exercise (−1.20 days; 95% CI −1.84 to −0.58) were most likely to reduce length of stay (very low-certainty evidence). The clinical benefit of isolated nutrition (OR 0.36; 95% CI 0.19–0.69) or combined multimodal prehabilitation (OR 0.18; 95% CI 0.07–0.47) was more pronounced among patients undergoing abdominal cancer surgery. No significant effects were observed for hospital mortality or health-related quality of life.

Conclusion

This meta-analysis confirms that prehabilitation meaningfully improves postoperative recovery in major oncologic surgery. Our findings demonstrate that nutritional and multimodal prehabilitation programs significantly reduce postoperative complications, intensive care admissions, and length of hospital stay, with the most consistent benefit seen in abdominal surgeries. Overall, these findings support the integration of structured, preferably multimodal, prehabilitation into standard perioperative care to enhance outcomes and reduce postoperative morbidity in patients undergoing major oncologic surgery.

A31 Cardiovascular subphenotypes and exploratory angiotensin ii therapy in high-risk major abdominal surgery

E. Antonucci1, F. Mulazzani1, F.F. Vezzulli2, J. Colombo1, G. Monti1

1Niguarda Metropolitan Hospital, Milan, Italy; 2University of Milan, Italy

Correspondence: E. Antonucci

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A31

Background

Myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery, is a proxy of perioperative cardiovascular susceptibility and is associated with increased risk of myocardial infarction, cardiac arrest, or death within 30 days [1, 2]. Conventional preoperative risk models may not capture mechanistic pathways leading to myocardial injury. Cardiovascular biomarker profiling, particularly based on renin, offers a potential strategy for physiology-informed patient phenotyping, with the potential for prognostic and predictive enrichment [3].

Clinical data supports the hypothesis that a relative angiotensin II deficiency, characterized by elevated precursor components such as renin, may contribute to refractory hypotension in vasoplegic states within the surgical population [4]. These patients may potentially benefit from targeted modulation of the renin-angiotensin system (RAAS) pathway [5].

The aim of this study was to assess whether an association exists between cardiovascular RAAS subphenotypes and early postoperative outcomes in high-risk patients undergoing major abdominal surgery. Furthermore, we aimed to preliminarily assess the feasibility, safety and hemodynamic effectiveness of angiotensin II infusion in patients requiring escalating vasopressor support during major abdominal surgery.

Material and methods

This is an observational prospective study framework including adult high-risk patients (ASA score 3) candidate to elective major abdominal surgery. Patients with preoperative requirement for vasoactive drugs, end-stage renal disease, recent kidney transplantation, and hyperaldosteronism were excluded. Written informed consent was obtained before surgery from all participants. The study was approved by the Comitato Etico Territoriale Lombardia 3 (protocol number 6603).

The first layer is a prospective cohort study designed to characterize cardiovascular RAAS subphenotypes using renin and assess postoperative myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (MINS). Renin serum concentration, measured by chemiluminescence, was recorded at baseline (within 48 h before surgical incision), and within 48 h after surgery. The population was divided in high or low baseline renin levels, based on its median value. The primary outcome was the incidence of MINS, defined as a high-sensitivity troponin T elevation attributable to myocardial ischemia (>20 ng/L with an absolute change >5 ng/L, or >65 ng/L), occurring within 72 h after surgery, irrespective of ischemic symptoms or electrocardiographic changes.

Secondary outcomes were early acute kidney injury, postoperative cardiovascular events, postoperative respiratory complications, and postoperative unplanned intensive care admission, according to perioperative plasmatic renin kinetics.

In a nested exploratory analysis, we included patients who received intraoperative angiotensin II infusion. According to institutional clinical practice, angiotensin II was considered in patients requiring escalating norepinephrine support (>0.1 mcg/kg/min) to maintain a mean arterial pressure >65 mmHg, correcting vasoplegic hypotension. Patients were not considered eligible for angiotensin II if they had received angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers within 12 h before surgery, had cardiac conditions potentially worsened by intense vasoconstriction, or had known hypersensitivity to synthetic angiotensin II. The main outcome of this nested study was the positive variation of mean arterial pressure from baseline to 10 minutes after the start of angiotensin II infusion.

Continuous and categorical variables were compared using nonparametric and exact tests, as appropriate.

Results

33 patients were included in the analysis and stratified according to the median baseline plasmatic renin concentration (17.3 pg/mL). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were generally balanced between high- and low-renin groups (Table 1). Patients with high baseline renin concentrations showed a significantly greater prevalence of diabetes mellitus.

Surgical procedures included hepatic (24%), esophagectomy (15%), pancreatic (15%), major intestinal (15%), urologic (3%), and other major abdominal surgeries (24%). Overall, 85% of procedures were performed using a robotic approach, whereas open surgery accounted for 15%.

Patients with high baseline renin concentrations showed a higher incidence MINS, compared with the low baseline renin group (75% vs. 24%; p = 0.003). No significant differences were observed regarding early postoperative acute kidney injury, respiratory complications, or unplanned ICU admission. No postoperative cardiovascular events were recorded, Table 2.

Absolute and relative postoperative renin increase were both non-significatively greater among patients who developed MINS (16 [−7 to 62] vs. −1 [−14 to 2] pg/mL; p = 0.063, and 76% [−39 to 195] vs. −16% [−65 to 19]; p = 0.087, respectively).

In the nested exploratory analysis, 4 patients received intraoperative angiotensin II infusion. Mean arterial pressure increased at the prespecified timepoint, together with parallel changes in cardiac index and systemic vascular resistance index, Figure 1.

No perioperative adverse events attributable to angiotensin II administration were observed.

Conclusions

Elevated preoperative plasmatic renin levels likely identify a subgroup of patients at increased risk of postoperative myocardial injury, supporting the concept that RAAS biomarker profiling may identify biologically distinct perioperative cardiovascular subphenotypes.

Preliminary exploratory observations also suggest that intraoperative angiotensin II administration may be feasible and hemodynamically effective in selected patients with vasoplegic hypotension requiring escalating vasopressor support, without incidence of adverse effects.

Statistically adequately powered data may inform the design of future biomarker-guided interventional trials.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A32 Effect of measured vs estimated body composition on propofol TCI performance: a proof-of-concept analysis

E. Tognoli1, V.A. Aleksandrov1, G. Catozzi1,2, F. Buono1,2, J.P. Van den Berg3, E. Bruno4

1Department of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Care, IRCCS Foundation – National Cancer Institute of Milan, Italy; 2Department of Pathophysiology and Transplantation, University of Milan, Italy; 3Department of Anesthesiology, University of Groningen, University Medical Center Groningen, Netherlands; 4Department of Predictive & Preventive Medicine, IRCCS Foundation – National Cancer Institute of Milan, Italy

Correspondence: V.A. Aleksandrov

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A32

Background

Target-Controlled Infusion (TCI) systems represent the current technological standard for propofol administration during total intravenous anesthesia. These systems rely on pharmacokinetic models incorporating patient-specific covariates, including body composition measurements. In the Schneider model, lean body mass (LBM) estimated using James’ formula contributes to the calculation of the elimination rate constant (K10), whereas the Eleveld model incorporates fat-free mass (FFM), estimated using Al-Sallami equations, in the calculation of V3 (peripheral compartment). However, formula-derived body composition may be inaccurate in oncologic patients with sarcopenic obesity. We conducted a proof-of-concept simulation to evaluate the impact of bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA)-measured versus formula-derived body composition on propofol infusion profiles.

Methods

A pharmacokinetic simulator implementing the Schneider and Eleveld propofol models was developed to compare infusion schemes generated using formula-derived versus BIA-derived body composition parameters. BIA measurements were obtained using the InBody970 system during routine preoperative assessment within an ongoing observational study on body composition in surgical oncology patients. Simulations were performed using data from a female patient aged 37 years, 150 cm in height, and 72 kg in weight. BIA-derived LBM and FFM were 34.4 kg and 37.2 kg, respectively. The Al-Sallami-derived FFM was 40.2 kg, while James formula-derived LBM was 42.9 kg. Propofol TCI was simulated to maintain a target plasma concentration of 3 mcg/mL for 60 minutes. The primary endpoint was total propofol dose administered during the infusion period.

Results

Within the Schneider model (Figure 1 A), the lower BIA-derived LBM (34.4 kg) produced a higher cumulative propofol dose compared with James formula-derived LBM (42.9 kg), demonstrating marked sensitivity of the model to LBM estimation, with total dose differences of 653.10 mg (LBM_estim) versus 576.84 mg (LBM_calc). In contrast, within the Eleveld model (Figure 1B), BIA-derived FFM resulted in a slightly lower cumulative propofol dose compared with Al-Sallami estimated FFM, with total doses of 508.82 mg (FFM_estim) versus 517.56 mg (FFM_calc).

Conclusions

BIA-derived body composition influences propofol TCI system performance differently depending on the pharmacokinetic model used, consistent with differences in how covariates are incorporated and weighted within each model. Incorporation of measured LBM may alter Schneider model behaviour inconsistently in sarcopenic obesity, whereas measured FFM appears to improve physiologic coherence and dosing performance within the Eleveld model. Overall, the Eleveld model combined with measured FFM may provide a more physiologically appropriate approach for obese sarcopenic patients. Prospective validation in a clinical sarcopenic population is warranted.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

Comparison of propofol target-controlled infusion (TCI) performance using measured versus estimated body composition in a single sarcopenic oncologic patient. Simulated infusion profiles and total admnistered dose are shown for the Schneider model (A) and the Eleveld model (B). Body composition was derived either from bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) or from formula-based estimates (James-derived lean body mass and All-Sallami-derived fat-free mass). Differences in cumulative dose reflect model-dependent sensitivity to covariate specification

A33 Analgesic efficacy of ultra-low-dose local anesthetic added to intrathecal morphine in open abdominal surgery

S. Di Stefano1, R. Didamo1, E. Trimarchi2, M.D. Randazzo2, R. Mallamace2, L. Cardia2

1ASP 5 Messina P.O. Taormina, Italy; 2A.O.U. University Polyclinic Hospital G. Martino, Messina, Italy

Correspondence: S. Di Stefano

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A33

Background

Analgesic management in laparotomic surgery remains a major challenge for anesthesiologists. Intrathecal morphine represents an effective strategy for both intraoperative and postoperative analgesia. However, its main limitation is the delayed onset of action, requiring a relatively long time before achieving full analgesic efficacy.

Materials and Methods

We conducted a retrospective observational study including 30 patients undergoing open abdominal surgery. All patients received subarachnoid anesthesia for analgesic purposes prior to induction of general anesthesia and were divided into two homogeneous groups:

The first group received intrathecal morphine alone at a dose of 1 mcg/kg ideal body weight (IBW) (MO Group).

The first group received intrathecal morphine alone at a dose of 1 mcg/kg ideal body weight (IBW) (MO Group).

The second group received intrathecal morphine at the same dose (1 mcg/kg IBW) combined with 5 mg of levobupivacaine (ULD Group).

The second group received intrathecal morphine at the same dose (1 mcg/kg IBW) combined with 5 mg of levobupivacaine (ULD Group).

The primary endpoint was to evaluate the analgesic efficacy of adding ultra-low-dose local anesthetic to intrathecal morphine compared with intrathecal morphine alone. The groups were compared in terms of postoperative intravenous morphine consumption and postoperative Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) pain scores. Secondary endpoints included intraoperative vasopressor and remifentanil requirements.

Results

Mean patient age was 71 ± 10 years, with a mean BMI of 27.09 ± 4.67 kg/m². Mean postoperative morphine consumption was 1.23 ± 1.07 mg, with a mean postoperative NRS score of 2 ± 0.83. The MO Group showed significantly higher postoperative morphine consumption compared with the ULD Group (1.73 ± 0.96 mg vs. 0.73 ± 0.96 mg, respectively; p = 0.008). Similarly, postoperative NRS scores were significantly lower in the ULD Group compared with the MO Group (1.67 ± 0.72 vs. 2.33 ± 0.82, respectively; p = 0.029).

Patients in the MO Group required intraoperative remifentanil more frequently (p = 0.025) in order to maintain adequate analgesia. Furthermore, patients who received remifentanil had higher postoperative morphine consumption on average compared with those who did not (1.56 ± 1.2 mg vs. 0.75 ± 0.62 mg; p = 0.042). Postoperative NRS scores followed the same trend, with lower pain scores observed in patients who did not require intraoperative remifentanil (1.67 ± 0.78 vs. 2.22 ± 0.81; p = 0.038). No significant differences were observed between the two groups regarding vasopressor use (p = 0.705) Table 1.

Conclusions

Effective intraoperative and postoperative pain management is essential in laparotomic surgery. The addition of ultra-low-dose local anesthetic to intrathecal morphine reduced intraoperative opioid requirements without significant hemodynamic effects. Moreover, it was associated with reduced postoperative morphine consumption and lower postoperative NRS pain scores.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A34 Fast-track inguinal hernia surgery: which anesthetic technique offers the best balance between recovery and efficacy?

S. Di Stefano2, M. Moscato2, C. Mazzeo1, E. Trimarchi1, L. Cardia1

1A.O.U. University Hospital G. Martino, Messina, Italy; 2Asp 5 Messina, Italy

Correspondence: S. Di Stefano

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A34

Background

Fast-Track protocols for ambulatory and day-surgery procedures emphasize the use of minimally invasive surgical approaches and short-acting anesthetic techniques that allow rapid postoperative recovery and early discharge. Lichtenstein inguinal hernia repair is widely performed within these pathways because of both its high prevalence in the general population and the progressive adoption of less invasive perioperative strategies.

Materials and Methods

This retrospective, observational, single-center study compared four different anesthetic approaches for patients undergoing Lichtenstein inguinal hernioplasty. A total of 68 patients were enrolled and divided into four groups according to the anesthetic technique used:

Group A: local anesthesia administered by the surgeon combined with sedation (n = 19);

Group A: local anesthesia administered by the surgeon combined with sedation (n = 19);

Group B: iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerve block performed by the surgeon using anatomical landmarks (blind technique) (n = 17);

Group B: iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerve block performed by the surgeon using anatomical landmarks (blind technique) (n = 17);

Group C: ultrasound-guided anterior transversus abdominis plane block (Anterior TAP block) (n = 17);

Group C: ultrasound-guided anterior transversus abdominis plane block (Anterior TAP block) (n = 17);

Group D: spinal anesthesia (n = 15).

Group D: spinal anesthesia (n = 15).

The primary endpoint was postoperative discharge time (TDPO), calculated in minutes from discharge from the operating room to actual hospital discharge. Secondary endpoints included intraoperative drug consumption and the incidence of intraoperative and postoperative complications.

Results

The mean age of the study population was 62 ± 13 years, with no significant differences in body mass index among groups. Mean operative time was 102 ± 23 minutes (p = 0.746). Group D showed a significantly longer TDPO compared with the other groups (954 ± 313 minutes; p = 0.001). Among the first three groups, Group C demonstrated the shortest TDPO, with statistically significant differences compared with Groups A and B. No cases of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), bowel perforation, or intravascular injection were reported. Overall, 41% of patients experienced no perioperative complications. Inadequate anesthesia occurred in 32% of cases, specifically in 47% of patients in Group A, 47% in Group B, and in none of the patients in Group C. Conversion to general anesthesia was required in 21% of patients receiving local anesthesia with sedation (Group A) Table 1.

Discussion

The optimal anesthetic management for patients undergoing Lichtenstein inguinal hernia repair in a day-hospital setting remains controversial because of the need to balance effective intraoperative analgesia with rapid postoperative discharge. Although spinal anesthesia provided the most reliable anesthetic block, it was associated with prolonged discharge times and potential complications such as urinary retention; moreover, it may be contraindicated in patients receiving anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. Local anesthesia combined with sedation demonstrated a higher failure rate and occasionally required conversion to general anesthesia. The anterior TAP block ensured effective intraoperative anesthetic management while allowing early discharge. However, its use may be limited by the need for operator expertise in ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia techniques. Both ultrasound-guided and landmark-based ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric blocks were associated with reduced TDPO, although the blind technique showed higher sedative requirements and a greater incidence of inadequate anesthesia.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A35 Implementation of an opioid-sparing protocol with serratus anterior plane block in breast surgery: impact on PONV and early postoperative recovery

S. Casanova, L. Accornero, N. Fiaccone, A. Gilardenghi, V. Trifiletti, M. Bonfiglio

Liguria Local Health Authority (ASL) – Section 4, Lavagna, Italy

Correspondence: V. Trifiletti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A35

Background

Pain management in oncological breast surgery (mastectomy and quadrantectomy) has shifted toward Regional Anesthesia (RA) techniques to minimize systemic opioid consumption and its related complications. This study aims to compare the efficacy of a protocol based on the Serratus Anterior Plane Block (SAPB) against a standard analgesic management based exclusively on opioids, evaluating the incidence of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting (PONV) and the timeliness of functional recovery.

Materials and Methods

A retrospective analysis was conducted on 167 patients divided into two cohorts:

2024 Protocol Group (n=82): General anesthesia (Fentanyl 100 mcg + Sevoflurane) + SAPB (Ropivacaine 0.375% 20 ml + IV Dexamethasone 8 mg). Postoperative analgesia: IV Paracetamol 1 g tid and IV Ibuprofen 600 mg as needed.

2024 Protocol Group (n=82): General anesthesia (Fentanyl 100 mcg + Sevoflurane) + SAPB (Ropivacaine 0.375% 20 ml + IV Dexamethasone 8 mg). Postoperative analgesia: IV Paracetamol 1 g tid and IV Ibuprofen 600 mg as needed.

2023 Control Group (n=85): Standard general anesthesia (Fentanyl 200 mcg). Postoperative analgesia: Morphine bolus (10 mg) followed by continuous infusion via elastomeric pump (20 mg/24h), combined with I’V Paracetamol 1 g tid and IV Ibuprofen 600 mg as needed.

2023 Control Group (n=85): Standard general anesthesia (Fentanyl 200 mcg). Postoperative analgesia: Morphine bolus (10 mg) followed by continuous infusion via elastomeric pump (20 mg/24h), combined with I’V Paracetamol 1 g tid and IV Ibuprofen 600 mg as needed.

Pain levels (VAS scale), PONV incidence, technique-related complications, and time to resumption of oral intake and mobilization were monitored.

Results

The protocol implemented in 2024 led to a drastic reduction in total opioid consumption (mean Morphine: 3 mg vs. 30 mg; Fentanyl: 100 mcg vs. 200 mcg). Despite the reduction in opioids, analgesic efficacy remained comparable (mean VAS score of 2 in both groups). A significant reduction in PONV was observed (20% in the 2024 group vs. 80% in the control group).

This facilitated a markedly faster functional recovery: 96% of patients in the new protocol group resumed oral intake and mobilization within 6 hours post-surgery, compared to 42% at 24 hours in the control group. No complications related to the regional anesthesia procedure were recorded.

Conclusions

Integrating the Serratus Anterior Plane Block into a multidisciplinary care pathway has proven to be an effective and safe strategy. The opioid-sparing technique not only ensures optimal pain control but also drastically reduces morphine-related side effects, accelerating functional recovery and optimizing hospital stay in alignment with modern ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A36 Efficacy of low-dose prilocaine in subarachnoid anesthesia for orthopedic surgery - elective knee arthroscopy: a randomized controlled trial

G. Sfregola, G. Montenero, S. Ruocco, S. Bufano, D. Galante

ASL FG, Cerignola, Italy

Correspondence: G. Sfregola

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A36

Background

Knee arthroscopy is one of the most frequently performed orthopedic procedures in the day-surgery setting. In this context, the choice of the local anesthetic for spinal anesthesia should ensure adequate surgical anesthesia, hemodynamic stability, and rapid postoperative recovery. Due to its intermediate duration of action, hyperbaric prilocaine may represent a valuable alternative to hyperbaric bupivacaine in fast-track protocols.

Objectives

To evaluate the efficacy and safety of low-dose hyperbaric prilocaine (30 mg and 50 mg) compared with hyperbaric bupivacaine 8 mg for spinal anesthesia in elective knee arthroscopy.

Materials and Methods

A prospective randomized controlled open-label study was conducted on 90 ASA I–II patients undergoing elective knee arthroscopy. Patients were randomized into three groups: P30 (hyperbaric prilocaine 30 mg), P50 (hyperbaric prilocaine 50 mg), and B8 (hyperbaric bupivacaine 8 mg). The following parameters were evaluated: intraoperative hemodynamic stability, sensory and motor block characteristics, motor recovery time, recovery of spontaneous micturition, intraoperative pain, adverse events, and patient satisfaction.

Results

The groups were homogeneous regarding demographic and clinical characteristics. Bupivacaine was associated with a higher incidence of intraoperative hypotension and greater ephedrine consumption compared with the prilocaine groups (p < 0.01). Motor recovery was significantly faster in the P30 group (95 ± 18 min) compared with P50 (135 ± 22 min) and B8 (210 ± 30 min) (p < 0.001). Recovery of spontaneous micturition was also significantly earlier in the prilocaine groups compared with the B8 group (p < 0.001). The P30 group showed a slightly higher incidence of intraoperative pain compared with B8 (13% vs 0%; p < 0.05), without the need for anesthetic conversion. Patient satisfaction was significantly higher in the prilocaine groups, particularly in the P30 group (p < 0.01).

Conclusions

Low-dose hyperbaric prilocaine, particularly at the 30 mg dose, represents a valid alternative to hyperbaric bupivacaine for spinal anesthesia in elective knee arthroscopy. It provides adequate anesthetic efficacy associated with greater hemodynamic stability, faster motor recovery, and earlier restoration of bladder function, thereby supporting fast-track and day-surgery protocols.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A37 Intravenous dexmedetomidine as an adjuvant to regional anesthesia in arthroscopic knee surgery

K. Musu1, M. Oggiano1, G.A. Grande1, M. Marchesini2

1Mater Olbia Hospital, Olbia, Italy; 2Pascale National Tumor Institute, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: K. Musu

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A37

Background

Ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia is widely used in arthroscopic knee surgery because it improves postoperative analgesia and anesthesia. Dexmedetomidine, a selective <alfa>2-adrenergic agonist, has recently gained interest as an adjuvant capable of prolonging peripheral nerve block duration and improving postoperative pain control.

Materials and methods

This study enrolled 63 ASA I–III patients aged 18–70 years undergoing elective arthroscopic meniscal surgery. Standard clinical practice was followed from January to June 2025; subsequently, dexmedetomidine endovenous (DEX) was introduced in accordance with the new hospital protocol implemented following the acquisition and availability of the drug. All patients provided informed consent for the processing of their data for study purposes. All patients received ultrasound-guided femoral nerve block with 10 mL mepivacaine 2% and ultrasound-guided subgluteal sciatic nerve block with 10 mL mepivacaine 2%. Patients who underwent surgery after June, receive continuous intravenous dexmedetomidine infusion (DEX group, 0.7–1 mcg/kg/h) instead of regional anesthesia alone (CTRL group). Postoperative pain was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) at 2, 6 and 12 hours. Secondary endpoints included sensory block duration (Hollmen scale), motor block duration (Bromage scale), total anesthesia duration, rescue analgesia requirement and adverse events. Statistical analysis was performed using Student’s t-test for continuous variables and the χ² test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical data, including the Bromage and Hollmen scales. Categorical variables are expressed as percentages. In all cases, a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results

Baseline demographic characteristics, ASA class and surgical duration were comparable between groups. The DEX group showed significantly lower postoperative NRS scores at 2, 6 and 12 hours compared with the CTRL group (Figure 1) (Table 1). Sensory and motor block duration were significantly prolonged in patients receiving intravenous dexmedetomidine, with slower regression of Bromage (Figure 2) (Table 2) and Hollmen scores (Figure 3) (Table 3). No patient required rescue analgesia. Adverse events observed in the DEX group included sedation in 50% of patients, bradycardia in 42% and hypotension in 8%. No major neurological complications or severe adverse events were reported. No adverse events were observed in the CTRL group

Discussion

Intravenous dexmedetomidine was associated with improved postoperative analgesia compared with the control group after arthroscopic knee surgery. This was evidenced by significantly lower NRS scores at 2 h, 6 h, and 12 h. Regarding block characteristics, dexmedetomidine was associated with a higher proportion of patients with a more pronounced motor block at 6 h postoperatively. Bromage score of 2 or more was observed in 66.7% of patients in the DEX group compared with 22.2% in the control group. No significant difference was observed at 2 h, while no residual motor block was present in either group at 12 h. Similarly, sensory block duration assessed by Hollmen score showed a greater proportion of patients with effective sensory block at 6 h in the DEX group compared with controls, whereas no significant differences were detected at 2 h or at 12 h (0% in both groups). These findings (Table 4) suggest that intravenous dexmedetomidine may prolong the duration of both sensory and motor components of peripheral nerve block while enhancing postoperative analgesia. The mechanism is likely related to <alfa>-adrenergic modulation of nociceptive transmission and synergistic effects with local anesthetics. From a clinical perspective, the improved analgesic profile may contribute to reduced postoperative pain.

Conclusions

Intravenous dexmedetomidine may represent a potentially useful adjuvant to ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia in arthroscopic knee surgery. Its intraoperative administration was associated with improved postoperative analgesia, as well as a prolongation of sensory and motor block and a reduction in postoperative pain scores over time. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution. Although a potential clinical benefit emerges, the observed prolongation of motor block may be associated with a delayed motor recovery, which could potentially influence functional recovery and discharge timing in fast-track surgical pathways. This aspect may have relevant implications in the context of enhanced recovery protocols and should be carefully balanced against the analgesic advantages. Further multicenter, prospective randomized controlled trials are warranted to better define the optimal dosing regimen, clarify the risk–benefit profile, and confirm the long-term clinical impact of intravenous dexmedetomidine as an adjuvant in peripheral nerve blocks.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.
