A38 Serratus posterior superior intercostal plane block (SPSIPB): a novel interfascial block in breast surgery

P.S. Mariotti, F. Santoro, V. Corritore, P. Vaira

Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza, San Giovanni Rotondo (Foggia), Italy

Correspondence: P.S. Mariotti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A38

Background

Breast cancer surgery, particularly nipple–areola complex (NAC)-sparing mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection, is associated with significant postoperative pain and opioid-related side effects that may impair recovery and increase the risk of chronic pain. Ultrasound-guided interfascial plane blocks, such as the serratus anterior plane block (SAPB), are widely used, while the novel serratus posterior superior intercostal plane block (SPSIPB) has recently been proposed to provide wider thoracic analgesia.

Objectives

This study aimed to compare the analgesic efficacy of SAPB and SPSIPB in patients undergoing NAC-sparing mastectomy with axillary dissection and its superiority in this surgical setting interpreted by patients as faster recovery and better comfort.

Methods

In this prospective, controlled clinical study, 60 female patients (ASA I–III) were allocated to receive either SAPB (n = 30) or SPSIPB (n = 30) before induction of general anaesthesia. The primary outcome was pain measured by the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) at rest and during movement at the end of surgery (T0) and 24 hours postoperatively (T24). Secondary outcomes included intraoperative remifentanil consumption, need for rescue analgesia, incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), and quality of recovery assessed by the QoR-15 questionnaire at T24. Data were analysed using non-parametric statistical tests.

Results

Baseline demographic and surgical characteristics were comparable between groups. Both techniques significantly reduced pain from T0 to T24; however, patients receiving SPSIPB reported significantly lower NRS scores at rest and during movement at both time points compared with SAPB. SPSIPB was also associated with significantly lower intraoperative remifentanil consumption and higher QoR-15 scores, indicating better early postoperative recovery. No statistically significant differences were found between groups in the incidence of PONV or the need for rescue analgesia Table 1.

Conclusions

Within a multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesic strategy, SPSIPB provided superior postoperative analgesia, reduced intraoperative opioid requirements, and improved quality of recovery compared with SAPB in patients undergoing NAC-sparing mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. These findings support the integration of SPSIPB as a valuable regional anaesthesia technique for breast surgery, although larger randomized trials are needed to confirm these results.

A39 Agreement between the MAIA artificial intelligence application (NYSORA) and experienced anesthesiologists in regional anesthesia planning for upper limb orthopedic surgery: a single-center retrospective agreement study

L. Bray, A. Ingrosso, A. Vergari, G. Bernardi, A. Fabretti, C. Memoli, C. Malatesta, L. Capuano, D. De Padova, D. Crupi

Department of Emergency, Anestesiology and Resuscitation Sciences, IRCCS A. Gemelli University Polyclinic Foundation, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: A. Ingrosso

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A39

Background

AI-based clinical decision support systems are increasingly developed for anesthesiology, but clinical validation remains limited [1]. Regional anesthesia is suitable for AI due to complex variables influencing technique selection [2]. MAIA (Medical AI Assistant, NYSORA) provides personalized recommendations based on structured patient data. We evaluated the agreement between MAIA and experienced anesthesiologists in elective upper limb orthopedic surgery.

Materials and Methods

We conducted a retrospective case series of 150 consecutive adult patients undergoing elective upper limb orthopedic surgery at Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli (Rome) between November 2025 and May 2026. Eligible cases included shoulder, arm, elbow, forearm, wrist, and hand procedures managed by anesthesiologists with >10 years of orthopedic anesthesia experience. Clinical variables (demographics, comorbidities, ASA status, medications, surgery) were extracted from medical records and processed through MAIA (v4.0.2) to generate recommendations. MAIA outputs included block type, local anesthetic agent, intended strategy, and dosing. These were compared with actual plans implemented by attending anesthesiologists. The primary outcome was inter-rater agreement assessed via Cohen’s weighted kappa with linear weighting [3]. Sensitivity analysis used quadratic weighting. Agreement was classified across five ordinal categories from total concordance to complete technique discordance. Secondary outcomes included discordance pattern analysis and clinical success (successful surgery without unplanned general anesthesia conversion).

Results

Overall agreement between MAIA and anesthesiologist decisions was 71.3% (107/150; 95% CI, 63.3–78.4). Total concordance (identical block, local anesthetic, intended use) occurred in 38.0% (57/150). Weighted kappa with linear weighting was 0.61 (95% CI, 0.51–0.71), indicating substantial agreement [4,5]. Sensitivity analysis yielded a kappa of 0.64. Local anesthetic discordances (33.3%) consistently reflected preference for mepivacaine over MAIA-recommended ropivacaine to reduce prolonged motor blockade and improve functional autonomy. Block type discordances (18.0%) related to teaching safety and procedural simplification. For wrist surgery, axillary block was frequently selected over supraclavicular block to minimize pneumothorax risk during resident procedures. For hand surgery, axillary block was favored over selective distal blocks to reduce needle insertions. Intended use discordances (7.3%) reflected factors not integrated into the AI, such as patient anxiety or positioning constraints. Regional anesthesia was omitted in 3.3% due to minimal invasiveness. Clinical success was achieved in all 145 performed blocks without general anesthesia conversion.

Conclusions

MAIA demonstrated substantial agreement with experienced anesthesiologists in upper limb regional anesthesia planning. Observed discordances reflected legitimate contextual clinical adaptations rather than algorithmic errors. MAIA may serve as a valuable first-pass clinical decision support tool, offering baseline recommendations requiring integration with clinician judgment. Optimal care depends on contextual factors, operator expertise, and patient specifics. Limitations include retrospective single-center design, lack of prospective validation, and absence of formal AI quality evaluation using DECIDE-AI or APPRAISE-AI frameworks [6,7]. Multicenter studies should evaluate if AI-guided planning improves clinical outcomes and efficiency.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A40 Blood lidocaine levels and clinical evaluation in intravenous regional anesthesia (bier block): our experience

F. Giulietti1, G. Giaccaglia2, D. Antonelli1, E. Antonelli3, C. Scala1

1Hospital Principe di Piemonte, Senigallia, Italy; 2Polytechnic University of Marche, Ancona, Italy; 3Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden

Correspondence: G. Giaccaglia

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A40

Background

Bier block, or intravenous regional anesthesia (IVRA), is a simple and effective anesthetic technique for short surgical procedures of the distal upper limb, generally lasting less than 60 minutes. Despite its advantages, the technique carries potential risks related to systemic toxicity from local anesthetic absorption.

Methods

This randomized double-blind study evaluated the clinical efficacy and systemic safety of lidocaine during IVRA, with simultaneous plasma measurements from both the operated limb and the systemic circulation. Twenty-four patients undergoing median nerve microneurolysis were divided into two groups according to lidocaine dose:

Group A: 2 mg/kg lidocaine (Table 1- Fig. 1)

Group A: 2 mg/kg lidocaine (Table 1- Fig. 1)

Group B: 3 mg/kg lidocaine (Table 2- Fig. 2)

Group B: 3 mg/kg lidocaine (Table 2- Fig. 2)

Each group included subgroups receiving either 0.5% or 0.75% lidocaine solutions.

After limb exsanguination with an Esmarch bandage, a tourniquet was applied to the arm at pressures at least 100 mmHg above systolic blood pressure. Lidocaine was infused slowly (about 6 mL/min), while venous pressure was monitored to prevent anesthetic leakage. An additional forearm tourniquet was used to compartmentalize anesthetic distribution.

Serial blood samples were collected from both the operated and contralateral limbs immediately after infusion, after reperfusion, and up to three hours later. Vital signs including blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygen saturation were continuously monitored.

Results

The procedure was clinically successful and well tolerated in all patients. No patient required additional sedation or analgesia, and surgeons benefited from excellent visualization due to ischemia. Group B patients experienced slightly longer postoperative analgesia, while approximately half of Group A patients reported mild discomfort during wound closure.

Only minor side effects were observed, including mild hypotension and one transient episode of bradycardia. Importantly, no signs or symptoms of systemic local anesthetic toxicity occurred, and no lipid rescue therapy was required.

Plasma analysis demonstrated very low systemic lidocaine concentrations throughout the study, always below the accepted toxicity threshold of 5 mcg/mL. However, concentrations measured in the operated limb were markedly higher, reaching values up to four times above the toxicity threshold before gradually decreasing over the following hours. Twenty-four-hour measurements showed almost complete disappearance of lidocaine in most patients.

Conclusions

The confirmed that IVRA with lidocaine is a safe, simple, and effective technique for short upper-limb surgery when strict technical precautions are respected. Although minimal anesthetic leakage into systemic circulation occurs, systemic concentrations remain well below toxic levels. The persistence of high local concentrations in the operated limb suggests temporary sequestration of lidocaine within tissue compartments, followed by gradual release into the circulation over time.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A41 T3-level MTP block combined with IP/PECS in breast surgery: our experience with an opioid-sparing multimodal protocol under locoregional anaesthesia, sedation and augmented reality

G. Galasso1, I. Esposito1, S. Guerriero1, C. Ferrigno1, M.M. Fabris1, A. Cicalese2, D. Carbone1

1Anesthesia and Intensive Care Unit, Emergency Department (DEA), Nocera–Pagani–Scafati, Nocera Inferiore (SA), Italy; 2Breast Unit ASL Salerno, Pagani (SA), Italy

Correspondence: G. Galasso

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A41

Background

Perioperative pain in breast surgery is still a clinically relevant issue, for early recovery and for the risk of chronic postsurgical pain. We evaluate, in our routine clinical practice, if a combined approach based on ultrasound-guided chest wall blocks, an opioid-sparing strategy and the use of an augmented reality headset, as part of the anaesthetic technique itself could provide adequate analgesia without opioids, in patients scheduled for mastectomy or quadrantectomy.

Materials and methods

The study is prospective observational single-center. We observed 20 patients aged 40 to 65 years undergoing breast surgery: 10 mastectomies and 10 quadrantectomies. Surgery was performed under locoregional anaesthesia combined with sedation and with the intraoperative use of an augmented reality headset, considered an active component of the anaesthetic technique. Each patient received midazolam 1 mg and ketamine 10 mg intravenously before block performance. In all cases an ultrasound-guided Midpoint Transverse Process to Pleura (MTP) block was carried out at the T3 level and combined with an interpectoral/pectoralis (IP/PECS) block, using 0.5% ropivacaine for a total volume of 20 mL. During surgery, continuous infusions of ketamine 0.25 mg/kg/h and magnesium sulfate 10 mg/kg/h were maintained. Postoperative analgesia consisted of paracetamol 1 g every 8 hours. We recorded intraoperative pain, NRS at awakening and at 3, 6, 12 and 24 hours, the need for rescue analgesia, time to oral intake and the presence of chronic pain at 3 months.

Results

None of the patients reported intraoperative pain. NRS values in the postoperative period and at the following time points remained below 3 in every case. No patient asked for NSAIDs as additional analgesia. Oral intake was resumed within 3 hours after surgery in all cases. At 3-month follow-up no chronic postsurgical pain was observed.

Conclusions

Combining a T3-level MTP block with an IP/PECS block, integrated with ketamine, magnesium sulfate, paracetamol and with an augmented reality headset used as an active component of the anaesthetic technique, in the setting of locoregional anaesthesia and sedation, proved to be in our experience a feasible and effective option for breast surgery, providing good acute pain control, fast recovery and absence of chronic pain at 3 months in the observed series. These results, coming from a small and uncontrolled series, will need to be confirmed in larger prospective studies.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A42 rethinking anesthesia in high-risk patients: thoracic spinal anesthesia for laparoscopic cholecystectomy in a patient with obesity and COPD

V. Fabbricatore, F. Barra, G. Cosenza, V. Pota, F. Coppolino, M.B. Passavanti, P. Sansone, M.C. Pace

University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: F. Barra

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A42

Background

Video-Laparoscopic Surgery (VLS) is considered the gold standard treatment for acute cholecystitis. However, the CO2 pneumoperitoneum required for the procedure presents significant physiological hurdles, particularly for patients with compromised respiratory function. The absorption of CO2 through the peritoneum, coupled with increased intra-abdominal pressure, leads to diaphragmatic splinting and a reduction in functional residual capacity (FRC). In patients suffering from Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), these factors exacerbate pre-existing ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatches. During acute exacerbations (AECOPD), the ability to compensate for exogenous CO2 load is severely impaired, often resulting in respiratory acidosis. Consequently, conventional general anesthesia (GA) with positive pressure ventilation carries a high risk of barotrauma and delayed weaning.

Case Report

We present the perioperative management of a 50-year-old female with Class II obesity (BMI > 35 kg/m^2) and acute-on-chronic respiratory failure due to AECOPD. Preoperative arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis revealed significant hypercapnia. To mitigate the risks of a difficult airway and further respiratory deterioration associated with endotracheal intubation, a neuraxial approach was selected.

Thoracic Spinal Anesthesia (TSA) was performed at the T10-T11 interspace using 12.5 mg of isobaric Ropivacaine and 7 mcg of Dexmedetomidine. Intrathecal dexmedetomidine was utilized to enhance sensory blockade and provide cooperative sedation without depressing respiration. Gas exchange was optimized via High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) therapy, which facilitated anatomical dead space washout and provided a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) effect to counter pneumoperitoneum-induced atelectasis. Intra-operative PaCO2 was monitored by serial ABG (Table 1).

Conclusions

This case highlights TSA as a sophisticated rescue strategy for high-risk surgical candidates. By maintaining spontaneous ventilation, we effectively circumvented the risks of ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI) and airway-related complications common in the obese population. The synergy between TSA and HFNC ensured hemodynamic stability and adequate CO2 clearance, even under the stress of a pneumoperitoneum. This awake laparoscopic approach offers a superior safety profile for patients where the conventional anesthetic paradigm carries unacceptable risks, aligning with the core tenets of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) in complex emergency settings.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A43 Ultrasound-guided multiple peripheral nerve blocks as sole anesthetic technique for pertrochanteric hip fracture fixation in a nonagenarian with critical aortic stenosis and severe comorbidities

V. Donatiello1, A. Scalvenzi1, L. Baiano1, V. Maffei1, A. Alfieri1, L. Pansa2, F. Coppolino2, M.B. Passavanti2, P. Sansone2, M.C. Pace2

1A.O.R.N. “Antonio Cardarelli” (National Relevance Hospital), Naples, Italy; 2University Hospital “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: L. Baiano

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A43

Background

Managing anesthesia for hip fracture surgery in frail elderly patients with severe comorbidities remains a major clinical challenge. Critical aortic stenosis (valve area less than 1.0 cm²) is associated with a fixed cardiac output and high perioperative risk, making both general anesthesia and neuraxial techniques potentially hazardous. Subarachnoid anesthesia may induce sudden decreases in systemic vascular resistance, leading to life-threatening hypotension, while general anesthesia carries risks of myocardial depression, hemodynamic instability, and postoperative pulmonary complications—particularly in patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In such contexts, peripheral nerve blocks may represent a viable alternative, allowing adequate surgical anesthesia while preserving hemodynamic stability. This case report describes the successful use of a multimodal locoregional anesthesia approach in a high-risk nonagenarian patient undergoing hip fracture fixation.

Case Report

A 92-year-old female was admitted for surgical treatment of a left pertrochanteric femoral fracture, scheduled for intramedullary osteosynthesis with a cephalomedullary nail. Her medical history included advanced senile dementia, severe COPD, and critical aortic stenosis with a valve area of 0.8 cm². Given the severity of the aortic stenosis, subarachnoid anesthesia was deemed contraindicated due to the risk of profound hypotension. General anesthesia was also considered high risk due to potential hemodynamic instability and respiratory complications.

After multidisciplinary evaluation and careful risk stratification, a decision was made to proceed with an ultrasound-guided locoregional anesthesia technique. Following acquisition of valid informed consent from the patient’s legal guardians for both the procedure and publication of the case, combined peripheral nerve blocks were performed. These included femoral, obturator, lateral femoral cutaneous, and sciatic nerve block at the gluteal level.

A mixture of ropivacaine 0.375% and dexamethasone 8 mg was used. The following volumes were administered: 15 mL for the femoral nerve, 20 mL for the sciatic nerve, 5 mL for the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, and 5 mL for the obturator nerve. Adequate sensory blockade was confirmed prior to surgery.

Intraoperative sedation consisted of intravenous ketamine 20 mg, providing effective anxiolysis and analgesia without compromising respiratory drive or hemodynamic stability. The surgical procedure was completed uneventfully. The patient maintained stable hemodynamic parameters throughout, with no episodes of hypotension, bradycardia, or oxygen desaturation.

Postoperative analgesia was managed with paracetamol 1000 mg every 8 hours, without the need for opioids. Pain control was satisfactory, and no signs of delirium or respiratory deterioration were observed. The patient’s recovery was consistent with expectations given her baseline clinical condition.

Conclusion

This case highlights the feasibility and effectiveness of a combined peripheral nerve block strategy as the sole anesthetic technique for hip fracture surgery in a frail, high-risk elderly patient with critical aortic stenosis. In situations where neuraxial anesthesia is contraindicated and general anesthesia poses significant risk, locoregional anesthesia offers a valuable alternative. By avoiding sympathetic blockade and minimizing systemic drug effects, this approach can preserve hemodynamic stability and reduce perioperative complications. Careful patient selection, ultrasound guidance, and a multimodal block strategy are essential to ensure adequate surgical anesthesia. This technique may be particularly advantageous in patients with severe valvular heart disease who are not contraindicated for deep peripheral nerve blocks.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A44 Strategies for prolonging neuraxial block with levobupivacaine: comparison among commonly used intrathecal adjuvants. a single-center, observational, retrospective study

S. Di Stefano1, G. Filoni1, E. Trimarchi2, L. Cardia2

1Asp 5 Messina P.O. San Vincenzo Taormina, Messina, Italy; 2A.O.U. Polyclinic G. Martino, Messina, Italy

Correspondence: S. Di Stefano

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A44

Background

The use of intrathecal adjuvants in combination with local anaesthetics for lower abdominal surgery allows modulation of neuraxial block. However, there is still no consensus in the literature regarding their benefits in terms of motor block duration and hemodynamic stability. While intrathecal opioids are widely used, α2-agonists, such as clonidine, remain uncommon in clinical practice due to the lack of agreement on their efficacy and optimal dosage.

Materials and Methods

This is a single-center, retrospective observational study. Data were collected after obtaining informed consent from all patients and were handled confidentially to ensure anonymity. A total of 80 patients undergoing lower abdominal surgery were enrolled and equally divided into four homogeneous groups, each consisting of 20 patients:

Group A: Levobupivacaine 0.5% 12.5 mg + Fentanyl 10 mcg;

Group A: Levobupivacaine 0.5% 12.5 mg + Fentanyl 10 mcg;

Group B: Levobupivacaine 0.5% 12.5 mg + Morphine 1 mcg/kg;

Group B: Levobupivacaine 0.5% 12.5 mg + Morphine 1 mcg/kg;

Group C: Levobupivacaine 0.5% 12.5 mg + Clonidine 15 mcg;

Group C: Levobupivacaine 0.5% 12.5 mg + Clonidine 15 mcg;

Group D: Levobupivacaine 12.5 mg.

Group D: Levobupivacaine 12.5 mg.

The primary endpoint was the duration of motor block, defined as the time from spinal injection to complete recovery of motor function (TRM). Secondary endpoints included onset of sensory and motor block, incidence of complications, correlations between anthropometric parameters and hemodynamic instability and their influence on block duration.

Results

The study population had a mean age of 61 ± 16 years, mean BMI of 27.43 ± 5.6 and mean preoperative haemoglobin (Hb) of 12.58 ± 1.68 g/dL. Arterial hypertension was present in 53.8% of patients and was significantly less frequent in group C compared to the other groups (p=0.020), as the use of antihypertensive therapy (p=0.008). The mean TRM was 242 ± 98 minutes. A statistically significant difference was observed among groups: group C showed a significantly prolonged motor block duration compared to all other groups (p=0.001). At the end of surgery, only 7.5% of patients had fully or partially recovered motor function (Bromage score 0 - 1), increasing to 30% at 1 hour postoperatively. No significant differences were observed in sensory and motor onset among groups (p=0.280). Overall, 32.5% of patients experienced complications. In Group C, 50% developed hypotension requiring vasopressor support; however, 41.3% of the total cohort required vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure >65 mmHg, without significant differences among groups. Advanced age, lower preoperative Hb levels, and higher BMI were significantly associated with hemodynamic instability (p=0.002) (Table 1).

A significant negative correlation was found between age and TRM (p=0.011; Y=346.38–1.697x), particularly in Group A (p=0.032) (Figure 1).

Conclusions

Intrathecal clonidine significantly prolongs motor block duration but is associated with a higher incidence of hemodynamic instability. Intrathecal opioids, although not affecting block duration, demonstrate a more favourable safety profile. These findings highlight the importance of a tailored approach in selecting intrathecal adjuvants, balancing efficacy and safety to optimize anesthetic management.

The study is currently under review by the local Ethics Committee.

A45 Comparative study of selective spinal anesthesia vs. combined peripheral nerve blocks for trimalleolar fracture surgery: the impact of peritibial fascia block on postoperative analgesia

S. Savino, F. Giordano, C. D’errico, R. Miccio, A. Imparato, C. Leone

New Hospital of the Amalfi Coast – ASL Napoli 3 Sud, Sorrento, Italy

Correspondence: S. Savino

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A45

Background

Trimalleolar fractures represent one of the most complex ankle injuries, requiring stable internal fixation and rigorous postoperative pain management. Traditionally, spinal anesthesia (SA) has been the gold standard due to its rapid onset and profound motor block. However, the rise of regional anesthesia has introduced peripheral nerve blocks (PNBs) as a viable alternative to prolong analgesia and reduce opioid consumption. This study compares the analgesic efficacy of selective spinal anesthesia using hyperbaric bupivacaine (Marcaine) against a combined femoral, sciatic, and adductor canal block, with both groups receiving a supplemental peritibial fascia block.

Methods

A prospective comparative study was conducted on 10 patients (n=10) scheduled for open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of trimalleolar fractures. Patients were randomized into two equal groups (n=5). Group A received selective spinal anesthesia with 5–7.5 mg of hyperbaric Marcaine 0.5%. Group B received a combined ultrasound-guided block consisting of the femoral nerve, sciatic nerve (popliteal approach), and the adductor canal. Crucially, all 10 patients in both groups received a supplemental peritibial fascia block to target the subcutaneous innervation often missed by major trunk blocks. Primary outcomes included the duration of effective analgesia (time to first rescue medication) and postoperative Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores.

Results

The data revealed a statistically significant difference in the duration of postoperative analgesia between the two cohorts. Group A (Spinal) experienced a rapid onset of anesthesia but reported a return of pain sensation significantly earlier than Group B, with a mean analgesia duration of 4.5 ± 1.2 hours. In contrast, Group B (Combined PNBs) showed a prolonged analgesic window, averaging 18.4 ± 3.6 hours.

The integration of the peritibial fascia block proved to be the most critical variable. In previous clinical observations, patients often reported incisional or tourniquet-like pain despite successful nerve blocks. In this study, the peritibial block effectively neutralized the superficial pain signals from the medial and lateral malleolar skin incisions. Patients in Group B, supported by this fascia block, required 60% less opioid-based rescue analgesia in the first 24 hours compared to Group A. Furthermore, Group B demonstrated earlier mobilization and higher satisfaction scores due to the absence of the rebound pain typically seen when spinal anesthesia wears off.

Discussion

While selective spinal anesthesia remains a reliable technique for the surgical phase, its analgesic profile is limited by the pharmacological half-life of the intrathecal agent. The transition from dense surgical anesthesia to the postoperative period is often abrupt. Conversely, the combined femoral, sciatic, and adductor canal blocks provide targeted, long-lasting desensitization of the deep structures.

The addition of the peritibial fascia block addresses the missing link in ankle anesthesia. By anesthetizing the terminal cutaneous branches that bridge the gaps between the major nerve territories, the peritibial block ensures a seamless analgesic cover. This study demonstrates that for complex trimalleolar repairs, a regional approach—specifically when bolstered by peritibial infiltration—offers superior pain control compared to selective spinal anesthesia alone.

Conclusion

In patients undergoing trimalleolar fracture surgery, the combination of femoral, sciatic, and adductor canal blocks, supplemented by a peritibial fascia block, significantly increases the duration of postoperative analgesia. This multimodal regional approach facilitates a smoother recovery, reduces the need for systemic opioids, and provides a superior analgesic profile compared to selective spinal anesthesia with hyperbaric Marcaine.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A46 Video-assisted thoracic surgery in a high risk patient under light sedation and a combination of fascial plane blocks: a case report

M. Cuomo, F. De Masi, M. Martone, P. Manganiello, R. Annunziata, M. Mariani, P. Rinaldi, F. Schettino, S. Cotena, R. Villani

A.O.R.N. A. Cardarelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: M. Martone

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A46

Background

Video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS) is a minimally invasive surgical technique. It generally requires general anesthesia, endotracheal intubation and one lung ventilation. However some patients with respiratory and cardiovascular comorbidities cannot tolerate general anesthesia with one-lung ventilation, resulting in failure of surgical treatment [1]. Non-intubated VATS combines the advantages of a non-intubated strategy with the benefits of a minimally invasive approach [2]. Ultrasound-guided fascial plane blocks provide safer alternative to more invasive approaches such as neuraxial and paravertebral blocks [3,4]. It has been demonstrated that the combination of two facial plane blocks improve analgesic coverage by targeting both true anatomical information and anatomical variations [4,5]. Anyway the evidence on whether it can provide surgical anesthesia is not yet sufficient [4]. Here we report the case of an urgent VATS in a high risk patient with an iatrogenic hemothorax, performed with sedation and the combination of Erector Spinae Plane (ESP) block and Serratus Anterior Plane (SAP) block.

Case report

A 64-year old woman, was transferred to our emergency operative room from the medicine ward, for a right iatrogenic retained haemothorax, previously treated with right intercostal artery embolization. The patient had been admitted to our hospital for hypercapnic respiratory failure, treated with high flow nasal cannula, and then, with non invasive ventilation (NIV). She suffered from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and chronic ischemic heart disease. At the arrival to the operative room, the patient was awake and oriented, she spontaneously breathed throw oxygen nasal cannula and she was haemodinamically stable. Because of her clinical conditions and comorbidties, it was collegially decided to perform a non-intubated VATS. The informed consent was obtained. The patient was monitored with an electrocardiogram using five electrodes and pulsoximeter; an invasive arterial pressure line was placed in the left radial artery. Bispectral index (BIS) and Density Spectral Array were used to monitor the depth of sedation. Emogasanalysis showed hypercapnia (67 mmHg), so a NIV with a face mask was started until the thoracoscopy The patient was placed on the left side, a light sedation was obtained by the endovenous administration of ketamine 30 mg, midazolam 1 mg and fentanyl 50 mcg. A multimodal prophylaxis of the postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) was obtained by the adminstration of Dexametasone 4 mg and Ondansetrone 4 mg. An ultrasound-guided Erector spinae Plane (ESP) block at the T5 level and a serratus anterior plane (SAP) block were performed; a 20 ml mixture containing ropivacaine 0,375% and mepivacaine 0,5% was used for each block. An uniportal VATS was performed to identify and control bleeding source and drain the residual haemothorax. Before the surgeon entered the pleural cavity, NIV was stopped and a 60% Venturi Mask was placed. A conservative fluid management was performed.The patient well tolerated the entire procedure without need of additional doses of sedative and/or analgesic. There was no coughing. BIS ranged from 60 to 80 corresponding to a Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale score between −1 and −2. Periferal oxygen saturation (SpO2) remained at 100% throwghout the procedure. Mean arterial pressure remained > 65 mmHg without need of vasopressors addition and she maintened an adequate urine output. No bleeding source was identified, a cleaning of pleural cavity was performed and a chest tube was placed. At the end of the procedure, the patient was repositioned in supine position and the NIV was restarted. RASS ranged between 0 and −1, the numeric rating scale (NRS) was 0, SpO2 was 100%, she was haemodinamically stable. Emogasanalysis showed a pCO2 of 56 mmHg and a pO2 of 180 mmHg with a FiO2 of 50%. The operative time was 45 minutes, the anesthetic time was 90 minutes. The patient was transferred to intensive care unit for monitoring.

Conclusions

The anesthesiological management of patients with multiple pathologies undergoing emergency thoracic surgery is a major challenge. The choice of a multimodal approach, performed with light sedation and the combination of ESP, SAP blockade and advanced cerebral monitoring, in accordance with the literature, minimized the impact on the respiratory, hemodynamic and neurological function of this fragile patient. The maintenance of spontaneous breathing, the reduction of opioid use and perioperative pain management also allowed for a gradual and independent recovery and stable postoperative vital signs.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A47 Tetra-block (ultrasound femoral, lateral femoral-cutaneous, obturator, and sciatic nerve blocks) in a Fahr’s syndrome patient with a medial femur fracture

S. Barbaro, R. Lomaistro, E. Scapini, A. Zagaria, M. Debitonto

Anaesthesia, Resuscitation and Pain Therapy Unit, Barletta, Italy

Correspondence: S. Barbaro

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A47

Background

Fahr’s syndrome is a rare disease of the central nervous system characterized by the presence of bilateral cerebral calcifications associated with a secondary cause [1]. In this case report we deal with the anesthesiological conduct adopted in a patient undergoing medial femur fracture surgery affected by Fahr’s syndrome. Locoregional anesthesia in orthopedic operations on the lower limbs reduces mortality and the occurrence of complications at 30 days [2]. Recent scientific publications do not pose an absolute contraindication to performing this technique in patients with pre-existing central neurological disease, but the best option should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis [3].

Case report

A 55-year-old Fahr’s syndrome patient came to the emergency department with a diagnosis of left femur fracture. Neurological symptoms include muscle rigidity, parkinsonism, and depression. On admission, calcemia was noted at 6.8 mg/dl and magnesemia at 1.1 mg/dl. In order to avoid the use of neuromuscular blocking drugs and avoid airway manipulation, it is decided to perform locoregional anesthesia. Calcemia and magnesemia were correct. Ultrasound-guided blocks of the femoral, lateral femoral-cutaneous, obturator, and sciatic (perpendicular sacral plexus block approach) nerves were performed with success (ecoplex+ 100 mm long 21-gauge 20°, VygonValueLife, Italy; Esaote MyLabX8 L4-15/C1-8, Italy). Levobupivacaine 0.5% was used (16 ml, 5 ml, 5 ml, and 16 ml, respectively). This results in a Bromage scale of 1 and a Hollmen scale of 4. Hemodynamic stability was noted. No anesthesia related complications were observed in the following weeks.

Conclusions

This rare case report demonstrates successful locoregional anesthesia in a patient with Fahr’s syndrome.

Informed written consent was obtained from the patient for the publication of this article.

A48 Peripheral nerve block-based anaesthesia for femoral intramedullary nailing in high-risk patients: a case series

A. Alfieri1,2, P. Bonagura1, L. Baiaino1, E. Sabatella1, V. Donatiello1, R. Punzo1, I. Biancogiglio1, E. Prisco1, V. Maffei1, P. Sansone2, M.C. Pace2, M.B. Pasasvanti2

1Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, A.O.R.N. A. Cardarelli, Naples, Italy; 2Department of Womens and Childrens Health and General and Specialized Surgery, University of Campania, L. Vanvitelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: P. Bonagura

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A48

Background

Femoral intramedullary nailing (IMN) is routinely performed under general anesthesia (GA) or neuraxial anesthesia (NA). However, both techniques may be associated with significant perioperative risks in frail and polymorbid patients, particularly in the presence of advanced cardiopulmonary disease, chronic anticoagulation, severe hemodynamic instability, or elevated risk of postoperative respiratory complications and delirium [1]. Peripheral nerve blocks (PNBs) are widely used for perioperative analgesia in orthopedic surgery, but evidence regarding their use as the sole anesthetic technique for major lower limb trauma procedures remains limited [2].

The present study describes our institutional experience with a multimodal ultrasound-guided PNB strategy as the exclusive anesthetic technique for femoral IMN in high-risk patients considered suboptimal candidates for GA or NA.

Case series

We performed a retrospective observational case series in a high-volume orthopedic trauma center performing approximately 420 femoral IMN procedures annually in patients aged >65 years. Ten consecutive adult patients undergoing femoral IMN between October 2025 and March 2026 were included.

Patients were selected on the basis of elevated anesthetic risk profile, including severe cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, chronic anticoagulant therapy, advanced frailty, or anticipated intolerance to GA-related hemodynamic stress.

All procedures were performed under combined ultrasound-guided femoral, sciatic, obturator, and lateral femoral cutaneous nerve blocks. A standardized anesthetic solution consisting of ropivacaine 0.5% was used in all patients. Sedation consisted of either intermittent midazolam (0.02–0.05 mg/kg) or dexmedetomidine infusion (0.4–0.7 mcg/kg/h), while maintaining spontaneous ventilation throughout the procedure.

Primary outcome was successful completion of surgery without conversion to GA or NA. Secondary outcomes included intraoperative analgesic adequacy, hemodynamic stability, postoperative pain control, opioid consumption, and complications.

Mean patient age was 74 ± 12 years, and 80% of patients were classified as ASA III-IV. Frequent comorbidities included coronary artery disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, atrial fibrillation requiring anticoagulation, and previous cerebrovascular disease.

All procedures were successfully completed without conversion to GA or NA (100% success rate). Mean surgical duration was 72 ± 18 minutes. Intraoperative analgesia was satisfactory in all cases, with median Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) pain score of 0 (IQR 0–1). Hemodynamic stability was preserved throughout surgery, with no episodes of clinically significant instability requiring continuous vasoactive support. No patient required airway management or ventilatory assistance.

Postoperative pain scores remained low during the first 24 hours, with minimal opioid consumption (median morphine equivalent 4 mg/24 h). Early mobilization within 24–48 hours was achieved in 80% of patients. No cases of local anesthetic systemic toxicity, persistent neurological deficits, postoperative delirium, or block-related infection were observed (Table 1).

Conclusions

A multimodal PNB strategy may represent a feasible and effective alternative to GA or NA for femoral IMN in carefully selected high-risk patients. In particular, this approach may be especially valuable in elderly frail patients, subjects with severe respiratory disease, limited cardiovascular reserve, chronic anticoagulation, or elevated risk of postoperative delirium.

Beyond anesthetic feasibility, this technique may contribute to improved perioperative physiological stability by avoiding airway manipulation, minimizing systemic anesthetic exposure, and reducing sympathectomy-related hypotension. Larger comparative studies are warranted to better define the role of PNBs as a primary anesthetic technique in orthopedic trauma surgery.

Consent to publish

All patients provided written informed consent for the anesthetic procedure and for the anonymous use of their clinical and perioperative data for scientific and publication purposes. All data were fully anonymized prior to analysis, in accordance with institutional policies and the Declaration of Helsinki.

A49 When blood pressure misleads: hemodynamic interpretation of pneumoperitoneum in a nonagenarian with severe multivalvular disease

A. Scalvenzi1, V. Donatiello1, L. Baiano1, V. Maffei1, A. Alfieri1, M.R. Pirolo1, M.B. Passavanti2, V. Pota2, M.C. Pace2

1A.O.R.N. Antonio Cardarelli, Naples, Italy; 2University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: A. Scalvenzi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A49

Background

Pneumoperitoneum during laparoscopic surgery induces significant hemodynamic changes, including increased systemic vascular resistance and reduced venous return. In patients with severe valvular disease, arterial pressure alone may not accurately reflect cardiovascular performance, particularly in elderly patients with limited physiological reserve.

Case presentation

A 91-year-old woman underwent laparoscopic nephroureterectomy in lateral decubitus position. Preoperative echocardiography revealed severe multivalvular disease, including severe mitral and aortic regurgitation, moderate aortic stenosis, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary hypertension (estimated PAPs 52 mmHg), with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (55%) and dilation of both atria and right heart chambers. The patient was in atrial fibrillation. Preoperative cardiology assessment classified the patient as at high, non-modifiable perioperative cardiovascular risk.

Following induction of general anesthesia and placement of invasive arterial monitoring, hemodynamic parameters were initially stable. Advanced hemodynamic monitoring was not employed, as atrial fibrillation may limit the reliability of derived dynamic indices.

Immediately after pneumoperitoneum insufflation, a marked hypertensive response was observed. Rather than indicating hemodynamic stability, this was interpreted as a consequence of increased afterload. In this setting, elevated systemic vascular resistance likely increased regurgitant flow across incompetent valves and reduced effective forward cardiac output.

Intraoperative management was guided by this physiological interpretation, focusing on optimizing anesthetic depth, maintaining low intra-abdominal pressure (10–12 mmHg), and controlling ventilation with a lung-protective strategy (PEEP 3 cmH20) to maintain end-tidal CO2 within 35–40 mmHg. Progressive hemodynamic stabilization was achieved, with systolic arterial pressure maintained around 130 mmHg and adequate heart rate control.

The postoperative course was uneventful from a cardiovascular standpoint. A transient reduction in urine output was observed during the first 48 hours, followed by progressive recovery and subsequent discharge.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case and any accompanying data.

Discussion and conclusions

This case highlights the potential dissociation between arterial pressure and effective cardiovascular performance during pneumoperitoneum. In patients with severe valvular disease, increased afterload may worsen regurgitant flow and impair forward circulation despite apparently acceptable blood pressure values. Additionally, increased pulmonary vascular resistance may further challenge right ventricular function in the presence of pulmonary hypertension.

In this context, the anesthetic approach should be guided by physiological reasoning rather than isolated hemodynamic values. Pneumoperitoneum represents a critical phase in elderly patients with advanced cardiac disease, in which hypertension should not be interpreted as a marker of stability.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A50 From static scores to dynamic signals redefining frailty as a real time system in perioperative medicine

V. Bellini, M. Madeo, S. Fedele, M. Panizzi, E.G. Bignami

Department of Medicine and Surgery, Division of Anesthesiology, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, University of Parma, Italy

Correspondence: E.G. Bignami

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A50

Background

Frailty is commonly described as a static condition, yet in clinical reality it behaves as an evolving and often elusive form of vulnerability. It does not simply exist, it unfolds. In the perioperative setting, where physiological balance is continuously challenged, this hidden instability becomes visible, exposing the limitations of conventional risk stratification [1,2].

Materials and methods

We conducted a narrative interdisciplinary review integrating evidence from anesthesiology, perioperative medicine, geriatrics, and data science. Literature was retrieved from PubMed MEDLINE and complementary sources between 2018 and 2026, focusing on frailty, artificial intelligence, continuous monitoring, wearable technologies, and point of care ultrasound. Approximately ninety studies were synthesized to construct a systems oriented conceptual framework.

Results

Frailty emerges as a dynamic expression of systemic instability, reflecting a progressive loss of coordination across interconnected physiological systems [3]. Static scores provide a snapshot, whereas a dynamic approach reveals trajectories, variability, and early signals of decompensation. Bedside tools such as point of care ultrasound allow direct and repeated visualization of physiological reserve, while continuous monitoring and wearable technologies extend observation across time, capturing subtle fluctuations that precede clinical deterioration [4,5]. Artificial intelligence acts as an integrative layer, transforming heterogeneous data into coherent patterns that support adaptive clinical reasoning [6]. Within this perspective, frailty is no longer a label to assign, but a signal to interpret, a trajectory that can be followed, anticipated, and potentially modified. This conceptual shift is summarized in a dynamic systems framework integrating clinical assessment, bedside evaluation, continuous monitoring, and artificial intelligence (Figure 1). This transformation, however, introduces parallel challenges, including data bias, limited generalizability, lack of transparency, and ethical implications that require careful governance [7].

Conclusions

Frailty should be understood as a dynamic and continuously evolving process rather than a fixed condition. The integration of clinical assessment, bedside evaluation, continuous monitoring, and artificial intelligence enables a shift toward a more attentive and responsive form of perioperative care. This approach does not merely improve prediction, it redefines clinical reasoning, moving from static categorization to real time interpretation. The future of perioperative medicine lies in the ability to recognize these dynamic patterns and translate them into timely, individualized, and meaningful clinical action.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A51 Multimodal opioid-free thoracic segmental spinal anesthesia for open gastrectomy in a high-risk patient: a case report

A. Fruncillo, P. Russo, A. Calabrese, C. Grandis, C. Chiumiento, F. Chiumiento

Complex Operative Unit (UOC) of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Emergency Department (DEA) Battipaglia–Eboli–Roccadaspide, Eboli, Italy

Correspondence: A. Fruncillo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A51

Body

Open gastrectomy for gastric cancer is traditionally performed under general anesthesia with systemic opioids and mechanical ventilation. However, in high-risk patients, this approach may increase postoperative pulmonary complications, perioperative hemodynamic instability, opioid consumption, and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols currently support multimodal opioid-sparing strategies aimed at reducing surgical stress response and accelerating postoperative recovery [1].

Thoracic segmental spinal anesthesia combined with erector spinae plane block (ESPB) may provide effective visceral and somatic analgesia while preserving spontaneous ventilation and cardiovascular stability [2,3]. Moreover, dexmedetomidine-based opioid-free anesthesia has shown benefits in reducing opioid requirements and improving postoperative recovery [5].

Case report

A 68-year-old woman (BMI 27 kg/m², ASA III) with antral gastric adenocarcinoma (T2N1M0) underwent open subtotal gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy. Her medical history included arterial hypertension, chronic ischemic heart disease (NSTEMI 4 years earlier, left ventricular ejection fraction 55%), severe PONV, and COPD GOLD III associated with chronic hypercapnia (baseline PaCO2 >50 mmHg). Preoperative spirometry demonstrated FEV1 <50% predicted and FEV1/FVC ratio <0.6.

Considering the elevated respiratory and cardiovascular risk, avoidance of general anesthesia and tracheal intubation was planned to preserve spontaneous ventilation and minimize perioperative sympathetic stress. Written informed consent was obtained for thoracic spinal anesthesia and bilateral ESPB, including possible conversion to general anesthesia if required.

Standard monitoring included ECG, pulse oximetry, invasive arterial pressure monitoring, and nasal capnography. Sedation was maintained using dexmedetomidine infusion at 0.4 mcg/kg/h without loading dose.

Thoracic segmental spinal anesthesia was performed at T7–T8 using a 25G Whitacre needle. Intrathecal administration included levobupivacaine 0.5% 10 mg and dexmedetomidine 10 mcg. Intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg was administered after spinal injection. A complete sensory block from T4 to L1 was achieved.

Bilateral ultrasound-guided ESPB was subsequently performed at T6 with levobupivacaine 0.25% 20 mL per side to prolong postoperative parietal analgesia after regression of neuraxial blockade.

Continuous norepinephrine infusion (0.02–0.05 mcg/kg/min) was titrated to maintain mean arterial pressure >65 mmHg throughout surgery [4]. Additional systemic analgesia included intravenous paracetamol and ketorolac without intraoperative opioid administration.

Surgery duration was 2 hours and 15 minutes without conversion to general anesthesia. Spontaneous ventilation was preserved throughout the procedure, with oxygen saturation consistently >93%. Hemodynamic stability was maintained with mean arterial pressure between 65 and 75 mmHg and heart rate between 58 and 70 bpm, without ischemic ECG changes or significant vasopressor boluses.

Postoperative pain control was satisfactory, with Visual Analog Scale scores of 1/10 at rest and 3/10 during coughing. No postoperative nausea or vomiting occurred. Only one rescue dose of morphine (2 mg IV) was required within the first 20 postoperative hours. Bowel canalization occurred on postoperative day 1, oral liquid diet was initiated on postoperative day 2, and discharge occurred on postoperative day 6 without respiratory, neurological, or cardiovascular complications.

Conclusion

Thoracic segmental spinal anesthesia combined with bilateral ESPB, dexmedetomidine sedation, and low-dose norepinephrine infusion may represent a feasible opioid-free alternative to general anesthesia for selected high-risk patients undergoing open gastrectomy. This multimodal ERAS-oriented strategy provided effective analgesia, preserved spontaneous ventilation, ensured hemodynamic stability, minimized postoperative opioid requirements and PONV, and facilitated postoperative recovery. Further prospective studies are required to confirm reproducibility and safety in larger populations.

Consent to publish

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and anesthetic management details.

A52 Opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) vs. opioid-based anesthesia (OBA) in the elderly patient: analysis of the hemodynamic stability of general anesthesia, pain control, and postoperative recovery

E. Fiocco, L. Rota, A. Di Sauro, A. Beltoja, G. Russo

ASST Lodi, Italy

Correspondence: E. Fiocco

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A52

Background

The progressive aging of the population will increasingly lead to the presence of elderly patients in hospital facilities. When undergoing surgery, particularly major surgery, these patients present a high risk of perioperative hemodynamic instability, postoperative complications, delirium, and prolonged length of stay. Opioid-free anesthesia (OFA), viewed from a different perspective, can be proposed as a potentially useful strategy to reduce surgical stress and hemodynamic variability, while simultaneously limiting opioid exposure. The aim of this study is to compare the use of an OFA approach versus opioid-based anesthesia (OBA) during general anesthesia in frail elderly patients, with hemodynamic stability as the primary outcome, and pain control, delirium, return of bowel function, and postoperative recovery as secondary outcomes.

Materials and Methods

We recruited patients aged 75 years and over, undergoing surgery across all specialties excluding Neurosurgery and Cardiac Surgery. Informed consent was collected for all patients. Patients were divided into two groups based on the anaesthetic technique performed: OBA (opioid-based anesthesia) and OFA (opioid-free anesthesia).

For each patient, baseline characteristics (comorbidities, ASA score, Clinical Frailty Scale) and peri-induction hemodynamic parameters (pre- and postinduction systolic blood pressure [SBP] up to 30 minutes, episodes of prolonged hypotension, episodes of severe hypertension, use of vasopressors, and fluid rescue) were collected. A composite indicator of relative blood pressure instability was defined (DropSBP>20%: a >20% reduction in post-induction SBP). Postoperative outcomes included: pain (NRS at 24 and 48 hours, use of rescue analgesia with both NSAIDs and opioids), delirium (clinically assessed by the presence/absence of agitation), time to return of bowel function, and length of hospital stay. Analyses were performed using the Mann-Whitney test, Fisher’s Exact/Chi-square test, and logistic regression for DropSBP>20%.

Results

A total of 64 patients were included (OBA n=39, OFA n=25), with comparable baseline characteristics and degrees of frailty between the groups. Relative hemodynamic instability was significantly more frequent in the OBA group (Figure 1): DropSBP>20% affected the vast majority of OBA patients (97%) compared to a minority of OFA patients (36%) (p<0.001), and multivariate analysis confirmed that belonging to the OFA group was an independent factor associated with a lower probability of DropSBP>20%. Episodes of prolonged hypotension, severe hypertension, and the use of vasopressors/fluid rescue were also more frequent in the OBA group. Acute postoperative pain control showed a better trend in the OFA group, with lower mean NRS scores at 24 hours and, using an NRS<4 cutoff, a higher proportion of patients compared to the OBA group (p<0.001 at 24 hours; p was not significant at 48 hours as pain control was comparable between the two groups). The incidence of delirium was higher in the OBA group but did not reach statistical significance due to the small sample size. The median time to complete return of bowel function was shorter in the OFA group (3 days) compared to the OBA group (4 days), and a delay was correlated with a prolonged length of stay.

Conclusions

In a population of frail elderly patients undergoing surgery, the OFA approach is associated with greater peri-induction hemodynamic stability, better acute postoperative pain control in the first 24 hours, and a comparable safety profile compared to conventional opioid-based general anesthesia. Despite the limitations due to sample size, the results support the use of OFA protocols in the surgical pathway of frail elderly patients. This preliminary analysis allowed us to establish some concepts regarding what we want to investigate, for which patients to apply OFA, and in which surgical settings to use it. The analysis will continue with a larger-scale study, utilizing more advanced monitoring and also examining organ-specific and long-term outcomes.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A53 Combined regional anaesthesia for femoral fracture surgery in a patient with sickle cell disease and achondroplasia

G. Aprile1, G. Bagnato2, R. Crescenti2, M. Giardina3, R. De Luca3, G. Genoese3, P. Calì3, A.T. Mazzeo3, I. Russo-Menna4, V.F. Tripodi3

1School of Anaesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Management Alma Mater Studiorum, University of Bologna, Italy; 2School of Anaesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Management, University of Messina, Italy; 3Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Human Pathology Department, University of Messina, Italy; 4Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) School of Medicine, Richmond, USA

Correspondence: G. Aprile

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A53

Background

Sickle cell disease (SCD) and achondroplasia (ACH) are rare medical conditions that pose substantial challenges in perioperative anaesthetic management. Their coexistence compounds the risk of vaso-occlusive crises (VOC) and acute chest syndrome (ACS), precipitated by hypoxia, hypothermia, acidosis, hypovolemia and uncontrolled pain. Tailored anaesthetic strategies are therefore essential to minimize physiological stress, optimize analgesia and maintain adequate oxygen delivery [1,2]. In patients with SCD undergoing orthopaedic surgery, perioperative complication rates range between 11.5% and 67%, depending on outcome definitions and institutional settings [1,3]. Current recommendations suggest preoperative transfusion with a target of Hb >10 g/dL and reduction of HbS below 30%, particularly in high-risk patients [4,5]. Regional anaesthesia (RA) is associated with reduced opioid requirements and improved respiratory function in SCD [4,5]. ACH poses additional challenges for general anaesthesia (GA), which may be complicated by hypoxia due to difficult airway anatomy secondary to midface hypoplasia, macroglossia and limited cervical mobility, with risk of spinal cord injury during airway manipulation [6,7]. Neuraxial anaesthesia may also be challenging because of spinal canal stenosis, reduced cerebrospinal fluid volume and unpredictable cephalad spread of local anaesthetic, leading to hypotension [6]. The coexistence of both conditions, however rare, creates a clinical dilemma.

Case report

A 50-year-old Caucasian male patient, ASA III, height 150 cm, weight 54 kg, BMI 24 kg/m², with known SCD and ACH, was admitted for elective open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a right mid-diaphyseal femoral shaft fracture following trauma. His past medical history included homozygous SCD treated with periodic erythrocyte exchange transfusions, hypertension, HCV infection previously treated, bilateral hip replacement and transurethral prostatectomy, all previously performed under Spinal Anaesthesia (SA) without complications. Airway evaluation showed: Mallampati class IV, limited mouth opening, reduced neck extension and prominent mandible. Lumbar examination revealed marked lordosis. Preoperative tests revealed Hb 9.9 g/dL, HbS 44.7%, WBC 18,900/mm³, Platelets 238,000/mm³, INR 1.20, aPTT 29.4, Fibrinogen 270 mg/dL and normal liver function tests. Manual erythrocyte exchange (350 mL phlebotomy + 1 leukoreduced PRBC) reduced HbS to 31.8%. Standard ASA monitoring was applied; venous access was already secured by an indwelling midline catheter. After fluid preload and administration of 1 mg midazolam IV, the patient was positioned in the right lateral decubitus with the operative side down, to limit cephalad spread. SA was performed at L3–L4 with a 25G Sprotte needle, injecting 1.5 mL of hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% and 10 µg of fentanyl slowly intrathecally. This low-dose regimen was chosen to mitigate the risk of excessive cephalad spread. The sensory block level was assessed and confirmed adequate for the surgery. To reduce postoperative pain, ultrasound-guided femoral and transgluteal sciatic nerve blocks were performed using 20 mL ropivacaine 0.75%, 5 mL mepivacaine 2% and 5 mL normal saline, all preservative-free. Sedation was achieved with midazolam 1 mg and fentanyl 40 µg IV, with spontaneous breathing and oxigen 2 L/min via nasal cannula. Intraoperative normothermia was maintained with a forced-air warming system. IV fluids administration consisted of 750 mL warm crystalloids and one unit of PRBC to optimize oxygen delivery and maintain Hb above 10 g/dL. The ORIF with plate fixation was completed in 100 min, without complications and minimal blood loss <150 mL. The postoperative course was uneventful; patient remained stable throughout the intensive care unit (ICU) observation and postoperative pain was absent, with a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) score of 0. On postoperative day 2, a further manual exchange (350 mL phlebotomy and 1 leukoreduced PRBC) reduced HbS to 28.7%. Written informed consent for publication was obtained from the patient.

Conclusion

This case demonstrates the feasibility of a purely locoregional and multimodal anaesthetic approach in a patient with both SCD and ACH undergoing orthopaedic surgery. Low-dose hyperbaric SA, peripheral nerve blocks and light sedation allowed avoidance of GA. This anaesthetic strategy may represent a useful option for selected orthopaedic procedures in patients with SCD and ACH; RA should be considered a first-line approach in similar cases. Beyond the individual case, perioperative care of haemoglobinopathy patients calls for institutional protocols covering risk stratification, transfusion strategy, prevention and management of VOC and ACS, criteria for ICU admission and acute and chronic pain pathways.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A54 Intraoperative regional cerebral oxygen saturation and its association with postoperative outcomes: a secondary analysis of the brain-promise randomized controlled trial

E. Antonioli1, A. Zucchini2, M. Cavallo1, A. Angelucci2, A. Aliverti2, M. Greco1, M. Cecconi1

1IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Milano, Italy; 2Politecnico di Milano, Italy

Correspondence: E. Antonioli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A54

Background

Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PNDs) represent a major source of morbidity in elderly and frail patients undergoing major non-cardiac surgery, being associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospitalisation, and long-term functional decline. Still, their intraoperative determinants remain incompletely characterized.

Cerebral hypoperfusion, detectable via near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS)-derived regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rSO2), is likely to be a significant contributor to postoperative cognitive decline. However, whether targeting intraoperative rSO2 can reduce postoperative cognitive decline remains to be established.

We conducted a secondary analysis of the BRAIN-PROMISE randomized controlled trial to evaluate whether NIRS-tracing derived desaturation features are associated with neurocognitive test performance in the early postoperative period.

Materials and methods

We analysed NIRS tracings from 183 patients enrolled in the BRAIN-PROMISE (BRAIN-targeted goal-directed therapy in high-risk Patients undergoing Major electIve SurgEry), a prospective single-centre RCT including high-risk patients undergoing major surgery under general anaesthesia (age above 65 years or frailty, ASA above II, invasive arterial monitoring planned). All patients provided written informed consent prior to enrolment. The trial was registered on clinicaltrials.gov in February 2020, with the trial identification number NCT04266574.

Regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rSO2) was continuously monitored using bilateral frontal NIRS sensors. Signals underwent preprocessing to correct artefacts, dropouts, and outliers, and bilateral values were aggregated using a worst-case strategy. Cerebral desaturation was defined as either a >10% decrease from baseline or an absolute rSO2 <60%.

Five NIRS-derived features were extracted: number of desaturation events, total desaturation time, desaturation AUC, nadir, and recovery time.

Neurocognitive performance was assessed preoperatively and at POD1 and POD3 using MMSE, TMT-A/B, RAVLT, and CAM-ICU.

Associations between intraoperative rSO2 burden and postoperative cognitive changes were evaluated using Spearman correlation analyses on the full cohort.

Results

Three of the intraoperative NIRS-derived features demonstrated clinically coherent associations with early postoperative neurocognitive performance. A higher absolute number of desaturation events was significantly correlated with greater MMSE decline at POD 3 (Spearman rho = +0.229, p = 0.010), indicating that rSO2 instability is associated with worse early global cognitive performance.

In addition, prolonged total time in desaturation and higher desaturation AUC were both significantly associated with TMT-B worsening at POD 3 (rho = +0.256, p = 0.015 and rho = +0.244, p = 0.020, respectively), suggesting that cumulative cerebral hypoperfusion, rather than the depth of any single desaturation episode, may represent the primary driver of postoperative executive dysfunction.

Nadir and recovery time did not reach statistical significance for any neurocognitive endpoint.

Conclusions

This secondary analysis of the BRAIN-PROMISE trial provides preliminary evidence that quantitative intraoperative rSO2 features estimating the burden of cerebral desaturation, particularly desaturation AUC, total time in desaturation, and absolute number of desaturation events, correlate with early postoperative neurocognitive decline, particularly in domains of global cognition (MMSE) and executive function (TMT-B).

These findings add to the limited but growing body of literature exploring the potential role of cerebral oximetry within multimodal perioperative monitoring strategies for high-risk surgical patients.

Further studies should investigate whether targeting intraoperative rSO2 through NIRS-guided hemodynamic optimization protocols can reduce the incidence of postoperative cognitive complications.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A55 End of life and euthanasia

N. Tiberii1, M.L. Simonetti2

1ASL Teramo, Italy; 2AST Ascoli Piceno, Italy

Correspondence: N. Tiberii

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A55

Background

In many European and non-European countries, euthanasia and/or assisted suicide practices are legal, while in Italy they constitute a crime and fall under the cases punished by articles 579 or 580 of the Penal Code. The suspension of treatment, on the other hand, is an inviolable right pursuant to art. 32 of the Constitution and Law 219/2017. With ruling 242/2019 of the Constitutional Court, in Italy it is possible to request medically assisted suicide at the express, voluntary, and repeated request of a patient who suffers intense physical and mental pain as a result of an irreversible disease that they themselves experience as unacceptable. The law also provides the possibility to express one’s wishes regarding medical treatments, as well as consent or refusal for diagnostic tests and therapeutic choices.

Materials and Methods

The preliminary study was developed by conducting a literature search consulting databases such as PubMed and Cochrane to design the research questions. A validated anonymous questionnaire was administered, after obtaining informed consent, to two types of sample representative of the population: a population that at the time of the study was not affected by diseases and a population belonging to associations of degenerative diseases; in both samples there was the possibility of self-defining as affected or not affected by a disease. The tool used for data collection consists of a sociodemographic section and a section containing 16 items related to personal choices on the topic addressed. The interviews were conducted in various Departments of the Territorial Health Authority of AP with prior authorization from the Health Directorate. Patient associations affected by oncological or rare diseases were instead sent via social platforms. Data collection was carried out from January to May 2023.

Results

A total of N= 344 questionnaires were analyzed. From the scientific literature, many studies have shown that the number of assisted suicide requests is continuously increasing due to the progressive aging of the population and the growing number of terminal illnesses. The results show that religion influences end-of-life choices; in particular, there is a strong disagreement among believers on topics such as assisted suicide or euthanasia, even if these were the only way to alleviate suffering, as religious people strongly support the preservation of life and therefore declare themselves against choices of end-of-life acceleration, compared to non-believers (p< 0.001) or agnostics. Subjects affected by a pathology are more favorable to forms of euthanasia as they do not find palliative care sufficient (p < 0.005), and their point of view has changed following their own health condition. A significant percentage of the sick sample has already prepared a living will, while the majority of healthy individuals declared that they were not even aware of it. The survey is considered appropriate for identifying some factors: being favorable to euthanasia is significantly associated with the following variables: non-religious orientation (p < 0.001), condition of disability or illness (p < 0.0023), having suffered intense pain during a phase of their life (p < 0.005).

Conclusion

One’s health condition and social status influence end-of-life issues; in particular, it is believed that the survey is appropriate for identifying certain factors: being in favor of euthanasia is significantly associated with the variables of non-religious orientation, widowed marital status, disability condition, and having experienced intense pain during a phase of one’s life. Nationality, high education level, and having provided care to a terminally ill family member, instead, were not found to be correlated. Observing the results, it is noted that a condition of disability or illness plays a fundamental role in decisions about end-of-life practices. The impact is significantly higher in the sample affected by illnesses regarding statements on decisions of non-treatment or euthanasia, as palliative care is found insufficient, and their point of view has changed following their own illness. A significant percentage of the sick sample has already made a living will for advance treatment directives, while the majority of the healthy sample stated that they were not even aware of it. In conclusion, decision-making is a multifactorial task dependent on religion, knowledge, relationships, and the subjective approach to end-of-life issues. It’s appropriate to evaluate the different situations and implement informational and specific interventions that allow people to make advanced and informed decisions about end-of-life care.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.
