A56 Impact of predictive hemodynamic strategy on carotid stump pressure and cerebral oxygenation: a randomised controlled trial

T. Torce, A. Russo, G. Fasano, F. Sessa, F. Del Tedesco, S.S. Melcore, F. Bruno, Y. tshomba, C. Vincenzoni, P. Aceto

A. Gemelli IRCCS University Hospital Foundation, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: T. Torce

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A56

Background

Maintaining stable systemic hemodynamics is crucial during carotid endarterectomy (CEA) to ensure adequate cerebral blood flow. Intraoperative hypotension frequently leads to decreased carotid stump pressure, increasing the risk of cerebral ischemia and the need for shunting. While conventional management is often reactive, the machine-learning-based Hypotension Prediction Index (HPI) offers a proactive approach by forecasting hypotensive events before they occur.

Objectives

To evaluate whether an HPI-guided hemodynamic strategy can better maintain cerebral perfusion, quantified by carotid stump pressure and regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rSO2), compared to standard reactive care.

Design and methods

Following the acquisition of written informed consent, 120 patients undergoing elective CEA were enrolled in this randomized controlled trial (NCT06926010). Participants were allocated 1:1 to either HPI-guided management (n=60) or a standard care control group (n=60). The intervention group received proactive hemodynamic optimization based on HPI alerts, while the control group received conventional reactive treatment. The primary endpoint was carotid stump pressure measured immediately after cross-clamping. Secondary endpoints included the time-weighted average (TWA) of hypotension (MAP <65 mmHg) and rSO2 levels via near-infrared spectroscopy.

Results

The HPI-guided approach significantly improved cerebral perfusion, resulting in higher mean carotid stump pressure (65.4 +/- 15.9 vs. 47.3 +/- 10.0 mmHg; p < 0.001) and a significantly lower incidence of its critical values (SP<50 mmHg) compared to controls (8.3% vs. 50%; p < 0.001). Patients in the HPI cohort experienced significantly less hypotension, evidenced by a lower TWA (0.11 +/- 0.11 vs. 0.26 +/- 0.16; p < 0.001) and fewer hypotensive episodes. This hemodynamic stability led to improved cerebral oxygenation during clamping (rSO2: 68.0 +/- 4.9 vs. 58.1 +/- 6.0; p < 0.001).

Conclusions

Integrating machine-learning-driven hypotension prediction into clinical practice significantly enhances cerebral perfusion during carotid surgery. By maintaining higher stump pressures and stabilizing cerebral oxygenation, this proactive strategy may positively impact surgical decision-making and reduce the need for intraoperative shunts.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A57 Performance of ARISCAT and LAS VEGAS scores for predicting postoperative pulmonary complications in thoracic surgery with one-lung ventilation: a prospective observational study

A. Prato Schmidt, C. T. Bevilacqua Filho, C. F. Andrade

Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre (HCPA), Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Porto Alegre, Brasil

Correspondence: A. Prato Schmidt

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A57

Background and Objectives

Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPC) are common after non-cardiac thoracic surgery with one-lung ventilation (OLV) and are associated with increased morbidity, prolonged hospital stay, and higher costs. Although the ARISCAT and LAS VEGAS risk scores are widely used in general surgery, their performance in this specific high-risk population remains poorly validated. This study aimed to evaluate the predictive accuracy of these scores for PPC and to identify additional independent risk factors in patients undergoing thoracic surgery with OLV.

Methods

This prospective observational study consecutively enrolled 115 adult patients undergoing elective or urgent non-cardiac thoracic surgery with OLV at two public teaching hospitals in southern Brazil (July 2023–September 2024). Preoperative ARISCAT and LAS VEGAS scores were calculated. The primary outcome was the incidence of in-hospital PPC within 30 days (composite endpoint including pulmonary infection, atelectasis, respiratory failure, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, aspiration pneumonitis, and pulmonary embolism). Multivariable logistic regression and ROC curve analysis with DeLong test were performed. Written informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.

Results

PPC occurred in 37.4% of patients. LAS VEGAS showed the best individual discrimination (AUC 0.648, p=0.005), followed by ARISCAT (AUC 0.598, p=0.067). Independent predictors identified by multivariable analysis were preoperative hemoglobin (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.62–0.95, p=0.013) and intraoperative noradrenaline use (OR 5.93, 95% CI 2.36–15.95, p<0.001). A combined model incorporating these two variables achieved an AUC of 0.772, significantly superior to the individual scores (DeLong test p<0.05), with 72% accuracy, 70% sensitivity, and 84% negative predictive value.

Conclusions

The ARISCAT and LAS VEGAS scores demonstrated only moderate predictive performance for PPC in thoracic surgery with OLV. A simple model based on preoperative hemoglobin and intraoperative noradrenaline use significantly improved risk stratification. These findings support targeted perioperative interventions (anemia correction and hemodynamic optimization) and highlight the need for thoracic-specific predictive tools in patients receiving one-lung ventilation.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A58 Right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling improvement with landiolol infusion in cardiogenic shock patients with atrial fibrillation

M. Pasetto1, G. Paissan1,2, M. Fasan1, L. Peluso1,2, A. Russo1, L. Gottin1,2

1Cardiothoracic and Vascular Intensive Care Unit, Hospital and University Trust of Verona, Italy; 2Department of Surgery, Dentistry, Gynecology and Paediatrics, University of Verona, Italy

Correspondence: M. Pasetto

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A58

Background

Atrial tachyarrhythmias frequently coexist with heart failure (HF) progression and may precipitate cardiogenic shock (CS). Rate and rhythm control strategies for atrial fibrillation (AF) in unstable patients are aimed at improving the energetic and mechanical interaction of the circulation, namely ventricular–arterial coupling (VAC). The ultra–short-acting beta1-selective adrenergic blocker landiolol is recommended by guidelines for the management of AF in unstable patients and has demonstrated improvement in hemodynamic variables and clinical outcomes in patients with HF or CS with tachyarrhythmias.

Aim

Evaluate the effect of landiolol infusion on RV VAC.

Methods

Prospective observational single-center cohort study, including adult patients admitted in our Center’s Cardiothoracic and Vascular Intensive Care Unit, since March 2025, presenting with acute HF or CS and with tachyarrhythmias. Hemodynamic profile evaluation before (T0), at 1 hour (T1) and 6 hours (T2) after landiolol infusion start, using minimally invasive pulse-contour monitoring and echocardiography. The most validated non-invasive measure of right VAC is the ratio of tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) to pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PAPs), with a validated prognostic thresold of 0,36 mm/mmHg. Conscious patients provided an informed consent for anonimized data acquisition.

Results

In this ongoing study we enrolled 9 patients treated with landiolol for CS due to or aggravated by AF; median age was 68 [57–72] years. Four patients were cardiac surgery cases, 3 were CS evolved from secondary cardiomyopaties, 2 were cardiac arrests. Three patients died in the ICU and other 2 in hospital (all were withdrawal of life support therapies); 4 were discharged home. Six cases were new onset AF. In 4 patients (44%) landiolol was effective in restoring sinus rhythm, all before T1; 3 of 5 that remained in AF already had permanent AF. RV-pulmonary artery coupling improved in all patients (p=0.0006, Friedman test – Figure 1), from a median 0,28 [0,13-0,43] mm/mmHg at T0 to a median 0,33 [0,23-0,61] mm/mmHg at T1 and to a median 0,37 [0,26-0,65] mm/mmHg at T2. TAPSE improved from median 10 [7,0–12,8] mm at T0 to median 10,2 [9,7–16] at T1 and median 13,5 [9,7–16] mm at T2 (p=0,0005) and PAPs decreased from median 36 [30–42] mmHg at T0 to median 30 [26–40] mmHg at T1 and median 27 [23–39] mmHg at T2 (p=0,0018). Right atrial pressure (RAP) also decreased from 18 [14–21] mmHg to 15 [13–17] mmHg at 1 hour and to 13 [12–15] mmHg at 6 hours. Landiolol median dose at T1 was 8 [6;10] mcg/kg/min.

Conclusions

These preliminary data showed that landiolol was effective in ameliorating RV mechanic and energetic performance in CS with AF.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A59 Cardiovascular performance improvement in cardiogenic shock patients with atrial fibrillation treated with landiolol

M. Pasetto1, G. Paissan1,2, M. Fasan1, M. Ceola Graziadei1, A. Russo1, L. Peluso1,2, L. Gottin1,2

1Cardiothoracic and Vascular Intensive Care Unit, Hospital and University Trust of Verona, Italy; 2Department of Surgery, Dentistry, Gynecology and Paediatrics, University of Verona, Italy

Correspondence: M. Pasetto

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A59

Background

Atrial tachyarrhythmias often coexist with worsening heart failure (HF) and can precipitate cardiogenic shock (CS). Effective treatment should address rate, rhytm and synchrony, aiming at improving the hemodynamic profile efficiency. Landiolol, a short-acting beta1-superselective blocker, is guideline-recommended for rhytm and rate control of atrial fibrillation (AF) and has demonstrated effectiveness in HF and CS patients. Cardiac Power Output (CPO) expresses the cardiovascular system energy output per unit time.

Aim

Evaluate whether rhytm/rate control with landiolol improves cardiovascular efficiency.

Methods

Prospective observational single-center cohort study, started 03/25. Adult patients with acute HF/CS and tachyarrhythmias admitted in our cardiothoracic ICU. Hemodynamic profile evaluation before (T0), at 1 h (T1) and 6 h (T2) after landiolol infusion start, with pulse-contour monitoring and echocardiography. Conscious patients were presented an informed consent for data preservation.

Results

In this ongoing study we enrolled 9 patients treated with landiolol for CS due to or aggravated by AF; median age was 68 [57–72] years. Four patients were cardiac surgery cases, 3 were CS evolved from secondary cardiomyopaties, 2 were cardiac arrests. Three patients died in the ICU and other 2 in hospital (all were withdrawal of life support therapies); 4 were discharged home. Six cases were new onset AF. In 4 patients (44%) landiolol was effective in restoring sinus rhythm, all before T1; 3 of 5 that remained in AF already had permanent AF. CPO improved from a median 0,58 [0,33-0,69] W before landiolol infusion to 0.68 [0,50-0,87] W at 1 h and 0.74 [0,58-0,85] W at 6 h, in a statistically significant manner (p=0.013, Friedman test). Adjusting the CPO computation for right atrial pressure for biventricular function evaluation, median increases were from a starting 0.47 [0,20-0,55] W to 0.48 [0,40-0,74] W at 1 h and to 0.62 [0,48-0,73] W at 6 h (p=0.013; Figure 1). CI improved from median 1,9 [1,4-2,2] l/min/m2 to 2,0 [1,9-2,9] l/min/m2 at 1 h and to 2,2 [1,9-3,1] l/min/m2 at 6h. A Mann-Whitney test showed non-significant differences between patients that reverted to sinus rhythm and patients that remained in AF (Table 1). Landiolol median dose at T1 was 8 [6;10] mcg/kg/min.

Conclusions

These preliminary data show that landiolol was effective in ameliorating cardiac mechanic and energetic performance in CS with AF.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A60 Awake carotid endarterectomy under locoregional anesthesia in high-risk patients: a case series

A. Alfieri1,2, M. Nutricati1, A. Scognamiglio1, P. Bonagura1, A. Scalvenzi1, V. Maffei1, P. Sansone2, M.C. Pace2, M.B. Passavanti2

1Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, A.O.R.N. A. Cardarelli, Naples, Italy; 2Department of Womens and Childrens Health and General and Specialized Surgery, University of Campania, L. Vanvitelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: A. Alfieri

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A60

Background

Carotid endarterectomy can be performed under general or locoregional anesthesia. Although large randomized data have not demonstrated a definitive superiority of one anesthetic technique over the other, locoregional anesthesia allows continuous clinical neurological monitoring during carotid cross-clamping and may be particularly attractive in selected high-risk patients [1,2]. Current evidence and contemporary reviews support awake neurological assessment as a valuable method for detecting cerebral hypoperfusion during carotid endarterectomy performed under regional anesthesia [2,3]. We report a 10-patient case series of carotid endarterectomy performed under locoregional anesthesia with intraoperative awake neurological monitoring.

Case Series

We reviewed 11 consecutive adult patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic or high-grade asymptomatic carotid stenosis at A.O.R.N. A. Cardarelli Hospital, Naples, Italy, between November 2025 and April 2026. All procedures were performed under locoregional anesthesia using ultrasound-guided superficial/intermediate cervical plexus block, supplemented when necessary by local infiltration performed by the surgeon. Light sedation was administered only when compatible with preserved cooperation and reliable neurological assessment. Intraoperative neurological monitoring consisted of repeated verbal contact, evaluation of consciousness and contralateral hand-grip testing before and during carotid cross-clamping. Hemodynamic management aimed to maintain systolic arterial pressure at or slightly above the patient’s baseline during cross-clamping, unless clinically contraindicated. The primary descriptive endpoints were technical feasibility, need for conversion to general anesthesia and occurrence of intraoperative neurological symptoms requiring selective shunt placement. Secondary endpoints included perioperative stroke, myocardial infarction, acute kidney injury, airway compromise, seizure, local anesthetic systemic toxicity, cervical hematoma, ICU admission, hospital length of stay and in-hospital mortality.

The median age was 76 years [IQR 70–81], all classified as ASA III–IV. Six patients underwent surgery for symptomatic carotid stenosis and four for asymptomatic high-grade stenosis. Relevant comorbidities included coronary artery disease in five patients, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in three, chronic kidney disease in three and previous stroke or transient ischemic attack in six. Locoregional anesthesia was successfully completed in all patients, with no conversion to general anesthesia. Mild intraoperative discomfort requiring additional local infiltration occurred in two patients. One patient developed transient contralateral hand weakness during carotid cross-clamping, which resolved after selective shunt placement. No intraoperative seizure, airway compromise or local anesthetic systemic toxicity occurred. No perioperative stroke, myocardial infarction, acute kidney injury or in-hospital death was observed. One patient developed a small cervical hematoma managed conservatively. Median hospital length of stay was 3 days [IQR 2–4].

Conclusion

In this case series, carotid endarterectomy under locoregional anesthesia was feasible and well tolerated in high-risk patients, allowing real-time clinical neurological monitoring during carotid cross-clamping. The technique avoided conversion to general anesthesia, enabled selective shunt placement based on awake neurological deterioration and was associated with a low rate of early postoperative complications. These observations support the role of locoregional anesthesia as a pragmatic strategy for selected patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy, particularly when continuous neurological assessment and avoidance of general anesthesia are clinically desirable.

Consent to publish

Written informed consent for the anesthetic procedure and for the anonymous use of clinical and perioperative data for scientific and publication purposes was obtained from all patients. All data were fully anonymized before analysis and reporting.

A61 Phenotype-guided intraoperative blood pressure management using advanced arterial waveform monitoring in major vascular surgery

A. Alfieri1,2, M. Nutricati1, P. Bonagura1, A. Scognamiglio1, A. Scalvenzi1, V. Maffei1, P. Sansone2, M.C. Pace2, M.B. Passavanti2

1Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, A.O.R.N. A. Cardarelli, Naples, Italy; 2Department of Womens and Childrens Health and General and Specialized Surgery, University of Campania, L. Vanvitelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: A. Scalvenzi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A61

Background

Major vascular surgery is characterized by abrupt haemodynamic changes related to anaesthetic induction, arterial clamping or declamping, endovascular manipulation, blood loss, reperfusion and pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Intraoperative hypotension should be interpreted not only as an isolated mean arterial pressure value, but as a time-dependent exposure in which both severity and duration contribute to postoperative organ injury. Recent perioperative consensus statements report that intraoperative MAP values below approximately 60–70 mmHg are associated with acute kidney injury, myocardial injury, myocardial infarction and mortality [1]. Patients undergoing abdominal aortic and other major vascular procedures may be particularly vulnerable to hypotension because of advanced age, chronic hypertension, atherosclerotic disease and renal impairment. HPI-guided haemodynamic management has been investigated in abdominal aortic surgery to anticipate hypotension and reduce hypotension burden [2]. European observational data further support time-weighted average MAP <65 mmHg as a clinically meaningful measure of intraoperative hypotension burden.

Case Series

We reviewed 12 adult patients undergoing major vascular surgery at A.O.R.N. A. Cardarelli Hospital, Naples, between January 2026 and April 2026, in whom intraoperative haemodynamic management was supported by advanced arterial waveform-derived monitoring in addition to standard invasive arterial pressure monitoring. HemoSphere with Acumen-HPI was used in seven patients, while MostCare/PRAM was used in five patients according to device availability and clinical preference. The intraoperative strategy aimed to maintain mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg, or above individualized higher targets in patients with chronic hypertension, carotid disease, chronic kidney disease or impaired cardiovascular reserve. Hypotensive episodes were interpreted according to the prevailing haemodynamic phenotype: vasoplegic hypotension, preload-dependent hypotension or low-flow hypotension. Therapeutic interventions included norepinephrine titration, targeted fluid challenge, packed red blood cell transfusion and selective inotropic support. The primary descriptive endpoint was intraoperative hypotension burden, defined as cumulative time with MAP <65 mmHg and time-weighted average MAP below 65 mmHg. Secondary endpoints included postoperative acute kidney injury, myocardial injury, ICU admission, hospital length of stay and in-hospital mortality.

All procedures were performed under standardized anesthetic management according to surgical indication and patient profile. Open aortic and lower-limb revascularization procedures were performed under general anesthesia, while carotid endarterectomy was performed under regional anesthesia with superficial and intermediate cervical plexus block and light sedation. In all cases, invasive arterial pressure monitoring was established before induction or block placement, and advanced arterial waveform-derived monitoring was used to guide blood pressure management.

The median age was 75 years [IQR 69–80], and all patients were ASA physical status III or IV. Surgical procedures included open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, endovascular aneurysm repair, carotid endarterectomy, femoro-popliteal bypass, aorto-bifemoral bypass and lower-limb revascularization. Median surgical duration was 215 minutes [IQR 168–263]. HemoSphere/HPI was used in seven cases and MostCare/PRAM in five. The dominant haemodynamic phenotype was vasoplegia in seven patients, preload dependency in four and low-flow hypotension in one. Median cumulative time with MAP <65 mmHg was 6.5 minutes [IQR 3.8–11.3], corresponding to a low overall hypotension burden. Median time-weighted average MAP <65 mmHg was 0.13 mmHg [IQR 0.06–0.29]. Norepinephrine was administered in ten patients, targeted fluid challenge in six, red blood cell transfusion in three and dobutamine in one. Postoperative acute kidney injury occurred in one patient with pre-existing chronic kidney disease after open abdominal aortic repair. No patient required renal replacement therapy. Three patients required planned postoperative ICU admission. No myocardial injury requiring invasive treatment and no in-hospital mortality were observed.

Conclusion

In this 12-patient case series of major vascular surgery, advanced arterial waveform-derived monitoring with HemoSphere/HPI or MostCare/PRAM was feasible and supported phenotype-guided intraoperative blood pressure management. This approach allowed hypotensive episodes to be interpreted according to their likely haemodynamic mechanism rather than treated solely according to arterial pressure values. The observed hypotension burden was low, and postoperative complications were limited in this high-risk cohort. These preliminary observations support further prospective evaluation of phenotype-guided haemodynamic management in vascular surgical patients.

Ethics and consent statement

The study was conducted on anonymized retrospective perioperative data. All patients had provided written informed consent for the anesthetic procedure and for the anonymous use of their clinical and perioperative data for scientific and publication purposes.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A62 Acute pain service (APS): implementation and clinical and cultural evolution in a tertiary-care center

A.Trotto, B. Bacer, C. Baraldi, E. Trapè, G. Mordenti, C. Ubaldi, F. Zoppi, A. Riccheo

Complex Operating Theatre Management and Southern Anesthesia Unit, Local Health Authority of Bologna (AUSL), Italy

Correspondence: C. Baraldi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A62

Background

The Acute Pain Service (APS) is a multidisciplinary organizational model designed to optimize postoperative and acute pain management through standardized protocols and advanced analgesic techniques, thereby reducing complications and improving clinical outcomes [1].

Established in our hospital in 2022, the service provides proactive surveillance for surgical and non-surgical patients. This study analyzes the service’s growth through the implementation of clinical and educational pathways over the years.

Materials and Methods

The service, managed by attending anesthesiologists and residents, evolved over time to its current configuration through a series of structured steps:

Initial phase (2022): launch in four surgical departments, followed by extension to all surgical specialties and creation of an in-house database. Residents performed twice-daily ward rounds to assess NRS scores, vital signs, adverse effects, and management of analgesic devices, including patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) and epidural or perineural catheters.

Conclusions

The evolution of the APS at OM specifically aimed to achieve the core standards currently considered essential for high-quality acute pain management: written evidence-based protocols, systematic pain assessment and documentation, dedicated trained staff, and 24/7 availability [2].

Transitioning to a proactive, hospital-wide, patient-tailored model supported by a robust organizational and educational framework, was key to fostering a shared “culture of pain control”, improving safety and quality of care for all patients experiencing acute pain.

A63 Continuous fascial plane blocks in thoracic trauma: development of a standardized protocol and impact on pain, opioid use and respiratory function

R. Nardini, C. Tani, R. Diodati, M. Luchini, A. Melai, R. Spina

San Giuseppe Hospital, Central Tuscany Local Health Authority (USL Toscana Centro), Empoli, Italy

Correspondence: R. Nardini

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A63

Background

Uncontrolled pain in thoracic trauma is a critical determinant of respiratory failure, increasing the risk of pulmonary complications and ventilatory escalation. In this context, neuraxial techniques, although effective, are often contraindicated due to coagulopathy, hemodynamic instability, or associated vertebral injuries, making alternative analgesic strategies necessary—safe and rapidly implementable. Fascial plane blocks, including the deep serratus anterior plane block (DSAPB) and the erector spinae plane block (ESPB), are increasingly used due to their favorable safety profile, ease of ultrasound-guided execution, and ability to provide effective analgesia. DSAPB is indicated for anterolateral rib fractures or chest tube-related pain, while ESPB is more suitable for posterolateral fractures. The use of continuous infusion catheters allows prolongation of analgesic effects and reduction in opioid consumption. However, protocols described in the literature are heterogeneous and non-standardized, limiting their transferability into clinical practice [1–6].

Objectives

To develop and implement a standardized internal protocol for the use of continuous catheter-based fascial plane blocks in thoracic trauma and to evaluate its efficacy and safety in a real-world clinical setting, identifying the most appropriate administration regimen.

Methods

An extensive literature review was conducted using an artificial intelligence platform querying biomedical databases, including studies on fascial plane blocks in thoracic trauma and continuous infusion protocols via catheter. Data selected based on relevance and methodological quality were used to construct an internal clinical protocol [1–6]. In parallel, a monocentric observational cohort of 15 consecutive patients with thoracic trauma admitted to the intensive care or high-dependency unit was analyzed. Inclusion criteria included multiple rib fractures and severe pain (NRS >4). All patients underwent ultrasound-guided fascial plane block (DSAPB or ESPB) with placement of a continuous infusion catheter, after informed consent, using sterile technique and dedicated systems for perineural analgesia. Initial bolus and infusion regimens were tailored based on clinical response and progressively standardized. In the absence of a control group, the analysis focused on intra-patient clinical response. The following outcomes were assessed:

Pain intensity (NRS scale)

Pain intensity (NRS scale)

Opioid consumption

Opioid consumption

Need and duration of respiratory support (high-flow oxygen therapy/non-invasive ventilation)

Need and duration of respiratory support (high-flow oxygen therapy/non-invasive ventilation)

Length of stay

Length of stay

Procedure-related complications

Procedure-related complications

Results

The cohort included 15 patients (mean age 62 years, range 29–93; 12 males, 3 females) with an average of 7 rib fractures and associated pulmonary contusions. 8 patients had bifocal fractures, 3 pneumothorax and 4 additional fractures. One patient required surgical stabilization of a flail chest. A total of 12 DSAPB and 3 ESPB were performed. Pain at admission was severe (mean NRS 9) and significantly decreased after the block (mean NRS 1). Considering a maximum bolus dose of ropivacaine <3 mg/kg and continuous infusion <0.4 mg/kg/h, the most effective initial bolus was ropivacaine 0.2% 30 mL (60 mg), ensuring adequate spread and rapid pain control. Among the infusion regimens used, ropivacaine 0.2% 20 mL every 2–4 hours provided the best balance between analgesic efficacy and safety, with significant opioid reduction and no signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity. All patients received multimodal analgesia, mainly with paracetamol and NSAIDs; 7 patients required opioids, primarily oral and at low doses. Five patients required respiratory support. In patients treated early with fascial blocks, a reduction in both the need and duration of respiratory support was observed, with discontinuation of high-flow oxygen on average in less than 2 days. In one case of delayed catheter placement (after 6 days of hospitalization), a marked clinical improvement was observed after treatment initiation, with discontinuation of respiratory support within three days. The mean catheter duration was 6 days. No major complications were observed; one case of catheter dislodgement required early removal. No events consistent with local anesthetic systemic toxicity or catheter-related infections occurred. Mean ICU stay was 6 days, while total hospital stay averaged 13 days.

Conclusions

Continuous catheter-based fascial plane blocks represent an effective and safe strategy for pain management in thoracic trauma. The protocol developed at our center, based on an initial bolus of ropivacaine 0.2% 30 mL followed by intermittent boluses of 20 mL every 2–4 hours, demonstrated a favorable efficacy and safety profile in clinical practice. The implementation of standardized protocols for continuous fascial blocks allows optimization of pain control, reduction in opioid use, and improvement in respiratory function. The protocol is easily reproducible and can be implemented even in non-hub settings. These findings support the structured integration of these techniques into thoracic trauma care pathways, highlighting the need for prospective multicenter studies to confirm their role and define optimal indications.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A64 Comparative analysis of postoperative analgesia in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: balanced general anesthesia with elastomeric pump vs. ultrasound-guided deep rectus sheath block

R. Miccio, S. Savino, F. Giordano, C. D’errico, V. Chierchia, A. Imparato, C. Leone

New Coastal Hospital – ASL Naples 3 South, Sorrento, Italy

Correspondence: C. Leone

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A64

Background

Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) is the gold standard for the treatment of symptomatic cholelithiasis. Despite its minimally invasive nature, postoperative pain remains a significant concern, often arising from both the surgical incisions (somatic pain) and peritoneal stretching/diaphragmatic irritation (visceral pain). Effective pain management is crucial for early discharge and the prevention of chronic pain. This study compares two different analgesic strategies: a traditional multimodal approach using a systemic elastomeric pump and a regional anesthesia technique involving the ultrasound-guided Deep Rectus Sheath Block (DRSB).

Methods

In this prospective randomized study, 30 patients (n=30) aged between 30 and 60 years, classified as ASA physical status I–III, were enrolled and divided into two equal groups (n=15).

Group A (Control - Elastomeric Group): Patients received standardized balanced general anesthesia. Postoperative analgesia was managed via an intravenous elastomeric pump containing a mixture of NSAIDs (Ketorolac), Tramadol, and antiemetics, delivering a continuous infusion over 24–48 hours.

Group A (Control - Elastomeric Group): Patients received standardized balanced general anesthesia. Postoperative analgesia was managed via an intravenous elastomeric pump containing a mixture of NSAIDs (Ketorolac), Tramadol, and antiemetics, delivering a continuous infusion over 24–48 hours.

Group B (Study - DRSB Group): Following induction of general anesthesia but prior to surgical incision, patients received a bilateral ultrasound-guided Deep Rectus Sheath Block. Under sterile conditions and sonographic guidance, 15–20 ml of 0.25% Levobupivacaine or Ropivacaine was injected into the space between the rectus abdominis muscle and its posterior sheath on both sides. Postoperative systemic analgesia was limited to on-demand rescue medication.

Group B (Study - DRSB Group): Following induction of general anesthesia but prior to surgical incision, patients received a bilateral ultrasound-guided Deep Rectus Sheath Block. Under sterile conditions and sonographic guidance, 15–20 ml of 0.25% Levobupivacaine or Ropivacaine was injected into the space between the rectus abdominis muscle and its posterior sheath on both sides. Postoperative systemic analgesia was limited to on-demand rescue medication.

The primary endpoint was the intensity of postoperative pain measured by the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at T0 (awakening), T2, T6, T12, and T24 hours. Secondary endpoints included total opioid consumption, time to first mobilization, and the incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV).

Results

The comparative analysis revealed significant differences in the analgesic profile over time.

At T0 and T2, Group B (DRSB) exhibited significantly lower VAS scores compared to Group A (p < 0.05). Patients in the DRSB group reported near-zero pain levels upon awakening, suggesting that the preemptive blockage of the anterior cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves provided superior immediate somatic coverage.

At T6 and T12, the analgesic efficacy in Group B remained stable. In Group A, despite the continuous infusion from the elastomeric pump, breakthrough pain was more frequent, particularly during coughing or movement (dynamic pain). The mean VAS score for Group B at T12 was 1.8 ± 0.5, compared to 3.4 ± 0.9 in Group A (Table 1).

By T24, the differences between the two groups began to narrow; however, the cumulative consumption of rescue opioids (Tramadol) was 55% lower in the DRSB group. Furthermore, Group B showed a faster return to mobilization (mean time 6 hours post-op) compared to Group A (mean time 9 hours), likely due to the reduced sedative effects of systemic analgesics and better control of movement-related pain. The incidence of PONV was also lower in Group B (13% vs 27%), reflecting the opioid-sparing effect of the regional block.

Discussion

The results demonstrate that the Deep Rectus Sheath Block is highly effective in neutralizing the parietal (somatic) component of pain following laparoscopic cholecystectomy. While the elastomeric pump (Group A) provides a steady state of systemic medication, it often fails to adequately cover the acute mechanical pain associated with trocar insertion sites.

The Deep Rectus Sheath Block specifically targets the terminal branches of the 7th to 11th intercostal nerves, which travel in the plane between the rectus muscle and the posterior sheath. By depositing local anesthetic in this deep compartment, clinicians can achieve a dense sensory block of the middle abdominal wall. This study highlights that regional anesthesia, when integrated into an ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocol, provides superior early analgesia compared to purely systemic methods. However, it is important to note that DRSB does not address the visceral (deep internal) component of pain; therefore, the combination with low-dose non-opioid systemic adjuvants remains ideal.

Conclusion

In patients aged 30–60 undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the ultrasound-guided Deep Rectus Sheath Block provides superior postoperative analgesia in the first 24 hours compared to a standard systemic elastomeric pump. The technique is associated with lower pain scores, reduced opioid requirements, fewer side effects, and faster functional recovery. DRSB should be considered a preferred component of the multimodal analgesic regimen for laparoscopic abdominal surgery

A65 Clinical diary as a supportive tool for pain assessment in primary fibromyalgia

S. Sorrenti1, M. Ciuffreda1, E. Pisello1, C. Pellegrino2, A. Monacelli2, G. Cucè3, G. Di Serafino4, C. Piangatelli1, D. Galante5

1Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, AST Ancona, Fabriano (AN), Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, UNIVPM, Ancona, Italy; 3Department of Public Health, University of Messina, Italy; 4Department of Pain Management and Palliative Care, AST Macerata, Italy; 5Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, ASL Foggia, Cerignola (FG), Italy

Correspondence: S. Sorrenti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A65

Background

Fibromyalgia is a chronic syndrome characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain, frequently associated with fatigue, sleep disturbances, cognitive impairment, and psycho-emotional symptoms. Although its etiopathogenesis remains incompletely understood, current evidence suggests that dysregulation of central pain modulation mechanisms and central sensitization play a key role in the development and maintenance of symptoms. Diagnosis, particularly in primary fibromyalgia, is mainly based on clinical criteria and exclusion of other conditions. In this context, pain assessment is essential but challenging, as pain perception and reporting are strongly influenced by emotional, psychological, and environmental factors. The present study aimed to evaluate the usefulness of a daily clinical diary as a supportive instrument for improving the objectivity of pain assessment in patients with primary fibromyalgia.

Materials and Methods

Data from 45 female patients aged between 15 and 45 years, with a confirmed diagnosis of primary fibromyalgia and undergoing pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatment, were analyzed. After obtaining informed consent and Ethics Committee approval, each patient received a 30-day clinical diary. Patients were instructed to complete the diary daily, recording the following parameters: principal pain locations (up to three sites), maximum pain intensity assessed using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), qualitative characteristics of pain, presence of nocturnal pain, impact of pain on daily quality of life, and effects on occupational and relational functioning. At the end of the 30-day period, patients underwent clinical re-evaluation. Analysis of the clinical diaries was performed only after verbal anamnesis had been collected, in order to minimize potential evaluation bias.

Results

Comparison between verbal anamnesis and data collected through the clinical diaries demonstrated that 60% of patients verbally overestimated pain intensity compared with the values recorded daily in the diary (Table 1). Similarly, 69% of patients overestimated the impact of pain on quality of life (Table 2), while 80% overestimated the impact on occupational and relational functioning (Table 3).

Conclusions

Systematic use of a clinical diary, preferably completed on a daily basis, appears to be a valuable tool for improving the objectivity of pain assessment in primary fibromyalgia. Daily recording may reduce the influence of emotional and contextual factors on pain perception and reporting, thereby supporting clinicians in obtaining a more accurate evaluation and facilitating a more personalized therapeutic approach.

Written informed consent was obtained from all patients prior to study participation, in accordance with ethical standards.

A66 MFAT outperforms BMAC in sustained pain control and synovial immunomodulation in knee osteoarthritis

F. Saturno1, G. Monaco1, A. Salerno1, A. Cianciola2, N. Cianciola2, E. Cianciola1

1ASL SaLerno, Sapri, Italy; 2Unicamillus, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: F. Saturno

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A66

Background

In chronic pain associated with knee osteoarthritis (OA), pro-inflammatory signaling mediated by interleukin-1 beta (IL-1B) represents a key therapeutic target for disrupting nociceptive feedback and peripheral sensitization. Although the efficacy of mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-based therapies is well established, comparative evidence regarding the durability of analgesic effects according to cellular source (bone marrow versus adipose tissue) remains limited, particularly in cohorts standardized for metabolic, biomechanical, and sex-related variables.

Objective

To evaluate the durability of analgesia and its correlation with synovial inflammatory marker modulation (IL-1B) at 12 months following treatment with Bone Marrow Aspirate Concentrate (BMAC) or Microfragmented Adipose Tissue (MFAT).

Materials and methods

A prospective pilot study was conducted on 40 patients (age 40–55 years; Kellgren–Lawrence grade II–III) affected by chronic knee pain refractory to conservative treatments. The cohort was balanced for sex (male:female ratio 1:1) and ethnicity (Caucasian). Written informed consent for clinical procedures and data collection was obtained from all participants in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

To minimize biomechanical confounding factors, only patients with sedentary occupational activity were included. Exclusion criteria comprised BMI >27 kg/m², uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (HbA1c >7.5%), active smoking, systemic inflammatory diseases, and previous intra-articular injections within the prior 6 months.

Patients were randomized to receive a single intra-articular injection of either BMAC (n=20) or MFAT (n=20). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Pain and functional outcomes were assessed using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and WOMAC score at baseline (T0), 6 months, and 12 months. Synovial fluid IL-1B levels were quantified through ultrasound-guided arthrocentesis followed by high-sensitivity ELISA analysis (sensitivity: 0.05 pg/mL).

Results

Both procedures achieved significant pain reduction at 6 months and demonstrated an excellent safety profile. However, differential long-term outcomes emerged at 12-month follow-up. The MFAT group showed significantly superior pain control (VAS T12: 2.8 ± 0.6) compared with the BMAC group, which demonstrated a trend toward pain recurrence (VAS T12: 3.9 ± 0.7; p<0.05) (Figure 1).

Biochemical analysis demonstrated persistent suppression of synovial IL-1B levels in the MFAT group at 12 months, whereas the BMAC group showed a progressive return toward baseline cytokine levels, suggesting reactivation of the inflammatory and nociceptive loop (Figure 1).

Conclusions

MFAT treatment provided more durable analgesia and superior stabilization of the synovial inflammatory microenvironment compared with BMAC over a 12-month follow-up period (Table 1). The persistence of clinical benefit strongly correlated with sustained IL-1B suppression, supporting the hypothesis that adipose tissue microfragmentation induces a more effective biological “re-setting” of the osteoarthritic joint.

Within the field of regenerative pain medicine, MFAT may represent a preferable autologous cellular source for the treatment of moderate knee osteoarthritis in metabolically and biomechanically standardized patient populations.

A67 Minimally invasive pulsed radiofrequency for trigeminal neuralgia: two-year follow-up in 50 patients

F. Saturno1, G. Monaco1, A. Salerno1, A. Cianciola1, N. Cianciola1, E. Cianciola1

1Asl Salerno, Sapri, Italy; 2Unicamillus, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: F. Saturno

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A67

Background

Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by severe facial pain, typically paroxysmal and stabbing in nature, caused by dysfunction of the fifth cranial nerve. The condition can be classified into primary (classical) trigeminal neuralgia, which is generally more responsive to pharmacological treatment, and secondary trigeminal neuralgia, resulting from compression of the trigeminal nerve by intracranial arteries, veins, tumors, or aneurysms.

We retrospectively analyzed our case series of patients treated with pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) of the trigeminal ganglion using a pterygopalatine fossa (PPF) approach between 2023 and 2024.

Case Series

A total of 50 patients underwent PRF treatment for trigeminal neuralgia using the PPF approach between 2023 and 2024. Clinical follow-up was performed at 6 months and 1 year after treatment.

At the 6-month follow-up, 40 out of 50 patients reported significant pain relief with a Visual Analog Scale (VAS) score <3. Among the 10 patients who experienced recurrence or worsening of pain symptoms, 8 underwent a second PRF procedure. At the latest follow-up, only one patient reported a VAS score >5 and was subsequently referred for neurosurgical evaluation.

Procedural Technique

Patients were positioned on a radiolucent operating table in the sitting position, with careful head stabilization. Mild conscious sedation was achieved using fentanyl and midazolam.

Fluoroscopic imaging of the skull was obtained in both anteroposterior (AP) and lateral projections to identify the boundaries of the pterygopalatine fossa. A 10-cm radiofrequency needle was introduced just above the mandibular notch, below the zygomatic arch, under lateral fluoroscopic guidance using a tunnel-vision approach. The needle was advanced into the superior portion of the pterygopalatine fossa, and its correct position was confirmed in the AP projection (Figure 1).

The needle was then connected to the radiofrequency generator. Sensory stimulation was performed at 50 Hz with a voltage between 0.1 and 0.4 V to evoke paresthesia in the affected trigeminal distribution. Motor stimulation at 2 Hz demonstrated thresholds approximately one-third higher than those observed during sensory stimulation.

Treatment consisted of two cycles of pulsed radiofrequency using the following parameters: 42 °C, 300 seconds, and 500 kHz.

Conclusions

Pulsed radiofrequency treatment of the Gasserian ganglion is undoubtedly a technically demanding procedure associated with potentially serious complications, widely reported in the literature, including decreased corneal reflex, masseter muscle weakness or paralysis, dysesthesia, temporary third and fourth cranial nerve palsy, and, most critically, intracranial hemorrhage.

Despite these concerns, our experience with 50 patients over a two-year period is encouraging. Forty-eight patients reported marked improvement in pain symptoms after treatment, while 8 patients required a second PRF procedure.

Careful patient selection remains essential. Only patients refractory to medical therapy and with significant impairment in quality of life should be considered candidates for this procedure. Furthermore, patients must be thoroughly informed about the possible complications and the realistic risk of treatment failure.

Informed Consent

Written informed consent was obtained from all patients included in this case series for both the procedure and the anonymous use of clinical data for scientific and educational purposes.

A68 Multimodal analgesia in major robotic pelvic surgery: spinal morphine versus sacral ESP block with postoperative ketamine infusion. A preliminary retrospective observational study

M. Quaraniello1, G. Galasso1, S. Giacometti1, F. Albano1, R. Baio2, D. Carbone1

1Complex Unit of Anesthesia and Intensive Care – Emergency Department (DEA) Nocera Pagani Scafati, Nocera Inferiore (SA), Italy; 2Complex Unit of Urology, Umberto I Hospital (PO), Nocera Inferiore, Nocera Inferiore (SA), Italy

Correspondence: M. Quaraniello

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A68

Background

Optimal perioperative analgesia in major robotic pelvic surgery should provide stable pain control, limit rescue analgesic requirements, attenuate the surgical inflammatory response, and support early functional recovery within enhanced recovery pathways. The optimal combination of neuraxial and locoregional techniques in this setting is still debated. We retrospectively compared two multimodal analgesic strategies in patients undergoing major robotic urologic and gynecologic surgery.

Methods

We conducted a preliminary single-center retrospective observational study including 15 patients aged 35 to 70 years. Surgical procedures comprised 10 urologic surgeries (7 prostatectomies, 1 total and 2 partial nephrectomies) and 5 gynecologic surgeries (3 hystero-adnexectomies and 2 adnexectomies). All patients received balanced general anesthesia with sevoflurane and remifentanil. Six patients received spinal analgesia with morphine 100 mcg, whereas 9 patients received a sacral erector spinae plane (ESP) block with ropivacaine 0.5% 10 mL and dexmedetomidine 10 mcg, followed by postoperative elastomeric ketamine infusion at 0.1 mg/kg/h. Outcomes included postoperative NRS pain scores at 3, 6, 12, 24, and 36 hours, 24-hour C-reactive protein (CRP), rescue analgesic requirements, and time to bowel canalization.

Results

Mean CRP at 24 hours was lower in the sacral ESP plus ketamine group than in the spinal morphine group (55.6 versus 115.4 mg/L). In the sacral ESP group, NRS remained below 3 throughout the observation period, with no need for rescue analgesia. In the spinal morphine group, NRS was below 3 at 3 and 6 hours, increased to approximately 4 at 12 hours, and worsened at 24 hours: all 6 patients required paracetamol rescue, with approximately 2 doses per patient during the first 24 hours; between 24 and 36 hours, all patients further required 1 g of paracetamol combined with 1 ampoule of ketorolac. Mean time to bowel canalization was approximately 18 hours in the sacral ESP group, compared with more than 24 hours in the spinal morphine group.

Conclusions

In this preliminary retrospective cohort, sacral ESP block combined with postoperative ketamine infusion was associated with a lower postoperative inflammatory response, more sustained analgesia, reduced rescue analgesic requirements, and earlier bowel recovery than spinal morphine. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the retrospective design, the small sample size, and the heterogeneity of surgical procedures, and warrant confirmation in larger prospective studies.

A69 Pulsed electromagnetic field therapy before platelet-rich plasma infiltration in knee osteoarthritis: a retrospective comparative study

A. Fruncillo, P. Russo, A. Calabrese, D. Giordano, C. Chiumiento, C. Grandis, F. Chiumiento

Complex Unit of Anesthesia and Intensive Care – Emergency Department (DEA) Battipaglia–Eboli–Roccadaspide, Italy

Correspondence: A. Fruncillo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A69

Background

Knee osteoarthritis is one of the leading causes of chronic pain and functional limitation in elderly patients and is frequently associated with synovial inflammation, suprapatellar joint effusion, impaired mobility, and chronic use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). In recent years, platelet-rich plasma (PRP) infiltrative therapy has gained increasing interest as a regenerative therapeutic option for symptomatic knee osteoarthritis.

Pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy has demonstrated analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiedematous properties in several musculoskeletal disorders. Experimental and clinical evidence suggests that PEMF may modulate inflammatory pathways, improve local microcirculation, and reduce soft-tissue edema, potentially creating a more favorable joint environment before regenerative infiltrative procedures. The aim of this report is to describe our clinical experience with wearable PEMF therapy before PRP treatment in patients affected by symptomatic knee osteoarthritis.

Materials and methods

We treated 50 consecutive patients with wearable PEMF therapy before PRP infiltrative treatment for symptomatic knee osteoarthritis.

Patients were males and females aged between 55 and 85 years with Kellgren-Lawrence grade II–III osteoarthritis associated with chronic pain, reduced walking tolerance, joint stiffness, and mild-to-moderate suprapatellar joint effusion documented by ultrasound examination. Twenty-eight patients presented Kellgren-Lawrence grade II osteoarthritis and 22 grade III disease.

Most patients were receiving chronic symptomatic therapy before enrollment, including daily or near-daily NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, diclofenac, ketoprofen, or coxibs/etoricoxib, frequently associated with antiedema supplements and intermittent analgesic therapy.

All patients underwent continuous wearable PEMF therapy for 20 days before the first PRP infiltration using a low-intensity non-ionizing pulsed electromagnetic field medical device approved for pain and soft tissue edema treatment. The device generated pulsed electromagnetic fields with a carrier frequency of 13.56 MHz and a maximum magnetic flux density of approximately 2000 μT through a flexible wearable antenna, allowing prolonged treatment during normal daily activities.

Clinical assessment included Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) pain score, NSAID consumption, walking tolerance, and clinical signs of inflammation before the first PRP infiltration.

Results

Mean baseline NRS score was 8.2 ± 0.8. After 20 days of pre-treatment with PEMF therapy, patients showed clinically relevant symptomatic improvement before the first PRP infiltration, with mean NRS decreasing to 5.1 ± 1.4.

A substantial reduction in NSAID consumption was observed: 38 patients (76%) reduced or discontinued their habitual anti-inflammatory therapy before the first PRP infiltration. In particular, 21 patients (42%) completely discontinued daily NSAID use during the pre-infiltrative period, while the remaining responders reported an estimated reduction of weekly analgesic consumption of approximately 50%.

Clinical and ultrasound evaluation before infiltration frequently suggested lower inflammatory burden, with reduction in joint swelling and ultrasound signs of suprapatellar effusion associated with improved walking tolerance. Thirty-four patients (68%) reported significant improvement in walking ability and daily activities, 9 patients (18%) experienced partial benefit, and 7 patients (14%) showed minimal or absent clinical response.

No severe adverse events related to PEMF therapy were reported. Mild transient local discomfort related to prolonged device application occurred in three patients and resolved spontaneously without treatment discontinuation (Table 1).

Conclusions

In our clinical experience, pre-treatment with wearable PEMF therapy before PRP infiltration was associated with reduction in pain intensity, lower NSAID consumption, improved walking tolerance, and decreased inflammatory signs in patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis.

The observed reduction in inflammatory burden before PRP infiltration may have contributed to a more favorable joint environment before regenerative treatment. The marked reduction in NSAID use observed in a large proportion of patients may also represent a clinically relevant advantage in an elderly population frequently exposed to chronic pharmacological therapy.

Although limited by the observational design and the absence of a control group, these preliminary findings suggest that PEMF therapy may represent a useful adjunctive strategy in the multimodal management of knee osteoarthritis before regenerative infiltrative procedures. Further prospective studies are needed to confirm these observations and to evaluate their impact on long-term PRP outcomes.

Consent to publish

Written informed consent for anonymous clinical data collection and scientific publication was obtained from all patients included in the study.

A70 Safety and effectiveness of low-dose transdermal buprenorphine in elderly patients with chronic non-cancer pain: a retrospective observational study

A. Calabrese, A. Fruncillo, P. Russo, D. Giordano, C. Grandis, C. Chiumiento, F. Chiumiento

Complex Unit of Anesthesia and Intensive Care – Emergency Department (DEA) Battipaglia–Eboli–Roccadaspide, Italy

Correspondence: A. Calabrese

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A70

Background

Chronic non-cancer pain is highly prevalent among elderly patients and is frequently associated with multiple comorbidities, polypharmacy, reduced functional reserve, and increased risk of opioid-related adverse events. In this setting, long-term opioid therapy is often limited by poor tolerability, opioid-induced constipation (OIC), cognitive adverse events, and treatment discontinuation. Transdermal buprenorphine has unique pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic properties, including high receptor affinity, prolonged analgesic activity, ceiling effect for respiratory depression, and potentially lower incidence of gastrointestinal adverse effects, making it a potentially suitable therapeutic option for elderly patients with chronic pain and cardiovascular or metabolic comorbidities [1,2].

The aim of this retrospective observational study was to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and tolerability of low-dose transdermal buprenorphine in elderly patients with chronic non-cancer pain treated in a real-world outpatient setting.

Materials and methods

A monocentric retrospective observational study was conducted between January 2025 and December 2025. Seventeen patients aged >65 years with moderate-to-severe chronic non-cancer pain were enrolled according to predefined inclusion criteria. One patient discontinued treatment because of cutaneous intolerance and was excluded from analysis.

Pain conditions included osteoarthritis, chronic low back pain, cervical pain, myofascial pain, and neuropathic pain. All patients presented at least one significant comorbidity, including hypertension, obesity, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, or cardiovascular disease.

Transdermal buprenorphine was initiated at the lowest effective dose (5 mcg/h) and titrated according to clinical response up to a maximum dose of 15 mcg/h. Treatment duration was at least 3 months in all analyzed patients.

Clinical efficacy was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS). Safety and tolerability evaluation included incidence of nausea/vomiting, neurological adverse events, cutaneous reactions, and assessment of opioid-induced constipation using the Bowel Function Index (BFI).

Results

Sixteen patients were included in the analysis. Mean baseline NRS value was 9.31, decreasing to 5.34 after at least 3 months of treatment, corresponding to a mean pain reduction of approximately 43%.

Only two patients reported mild nausea occurring 1–2 times per week during the first days of therapy, with progressive spontaneous resolution after treatment continuation. No severe vomiting episodes were observed and no patients required treatment discontinuation because of gastrointestinal adverse events.

No significant neurological adverse events such as dizziness, anxiety, visual disturbances, excessive sedation, or cognitive impairment were reported during follow-up. One patient older than 80 years experienced mild transient asthenia at a dose of 10 mcg/h, with spontaneous clinical improvement.

One patient discontinued therapy because of cutaneous intolerance related to the transdermal patch adhesive matrix.

Evaluation of bowel function demonstrated no statistically significant worsening of constipation after treatment initiation. According to BFI analysis and Wilcoxon signed-rank test, only one patient developed clinically significant opioid-induced constipation, while most patients reported no relevant changes in bowel habits (Table 1).

Conclusions

Low-dose transdermal buprenorphine showed favorable effectiveness and tolerability in elderly patients with chronic non-cancer pain and multiple comorbidities. Significant pain reduction was achieved with limited incidence of opioid-related adverse events, particularly opioid-induced constipation and neurological complications. These findings support the potential role of transdermal buprenorphine as a safe therapeutic option for long-term pain management in complex elderly patients requiring opioid therapy.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A71 Post-ischemic chronic pain management associated with subclinical epilepsy: a case report

A.A. Carrideo1, A. Discenza1,2, M. Pedone1, F. Cardinale2, T. Di Foggia1, N. Di Francesco1, G. Cinnella1,2

1Policlinico Riuniti Foggia, Italy; 2University of Foggia, Italy

Correspondence: F. Cardinale

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A71

Background

After ischemic stroke, patients may experience multiple complications due to the underlying cerebral injury, ranging from psychological to physical consequences (1). The most frequent are neurological complications, such as seizures (2) or chronic pain due to muscular spasticity (1). Epilepsy require the use of antiepileptic drugs which can cause impaired sleep regulation or slowed cerebral function (3). Muscle relaxant such as Cyclobenzaprine are used for spasticity and can be administered orally or intrathecally (4). Post stroke seizures are underestimated because more than one fifth of patients experience only electroencephalographic seizures (5), and the clinical manifestations varies from generalized seizures to focal and motor manifestation (6). Therefore, to achieve an optimal therapeutic response, patients - especially young adults - should be evaluated holistically, considering the impact of therapy and side effects in daily life activity (DLA) (7).

Case report

Patient of 36 y.o. woman with Marfan syndrome. In 2022 a ruptured aneurysm was surgically treated and was complicated by ischemic stroke. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data. After the brain injury she was admitted to intensive care unit (ICU). Once stabilized, she was transferred to physiatry department for the physical and logopaedic rehabilitation as she presented right-sided hemiplegia and aphasia. She was receiving levetiracetam for residual epilepsy. Over two years, she recovered about 80% of the previous mobility and sensibility in her right leg and regained full speech.

However, the antiepileptic therapy had side effects that seriously affected the patient’s quality of life (QoL), as she experienced difficulty in speaking and muscle weakness. Therefore, she discontinued the pharmacological treatment, with improvement of her DLA. A few months after the interruption, she developed muscle spasm, without evidence of clinical epilepsy, associated with chronic pain, compromising her QoL. This led the patient to consult the algologist in our pain department. The clinical evaluation through Numeral Rating Scale and Short Form Health Survey in Table 1, Panel A. To exclude subclinical epilepsy and confirm spasticity, an EEG was performed, showing slow theta activity in temporal region confirming a subclinical manifestation of seizures. After consulting the neurologist and considering the poor patient compliance to antiepileptic treatment, the algologist began a combo therapy with a low dose of Amitriptyline 6 mg once/day and Cyclobenzaprine 5 mg twice/day for symptom management.

This therapy was well tolerated by the patient, who reports in the follow up after 4 months a good QoL and no influence on DLA (Table 1 Panel B).

Conclusion

Although ischemic stroke is a rare pathology with favorable outcome and low mortality in younger adults, they may face psychological concerns about their future and a reduced QoL (7). The most common dysfunctions include fatigue, cognitive impairment, anxiety and depression, among others. Furthermore, the European recommendation on antiseizure therapy are based on low-quality evidence regarding the continuation and duration of the treatment (3).

Our patient discontinued antiepileptic therapy herself to achieve more satisfactory QoL and reduce problems in her DLA and work. Subclinical seizures, manifesting as an intense and painful spasticity led her to a clinical evaluation at our pain department. After consulting the neurologist who followed the patient, we decided to start a combo therapy with Amitriptyline and Cyclobenzaprine, to obtain a satisfying control both of seizures and spasticity. This tailored approach addressed the patient’s refusal of first line therapy. Our search did not find a similar association in literature, thus representing a novelty and a possible alternative for this subset of patient.

The relevance of our report could be found also in multidisciplinary approach to a subclinical manifested symptom of seizures, which lead the patient to go first to algologist instead of neurologist. Finally, we achieved successfully treatment of the underlying pathologies thus improving the QOL of the patient, as she referred an improvement.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A72 Efficacy of medical cannabis in the treatment of nociplastic pain: clinical impact on the management of pain and associated symptoms in fibromyalgia

A. Di Sauro, E. Fiocco, L. Rota, L. Tettamanzi, C.D. Votta, G. Russo

Ospedale Maggiore di Lodi, Italy

Correspondence: A. Di Sauro

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A72

Background

Fibromyalgia is a paradigmatic syndrome of nociplastic pain, characterized by central sensitization, systemic symptoms, and a poor response to conventional therapies. Recent evidence suggests a role for the endocannabinoid system in pain and mood modulation, hypothesizing that its dysfunction (Clinical Endocannabinoid Deficiency) may contribute to the pathogenesis of fibromyalgia. In this context, medical cannabis represents a potential pharmacological option for patients refractory to first-line therapies.

Materials and Methods

A retrospective observational study was conducted at a pain management clinic. The study included 12 female patients who provided informed consent, all with a confirmed diagnosis of fibromyalgia according to the EULAR/ACR criteria (median age 47 years, IQR 41–58). Inclusion criteria required refractoriness to first- and second-line therapies and at least 6 months of treatment with medical cannabis. The strains used were primarily “Bediol” (THC 6%, CBD 8%) in 58.3% of the patients, followed by “Bedrocan” (THC 22%, CBD <1%) in 25%, “Bedrolite” (THC <1%, CBD 8%) in 8.3%, and “Farmalabor” (THC 1%, CBD 5%) in 8.3%. Outcomes were assessed using the VAS, FIQR, GAD-7, PCS, PHQ-9, and GPE scales, administered at baseline (T0) and after 6 months (T6). Statistical analysis was performed using the Mann-Whitney U test, with significance set at p < 0.05.

Results

In the analyzed sample, the median THC dosage was 7.4 mg/day (IQR 3.825–21), while the median CBD dosage was 7.2 mg/day (IQR 1.275–21.125). Furthermore, 41.66% of the sample continued to use two or more adjuvants for symptom control; of these, 80% also resorted to the use of opioids. At the end of the follow-up, no statistically significant reduction in pain intensity was observed (VAS: median 10 at T0 vs. 9 at T6; p = 0.843). However, a significant improvement was recorded in physical function (FIQR Function: 72 vs. 51; p = 0.003), overall health status (FIQR Health: 18 vs. 13; p = 0.028), symptoms (FIQR Symptoms: 81 vs. 64; p = 0.008), and overall quality of life (FIQR Total: 84 vs. 61; p = 0.002). Scores related to anxiety (GAD-7: 16 vs. 10; p = 0.010), depression (PHQ-9: 19 vs. 12; p < 0.001), and catastrophizing (PCS Total: 40 vs. 25; p = 0.007) also improved significantly. The GPE questionnaire highlighted a subjective improvement (“much improved”) in the majority of patients. The most frequently improved aspects were sleep, pain, and mood, while side effects were limited.

Conclusions

In this sample of patients with severe and refractory fibromyalgia, medical cannabis proved effective in improving quality of life, physical function, and the emotional sphere, albeit without a significant reduction in pain perception. These results support the pathophysiological hypothesis of Clinical Endocannabinoid Deficiency and suggest that cannabis may represent a valid multidimensional therapeutic option in resistant cases, contributing to a restructuring of the subjective experience of pain and a recovery of functional autonomy.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A73 Integrated multimodal pain management and cannabis immunomodulation in an elderly patient with inflammatory arthritis, severe obesity and disabling mixed nociceptive-neuropathic pain

S. Di Franco, F. Miralto, M. Iannuzzi

Pellegrini Hospital (P.O.), ASL Naples 1 Central, Italy

Correspondence: S. Di Franco

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A73

Background

Chronic musculoskeletal pain in elderly patients with severe obesity, osteoarthritis, spinal degenerative disease and suspected inflammatory arthritis is frequently multifactorial and therapeutically challenging. In this setting, conventional analgesic escalation may be limited by cardiovascular comorbidities, anticoagulation, sleep-disordered breathing and frailty. Interventional pain procedures and cannabinoid-based therapy are increasingly considered within multimodal strategies for selected patients with refractory chronic pain, although causal interpretation of clinical and inflammatory changes remains difficult in single-patient observations [1–3]. We report a case in which a staged multimodal approach was associated with marked functional recovery, opioid discontinuation, weight loss and subsequent rheumatologic diagnosis.

Case report

A 79-year-old patient was referred to our pain clinic on 1 September 2025 for severe diffuse arthralgia involving both shoulders, hips and knees, bilateral coxofemoral synovitis, chronic low back pain radiating to the right lower limb and major walking limitation. The patient walked with a stick and reported neurogenic claudication after approximately 50 m, with increasing need for a walker. Physical examination showed painful limitation of both upper limbs, consistent with bilateral rotator cuff tendinous and fibrotic changes, more evident on the right side. Pelvic radiography documented bilateral coxarthrosis; lumbosacral and knee radiographs showed mild L2–L3 spondylolisthesis and bilateral knee demineralization. Lumbar spine and pelvic magnetic resonance imaging performed on 7 October 2025 confirmed multilevel disc disease from L2 to L5 and L5–S1 disc protrusion.

Relevant comorbidities included atrial fibrillation treated with flecainide and rivaroxaban, class II severe obesity, snoring and self-reported nocturnal apnoeas. Previous treatment with acetaminophen and an orthopaedic-prescribed analgesic regimen had provided insufficient relief. In October 2025, the patient started an anti-inflammatory dietary programme prescribed in our clinic and an acute-phase pharmacological strategy including transdermal buprenorphine 10 µg/h, amitriptyline 5 drops at night and etoricoxib 60 mg once daily for 5 days. Rheumatoid factor testing was requested and showed marked positivity, with a value of 1143 IU/mL on 6 December 2025.

Etoricoxib was discontinued. The patient continued transdermal buprenorphine 10 µg/h and low-dose amitriptyline, and started pharmaceutical cannabis with Bedrolite, providing cannabidiol 5 mg/day for 1 month. Rheumatoid factor decreased to 564 IU/mL. Buprenorphine was then reduced to 5 µg/h, amitriptyline was discontinued, and Bediol was added, providing cannabidiol 5 mg/day and tetrahydrocannabinol 5 mg/day for a further 30 days. Rheumatoid factor further decreased to 325 IU/mL.

Because of persistent focal pain generators, the patient underwent day-hospital diagnostic and therapeutic interventional pain treatment, consisting of a right genicular nerve block followed by pulsed radiofrequency of the genicular nerves, and continuous radiofrequency ablation of the sacroiliac joint using a palisade technique. Pain intensity decreased from numerical rating scale 7/10 to 2/10. At 15-day follow-up, the patient reported resolution of claudication-like walking limitation, no longer required a walking aid and discontinued transdermal buprenorphine.

At 6 months, the patient had lost 25 kg of body weight, denied resting dyspnoea and reported reduced nocturnal snoring. Rheumatologic evaluation performed on 17 March 2026 confirmed inflammatory arthritis and methotrexate therapy was initiated. Thirty days after rheumatologic treatment, rheumatoid factor was 226 IU/mL. The patient continued Bedrolite, providing cannabidiol 10 mg/day, as part of the analgesic strategy.

Conclusion

This case illustrates the potential value of a staged, multimodal pain pathway in an elderly, anticoagulated and obese patient with overlapping degenerative, neuropathic and inflammatory pain mechanisms. The combination of careful pharmacological de-escalation, low-dose cannabinoid-based therapy, weight-oriented lifestyle intervention and targeted radiofrequency procedures was associated with substantial pain reduction, opioid discontinuation and clinically meaningful functional recovery. The progressive reduction in rheumatoid factor occurred before and after rheumatologic disease-modifying therapy and should be interpreted cautiously, as a temporal association rather than proof of an immunomodulatory effect. Nevertheless, the case highlights how pain medicine assessment may reveal an unrecognized inflammatory disease and may act as a bridge between analgesic control, functional rehabilitation and definitive rheumatologic management.

Consent to publish

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and all related clinical details.
