A74 Chronic pain in ECMO survivors: an observational study on prevalence and functional impact

P.H. Dellakkada Liyanage1, A. Shinde2, M. Giacosa2, E.G. Intignano2, M. Belliato3, S. Natoli2,4

1Department of Molecular Medicine, University of Pavia, Italy; 2Department of Clinical-Surgical, Diagnostic and Pediatric Sciences, University of Pavia, Italy; 3Anesthesia and Cardiothoracic Intensive Care Unit, Fondazione IRCCS Policlinico San Matteo, Pavia, Italy; 4Pain Medicine Unit, Fondazione IRCCS Policlinico San Matteo, Pavia, Italy

Correspondence: P.H. Dellakkada Liyanage

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A74

Background

Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) is a life-saving intervention for refractory cardiopulmonary failure, but survivorship is increasingly burdened by impaired quality of life. This study aimed to evaluate the prevalence, clinical phenotypes, and functional impact of persistent post-ECMO pain.

Methods

A retrospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary care center ICU between July 2025 - January 2026. The cohort included 38 adult ECMO survivors from the Cardiac Surgery and General ICUs between the period from June 2023 - July 2025. To comprehensively assess pain profiles, patients were evaluated using the following questionnaires, Brief Pain Inventory (BPI), Douleur Neuropathique 4 (DN4), Leeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symptoms and Signs (LANSS), and Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI). Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics to evaluate the functional burden of pain and hypothesize underlying etiologies.

Results

Severe, active persistent pain was identified in 18.4% (7/38) of the cohort. Additional 5.3% (2/38) showed pain with neuropathic features scoring 0/10 on the standard BPI scale while demonstrating significant touch-evoked allodynia and dysesthesia on the LANSS and DN4 assessments. The reported pain presentations exhibited neuropathic characteristics, involving sudden paroxysmal bursts (n=6), tingling (n=5), allodynia (n=4), and vasomotor skin changes (n=4). All of the highly symptomatic patients had undergone large-bore Veno-Arterial (VA) cannulation, compared to none in the exclusive Veno-Venous (VV) group (21.9% incidence vs. 0%; p=0.323). Pain onset was completely independent of prolonged ICU length-of-stay (p=0.26). Furthermore, the CSI, stratified patients into distinct cohorts of localized pain (CSI < 40; n = 4) versus widespread central sensitization (CSI > 40; n = 3). Pain severity was a major driver of functional impairment, demonstrating a strong correlation with increased functional interference (R2=0.81, p=0.005). Standard monotherapies such as paracetamol or pregabalin, provided insufficient relief (30%), whereas significant pain reduction (up to 70%) was uniquely associated with individualized opioid-escalated multimodal regimens.

Conclusion

Chronic pain in ECMO survivors remains a highly complex, underestimated complication. Several mechanisms can underlie the development of this chronic pain, driven by a combination of suspected cannula-induced nerve trauma, polyneuropathy, and post-surgical mechanical or nociceptive pain. Furthermore, the onset of central sensitization can severely complicate the overall pain burden. To accurately identify and manage these refractory, mixed pain states, it is recommended to integrate comprehensive screening and referral to pain specialists into routine post- ECMO survivorship care. This facilitates the early detection of complex pain profiles and allows for the targeted application of appropriate pharmacological therapies.

Ethics and governance

This study was conducted as a retrospective observational study. The processing of health-related data for this research was conducted in accordance with Article 110 GDPR of the Italian Data Protection Code (Legislative Decree 196/2003 and subsequent updates). This legal framework allows for the processing of data for scientific research when obtaining written consent is prevented by specific objective reasons, such as the retrospective nature of the cohort and the significant clinical vulnerability of the survivors.

Despite the retrospective nature of the study, every effort was made to respect participant autonomy: For the telephone assessment phase, spontaneous and informed verbal consent was obtained from 100% of the included participants after a detailed explanation of the study objectives. Participants were informed of their right to withdraw at any time and were given the opportunity to ask questions regarding the use of their data.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A75 Regenerative medicine for osteoarthritis: preliminary outcomes of intra-articular autologous mesenchymal stem cell therapy

E. Cianciola1, G. Monaco1, A. Salerno1, A. Cianciola2, N. Cianciola2, F. Saturno1

1Asl Salerno, Sapri, Italy; 2Unicamillus, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: E. Cianciola

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A75

Abstract Introduction

Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common joint disease and one of the leading causes of disability in the elderly population. It affects approximately 4 million people and its prevalence increases progressively after the age of 45 years. OA is currently considered not only a degenerative disorder related to aging and biomechanical alterations, but also a pathological condition characterized by inflammation and immune imbalance within the joint.

Materials and Methods

We retrospectively analyzed 46 patients treated at our Pain Therapy outpatient clinic between January 2023 and January 2024. The mean age was 50 years (range 42–75 years), including 30 males and 16 females. Patients with advanced OA eligible for prosthetic surgery were excluded, while subjects with mild to moderate intra-articular lesions were selected.

Before treatment, all patients underwent three weekly intra-articular infiltrations with local anesthetic and triamcinolone depot 40 mg to reduce joint inflammation. Bone marrow mononuclear cells were harvested from the iliac crest under sterile conditions and local anesthesia (Figure 1). Approximately 60 mL of bone marrow aspirate was collected using a trocar inserted into the cancellous bone.

The Sepax Cell Processing System was used intraoperatively to isolate and concentrate mononuclear cells by removing erythrocytes and plasma. After approximately 15 minutes of processing, mesenchymal stem cells suspended in plasma were obtained and subsequently injected intra-articularly.

All patients received antibiotic prophylaxis with cefazolin 2 g preoperatively and were advised to avoid sports activities for one week after the procedure.

Results

No major postoperative complications were observed, including severe pain, edema, surgical-site infection, or ecchymosis at the harvesting site. However, patients reported a transient sensation of joint heaviness lasting approximately 15 days.

Clinical and radiological follow-up was performed after 9 months using the I.K.D.C. questionnaire, the V.A.S. pain scale, and MRI evaluation. Eleven patients (24%) experienced a pain reduction greater than 50%.

Conclusions

Intra-articular administration of autologous mesenchymal stem cells represents a promising alternative to high-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) infiltrations in the treatment of mild to moderate OA.

Mesenchymal preparations may reduce joint inflammation and promote cartilage regeneration. Despite the limited follow-up, our preliminary results are consistent with current literature and demonstrate that the procedure is safe, feasible, and associated with encouraging clinical outcomes.

Ethics Committee approval was obtained (or formally requested, as required by local regulations) before study initiation. Written informed consent for participation and publication of anonymized clinical data was obtained from all patients.

Informed Consent Statement

Written informed consent was obtained from all patients prior to treatment and for the anonymous use of clinical data for scientific and publication purposes.

A76 Ultrasound-guided brachial plexus block in Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease: challenging the avoidance of regional anesthesia in peripheral neuropathy

E. Cianciola1, G. Monaco1, A. Salerno1, A. Cianciola2, N. Cianciola2, F. Saturno1

1Asl Salerno, Sapri, Italy; 2Unicamillus, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: E. Cianciola

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A76

Background

Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (CMT) is the most common inherited peripheral neuropathy, with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 2,500 individuals. It is characterized by progressive demyelination of peripheral nerves, resulting in distal muscle weakness, atrophy, sensory impairment, and skeletal deformities.

Anesthetic management in patients with CMT remains controversial. Regional anesthesia has traditionally been avoided because of concerns regarding possible worsening of pre-existing neurological deficits, although current evidence supporting this risk is limited. Conversely, general anesthesia may expose these patients to unpredictable responses to neuromuscular blocking agents and potential metabolic complications.

Case Presentation

A 47-year-old woman with a long-standing diagnosis of CMT was referred for progressive deterioration of hand function, including reduced grip strength and inability to extend the fingers. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and she was not receiving chronic pharmacological therapy.

Physical examination revealed severe bilateral atrophy of the extensor and intrinsic hand muscles, including the thenar eminence, associated with tendon retraction and a characteristic claw hand deformity. The patient had previously undergone multiple orthopedic procedures for pes equinovarus and required braces and a cane for ambulation.

The patient was scheduled for reconstructive surgery of the right hand. Following multidisciplinary evaluation and discussion with the patient, a regional anesthetic approach was selected. Standard monitoring was applied in the operating room, and minimal sedation was administered with intravenous midazolam (2 mg).

An ultrasound-guided supraclavicular brachial plexus block was performed using levobupivacaine 0.5% (25 mg) combined with mepivacaine 2% (300 mg). Complete sensory blockade was achieved within 15 minutes, allowing surgery to proceed without conversion to general anesthesia.

The surgical procedure included Zancolli lasso technique, opponensplasty, and transfer of the extensor indicis proprius tendon. Total operative time was 45 minutes, with stable intraoperative hemodynamic and respiratory conditions throughout the procedure. No perioperative complications occurred.

Postoperative recovery was uneventful. No neurological worsening, respiratory impairment, or new sensory deficits were observed. The patient was discharged 24 hours after surgery with preserved baseline neurological status and satisfactory postoperative analgesia.

Discussion

The use of regional anesthesia in patients with hereditary neuropathies remains debated. The “double-crush” hypothesis suggests that already compromised nerves may be more vulnerable to secondary injury; however, clinical evidence supporting this concern in the setting of peripheral nerve blockade remains scarce.

In contrast, general anesthesia in patients with CMT may present relevant challenges, including increased sensitivity to non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents and the potential risk of hyperkalemia associated with succinylcholine administration. Avoidance of these pharmacological risks may represent a significant advantage of regional techniques.

The introduction of ultrasound guidance has significantly improved the safety profile of peripheral nerve blocks by enabling real-time visualization of neural structures, needle advancement, and local anesthetic spread, thereby increasing procedural precision and potentially reducing the risk of intraneural injection.

This case supports the growing evidence that ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia may represent a feasible and effective alternative to general anesthesia in selected patients with hereditary peripheral neuropathies.

Conclusions

This case demonstrates that ultrasound-guided brachial plexus block can be safely and effectively performed in patients with Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease when an individualized and carefully monitored anesthetic strategy is adopted.

Beyond technical feasibility, this experience supports a shift from precautionary avoidance toward a more balanced and patient-centered approach, in which theoretical risks are weighed against tangible clinical benefits.

Keywords

Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease; regional anesthesia; brachial plexus block; ultrasound-guided anesthesia; peripheral neuropathy.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and accompanying clinical information

A77 Use of pens in the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia refractory to other therapies: a case report

M. Caruso, M. Mura, A.M. Graziano, F. Bonadio, G. Bonadio, M. Oliviero, A. Monardo

Giovanni Paolo II Hospital, Lamezia Terme, Italy

Correspondence: M. Caruso

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A77

Background

Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most common and fearful chronic complication of Herpes Zoster infection. In young subjects it occurs in about 20% of cases, it rises up to 70% in elderly people. Neuropathic pain is usually localized in the skin region where the eruption of the vesicles has occurred, it is felt when they are healing or even a few days before their appearance and it can last several years if it isn’t adequately treated. The most affected dermatomal sites are the thoracic and trigeminal ones. The pain is more frequently continuous, very intense, disabling, stabbing, burning, exacerbated by contact and associated with hyperalgesia and allodynia due to unilateral inflammation of the cranial or spinal nerves and their ganglia caused by the neurotropic virus. Tingling and itching may also occur. PHN is associated with depression, insomnia, weight loss and severely impaired quality of life. PENS (Percutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) has proven to be an effective treatment in this condition; it consists of delivering a low-frequency electrical current through an electrode placed subcutaneously near the nerve endings in the area to be treated. It is a minimally invasive therapy indicated for chronic peripheral neuropathic pain as it acts on the afferent nociceptive pathways, reducing the transmission of the pain signal. Electric fields have also been shown to have effects on immune modulation by reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1b and IL-6 and increasing the activity of descending inhibitory pathways, both noradrenergic and serotonergic. A series of studies have demonstrated its long-term efficacy with a significant level of pain relief [1,2]. The method can be easily repeated.

Case report

The patient under examination came to our observation for continuous, unbearable, stabbing, burning, disabling pain (NRS 10), associated with hyperalgesia and allodynia in the left intercostal region with radiation to the left hemiabdomen following a Herpes Zoster infection not adequately treated. She was already undergoing treatment without benefit with Gabapentin 300 mg x 3, Lidocaine 5% medicated patches and Tapentadol 50 mg x 2 (higher dosages caused her dizziness, drowsiness and nausea). Two sessions of PENS were performed two months apart: two 10 cm electrodes were introduced under ultrasound guidance to a depth of about 1 cm from the skin surface in a medio-lateral direction and subcutaneous course parallel to the ribs at the level of T7-T9, and two electrodes were introduced at the subcutaneous level anteriorly on the distal extension of the previous ones. Gradual stimulation was performed starting from the patient’s perception up to the maximum value of 20 mA for a total treatment time of one hour. No periprocedural complications. The patient found a partial benefit after just a few days from the first session with improvement in painful symptoms (NRS 5–6) and quality of life without side effects. The painful area gradually reduced in extension and oral therapy was gradually tapered off.

Conclusion

PENS is very effective in pain reduction and improvement of quality of life in 74-year-old patient affected by PHN; it has no side effects.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A78 Efficacy of high-frequency peripheral neuromodulation (BioWave pens) in refractory classical trigeminal neuralgia: a case report

M. Candriella1, A. Berardi2, A. Napoli2, L. Cancelliere1, E. Caputo1, R. Vaschetto3, A. Sala1

1Simple Departmental Unit of Pain Therapy, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy; 2Postgraduate School in Anesthesia, Intensive Care, Pain Medicine and Critical Care, UPO University, Novara, Italy; 3Simple Departmental Unit of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy

Correspondence: M. Candriella

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A78

Background

Classical trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by paroxysmal lancinating pain and severe allodynia, often resulting from hyperexcitability of second-order neurons. Standard clinical management includes gabapentinoids and antidepressants; however, these medications are frequently poorly tolerated in geriatric patients. Among interventional approaches, Pulsed Radiofrequency (PRF) is widely employed because of its non-ablative neuromodulatory effect, although its efficacy is often time-limited, with significant recurrence rates.

Percutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (PENS) using percutaneous electrodes with microneedles has emerged as a promising alternative. Unlike conventional TENS, PENS generate a low-frequency electrical field within deep tissues. This mechanism overcomes cutaneous impedance and induces a hyperpolarization-mediated conduction block, thereby inhibiting nociceptive transmission along A-delta and C fibers.

Case Presentation

An 89-year-old male patient was referred to the Pain Medicine Unit in 2016 with a diagnosis of right-sided classical trigeminal neuralgia involving the V2 and V3 branches, persisting for approximately 20 years. The clinical presentation was characterized by spontaneous lancinating pain crises and attacks triggered by minimal tactile stimuli.

The patient’s medical history included arterial hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral hypoglycemic agents, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). No drug allergies were reported.

In 2006, the patient had undergone microvascular decompression surgery according to the Scarpetta technique.

The patient proved refractory to multiple pharmacological treatment lines, including opioids, gabapentinoids, antidepressants, and neurotrophic supplements, and was currently taking pregabalin 50 mg in the morning and 75 mg in the evening. More recently, pulsed radiofrequency treatment had been performed on the second and third peripheral trigeminal branches using E-dose technology. This intervention provided symptomatic relief lasting only 30 days, followed by rapid recurrence of baseline pain, with an NRS score of 8 and a DN4 (Douleur Neuropathique 4) score of 5/10.

Given the patient’s advanced age and frailty, further surgical intervention was ruled out, and a sequential non-invasive neuromodulation protocol was initiated.

Treatment was started using PENS (device for hospital using). Percutaneous micro-needle electrodes designed to overcome cutaneous impedance were applied in monopolar configuration over the right Gasserian ganglion, with a dispersive electrode placed over the right scapular region. The session lasted 30 minutes, with progressive increase of stimulation intensity up to 22.5%.

To prevent the rapid recurrence previously observed following PRF, the protocol was subsequently continued at home using the portable PENS device equipped with reusable monopolar electrodes without microneedles.

The patient underwent daily 30-minute sessions for 15 consecutive days. A second in-hospital treatment was then administered (maximum intensity achieved: 19.5%), followed by an additional 15-day home-treatment cycle.

After the initial 15 days, the patient reported complete disappearance of painful paroxysms. Clinical parameters demonstrated a reduction of the NRS score from 8 to 0. Previously documented allodynia was no longer elicitable by tactile stimulation, and the patient resumed normal eating and speaking without the need for rescue analgesics. No adverse events or dermatological complications were reported.

Conclusion

The combined PENS protocol proved superior to pulsed radiofrequency in this case of severe classical trigeminal neuralgia. The observed success may be attributed to the unique kinetics of the PENS signal: whereas PRF provides a localized intermittent stimulus, the continuity ensured by the PENS system may maintain a persistently elevated neural activation threshold.

The sinusoidal waveform technology also provides superior tissue penetration, proving effective in cases where low-frequency currents are poorly tolerated. The absence of symptoms after two decades of chronic disease suggests that continuous peripheral neuromodulation may induce reversible neural plasticity within the trigeminal system.

Furthermore, this approach reduces pharmacological burden, a critical safety consideration in very elderly patients.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A79 Feasibility and applicability of telemedicine follow-up of patients undergoing radiofrequency procedures for pain management and analysis of clinical outcomes: preliminary data from a prospective observational pilot study

M. Candriella1, A. Berardi2, A. Napoli2, L. Cancelliere1, E. Caputo1, R. Vaschetto3, A. Sala1

1Simple Departmental Unit of Pain Therapy, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy; 2Postgraduate School in Anesthesia, Intensive Care, Pain Medicine and Critical Care, University of Eastern Piedmont (UPO), Novara, Italy; 3Simple Departmental Unit of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy

Correspondence: M. Candriella

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A79

Background

Telemedicine represents an increasingly widespread tool in the management of acute and chronic diseases, with evidence of non-inferiority compared to in-person evaluations in specific clinical settings (1). However, in the field of pain management, limitations persist regarding the standardization of protocols and a lack of data on the application of remote monitoring (2,3).

Objectives

This study aims to evaluate the feasibility and patient satisfaction of a telehealth follow-up program for patients suffering from chronic pain who underwent radiofrequency (RF) treatment. The secondary objective is to assess post-procedural clinical improvement.

Materials and Methods

This prospective observational study is conducted on adult patients (age > 18 years) undergoing interventional pain procedures using continuous or pulsed radiofrequency on any anatomical site. Patients are enrolled during the pre-admission phase and followed via telehealth visit approximately 30 days after the procedure. The protocol includes subsequent evaluations at 3, 6, and 12 months.

Collected data include demographic characteristics, Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) scores (baseline, follow-up at 24 h, 7 days, 15 days, and 30 days), and rescue analgesic therapy. Satisfaction and usability are evaluated through a validated English-language questionnaire (TUQ - Telemedicine Usability Questionnaire).

Written informed consent is obtained for each patient for both the RF procedure and study data collection. According to current institutional policy, specific consent for performing the telehealth visit is no longer required, as it is equivalent to an in-person follow-up visit. Telehealth follow-up visits are conducted using the ‘Fenix Televisita’ application already in use at AOU Maggiore della Carità in Novara.

Upon discharge after pain procedure, patients receive: discharge papers with the telemedicine appointment, a brief instruction manual, and a referral for the telehealth service. The link for the telehealth connection is sent automatically to the email address provided by the patient upon acceptance of the referral by the CUP of the Piedmont Region.

Results

Currently, 6 patients (mean age 62.5 years, range 39–81 years) treated with radiofrequency techniques have been enrolled. The telemedicine program proved feasible in 100% of cases, with a 30-day follow-up completion rate of 100% (Table 1- Fig. 1)

Patients reported a high degree of satisfaction (mean TUQ score 6.73 ± 0.32 SD). Specifically, all patients assigned the maximum score (7) for the time saved by not traveling to the hospital and for the ability to communicate effectively (Table 2).

Regarding the secondary objective, a significant reduction in pain intensity was recorded: the mean NRS score decreased from 7.5 ± 1.38 SD at baseline to 1.17 ± 1.47 SD at 30 days, confirming the clinical benefits of the procedures. Four patients reported taking rescue analgesics only once (Table 1).

Discussion and Conclusions

Although the study is still in its early stages and larger sample sizes are needed to confirm these findings, the implementation of telehealth follow-up proved highly feasible and applicable in the field of pain management (4). Technology did not represent a barrier, but rather a facilitator of the care pathway. The results support the integration of mHealth models to optimize follow-up care, ensuring high quality standards and reducing the logistical impact on patients (5).

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A80 Use of the NECPAL assessment tool to identify palliative care needs in patients with heart failure

A. Rea, A. Frenez, A. Busnardo, F. Ganzaroli, G. Scaramuzzo, L. Gulmini, C.A. Volta, S. Spadaro

Translational Medicine, University of Ferrara, Italy

Correspondence: A. Rea

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A80

Background

Palliative care represents an active, comprehensive, and multidimensional approach aimed at people of all ages affected by severe illnesses characterized by significant health-related suffering, particularly in advanced stages of disease. Its primary goal is to improve patients’ quality of life, while also supporting their families and caregivers through careful management of symptoms and psychological, social, and spiritual needs.

Despite increasing evidence of its benefits, numerous studies highlight a marked discrepancy between the need for palliative care and actual access to dedicated services, especially among non-oncological patients, who are frequently underrepresented in palliative care pathways.

In this context, the present study aims to evaluate the need for palliative care in patients affected by heart failure, a chronic condition with a high clinical and prognostic impact. The analysis was conducted in three different care settings: the cardiology ward, the cardiac intensive care unit (CICU), and the outpatient heart failure clinic, in order to explore the different clinical and healthcare characteristics of patients and identify possible critical issues in the early recognition of palliative care needs.

Methods

The main assessment tool used was the NECPAL instrument, developed in 2013, which is practical and easy to apply for the early identification of patients with advanced chronic diseases and limited life expectancy who may require palliative care interventions.

NECPAL is suitable for all healthcare and social care settings, combining a quantitative, qualitative, and multifactorial assessment that includes the “Surprise Question” (SQ), severity and progression parameters, geriatric syndromes, emotional aspects, comorbidities, healthcare resource utilization, and disease-specific indicators for selected conditions.

To complement the comprehensive assessment provided by the NECPAL tool, standardized instruments such as the Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) and the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) were also employed. These tools represent valuable supports for conducting a multidimensional evaluation of the patient’s health status and functional capacity.

Results

The analysis showed that 32.9% of patients (23/70) were NECPAL-positive; moreover, all patients with a positive Surprise Question were also NECPAL-positive. Despite this, none of the identified patients had been included in a palliative care pathway, except for two patients who had been referred to palliative care due to a previous oncological disease.

Another finding emerging from the study is that advanced age, greater frailty, the presence of multiple comorbidities, and poorer functional status were significantly associated with NECPAL positivity (Figure 1 – Table 1). However, defining the need for palliative care remains complex and requires an individualized assessment. Tools such as the Surprise Question and parameter Q2_2, in which clinicians are asked whether they consider palliative care appropriate for the patient, include a subjective component dependent on the clinician’s experience, thereby limiting the objectivity and generalizability of the NECPAL tool.

NECPAL demonstrated a high negative predictive value, proving effective in identifying patients who do not require palliative care, but showed low specificity, with a tendency to overestimate patients at risk. While this characteristic may facilitate earlier integration of palliative care, it may also lead to challenges in resource management and allocation.

The main limitations of the study include the small sample size, the subjective component in the assessment of the Surprise Question and Q2_2, and the lack of direct patient involvement.

Conclusions

The study demonstrates that NECPAL is a useful tool for the early identification of heart failure patients with palliative care needs. Test positivity was associated with advanced age, greater frailty, the presence of comorbidities, and higher mortality. However, NECPAL should not be considered a purely prognostic tool and must be integrated with other clinical assessment instruments; furthermore, adequate healthcare professional training is required. Strengthening community-based healthcare networks and increasing the availability of professionals dedicated to palliative care is also necessary, in order to support specialists both in hospital and outpatient settings.

A multidimensional and multidisciplinary approach remains essential to ensure appropriate, personalized, and timely care for critically ill patients. Nevertheless, at present, cardiology patients who could potentially benefit from a palliative care pathway are still frequently not identified by dedicated services.

A81 Clinical and organizational impact of a structured in-hospital specialist palliative care service: a three-year retrospective analysis of 2,220 consultations

D. Marelli1, M. Romelli1,2, S. Amati1, C. Cornali2, D. Martinelli2, E. Sosta2, M. Zigliani2, C. Chelazzi1,2

1Department of Medical and Surgical Specialties, Radiological Sciences, and Public Health, University of Brescia, Italy; 2Complex Unit of Palliative Care and Home Care (ADI), ASST Spedali Civili of Brescia, Italy

Correspondence: D. Marelli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A81

Background and Aims

The integration of in-hospital palliative care teams is a strategic priority to address clinical complexity and optimize hospital resource allocation. This retrospective pre-post study compared an external palliative care consultation model active in 2022 with a structured in-hospital specialist palliative care service implemented from January 2023 onward. The study aimed to evaluate the impact of this organizational integration on referral timing, patient clinical characteristics, and discharge outcomes.

Methods

A retrospective analysis was conducted on 2,220 patients evaluated between January 2022 and December 2024. Patients were categorized by year of consultation: 2022 (N=472), 2023 (N=685), and 2024 (N=1,063). Key metrics included latency (days from admission to first palliative care referral), diagnosis (oncological vs. non-oncological), Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), and discharge outcomes.

This study was conducted as part of standard care activities and in accordance with Good Clinical Practice and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the Local Ethics Committee (protocol no. 0032664/25).

Results

The service experienced a 125% increase in annual consultation volume by 2024. Median referral latency decreased from 10 days (IQR 5–18) in 2022 to 7 days (IQR 3–15) in 2024 (p<0.001, Figure 1). Latency data were unavailable for 475 patients (21.4% of the cohort).

The proportion of non-oncological patients increased from 22.5% in 2022 to 30.4% in 2024, while median KPS remained low across years (40% median). Discharges to hospice nearly doubled, increasing from 14.8% in 2022 to 27.5% in 2024. Discharge to home palliative care increased from 20% in 2022 to 29% in 2024, while the proportion of patients dying in hospital decreased from 18.0% to 15.8%.

Conclusions

The implementation of a structured in-hospital specialist palliative care service was associated with earlier referral and improved transition toward hospice and home palliative care services. Although patients remained severely functionally impaired throughout the study period, the progressive increase in non-oncological referrals suggests a broader integration of palliative care within hospital practice.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A82 Intrathecal drug delivery: not last resort. Impact on symptom burden within an integrated pain and palliative care model

G. Armento1, I. Lanfranca1, C. Rabanal1, L. Guido1, M. Allodi1, G. Di Nardo1, E. Dimo2, V.A. Guardamagna1

1European Institute of Oncology (IRCCS), Milan, Italy; 2Campus Bio-Medico University of Rome, Italy

Correspondence: G. Armento

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A82

Background

Refractory cancer pain is associated with high symptom burden, opioid-related toxicity, and progressive functional impairment. Although intrathecal drug delivery (IDD) is traditionally considered a pain-focused intervention, its impact on multidimensional symptom burden and clinical complexity in advanced cancer patients remains poorly explored in real-world settings.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective real-world analysis in a comprehensive cancer center (IRCCS), within an integrated Pain Therapy and Palliative Care Unit. Data collection was embedded in routine clinical care within a dedicated integrated supportive care pathway.

Data collection was embedded in routine clinical care within a dedicated integrated supportive care pathway.

Patients undergoing intrathecal drug delivery (IDD) implantation for refractory cancer pain were retrospectively selected if complete clinical documentation was available at baseline and at 24 hours, 48 hours, 7 days, 14 days, 30 days, and 60 days after implantation.

Clinical data were extracted from structured electronic medical records specifically designed for comprehensive cancer pain assessment and longitudinal symptom monitoring. The institutional chart format allows multidimensional pain profiling beyond pain intensity alone, including pain mechanisms, temporal characteristics, breakthrough pain features, analgesic response, and functional impact, according to clinically oriented cancer pain assessment models.

Pain intensity was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), systemic opioid consumption was converted into oral morphine equivalents (MME), and symptom burden was evaluated using the Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS). Baseline performance status, oncologic history, and algological pain phenotype were also collected.

All patients provided informed consent for the use of anonymized clinical data for research purposes.

Results

Thirty-eight patients with refractory cancer pain were included. At baseline, patients presented with severe pain (median NRS 9) and high systemic opioid exposure (median 260 mg/day MME).

Following IDD implantation, pain intensity significantly decreased (median NRS 4.5; p < 0.0001), with 65.8% of patients achieving > or = 30% pain reduction and 47.4% achieving > or =50% reduction.

A marked opioid-sparing effect was observed, with median opioid consumption decreasing to 50 mg/day MME (p < 0.0001)-Figure 1-. Overall, 78.9% of patients achieved > or = 30% opioid reduction, while 31.6% discontinued systemic opioids entirely.

Symptom burden improved across multiple ESAS domains, including fatigue, anxiety, depression, drowsiness, nausea, appetite loss, and overall well-being (Figure 2).

The median number of adjuvant analgesic medications decreased from 2 to 1 (p = 0.024).

Clinical benefit was observed even in patients with poor baseline performance status, including bedridden patients and subjects with ECOG > or =2.

Conclusions

Within an integrated Pain Therapy and Palliative Care model, intrathecal drug delivery provided clinically meaningful benefits extending beyond analgesia alone.

In advanced cancer patients with high symptom burden and complex pain phenotypes, IDD was associated with reduced opioid exposure, improvement in multidimensional symptoms, and reduced treatment complexity, supporting its role as a comprehensive supportive care intervention in real-world oncologic practice.

IDD may represent a strategy for pharmacological de-intensification in frail advanced cancer patients with high symptom burden.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A83 Identification of the potential donor outside the intensive care unit: the model of ARNAS Garibaldi-Catania

S. Cefalù1, I.G. Bonanno1, D.E. DI Stefano1, A. Leuzzi1, G. Bufalino1, A. Salice1, L.S.A. Muscarà1, F. Tornitore1, A. Pecora1, G. Zuccaro1, M. Falcone1, C. Geraci1, R. Nicoletti1, B. Longo1, A.D. Vilardi1, A. Scafidi3, G. Panarello2, G. Burgio2, G. Battaglia3, B. Piazza4

1Arnas Garibaldi, Catania, Italy; 2ISMETT – Mediterranean Institute for Transplantation (IRCCS), Palermo, Italy; 3CRT, Sicily, Italy; 4ASP-Palermo, Termini Imerese, Italy

Correspondence: S. Cefalù

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A83

Background

Donation after Circulatory Death (DCD) has become a fundamental resource to expand the organ donor pool for transplantation. Type 3 (Controlled) DCD is performed following an expected cardiac arrest (CA) after the withdrawal of life-sustaining treatments (WLST).

Intensive Care Oriented to Organ Donation (ICOD) is defined as the initiation or continuation of intensive care (e.g., intubation and mechanical ventilation) in patients with conditions where intensive treatment has been deemed futile for the patient’s prognosis.

ICOD incorporates the option of organ donation into end-of-life care, in accordance with the patient’s wishes and values. Potential Type 3 DCD donors can therefore be identified in Intensive Care Units (ICU), stroke units, neurology, neurosurgery, coronary care units, medical wards, and emergency departments.

A primary task of the Hospital Procurement Coordination (COP) is training, which is essential to maintain an efficient procurement network, particularly within the ICOD framework.

Purpose

The aim of this study was to compare the number of DCD procedures before and after the implementation of procurement activities outside the ICUs at ARNAS Garibaldi in Catania. This included the admission of patients specifically for ICOD to verify whether there was a significant increase in organ procurement following the start of these activities.

Materials and Methods

We analyzed the number of DCD procurements performed at ARNAS Garibaldi from 2023 to 2026 (data updated to February 28, 2026).

Starting from mid-2024, the Hospital Transplant Coordination (COP) at ARNAS Garibaldi implemented a comprehensive training and awareness program. This initiative targeted not only the internal ICU staff but also extended to other clinical departments, focusing specifically on DCD and ICOD protocols. This was achieved through annual corporate courses and ‘in-house’ training sessions at the Emergency Department and Neurology departments, conducted by the COP team.

Patients were admitted to the ICU after verifying their donation status in the National Transplant Information System (SIT) or through family interviews conducted by the COP staff, following referrals from ward physicians or intensivists, in compliance with SIAARTI (Italian Society of Anesthesia, Analgesia, Resuscitation, and Intensive Care) guidelines on ICOD.

The medical team responsible for the decision to limit treatments was always distinct from the team exploring donation eligibility; the latter was exclusively managed by the COP members.

The data shows a significant increase in DCD donations from the beginning of 2025 to the present. As shown in Figure 1 and Table 1. The number of DCD procedures in 2025 was 8, representing an increase of over 150% compared to 2024 (3 DCD) and 2023 (3 DCD).

Conclusions

The identification of the potential donor is the cornerstone of the donation and transplantation process. The possibility of organ and tissue donation must be an integral part of the hospital’s end-of-life care pathway. Systematically considering eligibility for controlled DCD following the decision to limit treatment in the ICU, combined with ICOD protocols, has proven to be a successful strategy in expanding the donor pool at ARNAS Garibaldi in Catania.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A84 The prophylactic use of tranexamic acid in orthotopic liver transplantation: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial

A. Prato Schmidt1, E. S. Martinelli2, V. C. de Moura1, M.J. C. Carmona3, L.M. Malboussion3

1Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre (HCPA), Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Porto Alegre, Brazil; 2Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Porto Alegre, Brazil; 3Hospital das Clínicas, University of São Paulo, Brazil

Correspondence: A. Prato Schmidt

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A84

Background

Perioperative bleeding in orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT) is primarily driven by hyperfibrinolysis and complex coagulopathy in end-stage liver disease. Tranexamic acid (TXA), a potent antifibrinolytic agent, reduces bleeding in many surgical settings, but its prophylactic efficacy and safety in OLT remain debated.

Methods

This prospective, multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 138 adult patients undergoing OLT at two tertiary centers in Brazil. Patients were randomized to receive TXA (10 mg/kg bolus followed by 1 mg/kg/h infusion until skin closure) or equivalent 0.9% saline (placebo). The primary outcome was the incidence of major bleeding within 24 hours of surgical incision (composite endpoint: hemoglobin drop more than 4 g/dL or postoperative Hb lower than 8 g/dL with transfusion, more than 4 units RBC transfused, or surgical reintervention). Secondary outcomes included RBC transfusion requirements, hospital length of stay, thromboembolic events, infections, and mortality. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrollment. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04753151) and ReBEC (RBR-3jwv5kh).

Results

Major bleeding occurred in 48.5% of the TXA group versus 62.9% in the placebo group (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.56–1.04; P=0.09). In prespecified subgroup analyses, TXA significantly reduced major bleeding in patients with MELD 3.0 lower than 9 (14.2% vs 50.0%; P=0.006) and Child-Pugh class A (17.2% vs 50.0%; P=0.007). The TXA group required fewer intraoperative RBC transfusions (median 0 [IQR 0–3] vs 2 [IQR 0–5] units; P=0.008) and had shorter hospital length of stay (median 20 [14–31] vs 25 [18–37] days; P=0.04). MDRO colonization was lower in the TXA group (23.5% vs 42.9%; P=0.02). No differences were observed in thromboembolic complications, seizures, graft dysfunction, or 30-day mortality.

Conclusions

Prophylactic low-dose TXA did not significantly reduce the overall incidence of major bleeding in OLT. However, it was associated with reduced RBC transfusion requirements, shorter hospital stay, and lower MDRO colonization, with greater benefits in lower-risk patients (low MELD and Child-Pugh A), without increasing thromboembolic risk. These findings support selective use of TXA in less severe liver disease and justify larger multicenter confirmatory trials.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A85 Prehabilitation in liver transplant candidates: development and implementation of a structured multidisciplinary program

T. Buzzigoli1, G. Pratesi2, A. Fortini2,3, F. Forfori1, G.L. Biancofiore2

1School of Anesthesiology, Department of Surgical, Medical, Molecular, and Critical Area Pathology, University of Pisa, Italy; 2Department of Anaesthesia and Transplant Intensive Care, Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria Pisana, Pisa, Italy; 3Department of Anaesthesia, Nuovo Ospedale Apuano, Azienda USL Toscana Nord Ovest, Massa, Italy

Correspondence: T. Buzzigoli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A85

Background

Patients with advanced liver disease frequently present with frailty, sarcopenia, malnutrition, and impaired functional capacity, all of which negatively affect perioperative and post-transplant outcomes [1–3]. Consequently, prehabilitation has progressively gained attention as a strategy aimed at improving physical and nutritional status before liver transplantation and has recently been incorporated into ERAS recommendations for liver surgery [4]. Nevertheless, data regarding the implementation and real-world feasibility of structured multidisciplinary prehabilitation programs in liver transplant candidates remain scarce [6,7].

Methods

A prospective, multidisciplinary, open-label, single-arm study was conducted on adult patients assessed for liver transplantation at our center between October 2022 and the December 2025. All adult patients (age above 18 years old) with liver disease regardless of etiology were enrolled; exclusion criteria included very high MELD score, decompensated disease, untreated varices, significant recurrent paracentesis, encephalopathy, major hematochemical or hemodynamic abnormalities, cardiological contraindications, history of recurrent falls, and combined multi-organ transplant candidacy. The prehabilitation program consisted of an in-person baseline assessment — integrating physical therapy and nutritional evaluation — followed by remote follow-up contacts every two weeks until transplantation, de-listment, or death. Frailty was assessed using the Liver Frailty Index® (LFI) [5]; physical activity was measured with the IPAQ-SF at baseline (T0), 15 days (T15), and 45 days (T45) post-enrollment. Adherence was defined as compliant when greater or equal than 66%. Safety was evaluated as the number of exercise-induced adverse events. Patient satisfaction was assessed via a validated post-operative questionnaire. Informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Results

During the first two and a half years of implementation, 560 patients were enrolled (Figure 1). Only 7% of enrolled patients lived within the hospital catchment area, whereas the vast majority originated from outside the Pisa area, further supporting the remote follow-up model adopted. At baseline, 77.9% of patients were classified as frail or pre-frail (mean LFI: 3.87 ± 0.52), and 52% were inactive according to the IPAQ-SF. Among the patients who initiated or completed follow-up, mean adherence consistently exceeded the predefined 66% acceptability threshold. No exercise-induced adverse events were recorded. Patients classified as inactive or sufficiently active at baseline demonstrated a statistically significant increase in physical activity between T0 and T15 (p<0.001), maintained at T45 (Figures 2, 3 and 4). Post-operative questionnaires revealed that 85% of respondents deemed the program adequate without modifications.

Conclusions

The prehabilitation program proved appropriate, feasible, safe, effective in increasing preoperative physical activity levels, and well-received by patients. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first multidisciplinary prehabilitation pathway for liver transplant candidates implemented in Italy, offering a replicable model for other national and international transplant centers.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A86 Organization of the hospital procurement coordination (COP) in a large hospital: the ARNAS Garibaldi Catania model

I.G. Bonanno1, D.E. Di Stefano1, S. Cefalù1, G. Bufalino1, A. Leuzzi1, B. Longo1, A. Salice1, C. Geraci1, R. Nicoletti1, A. Vilardi1, G. Burgio2, G. Panarello2, A. Scafidi3, G. Battaglia3, F. Tornitore1, A. Pecora1, G. Zuccaro1, M. Falcone1, l. Muscarà1, B. Piazza4

1Arnas Garibaldi, Catania, Italy; 2ISMETT, Palermo, Italy; 3Sicilian Regional Transplant Center, Palermo, Italy; 4ASP Palermo, Termini Imerese, Italy

Correspondence: I.G. Bonanno

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A86

Background

The Hospital Procurement Coordination (COP) is the operational unit responsible for coordinating, managing, and optimizing the entire organ and tissue donation process within a healthcare facility. It is led by the Local Coordinator, who reports directly to the Medical Health Management (DSA).

Training is a strategic pillar of the COP: staff must possess advanced technical and interpersonal skills, maintained through continuous professional development.

The use of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) in the context of Donation after Circulatory Death (DCD) is a fundamental advanced technique to preserve organ function post-cardiac death and prior to transplantation, minimizing ischemic injury.

This study aims to demonstrate how the unique organizational structure of the COP at ARNAS Garibaldi in Catania has led to a significant increase in procurement activity from 2016 to the present. The cornerstones of the ARNAS Garibaldi COP activity are the continuous training of its personnel and close collaboration with centers of excellence.

Materials and Methods

The COP of ARNAS Garibaldi, a 614-bed hospital facility acting as a hub for neuroradiology, STROKE, neurosurgery, and emergency medicine, oversees procurement for two adult Intensive Care Units (ICUs) (totaling 28 beds), one Pediatric ICU (4 beds), one Hospice unit, two mortuaries, and all other clinical departments.

The Coordination Office has a dedicated onsite headquarters. In May 2021, the Simple Operational Unit of Organ and Tissue Donation Procurement was established, assigned to the Local Coordinator (LC) with a 34% hourly commitment, supported by the Hospital Committee for Organ and Tissue Donation.

The COP team consists of 7 Anesthesia and Intensive Care physicians, 1 Nursing Coordinator, 6 Registered Nurses, 2 Psychologists, and 2 Perfusionists.. Each member has dedicated hours, duties, and institutional objectives focused on organ procurement and donation. Shift assignments are overseen by the LC in collaboration with the Directors of the Anesthesia and ICU Departments to ensure 24/7 availability for procurement and donation procedures.

Four institutional procedures were formalized for Donation after Brain Death (DBD), DCD, DCD II Lung, and Tissues, along with protocols for End-of-Life Management and family communication.

The COP is activated by clinical departments via a dedicated short-code number. The Nursing Coordinator performs daily monitoring of patients with brain injury in the ICU, Emergency Department (DEA), and STROKE unit, as well as monitoring the mortuary.

Staff are continuously engaged in training to maintain high-level competencies. Furthermore, they promote training initiatives for all ARNAS personnel.

In this context, a partnership was established with ISMETT (Mediterranean Institute for Transplantation and Highly Specialized Therapies) in Palermo for ECMO training: since 2022, 6 doctors and 6 nurses have completed 15-day clinical rotations at ISMETT.

In 2022, ARNAS Garibaldi acquired an ECMO machine for the Anesthesia and ICU Department and hired two perfusionists.

From 2021 to date, 21 DCD III donations have been performed: 11 in collaboration with ISMETT and 10 independently.

Thanks to the expertise gained in Regional Normothermic Perfusion (RNP) via ECMO for DCD donations, the Garibaldi Centro ICU staff successfully utilized Venovenous (VV) ECMO as rescue therapy for patients with ARDS, achieving excellent outcomes.

Additionally, collaboration with the Veneto Eye Bank Foundation (Mestre) allowed for the specialized training of a COP physician in corneal harvesting.

Conclusions

Our study demonstrates the importance of a functional COP organization, which has led to optimal results in expanding the donor pool and increasing organ procurement at ARNAS Garibaldi (Figure 1).

We emphasize the necessity of continuous staff training, which enabled clinical autonomy in managing DCD III ECMO and corneal harvesting. Furthermore, this training facilitated the extension of ECMO beyond procurement, integrating it into international protocols for treating ICU patients with ARDS.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A87 Hemodynamic monitoring in liver transplantation: LiDCOTM versus pulmonary artery catheterization

P. Balagna, C. Stratta, C. Melchiorri

University Hospital “City of Health and Science” Anesthesia and Intensive Care 2, Molinette Hospital, Turin, Italy

Correspondence: P. Balagna

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A87

Background

Liver transplantation is a surgical procedure of extreme complexity, characterized by marked hemodynamic instability. This instability stems from the pathophysiology of cirrhosis, which is defined by a hyperdynamic state and reduced systemic vascular resistance. In this clinical context, accurate hemodynamic monitoring is essential to guide fluid therapy and pharmacological interventions.

Objectives

The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical agreement and interchangeability between two different methods of cardiac output (CO) monitoring during liver transplantation: the pulmonary artery catheter (PAC - Swan-Ganz), the traditional but highly invasive gold standard, and the LiDCO™ system, a minimally invasive method based on pulse power analysis of the pressure waveform. A secondary objective involved the analysis of agreement in hemoglobin (Hb) measurements between the central laboratory (gold standard), arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis, and continuous non-invasive LiDCO™ monitoring.

Materials and Methods

Patients undergoing orthotopic liver transplantation at the Molinette Hospital in Turin were prospectively analyzed. Written informed consent was obtained prior to data collection. To compare cardiac output, 24 paired measurements were performed (6 patients across 4 surgical phases: incision, clamping, unclamping, and closure). Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman analysis and the calculation of Percentage Error (PE), adopting an interchangeability threshold of 30% according to the Critchley & Critchley criteria. For hemoglobin comparison, the laboratory values obtained during the four surgical phases were compared with concurrent ABG and LiDCO™ measurements.

Results

The LiDCO™ system demonstrated clinical interchangeability with the PAC during phases of surgical stability. However, under conditions of high cardiac output and rapid volemic variations (typical of reperfusion in liver transplantation), the overall Percentage Error (37.9%) suggests that the two methods are not fully interchangeable. Specifically, LiDCO™ tended to underestimate extreme values compared to PAC thermodilution. Regarding hemoglobin monitoring, the data indicate that ABG analysis is more interchangeable with laboratory results than the LiDCO™ system, which showed a wider dispersion of values and greater instability regarding point-of-care accuracy.

Conclusions

Invasive hemodynamic monitoring with the PAC remains the gold standard in the management of cirrhotic patients undergoing liver transplantation. Although LiDCO™ shows acceptable clinical agreement during stable phases, the overall Percentage Error exceeding 30% and the underestimation of extreme values limit its interchangeability with the PAC, particularly during reperfusion (Figure 1). Similarly, for hemoglobin monitoring, LiDCO™ proved useful for trend monitoring but was less accurate than ABG for clinical decisions based on single-point values.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A88 Hyperbaric oxygen therapy in pediatric carbon monoxide poisoning with beta-thalassemia trait: a case report

S. Sorrenti1, M. Ciuffreda1, E. Pisello1, C. Pellegrino2, A. Monacelli2, G. Cucè3, V. Zanon4, C. Piangatelli1, D. Galante5

1Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, AST Ancona, Fabriano (AN), Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, UNIVPM, Ancona, Italy; 3Department of Public Health, University of Messina, Italy; 4ATIP-Care, Department of Underwater and Hyperbaric Medicine, Padova, Italy; 5Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, ASL Foggia, Cerignola (FG), Italy

Correspondence: S. Sorrenti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A88

Background

Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning is a rare but potentially life-threatening condition and remains the leading cause of poisoning in developed countries. Diagnosis may be challenging because of the highly heterogeneous clinical presentation and the presence of non-specific symptoms. Coexisting conditions affecting oxygen transport and tissue oxygenation may significantly increase the risk of complications, even in cases with apparently mild intoxication. Pediatric patients represent a particularly vulnerable population due to their higher metabolic demand and reduced physiological reserve.

Case Report

A pediatric patient younger than 12 years of age, of African descent, was admitted to the Emergency Department following accidental carbon monoxide poisoning caused by prolonged exposure to a charcoal brazier in a closed environment. Medical history revealed beta-thalassemia trait without previous clinically significant manifestations. Laboratory findings showed hemoglobin values slightly below the normal range, associated with reduced mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), consistent with microcytic anemia. Carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) level at admission was 8%. The patient did not present neurological, respiratory, or cardiovascular symptoms related to acute CO poisoning.

Following interdisciplinary evaluation involving the emergency physician and the Pavia Poison Control Center, the patient was transferred to the nearest hyperbaric medicine facility. Considering the coexistence of microcytic anemia and the potential increased risk of tissue hypoxia related to impaired oxygen transport, hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) was initiated despite COHb levels below the standard pediatric treatment threshold.

HBOT was performed at 2.8 atmospheres absolute (ATA) for 23 minutes, followed by a decompression phase at 2 ATA for 50 minutes. Treatment was well tolerated, and no intra-procedural or post-procedural complications occurred. Clinical monitoring remained stable throughout hospitalization, with progressive normalization of laboratory parameters and no delayed neurological manifestations observed.

Written informed consent for publication of clinical data was obtained from the patient’s legal guardians prior to inclusion in this report.

Conclusion

Current guidelines generally recommend HBOT in pediatric carbon monoxide poisoning when COHb levels exceed 10%. However, beta-thalassemia trait may alter oxygen transport dynamics, and the coexistence of microcytic anemia with CO poisoning can significantly worsen tissue hypoxia, potentially increasing the risk of systemic and neurological complications. This case highlights how anemia may represent an additional risk factor supporting off-label HBOT indication even in patients with COHb levels below conventional thresholds. Furthermore, it underlines the importance of individualized clinical assessment and interdisciplinary collaboration in the management of complex toxicological emergencies.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A89 Transient intrahepatic portal venous gas following 33% hydrogen peroxide ingestion: a case managed without hyperbaric oxygen therapy

A. Franci1, S. Honsell2, V. Tabolli2, V. Brizzi1, A. Cardoni1, E. Cipriani1, G. Fulceri1, C. Fabiani1, C. Grillandini1, M. Orlandi1, F. Pelagatti1, F. Socci1, A. Valletta1, M. Bonizzoli1

1Emergency and Trauma Intensive Care, Careggi University Hospital (AOU Careggi), Florence, Italy; 2University of Florence – Postgraduate School in Anesthesia, Intensive Care, Critical Care and Pain Medicine, Italy

Correspondence: V. Tabolli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A89

Background

Ingestion of concentrated hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) may cause caustic gastrointestinal injury and intravascular gas formation, including portal venous gas and systemic gas embolism [1,2]. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is commonly considered in patients with neurological manifestations or evidence of systemic embolization [3,4]. However, the management of isolated portal venous gas without neurological involvement remains controversial.

Case report

A 59-year-old woman accidentally ingested a small amount of 33% H2O2 after mistaking it for water mixed with an orange soft drink. She immediately spat out the liquid and contacted emergency medical services. At presentation, she was clinically stable, neurologically intact, and reported mild epigastric discomfort with two episodes of vomiting.

Laboratory testing was unremarkable except for mild elevation of aspartate aminotransferase (AST 48 U/L). Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) demonstrated intrahepatic portal venous gas with periportal edema, without spleno-porto-mesenteric thrombosis (Figure 1). Cranial CT angiography excluded cerebral gas embolism.

Following multidisciplinary discussion involving the Poison Control Center and hyperbaric specialists, the patient was transferred to a tertiary hyperbaric-capable center for close monitoring and possible HBOT. Given the absence of neurological deficits, hemodynamic instability, or radiological evidence of systemic embolism, a watchful waiting approach was adopted. Treatment included intravenous proton pump inhibitor therapy, neurological surveillance, and prophylactic anticoagulation.

Repeat abdominal CT performed approximately 12 hours after exposure showed near-complete resolution of portal venous gas (Figure 2). The patient remained asymptomatic during 72 hours of observation and was discharged after normalization of liver enzymes.

Conclusions

Accidental ingestion of concentrated H2O2 may result in portal venous gas even in minimally symptomatic patients. Early abdominal CT and cranial imaging are essential to assess the extent of injury and exclude systemic embolism.

In clinically stable patients without neurological manifestations, conservative management with close monitoring in a hyperbaric-capable center may represent a safe strategy, reserving HBOT for cases with clinical deterioration or evidence of systemic gas embolism.

Consent to publish

Written informed consent for publication was obtained from the patient.

A90 Extracellular vesicle proteomics identifies candidate plasma biomarkers of acute carbon monoxide poisoning

A. Burgener1, T. Esposito1,2, F. Moretto1,2, M. Manfredi1, E. Barberis3, C. Didò3, R. Girardi1, G. Cammarota4, A. Giovanniello5, R. Vaschetto1,2

1Department of Translational Medicine, University of Eastern Piedmont, Novara, Italy; 2“Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital – Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Novara, Italy; 3Department of Science and Technological Innovation, University of Eastern Piedmont, Alessandria, Italy; 4SS. Antonio and Biagio and Cesare Arrigo University Hospital – Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Alessandria, Italy; 5Habilita I Cedri Nursing Home, Fara Novarese, Italy

Correspondence: A. Burgener

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A90

Body

Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning may lead to acute toxicity and delayed neurological sequelae. Current clinical markers, including carboxyhemoglobin levels, have limited ability to reflect biological injury or predict clinical evolution. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) may provide a circulating readout of inflammatory and vascular responses triggered by CO exposure. In this study, we analyzed plasma samples from patients with confirmed acute CO poisoning and healthy controls enrolled in a multicenter observational cohort. The study was conducted after informed consent had been obtained from all patients. Blood samples were collected before hyperbaric oxygen therapy and, when available, after treatment. EVs were isolated from plasma and subjected to untargeted proteomic analysis to identify candidate biomarkers associated with CO intoxication. Proteomic profiling quantified more than 800 proteins and identified 69 differentially represented proteins in EV preparations from CO-poisoned patients compared with controls. Among these, Leucina-rich alpha-2-glycoprotein 1 (LRG1) and Alpha-2-macroglobulin (A2M) emerged as increased and decreased candidate markers based on statistical analysis. Candidate proteins were subsequently evaluated by ELISA in circulating EV samples from the study cohort. ELISA validation confirmed their significant modulation in patients with acute CO poisoning compared with healthy controls. These findings support the presence of a distinct EV-associated molecular signature in CO intoxication and suggest that EV-derived proteins may reflect early inflammatory and tissue-response pathways activated by CO exposure. The two validated markers, LRG1 and A2M, warrant further investigation in larger cohorts to assess their potential role in risk stratification, monitoring of treatment response, and prediction of delayed neurological sequelae.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A91 Early postoperative risk stratification after cardiac surgery using MR-proADM: a preliminary single-centre study

L. Rodigari1, R. Traversi2, G. Carlin2, A.C. Trompeo1, L. Brazzi1,2, G. Montrucchio1,2

1University Hospital “City of Health and Science” of Turin, Anesthesia and Intensive Care 1U, Italy; 2University of Turin, Department of Surgical Sciences, Italy

Correspondence: G. Carlin

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A91

Background

MR-proADM is a stable biomarker of adrenomedullin1, a vasodilatory peptide involved in vascular regulation and systemic inflammatory response. Cardiac surgery and the use of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) represent a complex setting2 in which proADM and other biomarkers of inflammation could improve early postoperative risk stratification.

Objectives

To evaluate the ability of proADM and other biomarkers to predict prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay (LOS) and the postoperative complications.

Methods

This is an interim analysis of an ongoing prospective trial including patients undergoing cardiac surgery with or without CPB. Several biomarkers were measured including proADM. Blood samples were collected at ICU admission (T0) and repeated at 24 hours (T1), on postoperative day (POD) 3 (T3) and on POD 7 (T7). Complication was defined as the presence of at least one of the following events during ICU stay: Acute kidney injury; Hemorrhagic shock; infections with or without septic shock; ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke; use of temporary mechanical circulatory support; others including seizures, postoperative myocardial infarction (MI), need for open chest at the end of surgery. Univariate and multivariate logistic models were built for both outcomes. The study was approved by the local Ethics Committee and conducted in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration.

Results

87 patients were included from Mars to June 2025. proADM was associated with ICU LOS >24h, showing the best discriminative performance among the biomarkers analyzed (Table 1). In the overall population, the mean proADM level at admission (T0) was 1.69 vs 2.71 nmol/l at T1. However, in patients with prolonged ICU LOS, these values were significantly higher: at T0, MR-proADM was 2.48 vs 1.165 nmol/l in patients discharged within 24 hours (p<0.0001), while at T1 it reached 3.99 vs 1.47 nmol/l (p<0.0001). In the multivariate model, MR-proADM maintains an independent association with prolonged ICU LOS (OR 3.854 CI95% 1.451–10.234, p=0.0062) alongside SAPSII, after adjustment for preoperative disease severity, urgency of surgical procedure, and operative duration (Table 2). Regarding complications, MR-proADM, lactate, CRP, and NT-proBNP were significant in univariate analysis (Table 3). MR-proADM at T0 was significantly higher in patients who developed complications compared to those without (2.73 vs 1.39 nmol/l, p<0.0001), and this difference was further amplified at T1, with values reaching 4.58nmol/l in patients with complications vs 1.93nmol/l in those without (p<0.0001); however, in the multivariate model MR-proADM failed to reach statistical significance (OR 1.458 CI95% 0.832–2.556, p= 0.1877). only SAPSII remained an independent predictor (Table 4).

Discussion

This analysis evaluates the role of proADM and other blood biomarkers in predicting ICU LOS and the occurrence of postoperative complications in cardiac surgery. The analysis integrates biomarkers with clinical characteristics and severity scores identifying which variables independently contribute to perioperative prognosis. Regarding ICU LOS, proADM emerged as the biomarker with the best discriminative performance. In univariate analysis baseline proADM levels showed a significant association with prolonged ICU LOS. This finding is consistent with the pathophysiology of adrenomedullin, a marker of endothelial dysfunction, a central feature of the response to CPB. The multivariate model extends this finding, showing that MR-proADM retains a significant role even after adjustment for preoperative severity, surgical urgency and procedure duration. This suggests that proADM reflects a pathophysiological component not fully captured by traditional scores, likely related to acute vascular dysfunction induced by CPB and surgical stress, providing complementary information for early risk stratification. Regarding postoperative complications, univariate analysis showed a significant association between complications and several biomarkers, particularly proADM, lactate, CRP, and NT-proBNP. However, in the multivariate model only SAPSII maintained an independent association. This suggests that, although proADM is correlated with the development of complications, its prognostic value is mediated or absorbed by preoperative severity. Furthermore, the heterogeneity of complications may have reduced its predictive precision. Our study confirms proADM as a sensitive marker for early identification of patients at higher risk of postoperative instability, while defining its limitations in predicting specific complications, where structured clinical scores such as SAPSII retain greater discriminative power.

Conclusions

proADM represents a promising biomarker for the early prediction of prolonged ICU LOS in cardiac surgery. Its role in predicting complications appears less robust and warrants further investigation with prospective trials to confirm the clinical utility of proADM in cardiac surgery. Nevertheless, as enrollment is still ongoing, the strength of these findings is expected to increase with the growing sample size.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A92 MR-proADM as a dynamic biomarker of disease severity, treatment response and prognosis in sepsis in the intensive care unit

F. Squillacioti1,2, F. Civale1,3, F. Marinelli1, A. Marra2, F. Ferraro3

1UOC Anesthesia and Intensive Care, San Giuliano Hospital, ASL Napoli 2 Nord, Giugliano in Campania, Italy; 2Department of Neuriosciences, Reproductive and Odontostomatological Sciences, University of Naples Federico II, Italy; 3Department of Woman, Child, General and Specialistic Surgery, University of Campania L. Vanvitelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: F. Squillacioti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A92

Background

Sepsis and septic shock are leading causes of mortality in the intensive care unit, with diagnosis and prognostication remaining clinically challenging [1,2]. Mid-regional-pro-adrenomedullin (MR-proADM), a stable surrogate of adrenomedullin, may reflect endothelial dysfunction, vasoplegia and immunomodulation impairment [3–5]. This study evaluated MR-proADM as a biomarker of disease severity, treatment response, prognosis and diagnosis in critically ill septic patients [6,7].

Materials and Methods

According to the Declaration of Helsinki, we conducted a single-centre retrospective observational study in the ICU of San Giuliano Hospital between June and December 2025. Adult patients were included if they had sepsis or septic shock at ICU admission or developed them during ICU stay, according to Sepsis-3 criteria, with MR-proADM measurement at the time of clinical suspicion of sepsis(T0). Of 24 patients analyzed, 12 met inclusion criteria at ICU admission and 12 during ICU stay. Anonymously demographic, clinical, laboratory data, among which MR-proADM, procalcitonin(PCT), lactate, C-reactive protein(CRP) and SOFA score, were assessed at T0. MR-proADM and PCT were reassessed at 48 and 96 hours. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality; the secondary outcome was diagnostic value of MR-proADM and PCT at admission. Biomarker performance was assessed using ROC analysis, Youden-derived cut-offs, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and logistic regression models.

Results

28-day mortality was 62.5%. Non-survivors had higher SOFA score, lactate and MR-proADM at T0 than survivors (p<0.05) (Table 1). MR-proADM at T0 showed good discrimination for 28-day mortality, with AUROC 0.83(95% CI 0.61–1.00), exceeding SOFA(0.77), PCT(0.68) and CRP(0.57), and ranking below lactate (0.89) (Fig. 1). No deaths occurred in patients with MR-proADM <3.2 nmol/L (Fig. 2), and this cut-off was associated with significantly different survival (p<0.0018). 96-hour MR-proADM clearance added prognostic value, discriminating mortality with an AUROC of 0.85(95% CI 0.68–1.00), while PCT clearance remained non-discriminatory even above 80% (AUROC 0.47) (Fig. 3). At 96-hour a MR-proADM clearance <40% (p=0.0027) (Fig. 4) or a value >2.5nmol/L was associated with higher mortality (p=0.006) (Fig. 5). For sepsis/septic shock diagnosis at admission, MR-proADM showed the highest AUROC 0.97(95% CI 0.89–1.00) (Fig. 6).

Conclusion

MR-proADM was associated with sepsis severity, 28-day mortality and diagnostic discrimination at ICU admission. Its 96-hour clearance appeared more informative than PCT kinetics and may help identify persistent endothelial-organ dysfunction, complementing the infection-role of PCT [8]. Although sepsis remains a clinical diagnosis, MR-proADM may serve as an adjunctive tool for risk stratification and dynamic prognostic assessment, pending validation by larger prospective multicentre studies.

Local ethical committee approval and informed consent were obtained for the publication of this scientific article.
