A93 Successful VV-ECMO management in a severely obese patient with influenza-induced ards and moyamoya syndrome: a case report

G. Zuccaro, I.G. Bonanno, A. Leuzzi, A. Salice, D.E. Di Stefano, C. Geraci, S.L. Orlando, R. Nicoletti, L.S. Muscarà, M. Falcone, A. Pecora, F. Tornitore, G. Bufalino, T. Locicero, A.D. Vilardi, S. Cefalù

Arnas Garibaldi, Catania, Italy

Correspondence: G. Zuccaro

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A93

Background

Severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a leading cause of refractory respiratory failure in intensive care units (ICU). In the most severe cases, veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) remains a cornerstone rescue therapy. However, its management is particularly complex in obese patients with concomitant thrombotic conditions or cerebrovascular conditions. Moyamoya syndrome—a rare vasculopathy characterized by progressive occlusion of the main intracranial arteries and the development of pathological collateral circulation—presents a significant clinical complication. We report the case of a patient with severe influenza-related ARDS associated with bilateral ischemic stroke in a suspected Moyamoya pattern, successfully treated with VV-ECMO.

Materials and Methods

A 44-year-old male with severe obesity (BMI 44 kg/m²), obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS), and a history of hepatitis was admitted on January 13, 2026, for acute respiratory failure and suspected stroke. Following seven days of home-treated fever and cough, the patient experienced rapid respiratory and neurological deterioration, requiring intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation. Brain CT showed multiple areas of acute cerebral ischemia, while chest CT revealed diffuse ground-glass opacities. Upon transfer to our center, CT angiography and brain MRI documented bilateral occlusion of the middle cerebral arteries with a puff of smoke-pattern, consistent with Moyamoya syndrome. At ICU admission, the patient presented with severe hypoxemic-hypercapnic respiratory failure (P/F ratio < 200) and tested positive for Influenza A. Protective ventilation, empirical antibiotic therapy (piperacillin/tazobactam), and antiviral therapy (oseltamivir) were initiated. Despite maximal conventional treatment, the respiratory status worsened (P/F 64), necessitating right femoro-jugular VV-ECMO cannulation and ultra-protective ventilation on day 8. The patient remained on extracorporeal support for 10 days and 14 hours.

The clinical course was complicated by coagulation abnormalities, with D-dimer levels rising from 26,676 ng/mL to a peak of 103,272 ng/mL on day 14, accompanied by an increasing oxygenator pressure gradient (Delta P) and fungal superinfection (Candida parapsilosis).

Given the high thrombotic and cerebrovascular risk in the context of Moyamoya syndrome, a continuous infusion of tranexamic acid (3 g/24 h) was introduced, resulting in a progressive reduction of D-dimer levels.

Concurrently, elevated beta-D-glucan levels prompted further cultures; bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and urine cultures were positive for Candida parapsilosis, whereas blood cultures remained negative. Antimicrobial therapy was escalated to meropenem, linezolid and caspofungin.

From day 16, gas exchange began to improve, allowing for ECMO weaning and decannulation on day 19. A percutaneous tracheostomy was performed on day 21.

Following sedation tapering, the patient showed neurological improvement, regaining consciousness, speech, and motor function in all four limbs.

On March 20th, the patient was transferred to the rehabilitation unit in stable clinical condition.

Conclusions

This case demonstrates that VV-ECMO can be an effective life-saving strategy for refractory influenza-related ARDS, even in patients with complex cerebrovascular pathology.

The coexistence of bilateral ischemic stroke and suspected Moyamoya syndrome made anticoagulation management during ECMO exceptionally delicate, requiring a constant balance between thrombotic and hemorrhagic risks.

The use of tranexamic acid in a selected context of severe hyperfibrinolysis may represent a valuable therapeutic option for managing coagulopathic complications during extracorporeal support.

This case underscores the necessity of an integrated multidisciplinary approach in the management of complex critically ill patients.

Ethics approval and consent to participate

As this manuscript is a case report of a single patient treated according to standard clinical practice, institutional ethics committee approval was not required. Informed consent to participate was obtained from the patient’s legal guardian for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A94 Combined use of hemoadsorption devices (CytoSorb®) and iloprost in critically ill patients with septic shock, severe metabolic acidosis and peripheral microvascular impairment: a case series

F. Tornitore, I.G. Bonanno, D.E. DI Stefano, A. Pecora, A. Leuzzi, A. Salice, G. Bufalino, G. Zuccaro, L.S.A. Muscarà, M. Falcone, C. Geraci, S.L. Orlando, R. Nicoletti, G. Restuccia, G. Di Giovanni, T. Locicero, A. Vilardi, F. Melicchio, S. Cefalù

Arnas Garibaldi, Catania, Italy

Correspondence: F. Tornitore

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A94

Background

Critically ill patients with septic shock and severe metabolic derangements frequently develop multiorgan failure and peripheral microcirculatory dysfunction, including acrocyanosis.

The cornerstones in the treatment of metformin-associated lactic acidosis are correction of metabolic acidosis (using bicarbonates), hemodynamic support (fluid and vasopressor therapy), and hemodialysis/CRRT for the direct elimination of metformin and the removal of excess lactate.

The integration of hemoadsorption devices such as CytoSorb® is employed as an adjuvant therapy to standard dialysis. The addition of CytoSorb®may offer specific advantages, as it reduces the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines driving pathological vasodilation and contributes to the removal of toxic mediators and drugs that complicate the clinical presentation.

The co-administration of iloprost may improve peripheral perfusion through vasodilatory and antiplatelet effects.

We describe two cases in which the combined use of CytoSorb®and iloprost was implemented in the setting of severe systemic illness with peripheral hypoperfusion.

Methods

We report two cases of middle-aged women admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with severe systemic illness complicated by metabolic and hemodynamic instability and peripheral microvascular impairment Fig 1.

The first case concerns a 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, thyroid disorder, admitted for urosepsis due to Escherichia coli associated with obstructive uropathy (left hydronephrosis due to ureteral stone). On admission, she presented with oligoanuria, hyperlactatemia, markedly elevated procalcitonin (>100 ng/mL), septic shock and progressive respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support (norepinephrine, adrenaline, and argipressin). Due to acute kidney injury and metabolic derangement whit hyperlactatemia, CRRT was initiated and integrated with CytoSorb®.

The second case involves a 50-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and Hashimoto thyroiditis.The patient presented with symptoms of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; however, cultures showed no growth, suggesting a probable viral gastroenteritis. Due to acute severe metabolic acidosis, hyperlactatemia, dehydration, acute kidney injury and progressive respiratory failure, she required invasive mechanical ventilation, and high-dose norepinephrine. CRRT (CVVH/CVVHDF) was initiated and subsequently combined with CytoSorb® due to persistent metabolic acidosis.

In both cases, patients developed peripheral acrocyanosis involving multiple extremities, consistent with severe microcirculatory impairment. Vascular consultation excluded indications for urgent surgical intervention and suggested initiation of iloprost infusion, along with adjunctive measures (anticoagulation, local warming, and device removal when indicated).

Results

In both patients, the integration of CRRT with CytoSorb® was associated with progressive improvement in metabolic parameters, including acid–base balance and lactate clearance, as well as stabilization of respiratory and hemodynamic status.

In the first case, after three CytoSorb® cycles, renal function recovered with restoration of diuresis, allowing discontinuation of CRRT. Vasopressors were progressively weaned and discontinued, followed by successful ventilatory weaning, extubation, and transition to non-invasive respiratory support. The infectious source (E. coli) was treated with targeted antibiotic therapy (initially piperacillin/tazobactam, then meropenem). Peripheral acrocyanosis showed partial but progressive improvement without need for surgical intervention.

In the second case, the multimodal approach led to resolution of severe metabolic acidosis, improvement in renal function, and discontinuation of extracorporeal support. The patient was successfully extubated shortly thereafter. Vascular findings improved with regression of acrocyanosis, restoration of distal perfusion, and improved Doppler signals. Immunological and hematological workup excluded autoimmune vasculitis or thrombotic microangiopathy.

Both patients were eventually transferred to a lower-intensity care setting in stable clinical condition, with recovered or improving organ function and reduced peripheral ischemic signs.

Conclusions

These cases highlight the potential role of a combined strategy including CRRT with CytoSorb® and iloprost in critically ill patients with severe metabolic derangement or septic shock complicated by peripheral microvascular dysfunction. Hemoadsorption may contribute to systemic stabilization, while iloprost may support peripheral perfusion in the absence of surgically correctable vascular lesions.

Although causality cannot be established, the observed clinical improvement suggests that this integrated approach may represent a valuable adjunct in selected patients with multiorgan failure and microcirculatory impairment. Further studies are warranted to better define indications, timing, and clinical impact of these therapies in critical care settings.

Conflict of Interest

The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

Ethics approval and consent to participate

As this manuscript is a case series of patients treated according to standard clinical practice, institutional ethics committee approval was not required. Informed consent to participate was obtained from the patients’ legal guardians for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A95 Refractory atrial flutter in septic cardiomyopathy in endotoxemic shock treated with triple inotropic therapy

G. Sagristani, A. Diana, F. De Vivo, C. Morrone, G. Cosenza, F. Coppolino, V. Pota, P. Sansone, M.B. Passavanti, M.C. Pace

University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: G. Sagristani

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A95

Background

Sepsis is a systemic inflammatory response syndrome that arises from a dysregulated immune response to pathogens infection leading to potentially life-threatening organ dysfunction [1].

Case report

A 75-year-old patient with seven previous coronary stents placed in three different sessions (last one 2020). He underwent prostatectomy in 2019.

Informed consent to publish had been obtained

The patient underwent cholecystectomy, initially approached laparoscopically and subsequently converted to open surgery due to extensive intra-abdominal adhesions.

On the first postoperative day, the patient developed hemodynamic instability associated with atrial flutter (HR 150 bpm) and severe hypotension (BP 70/30 mmHg). Laboratory findings revealed metabolic acidosis (lactate >2 mmol/L), oliguria, and clinical signs of dehydration. The patient was apyretic but reported severe abdominal pain (NRS 8).

Initial resuscitation included cautious volume expansion with 500 mL balanced crystalloids over 20 minutes due to limited fluid tolerance.

Electrical cardioversion under sedation was attempted without restoration of sinus rhythm. Pharmacological management included amiodarone loading followed by continuous infusion. Norepinephrine was initiated to maintain a diastolic arterial pressure >50 mmHg.

Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) excluded significant pericardial effusion and free intra- abdominal fluid, although doubtful pelvic collections were noted. [2] Subsequent abdominal CT scan revealed intestinal perforation.

The patient underwent urgent surgical source control. Intraoperative cultures were obtained and broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy was initiated (meropenem, vancomycin, and caspofungin).

Despite treatment, the patient developed refractory septic shock requiring high-dose norepinephrine (>0.25 µg/kg/min). Adjunctive therapy included argipressine infusion and hydrocortisone (200 mg/day).

On postoperative day two, echocardiography revealed a severe reduction in left ventricular ejection fraction (EF 10%), consistent with septic cardiomyopathy and cardiogenic shock. Endotoxin activity assay (EAA) was elevated (0.7).

Hemoperfusion with polymyxin B (PMX-HP) was initiated. Vasopressin was discontinued and replaced with adrenaline (0.2 µg/kg/min), while norepinephrine was continued (0.15 µg/kg/min).

Following the second hemoperfusion cycle and reduction of endotoxin levels (EAA <0.6), a significant improvement in cardiac function was observed (EF increased to 35%). Sinus rhythm was restored, and hemodynamic parameters progressively stabilized. [1,2]

Conclusion

This case highlights limitations of standard fluid resuscitation, rapid progression to mixed shock, and the role of endotoxemia in septic cardiomyopathy. The improvement after hemoperfusion suggests a potential therapeutic role in selected patients. Septic cardiomyopathy is a reversible condition. A multimodal approach combining vasopressors, inotropes, and hemoperfusion may be effective in refractory cases.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A96 Clinical application of additional cartridge in septic shock: case report

S.T. Saglimbene, V. Drago, M.L. Granata, S. De Luca, G. Leonardi, G. Magro, C. Nicocia, M.T. Montalto, F.M.S. Messina, L.C. Cavallo, G. Cammarata, M. Quercio, A. Ancona, F. Papa, S. Zappalà, C. Guarneri, G. Rapisarda

Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Santa Marta and Santa Venera Hospital, ASP-CT, ACIREALE, Italy

Correspondence: S.T. Saglimbene

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A96

Background

Sepsis causes a continuous release of inflammatory mediators, which can damage cells and lead to severe immune impairment. Haemoperfusion by the CytoSorb® adsorbent aims to eliminate damage-associated molecular patterns, pathogen-associated molecular patterns and excessive cytokines {1}.

Case Report

A 43-year-old woman, with a medical history of nephrolithiasis, presented to the Emergency Department with a one-week history of abdominal pain and fever. Upon admission, the following investigations were performed: blood tests (creatinine 3.62mg/dL, WBC 22.9 x 10³/uL, PLT 72 x 10³/uL, GOT 247UI/L, GPT 194UI/L, total bilirubin 1.63mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.14mg/dL, troponin 1449ng/L, CRP 188mg/L, D-dimer 6881ng/mL), Arterial Blood Gas analysis (ABG) (pH 7.18, pCO2 29mmHg, pO2 59.2mmHg, BE −17.6mmol/L, HCO3 11.9mmol/L, Lac 10.17mmol/L, SpO2 82.3%), CT scan (Thorax/Abdomen) with evidence of pericardial fluid, pleural effusion, interstitial oedema, significant congestive hepatomegaly, gallbladder wall thickening with pericholecystic fluid due to inflammation, enlarged kidneys with multiple microlithiasis and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. The patient was initially admitted to the Nephrology department, but appeared in severe distress, dyspnoeic, with diffuse crackles and oligo-anuria. Consequently, she underwent sedation and endotracheal intubation and she was admitted to ICU. Mechanical ventilation was performed and haemodynamic support with dopamine, was started alongside diuretic stimulation. Blood tests showed: creatinine 3.83mg/dL, WBC 38.3 x 10³/uL, PLT 115 x 10³/uL, GOT 522UI/L, GPT 346UI/L, total bilirubin 1.51mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.23mg/dL, troponin 4733ng/L, CRP 234mg/L, PCT 199.79ng/mL and D-dimer 6899ng/mL. Surveillance swabs identified Staphylococcus aureus in the pharyngeal swab. Initial ICU ABG: pH 7.12, pCO2 65.2, pO2 75, BE −8.2, HCO3 17.4, Lac 8.32. Empirical antibiotic therapy was administered and CRRT was performed 90 minutes after admission. Twelve hours post-admission, a follow-up CT scan showed further deterioration of the pulmonary, hepatic and renal status. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy and ureteral stent placement. Dopamine was discontinued and inotropic support with noradrenaline and argipressin was administered. CRRT was resumed, maintaining urine output >0.5 ml/h; the patient received transfusions of packed red blood cells, platelets, and plasma, along with hydrocortisone and antioxidants.

Forty hours after admission, three consecutive 24-hour cycles of haemoadsorption were performed using the CytoSorb® cartridge on the OMNI SYSTEM during CRRT with calcium citrate. Pre-treatment values: creatinine 2.44mg/dL, WBC 32.9 x 10³/uL, PLT 37 x 10³/uL, GOT4321 UI/L, GPT 3026UI/L, total bilirubin 2.47mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.38mg/dL, troponin 4733ng/L, CRP 232mg/L, PCT 91.55ng/mL, D-dimer 6435ng/mL, IgA 121mg/dL, IgG 497mg/dL, IgM 71mg/dL. ABG: pH 7.43, pCO2 33.8, pO2 110.7, BE −2.2, HCO3 23, Lac 5.26. Post-first cycle values: creatinine 1.62mg/dL, WBC 33.9 x 10³/uL, PLT 35 x 10³/uL, GOT 1597UI/L, GPT 2717UI/L, total bilirubin 1.45mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.74mg/dL, troponin 4717ng/L, CRP 165mg/L, PCT 40.47ng/mL, D-dimer 7141ng/mL, IgA 168mg/dL, IgG 675mg/dL, IgM 92mg/dL. ABG: pH 7.45, pCO2 44, pO2 106.7, BE 6.4, HCO3 29.6, Lac 2.82. Post-second cycle values: creatinine 1.15mg/dL, WBC 38.1 x 10³/uL, PLT 35 x 10³/uL, GOT 753UI/L, GPT 2113UI/L, total bilirubin 1.30mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.59mg/dL, CRP 101mg/L, PCT 18.73ng/mL, D-dimer 23264ng/mL, IgA 213mg/dL, IgG 794mg/dL, IgM 115mg/dL. ABG: pH 7.52, pCO2 41, pO2 68.7, BE 10, HCO3 32.8, Lac 1.80. Post-third cycle values: creatinine 0.86mg/dL, WBC 41.6 x 10³/uL, PLT 44 x 10³/uL, GOT 396UI/L, GPT 1355UI/L, direct bilirubin 0.28mg/dL, CRP 40mg/L, PCT 8.4ng/mL, D-dimer 21307ng/mL. ABG: pH 7.45, pCO2 44, pO2 75.3, BE 6.0, HCO3 29.2, Lac 1.62. During treatment, noradrenaline support was gradually reduced and discontinued 44 hours after starting therapy with haemoadsorption using CytoSorb®. Following the three cycles, CRRT was performed for a further 24 hours. Argipressin and furosemide infusions were also discontinued. A post-CRRT CT scan led to a second exploratory laparotomy, which ruled out colonic perforation. A liver biopsy was performed, revealing massive geographic hepatocellular necrosis due to acute liver failure secondary to sepsis. Twenty-four hours later, following sedation and ventilator weaning, the patient was successfully extubated. She was afebrile, alert and cooperative, within 72 hours oxygen support was discontinued followed by spontaneous breathing on room air. The patient was transferred back to the Nephrology department on day 11, with the following laboratory results: creatinine 0.51mg/dL, WBC 13.7 10³/uL, PLT 299 x 10³/uL GOT 48UI/L, GPT 176UI/L, total bilirubin 0.97mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.27mg/dL CRP 16mg/L, PCT 0.33ng/mL, D-dimer 5071ng/mL. ABG: pH 7.49, pCO2 28, pO2 90.5, BE −1.7, HCO3 24.0, Lac 1.07. On day 18, she was transferred to the Surgical department and she was discharged home on day 21 with the following laboratory results: creatinine 0.55mg/dL, WBC 6.0 x 10³/uL, PLT 235 x 10³/uL, GOT 32UI/L, GPT 58UI/L, total bilirubin 0.85mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.18mg/dL CRP 17mg/L, PCT 0.1ng/mL. Informed consent for publication was obtained from the patient.

Conclusions

Haemoadsorption by CytoSorb® cartridge may represent an effective therapeutic option for stabilising patients in septic shock. It can reduce inflammatory markers and vasoplegia, rebalance metabolic parameters and subsequently improve organ function.

A97 Vancomycin-resistant enterococcus faecium bloodstream infections in a peripheral icu-inclusive hospital: a biennial antibiogram strategy to guide empirical therapy and rapid diagnostics integration

F. Russo1, M.C. Russo2, A. Milone1, P. Rumma3, A. Vitiello1, C. Candurro1, F.D. Precone4

1Po Villa Malta Asl Salerno Uoc Anestesia E Rianimazione, Sarno, Italy; 2Po Villa Malta Asl Salerno Uoc Cardiologia E Utic, Sarno, Italy; 3Po Villa Malta Asl Salerno Uosd Laboratorio, Sarno, Italy; 4Po Villa Malta Asl Salerno Uoc Medicina Generale, Sarno, Italy

Correspondence: F. Russo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A97

Background

Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE), particularly Enterococcus faecium, carry roughly twofold attributable mortality in bloodstream infections (BSI) versus vancomycin-susceptible bacteraemia [1]. In Italy, AR-ISS reported a VRE prevalence of 32.4% among invasive E. faecium isolates in 2023 [2]. Peripheral hospitals with ICU activity face a specific challenge: annual Enterococcus BSI isolate counts routinely fall below the CLSI M39 minimum threshold of 30 isolates per species [3]. As a consequence, empirical therapy in critical patients lacks local microbiological grounding.

Methods

All Enterococcus spp. isolates from blood cultures (BACTEC FX) at a peripheral hospital in Southern Italy (<150 beds, including ICU and coronary care unit [UTIC]) between January 2024 and December 2025 were included. A biennial aggregation strategy was applied as the reporting unit, consistent with multi-year pooling anticipated by CLSI M39 [3] and quantified for low-volume settings by Tran et al. [4]. CLSI M39 deduplication was applied. Identification and susceptibility testing used VITEK 2 (bioMerieux) with EUCAST v14.0 breakpoints; vancomycin resistance defined as MIC >4 mg/L. Susceptibility percentages reported with Wilson 95% CI. Hospital and territorial ceftriaxone consumption data were obtained from the institutional pharmacy and regional prescribing databases.

Results

Twenty-eight isolates with interpretable susceptibility data were included (14 E. faecalis, 14 E. faecium) from 29 deduplicated episodes. ICU and UTIC accounted for 55.2% of episodes; internal medicine for 27.6%. E. faecium vancomycin resistance was 50.0% (7/14; 95% CI 26.8–73.2%) versus the 2023 AR-ISS national average of 32.4%. Ampicillin resistance in E. faecium (93%) is in line with Italian and European surveillance (>85–90%); the local-specific finding is the 50% vancomycin resistance. High-level gentamicin resistance (HLGR) was 79% in E. faecium and 43% in E. faecalis; aminoglycoside-based synergistic regimens were therefore ineffective. One E. faecium isolate showed concurrent vancomycin and linezolid resistance. Linezolid susceptibility was 93% in E. faecium and 100% in E. faecalis; tigecycline susceptibility was 100% in both species (Table 1). In 2024, hospital ceftriaxone consumption was 17.4 DDD/100 patient-days, 36% above the national average of 12.8 [5]; territorial consumption in ASL Salerno (0.55 DDD/1000 inhabitants/day) was more than twice the national average (0.24).

Clinical and stewardship implications

The local E. faecium vancomycin resistance rate of 50% renders empirical glycopeptide coverage unreliable in critically ill patients with VRE risk factors (transfer from long-term care, recent hospitalisation, documented colonisation). The institutional antimicrobial stewardship committee (GLAS) revised the empirical approach: for high-risk ICU/UTIC patients, empirical linezolid or high-dose daptomycin (10–12 mg/kg) with intravenous fosfomycin as combination partner replaced the prior glycopeptide-based regional regimen. Systematic integration of rapid molecular diagnostics (BioFire FilmArray BCID2) for vanA/vanB detection at blood culture positivity was introduced in parallel. For E. faecalis BSI with confirmed HLGR, ampicillin-ceftriaxone replaced ampicillin-gentamicin (Figure 1). The combined hospital and community ceftriaxone exposure is biologically consistent with E. faecium expansion [6] and supports the stewardship rationale of the revised algorithm.

Conclusions

Biennial aggregation enables peripheral hospitals below the CLSI M39 threshold to generate locally applicable data for empirical therapy in critically ill patients. In our setting, an E. faecium VRE rate of 50% combined with hospital and community ceftriaxone overuse made glycopeptide-based empirical coverage unreliable in critical patients and motivated a risk-stratified algorithm integrating rapid molecular diagnostics now embedded in the ICU empirical workflow.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A98 Analysis of antibiotic consumption according to the aware classification in the intensive care unit (ICU): comparison 2024–2025

F. Ratti1, C. Ammendola2, M.R. Sarno3, M. Casale3, P. Di Filippo3, P. Maiolino3

1University of Naples Federico II, Italy; 2University of Salerno, Italy; 3National Cancer Institute IRCCS – G. Pascale Foundation, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: F. Ratti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A98

Background

The appropriateness of antibiotic prescribing is a priority in high-complexity settings such as the ICU, both for containing antimicrobial resistance and for ensuring the economic sustainability of the healthcare system. In this context, the World Health Organization’s Access [1]. Watch and Reserve (AWaRe) classification is a useful tool for monitoring and guiding antibiotic consumption toward more appropriate and conscious use. In an oncology research institute, continuous awareness-raising activities are carried out for healthcare personnel through training courses organized with the support of the Hospital Pharmacy Unit. The latter plays a fundamental role in regulating the use of Reserve [2] antibiotics, whose use is subject to the completion of a medical report supported by an antibiogram. Furthermore, starting in 2025, the update of monitoring forms by AIFA contributed to reducing the use of these antibiotics.The aim of this study is to analyze and compare antibiotic consumption and costs in the ICU, assessing overall expenditure trends and the distribution of consumption across the AWaRe categories.

Materials and Methods

A retrospective analysis was conducted on antibiotic consumption in the ICU. Data were obtained from the hospital software, collecting for each drug both the number of units used and the corresponding expenditure. The analysis considered the years 2024 and 2025, categorizing antibiotics into the three AWaRe groups to evaluate prescribing trends and their economic impact [3]. The study has a descriptive design and aims to highlight how antibiotic use changed between the two years examined. Informed consent and data processing authorization were obtained.

Results

The comparison between 2024 and 2025 revealed changes in consumption across the three AWaRe categories. In 2024, total antibiotic consumption amounted to 6,434 units, of which 28.4% Access, 47.7% Watch and 23.9% Reserve (Figure 1). In 2025, total consumption was slightly lower (6,163 units), with a different distribution: 35.8% Access, 48.0% Watch and 16.1% Reserve (Figure 2). The analysis shows an increased use of Access antibiotics (+20.8%), stability in the Watch category, and a reduction in Reserve antibiotics (–35.4%) (Figure 3). The latter represents the main factor determining the decrease in expenditure observed in 2025, with costs decreasing from €68,147.59 in 2024 to €45,201.53 in 2025.The economic analysis highlighted an overall reduction of approximately 33.7% compared with 2024.

Conclusions

The analysis of antibiotic consumption in the ICU between 2024 and 2025 shows a reduction in overall use, with a decrease of Reserve antibiotics and, consequently, a reduction in the annual economic impact. The increase in the proportion of Access antibiotics indicates a progressive realignment toward the use of lower-risk molecules, in line with the national objectives defined by the PNCAR [4]. This trend was further supported by the 2025 update of AIFA monitoring forms, which contributed to promoting more appropriate use of Reserve antibiotics.The data highlight a reduction in annual expenditure and increased attention and awareness in the use of antibiotics in intensive care over the two years analyzed, supported by the collaboration and guidance of the Hospital Pharmacy Unit.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A99 “From the stable to the ICU: critical encephalitis in q fever due to Coxiella burnetii” a case report

F. Pulice, T. Perricelli, V. Alagna, D. Battaglia, F. Galeno, F. Costantino, L. Bocchino, A. Monardo

Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Ospedale Lamezia Terme, Italy

Correspondence: F. Pulice

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A99

Background

Q Fever caused by Coxiella burnetii is a zoonotic infection typically associated with occupational exposure to livestock [1]. Transmission occurs primarily via inhalation of contaminated aerosols. C. burnetii is an obligate intracellular pathogen with tropism for monocytes and macrophages [2] [3]. Acute infection is generally self-limiting but in selected cases, infection may progress to severe, life-threatening disease with extrapulmonary involvement (Fig. 1), including encephalitis and endocarditis [2]. Encephalitis is rare, and diagnosis is often delayed [4].

Case Report

A 77-year-old man with chronic kidney disease and diabetes was admitted to the ICU because of acute respiratory failure associated with progressive neurological deterioration during hospitalization in a medical ward, reaching a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3, persistent fever and hypotension. Laboratory investigations showed neutrophilia (12.8 ×10^9/L) and mildly elevated procalcitonin levels (0.23 ng/mL). Chest and abdominal CT scans were unremarkable, while blood and urine cultures were negative.

Electroencephalography (EEG) demonstrated diffuse slowing of cerebral activity, while brain CT excluded ischemic and hemorrhagic lesions. Given the suspicion of neurological-origin respiratory failure, lumbar puncture was performed. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis (99% lymphocytes), elevated albumin (530 mg/L), and increased IgG levels (100 mg/L). CSF analysis for common bacterial and viral pathogens was negative. Viral or atypical bacterial encephalitis was suspected, prompting an extended microbiological work-up including West Nile virus, Tick-borne encephalitis, Zika virus, Chlamydia spp., Coxiella burnetii, tuberculosis, and leishmaniasis. Serological testing demonstrated positivity for C.burnetii IgG and IgM antibodies, later confirmed by repeat serum sampling and antibody titer assessment.

Considering the patient’s occupational exposure to livestock, together with serological findings, a diagnosis of Q Fever encephalitis was established. The case was reported to the public health authorities. Given the severity of encephalitis and the lack of established guidelines, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days was combined with rifampicin 600 mg daily for 14 days, based on the documented activity of both agents against C. burnetii and their adequate CSF penetration. Therapy led to gradual neurological improvement up to GCS 13 and EEG normalization. Due to difficulty in weaning, a tracheostomy was performed. Transesophageal echocardiography excluded infective endocarditis. Serial monitoring of antibodies titers was carried out throughout hospitalization.

Conclusions

Q Fever should be considered in encephalitis of unclear origin, particularly in patients with occupational livestock exposure. Early multidisciplinary management, prompt serology, and targeted antimicrobial therapy are crucial for favorable outcomes.

The authors would like to acknowledge all members of the study group for their collaboration and intellectual contribution to this work.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A100 Microbiological diagnostic resources and infection surveillance in intensive care units: a multicenter survey from southern Italy

M. Tescione, A. Piccolo, C. Santoro, E.G. Vadala’, S. Pangallo, M.L. Foti, N. Polimeni, A. Serrano’, F. Vaccaro, A. De Lorenzo, S. Pantano, S. Macheda

Complex Unit of Intensive Care and Anesthesia, “Bianchi Melacrino Morelli” Metropolitan Hospital, Reggio Calabria, Italy

Correspondence: C. Santoro

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A100

Background

Microbiological diagnostics and infection surveillance are fundamental components in the management of severe infections and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) among critically ill patients admitted to Intensive Care Units (ICUs). Early pathogen identification, rapid antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and timely integration of antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) interventions are essential to optimize antimicrobial therapy, support infection prevention strategies, and improve clinical outcomes in sepsis and septic shock. However, substantial variability in diagnostic resources, surveillance systems, and stewardship infrastructures may persist between tertiary referral hospitals and peripheral centers, particularly in geographically heterogeneous healthcare settings. The aim of this study was to evaluate the current organization of microbiological diagnostic resources, infection surveillance systems, and AMS integration across ICUs in Calabria, Southern Italy.

Methods

A preliminary multicenter cross-sectional survey was conducted among ICUs in Calabria between January and December 2024. A structured electronic questionnaire based on SIAARTI, ESCMID, ECDC, and WHO recommendations was administered to participating centers. Collected variables included ICU organizational characteristics, availability of conventional and advanced microbiological diagnostic techniques, implementation of AMR and healthcare-associated infection surveillance systems, screening protocols for multidrug-resistant organisms, antimicrobial stewardship activities, diagnostic–therapeutic pathways (PDTA), microbiological feedback mechanisms, infection - control audits, and digital data management systems. Data were collected anonymously at institutional level and analyzed descriptively.

Results

Seven ICUs participated in this preliminary analysis, including three HUB hospitals and four SPOKE centers. Preliminary mortality and organizational analyses highlighted marked differences between HUB and SPOKE hospitals in both clinical outcomes and diagnostic - stewardship integration (Figure 1). All participating ICUs reported access to conventional microbiological cultures and routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing. However, advanced diagnostic technologies, including MALDI - TOF mass spectrometry, multiplex PCR assays, and rapid phenotypic susceptibility testing, were available in 100% of HUB centers but only partially implemented in SPOKE hospitals. Real-time computerized infection surveillance systems integrated with microbiology laboratories were present exclusively in HUB ICUs, whereas most SPOKE centers relied on manual or delayed reporting systems. Formal AMR and healthcare-associated infection surveillance programs were available in 85.7% of participating centers. Structured AMS diagnostic–therapeutic pathways were implemented in all HUB ICUs but only partially adopted in SPOKE hospitals. Gap implementations between HUB and Spoke are shown in Figure 2 and Table 1. All centers reported routine screening programs for multidrug-resistant organisms and annual infection-control training activities. Marked variability was also observed in microbiological feedback integration, frequency of stewardship audits, and digital surveillance infrastructure. HUB hospitals demonstrated a higher degree of multidisciplinary integration between intensivists, microbiologists, infectious disease specialists, pharmacists, and stewardship teams. Preliminary mortality analysis showed higher crude ICU mortality in SPOKE hospitals (median 31.0%) compared with HUB centers (25.6%). Similarly, sepsis/septic shock-related mortality appeared numerically higher in SPOKE ICUs, although substantial variability was observed across centers.

Conclusions

This preliminary multicenter survey highlights substantial heterogeneity in microbiological diagnostic resources, infection surveillance systems, and AMS integration across ICUs in Southern Italy. HUB hospitals demonstrated more advanced diagnostic infrastructures, stronger stewardship integration, and greater digital surveillance capability, whereas SPOKE centers showed partial implementation, particularly regarding rapid diagnostics and real-time surveillance systems. Despite these differences, all participating ICUs reported strong engagement in infection prevention and microbiological screening activities, representing a valuable foundation for future regional harmonization initiatives. Expanding access to rapid microbiological diagnostics, strengthening stewardship governance, and implementing integrated digital surveillance networks may improve infection management, optimize antimicrobial use, and support AMR containment in critically ill patients.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A101 Predictive factors of antibiotic de-escalation in patients with septic shock admitted to the intensive care unit

M. Pazzi1, T. Meconi1, V. Manetti1, R. Papa1, P. Ballo2, D. Conti1

1Emergency Department and Critical Care Area, Anesthesia and Intensive Care Unit, Santa Maria Annunziata Hospital, Florence, Italy; 2Cardiology unit, Santa Maria Annunziata Hospital, Florence, Italy

Correspondence: M. Pazzi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A101

Background

The antibiotic de-escalation strategy in septic shock patients plays a crucial role in balancing clinical effectiveness with the containment of antimicrobial resistance.[1,2] This study aimed to identify predictive factors for antibiotic de-escalation in patients with septic shock admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) and to evaluate its impact on the length of ICU stay.

Materials and Methods

This single-center retrospective observational study was conducted in the ICU of Santa Maria Annunziata Hospital and included patients admitted between January 2024 and September 2025 with a diagnosis of septic shock. Patients were divided into two groups: Group 1 (de-escalation) and Group 2 (no de-escalation). Clinical, microbiological, and anthropometric data were collected, including sepsis scores and surveillance swabs. Treatments and major supportive interventions were also recorded. Written informed consent was obtained from all enrolled patients, and the study protocol is currently under review by the local Ethics Committee.

Results

A total of 92 consecutive patients were included. De-escalation was performed in 35 (38%) patients. There were no differences in the duration of antibiotic treatment between the two groups or in ICU mortality. Group 1 had a higher Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score (10.2 ± 3.1 vs 8.7 ± 2.5, p = 0.017), a higher prevalence of positive surveillance swabs at admission (p < 0.001), and more frequent positive culture tests (p = 0.029). Patients in Group 1 also had longer ICU stays (p = 0.009) and a greater use of Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT) (5 [14.3%] vs 2 [3.5%], p = 0.050). No difference in the timing of de-escalation was observed according to the type of infection (pulmonary, abdominal, urinary, or other) (p = 0.46). Multivariate analysis identified advanced age and low body mass index (BMI) as independent factors associated with de-escalation (p = 0.043 and p = 0.016, respectively).

Conclusions

Patients undergoing antibiotic de-escalation were older, had lower BMI, and greater severity at ICU admission. They also experienced longer ICU stays, likely reflecting the need for more invasive supportive therapies. In this context, the presence of an antibiotic stewardship program, together with the implementation of rapid diagnostic tests[3], may further promote a more rational and targeted use of antibiotics in the ICU.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A102 Early predictors of pneumonia in ICU blunt chest trauma patients: a retrospective study from a level 1 trauma center

F. Guerriero1, I. Pattarino1, C. Medina2, S. Scabini3, S. Corcione3, D. Vita3, F. Agliata1, A. Giachetti1, S. Binello4, B. Vittoni4, M. Berardino1

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A102

Background

Hospital-Acquired (HAP) and Ventilator-Associated pneumonia (VAP) represent a common complication in patients with blunt chest trauma (BCT), contributing to morbidity and mortality. Early diagnosis remains challenging due to the radiological and clinical overlap between infectious and trauma-related pulmonary features. Despite advances in critical care, the ability to promptly identify patients at risk remains limited. Thoracic Trauma Severity Score (TTSS) is a predictor of chest trauma-related complications, including pneumonia. CT-based TTSS (CT-TTSS) allows ARDS risk determination according to values stratification: scores above 13 corresponds to high risk, while scoring below 8 carry minimal risk. In intermediate-range patients (8–13), predictive sensitivity decreases. Pneumonia risk stratification through TTSS remains underexplored. This study aims to identify HAP and VAP predictive factors in BCT patients, in order to facilitate early risk evaluation and timely preventive and therapeutic strategies implementation.

Materials and methods

A retrospective observational study was conducted at CTO Hospital, in Turin, between January 2022 and December 2023, including adult patients with BCT who need Intensive Care Unit (ICU) stay for longer than 48 hours after trauma. The study protocol was approved by the Local Ethics Committee (LEC). Informed consent was obtained from contactable patients. Regarding deceased and/or non-contactable patients, a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) was performed and enrollment proceeded without consent, in accordance with approval granted by LEC. Collected data included demografic and clinical characteristics, trauma-related variables, severity scores and ICU parameters. Microbiological data and antibiotic therapy were additionally recorded for pneumonia patients. Risk factors were analysed using logistic regression models.

Results

244 patients were included (median age 54, IQR 38–66; male gender 74,2%); 88 presented pneumonia (36%) and 44% of these cases occurred during the first five days of hospitalization. Enterobacteriaceae were the most frequent isolated pathogens (62%) and Pseudomonas Aeruginosa accounted for 35% of pneumonia, of which 35% exhibited a carbapenem-resistant profile. Therapeutic escalation was required in half of the cases. CT-TTSS on ED admission and ICU admission SOFA score were independently associated with pneumonia development (respectively, OR 1.10, 95% CI 1.02–1.19, p 0.013 and OR 1.26, CI 1.10–1.44, p < 0,001). Analyzing specifically CT-TTSS groups according to ARDS risk classification, we found out that compared to low -risk patients, higher scores corresponds to increasing odds, both in intermediate range (OR 2.23, CI 1.10–4.53 p= 0.027) and high risk (OR 3.20, CI 1.41–7.28, p=0.005) group.

Conclusions

The results suggest that early recognition of elevated TTS and SOFA scores may guide the implementation of preventive measures and targeted protocols in BCT patients who need more than 48 hours ICU stay after trauma. Future studies will enable to define pneumonia specific predictive score in thoracic trauma.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A103 Critical care management during a large foodborne botulism type B outbreak: respiratory strategy and infectious complications in 28 patients

F. Gencarelli1, M. Madeo2, S. Fresilli3, A. Mesiti4, G. Gemelli4, I. Germanò1, B. Calandra1, C. Biscardi1, D. Veltri1, A. Pasqua4, M.F. Bianco1, O.S. Cava1

1Intensive Care and Anesthesiology, Annunziata Hospital, Cosenza, Italy; 2Anesthesiology, Critical Care and Pain Medicine Division, Department of Medicine and Surgery, University of Parma, Italy; 3Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milan, Italy; 4Intensive Care Unit, Department of Medical and Surgical Sciences, University Hospital Mater Domini, Catanzaro, Italy

Correspondence: F. Gencarelli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A103

Background

Foodborne botulism is a rare but potentially fatal neuroparalytic disease caused by botulinum neurotoxin, with respiratory failure representing the main life-threatening complication [1]. Large outbreaks remain uncommon and may generate major organizational challenges for emergency departments and intensive care units, particularly because diagnosis is primarily clinical and treatment often precedes laboratory confirmation [2,3]. We describe the critical care management of a large botulinum neurotoxin type B outbreak, focusing on respiratory strategy, infectious complications, gastrointestinal dysautonomia, and multidisciplinary coordination (Figure 1).

Materials and methods

We retrospectively analyzed 28 patients hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed botulinum neurotoxin type B intoxication after a shared exposure to commercially prepared food. Clinical presentation, intensive care unit admission, ventilatory support, antitoxin administration, infectious complications, gastrointestinal dysfunction, and outcomes were collected from medical records. Respiratory management was based on repeated bedside assessment of cranial nerve involvement, bulbar dysfunction, secretion burden, cough effectiveness, work of breathing, gas exchange, and diaphragmatic function. High-flow nasal cannula and non-invasive ventilation were used cautiously, with a low threshold for intubation when airway protection or ventilatory pump function deteriorated [4–6].

Results

Twenty-eight patients were diagnosed with foodborne botulism. Fourteen patients (50%) required intensive care unit admission because of acute respiratory failure and progressive cranial nerve dysfunction. All patients received high-flow nasal cannula and/or non-invasive ventilation, whereas only two patients (7%) required invasive mechanical ventilation. Both intubated patients developed aspiration pneumonia followed by multidrug-resistant pulmonary infection. Gastrointestinal dysautonomia was frequent: all patients developed constipation, and severe ileus requiring pharmacological intervention occurred in the most severely affected patients. Seven critically ill patients received botulinum antitoxin. No patient required tracheostomy. No deaths occurred. Mean intensive care unit length of stay was 5.3 ± 4.4 days, and mean hospital length of stay was 8.7 ± 4.3 days.

Conclusions

In this large foodborne botulism type B outbreak, early clinical recognition and a structured respiratory management strategy may have contributed to limiting invasive mechanical ventilation. Botulism remains a critical care disease requiring coordinated multidisciplinary management, prompt antitoxin consideration, close respiratory monitoring, airway protection, infectious complication surveillance, and active management of autonomic gastrointestinal dysfunction.

The study is currently under review by the local Ethics Committee.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A104 Shock after second-trimester fetal loss complicated by Escherichia coli infection and reversible septic cardiomyopathy: the role of angiotensin II

V. Lomonaco1, E. Moro2, D. Gaetano1, C.A. Ajmone Cat2, L. Tritapepe2

1Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, AORN Sant’Anna e San Sebastiano, Caserta, Italy; 2Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, AO San Camillo Forlanini Hospital, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: E. Moro

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A104

Background

Obstetric septic shock is a rare but life-threatening condition that may rapidly evolve into refractory vasoplegia requiring multiple vasopressors. Angiotensin II is a non-catecholaminergic vasopressor targeting the renin–angiotensin system and has emerged as a rescue therapy in catecholamine-resistant distributive shock.

Case report

A 42-year-old woman with hypothyroidism and pregnancy following assisted reproductive technology was admitted at 17+6 weeks for pelvic pain. After confirmation of intrauterine fetal death, labor was induced. Shortly after delivery, she developed fulminant septic shock characterized by severe hypotension (47/31 mmHg), hyperlactatemia (peak 8 mmol/L), and multiorgan dysfunction.

She required intensive care support including norepinephrine (up to 0.33 mcg/kg/min), vasopressin, invasive mechanical ventilation, continuous renal replacement therapy, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Blood and placental cultures were positive for Escherichia coli, and targeted therapy with piperacillin/tazobactam was initiated.

An early multimodal vasopressor strategy was implemented, combining catecholaminergic and non-catecholaminergic agents to address different pathophysiological pathways of vasoplegia. Despite escalation of norepinephrine and vasopressin, persistent distributive shock was observed. Angiotensin II was introduced (starting at 22 ng/kg/min) as part of a triple-agent vasopressor strategy, resulting in progressive hemodynamic stabilization, lactate clearance, and reduction of vasopressor requirements.

The clinical course was further complicated by septic cardiomyopathy (left ventricular ejection fraction 30–35%), treated with levosimendan, with complete recovery (ejection fraction 62%). Additional complications included acute respiratory failure, severe anemia requiring transfusion, retained products of conception, uterine arteriovenous malformation treated with embolization, and psychological sequelae.

The patient was discharged in stable condition with preserved cardiac function at follow-up echocardiography.

Conclusion

This case highlights the potential role of an early multimodal vasopressor strategy in refractory septic shock, integrating norepinephrine, vasopressin, and angiotensin II to target complementary mechanisms of vasoplegia. In this setting, angiotensin II was associated with rapid hemodynamic stabilization, lactate clearance, and reduction in catecholamine requirements.

Consent to publish

Written informed consent for publication was obtained from the patient.

A105 Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome complicated by multiple organ failure: case report and role of Oxiris treatment

R. Leo1, C.A.T. Lo Giudice1, F. Suaria2, M. Frisina1, M. Scivoli1, A. Barbagallo1, A. Merendino1, P. Giaquinta1, G. Terranova1, G. Filoni1

1San Vincenzo Hospital, Taormina, Messina, Italy; 2Gaetano Martino University Hospital, Messina, Italy

Correspondence: R. Leo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A105

Background

A 38-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with pelvic-abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, and hypotension refractory to fluid resuscitation. Contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT showed bilateral pleural effusion and hilar congestion without significant abdominal abnormalities.

Due to progressive clinical deterioration, the patient was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU).

Case Report

At ICU admission, the patient was febrile, tachypneic, hemodynamically unstable, and oliguric despite low-flow oxygen therapy through Ventimask. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed hyperlactatemia (5.3 mmol/L).

Laboratory findings demonstrated severe systemic involvement with leukopenia/neutropenia (WBC 2.45), acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.85 mg/dL), electrolyte imbalance, coagulation abnormalities, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 241.8 mg/L; procalcitonin 68 ng/mL), and increased cardiac-muscular injury markers including troponin, CPK, CPK-MB, and myoglobin.

Contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT scan revealed bilateral pleural effusions occupying approximately 50% of the lung fields, predominantly on the right side, associated with ascites. A CT-guided right pleural drainage was performed. The drained citrine-yellow pleural fluid was sent for microbiological and cytological analysis. Persistent renal retention of contrast medium administered approximately 24 hours earlier suggested associated renal impairment despite preserved renal morphology.

Empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy, vasopressor support, diuretics, and fondaparinux were initiated.

Despite treatment, the patient developed worsening respiratory failure and persistent hypotension requiring escalation of vasopressor support and high-flow oxygen therapy.

Blood cultures collected during admission to the Internal Medicine ward resulted positive for multidrug-resistant Group A Streptococcus pyogenes, while rectal swab was positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae. Piperacillin/tazobactam therapy was continued and fosfomycin was added.

Due to severe respiratory deterioration and worsening gas exchange, the patient underwent sedation, neuromuscular blockade, orotracheal intubation, and invasive mechanical ventilation.

On ICU day 4, persistent inflammatory activation and worsening organ dysfunction were observed, with elevated inflammatory markers and progression toward multiple organ failure (MOF).

Considering the possible role of cytokine storm and systemic hyperinflammation, extracorporeal blood purification with continuous veno-venous hemodialysis (CVVHD) using the Oxiris filter was initiated. Two treatment cycles of 72 hours each were performed.

Over the following days, progressive improvement in hemodynamic stability and respiratory function was observed, with reduction of vasopressor support and improvement in gas exchange. A subsequent blood culture performed on ICU day 6 was positive for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), leading to replacement of fosfomycin with vancomycin.

On ICU day 10, after gradual sedation reduction and respiratory weaning, the patient was successfully extubated and later transferred to a lower-intensity care ward.

Conclusion

This case highlights the severe clinical course of streptococcal toxic shock syndrome caused by Group A Streptococcus pyogenes complicated by multiple organ failure. Early intensive care management, prompt antimicrobial therapy, invasive organ support, and extracorporeal blood purification with Oxiris were associated with progressive clinical recovery and favorable outcome.

The study is currently under review by the local Ethics Committee.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A106 Therapeutic drug monitoring to assess the adequacy of antibiotic prophylaxis with cefazolin in urologic and non-cardiac thoracic surgery: clinical implications from preliminary results

E. Giusiano1, G. Ferrero1, V. Blua1, A. Palermiti2, C. Martino2, E. Ceraolo3, A. D’Avolio2, L. Brazzi1,3, G. Montrucchio1,3

1University of Turin – Department of Surgical Sciences, Italy; 2University of Turin – Department of Medical Sciences, Italy; 3University Hospital “City of Health and Science”, Turin, Italy

Correspondence: E. Giusiano

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A106

Background

Surgical site infections (SSIs) are frequent healthcare-associated infections responsible for significant morbidity, mortality, and costs for healthcare systems. Antibiotic prophylaxis (AP), particularly with cefazolin, is essential for prevention. However, doubts persist about the optimal timing of administration, dosage, and redosing, which may vary depending on patient characteristics, surgical setting, and perioperative complications. This study aimed to evaluate AP through a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) approach, by measuring cefazolin plasma concentrations and comparing them with minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values of pathogens responsible for SSI and with literature cut-offs associated with a higher infection risk. Secondary aims were to correlate PK data with clinical variables and SSI occurrence and to identify reference values for assessing AP adequacy.

Materials and Methods

A single-centre prospective observational study was conducted at a University Hospital in Italy from October 2023 to June 2025, involving urological and non-cardiac thoracic surgeries. All recruited patients provided specific informed consent. Cefazolin was administered according to best clinical practice (2 g within 1 hour before incision followed by a 1 g redose after 2 hours). Blood samples were collected at specific time points during surgery and concentrations measured using UHPLC–MS/MS. Clinical and outcome data on SSI were collected.

Results

Sixty-seven patients were included (69% thoracic, 31% urological), with a mean (SD): age 65 (12) years, body mass index (BMI) 24.6 (4.3) kg/m², eGFR 72 (29) mL/min. No superficial SSIs were found, but 6 cases of organ/space SSIs occurred. The average total cefazolin plasma concentration at closure (T4) was 114.25 (85.87) mg/L (22.85 mg/L free fraction). Free T4 was below 4 mg/L (EUCAST MIC for S. aureus [1]) in only 2 (3%) cases, but below 16 mg/L in 22 (33%) cases. Total T4 was below 104 mg/L (best available literature option [2]) in 39 (58%) cases. An interval between redosing administration and surgery completion exceeding 2 hours and eGFR > 50 mL/min correlated with significantly lower T4, unlike BMI >= 25 kg/m².

Conclusions

In the absence of well-established MIC or concentration cut-off values in the literature, according to our data, cefazolin 2 g given before incision and redosing with 1 g after 2 hours appear to provide adequate coverage for the initial surgery phase. However, additional doses, depending on surgery duration and patient characteristics (e.g., eGFR), may be necessary to maintain adequate concentrations until closure. Further analyses, including assessment of AUC and infection rates, are ongoing and may provide additional information.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A107 The role of serum cholinesterase levels in monitoring covert immunosuppression in critically ill patients with septic shock: evidence from a monocentric retrospective analysis

A. Frattari, F. Cedrone, E. Polilli, L. Agostinone, R. Frontera, R. Zocaro, G. Parruti

ASL Pescara, Pescara, Italy

Correspondence: A. Frattari

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A107

Background

Sepsis is a leading cause of mortality in intensive care units (ICUs) and, in the current dearth of evidence, identification of early, reliable, and possibly inexpensive prognostic biomarkers of covert immunosuppression is crucial for patients’ risk stratification and management. Serum cholinesterase levels, an enzyme reflecting hepatic synthetic function and systemic inflammation, have been suggested as a potential marker of survival, but their independent prognostic value in critically ill septic patients remains unclear.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective observational study on 259 consecutive adult patients admitted to a tertiary ICU for sepsis or septic shock, or who developed sepsis during ICU stay, between September 2024 and October 2025. Clinical and laboratory data collected included age, sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index, herpesvirus reactivation, CD4+ T-cell count, serum cholinesterase levels, immunoglobulin administration, and multidrug-resistant (MDR) status.

Survival analysis was performed using Cox proportional hazards regression. After assessment of model assumptions using Schoenfeld residuals, a final multivariable Cox model was built including only variables that satisfied the proportional hazards assumption. Hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated to evaluate the association between cholinesterase levels (<1600 vs >1600 U/L) and survival, and compared using log-rank test.

Results

Serum cholinesterase levels >1600 U/L emerged as the strongest independent protective factor for survival in the studied cohort (HR 0.21, 95% CI 0.09–0.46) after adjustment for age, sex, comorbidity burden, viral reactivations, lymphocytopenia, and CD4+ T-cell counts (Table 1 and Figure 1). Other variables —including sex, age, Charlson Comorbidity Index, herpesvirus reactivations, severe lymphocytopenia, CD4+ T-cell counts — where not independently associated in the multivariate analysis (Table 1).

Conclusions

In our study we found that serum cholinesterase levels >1600 U/L were independently and strongly associated with improved survival, suggesting they may serve as a simple and reliable prognostic biomarker of covert immunosuppression ensuing in otherwise immunocompetent critically ill patients. Persistent cholinesterase drop during sepsis is an easily assessable and interesting biomarker of dysregulated inflammation. Our findings highlight the need for prospective studies to validate its predictive value and explore more in dept the possible contribution of other, similarly accessible biomarkers of acute immune disfunction.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A108 Position paper on sepsis and septic shock: the right to early diagnosis and prompt access to the most appropriate treatments and pathways of care

V. Fava1, M. Bassetti2, E.G. Bignami3, N. Latronico4, C. Mussini5, A. Taraschi6

1Active Citizenship APS (Cittadinanzattiva), Rome, Italy; 2Department of Health Sciences, University of Genoa, Italy; 3Department of Medicine and Surgery, University of Parma, Italy; 4Department of Medical and Surgical Specialties, Radiological Sciences and Public Health, University of Brescia, Italy; 5Department of Infectious Diseases, Modena University Hospital, Italy; 6Local Health Authority of the City of Turin, Italy

Correspondence: V. Fava

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A108

Body

Sepsis and septic shock are time dependent emergencies associated with high mortality and morbidity, and major organizational burden across healthcare settings. In Italy, approximately 250,000 cases are reported annually, with a significant impact on clinical outcomes, healthcare resource utilization, and variability of care delivery. Despite the availability of international guidelines, real world management remains heterogeneous across healthcare facilities and care settings. The aim of this study was to identify the main clinical and organizational barriers to early diagnosis, treatment, and continuity of care in sepsis and septic shock, with particular attention to care pathways, multidisciplinary coordination, and continuity between hospital and community care.

A national civic investigation was conducted between 2025 and 2026 using a multi stakeholder approach. Data were collected through online surveys completed by 172 healthcare professionals, including anesthesiologists intensivists, infectious disease specialists, emergency physicians, and other clinicians. Additional contributions were obtained from patient associations and through qualitative interviews with representatives of scientific societies and general practitioners. Diagnostic, therapeutic, organizational, and communication related aspects of sepsis management were analyzed.

The lack of shared diagnostic and therapeutic pathways emerged as the main critical issue. Approximately one third of healthcare facilities reported the absence of dedicated hospital protocols for sepsis and septic shock. More than 70% of respondents identified significant multidisciplinary coordination problems and relevant differences in quality of care between daytime and nighttime or holiday shifts, particularly related to access to microbiological diagnostics. Post acute management was identified as a critical unmet need, with over 70% of facilities lacking structured follow up pathways and organized hospital–community integration, despite the high prevalence of physical, cognitive, and psychological sequelae among survivors.

These findings highlight how organizational fragmentation and variability in care delivery continue to limit the effective implementation of available clinical expertise. Uniform implementation of sepsis specific clinical pathways, guaranteed 24/7 access to rapid diagnostics, continuous multidisciplinary training, and strengthened hospital–territory integration represent key priorities to improve outcomes and reduce unwarranted variability in sepsis management, in line with clinical and organizational priorities (Figure 1).

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

The 10 final recommendations of the Position Paper outline the key priorities to improve sepsis clinical management in Italy, including standardized care pathways, strengthened early diagnosis, enhanced multidisciplinary coordination, and the development of more structured and integrated models of care

A109 Hemorrhagic shock and severe sepsis due to disseminated abdominal tubercolosis with paralytic ileus and tuberculous meningitis: the role of intensive critical care management in a young patient

A. Diana, C. Morrrone, F. De Vivo, G. Sagristani, G. Cosenza, F. Coppolino, V. Pota, S. Pasquale, M.B. Passavanti, M.C. Pace

University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: A. Diana

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A109

Background

Disseminated tuberculosis is a severe form of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection associated with high morbidity and mortality. It may involve multiple organ systems, including the abdomen and central nervous system, and can rapidly progress to severe sepsis and mixed hemorrhagic-septic shock. Early recognition and prompt intensive care management are essential to improve outcomes.

Case report

We report the case of a 20-year-old patient from a tuberculosis-endemic region who presented with acute diffuse abdominal pain, progressive asthenia, and massive rectal bleeding. The clinical presentation was consistent with abdominal tuberculosis complicated by paralytic ileus, leading to rapid hemodynamic deterioration and severe hemorrhagic shock. Immediate activation of the intensive care team and initiation of a massive transfusion protocol were required.

Despite initial resuscitation, the patient developed a cardiocirculatory arrest secondary to profound hypoperfusion, complicated by hypoxic brain injury. During the intensive care unit stay, neurological manifestations occurred, including recurrent epileptic seizures, successfully controlled with levetiracetam. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis confirmed tuberculous meningitis.

Advanced airway management was required, including orotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation, followed by tracheostomy because to prolonged ventilatory dependence. Hemodynamic instability required continuous infusion of norepinephrine and vasopressin. Standard four-drug antituberculous therapy was initiated in combination with dexamethasone. The clinical course was further complicated by sepsis-associated thrombocytopenia and ethambutol-induced retrobulbar optic neuritis.

Conclusions

Abdominal tuberculosis may rarely present with paralytic ileus and massive gastrointestinal bleeding, mimicking an acute surgical abdomen and delaying diagnosis. Central nervous system involvement in the form of tuberculous meningitis significantly worsens prognosis.

This case highlights the pivotal role of early and aggressive intensive care management in mixed hemorrhagic and septic shock due to disseminated tuberculosis, based on advanced hemodynamic support, invasive mechanical ventilation, and management of neurological and pharmacological complications. Early recognition of atypical infectious presentations in the intensive care setting is essential to improve survival and neurological outcomes.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient’s legal representative for publication of this case report and accompanying clinical information. All identifying information has been removed to preserve patient anonymity.

A110 Targeted use of IgM- and IgA-enriched immunoglobulins in septic shock: survival benefits from a precision-based dosing algorithm

A. Bucaletti, A. Capone, E. Zendra, F. Celli, D. Fiumanò, S. Simoncini, I. Gatti, M.C. Michelini, C. Santorsola, R. Zanotti, G. Richini, A. Corona

ASST Valcamonica, Breno (BS), Italy

Correspondence: A. Bucaletti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A110

Background

Septic shock remains associated with high mortality despite early antimicrobial therapy, source control, and advanced organ support. A relevant proportion of patients develop marked immune dysregulation, including depletion of circulating immunoglobulins and impairment of cellular immune competence. This biological heterogeneity may partly explain the inconsistent results of previous studies on adjunctive immunoglobulin therapy, many of which adopted fixed-dose strategies without accounting for timing, organ dysfunction, renal clearance, or baseline immune profile. Previous evidence suggests that timing of IgM- and IgA-enriched immunoglobulin administration may influence outcome, supporting a more individualized treatment approach [1]. We therefore evaluated the impact of adjunctive IgM- and IgA-enriched immunoglobulins (IGAM) in septic shock using a center-developed precision-based dosing strategy, the P.R.I.O.R.I.T.Y. score [Plasma Immunoglobulins, CD4+/CD8+ Ratio, Initiation timing, Organ dysfunction, Renal function, Indicated dose, Therapy escalation, Yield prediction], designed to individualize dose intensity according to biological and clinical severity.

Methods

We performed a prospective propensity score-matched observational study in adults with septic shock admitted to ICU. Patients received either standard care alone (Group B) or standard care plus adjunctive IGAM (Group A). IGAM was administered for 72 hours at 250–500 mg/kg/day according to the institutional P.R.I.O.R.I.T.Y. algorithm. Matching was used to reduce baseline imbalance between treated and untreated patients. Primary endpoints were ICU, hospital, and 180-day survival. Secondary endpoints included ICU-acquired infections, duration of mechanical ventilation, duration of vasoactive therapy, and ICU/hospital length of stay. Immune monitoring included serial measurements of serum IgG, IgA, and IgM and lymphocyte subsets (CD3+, CD4+, CD8+) to explore the relationship between treatment and immune reconstitution. Multivariable analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of survival and to test whether the observed association between IGAM exposure and outcome persisted after adjustment for relevant clinical covariates.

Results

A total of 330 adults with septic shock were analyzed. Adjunctive IGAM was associated with numerically higher ICU survival (73.9% vs 61.9%, p=0.2198) and significantly higher 180-day survival (70.3% vs 58.2%, p=0.0393). In multivariable logistic regression, IGAM emerged as an independent protective factor for survival (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.20–0.80, p=0.002). The survival signal was accompanied by a biologically coherent pattern of immune recovery. Among survivors, IgM exceeded 1.5 g/L at 72 hours (p=0.00005), with parallel increases in IgG and IgA concentrations and recovery of CD3+, CD4+, and CD8+ lymphocyte subsets, suggesting enhanced immune reconstitution rather than a transient replacement effect only. This finding is clinically relevant because the treatment strategy was not uniform but calibrated according to the P.R.I.O.R.I.T.Y. score, integrating timing of initiation, renal function, organ dysfunction, and baseline immune status into dose selection.

IGAM exposure was also associated with lower ICU morbidity and reduced organ support burden. Treated patients had fewer secondary infections (p=0.0131), shorter duration of mechanical ventilation (p=0.0017), shorter vasoactive support (p=0.0001), and shorter hospital stay (p=0.0388). These findings suggest that the benefit of treatment may extend beyond crude mortality reduction and may influence the trajectory of organ dysfunction, ICU-related complications, and pace of recovery. The overall pattern supports the concept that early and individualized IGAM administration may be particularly valuable in patients with septic shock characterized by both hemodynamic instability and measurable immune impairment. Rather than behaving as a generic adjunct, IGAM appeared to perform best when embedded in a phenotype-oriented framework able to address who to treat, when to treat, and how much to administer. This interpretation is consistent with previous reports emphasizing the relevance of timing and patient selection in maximizing the effect of IgM- and IgA-enriched preparations [1], while also fitting within the broader, though methodologically heterogeneous, literature on intravenous immunoglobulins in sepsis [2].

Conclusions

In this prospective propensity score-matched study, early and personalized IGAM administration was associated with improved long-term survival, enhanced immune reconstitution, fewer secondary infections, and shorter duration of organ support in septic shock. These findings support a precision-based, rather than fixed-dose, approach to adjunctive immunoglobulin therapy and suggest that treatment efficacy may depend on integration of biological and clinical profiling into bedside decision-making. The P.R.I.O.R.I.T.Y.-guided strategy may therefore represent a practical framework for translating immunological heterogeneity into individualized treatment. Randomized controlled trials are warranted to validate this approach and to define which septic shock phenotypes derive the greatest benefit from targeted IGAM use.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.
