A111 When presepsin fails to fall: a dynamic marker of mortality and prolonged ICU stay in sepsis and septic shock

A. Capone, E. Zendra, F. Celli, D. Fiumanò, A. Bucaletti, S. Simoncini, I. gatti, M.C. Michelini, C. Santorsola, R. Zanotti, G. Richini, A. Corona

ASST Valcamonica, Breno (BS), Italy

Correspondence: A. Capone

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A111

Background

Sepsis and septic shock remain major causes of ICU morbidity and mortality, and early risk stratification is still challenging despite the availability of conventional biomarkers such as procalcitonin (PCT), C-reactive protein (CRP), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Presepsin, the soluble CD14 subtype released during monocyte-macrophage activation in response to bacterial infection, has emerged as a promising biomarker for both diagnosis and prognostic assessment. Beyond its early diagnostic role, recent evidence suggests that biomarker kinetics may be more informative than isolated baseline values, particularly in critically ill patients with prolonged organ dysfunction and heterogeneous inflammatory trajectories. Persistent elevation, delayed decline, or failure to normalize may identify patients with ongoing dysregulated host response, more severe disease evolution, and delayed recovery. We therefore evaluated the kinetic behavior of presepsin in a real-world ICU cohort of septic patients, comparing its temporal profile with PCT, CRP, and IL-6 and exploring its association with mortality, prolonged ICU stay, and intensity of organ support.

Methods

This prospective observational study was conducted in the ICU of ASST Valcamonica between August 2022 and August 2025. Consecutive adult patients admitted with sepsis or septic shock were included. Presepsin was measured daily from ICU admission until discharge or death, together with PCT, CRP, and IL-6. Biomarker kinetics were analyzed according to survival status and ICU length of stay (LOS), using a predefined threshold of more than 14 days versus 14 days or less. Clinical and demographic variables included age, sex, comorbidity burden, need for continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), vasoactive support, duration of mechanical ventilation, and ICU stay. Survivors and non-survivors were compared using descriptive statistics, with particular attention to baseline values, end-of-ICU values, and persistence of abnormal presepsin levels beyond day 7. The analysis was designed to reflect bedside applicability rather than laboratory discrimination alone.

Results

A total of 215 patients were enrolled during the study period, with a male-to-female ratio of 1.5:1 and a median age of 72 years (IQR 55–74). Patients with prolonged ICU stay showed less favorable biomarker trajectories than those with shorter LOS. Baseline median (IQR) PCT values were 7.5 ng/mL (4.8–12.6) in survivors and 7.5 ng/mL (5.1–13.9) in non-survivors, decreasing at ICU end to 0.8 ng/mL (0.4–1.3) and 1.1 ng/mL (0.7–2.4), respectively; baseline and end-of-course differences were not significant (p>0.05). Baseline CRP values were 168 mg/L (122–231) in survivors and 181 mg/L (136–248) in non-survivors, falling to 42 mg/L (18–76) and 71 mg/L (34–129), respectively; baseline differences were not significant, whereas end-of-ICU values were significant (p<0.01). Baseline IL-6 values were 410 pg/mL (285–690) in survivors and 465 pg/mL (310–820) in non-survivors, decreasing to 118 pg/mL (62–210) and 276 pg/mL (154–498), respectively; only end-of-ICU differences were significant (p<0.01). Baseline presepsin values were 1,760 pg/mL (1,420-2,280) in survivors and 1,980 pg/mL (1,560-2,740) in non-survivors (p>0.05); at ICU end, presepsin decreased to 420 pg/mL (290–610) in survivors but remained markedly elevated in non-survivors at 4,850 pg/mL (3,920-6,340) (p<0.001). This represented the clearest separation between groups among all analyzed biomarkers. CRRT was required in 12% of survivors and 31% of non-survivors (p<0.01), vasoactive support in 52% and 86%, respectively (p<0.001), and median duration of mechanical ventilation was 7 days (IQR 4–12) versus 13 days (IQR 8–21) (p<0.01). Patients with prolonged LOS also showed more sustained presepsin elevation than those discharged earlier. Overall, while PCT, CRP, and IL-6 declined in survivors and remained higher in non-survivors, their baseline values did not discriminate outcome as effectively as the longitudinal behavior of presepsin. In contrast, failure of presepsin to normalize over time, especially after the first week of ICU stay, consistently identified patients with longer organ support exposure, more complicated ICU course, and higher risk of death.

Conclusions

Daily monitoring suggests that presepsin is a valuable dynamic prognostic marker in septic ICU patients. More than a simple diagnostic adjunct, it appears to reflect the trajectory of critical illness over time. Persistent elevation beyond day 7 was associated with ICU mortality, prolonged LOS, higher CRRT exposure, greater vasoactive requirements, and longer mechanical ventilation. Compared with PCT, CRP, and IL-6, presepsin showed the strongest end-of-course separation between survivors and non-survivors, supporting its role as a longitudinal bedside marker of unfavorable evolution. These findings suggest that serial presepsin assessment may help identify high-risk patients who require closer monitoring, therapeutic reassessment, or escalation of care. Larger studies are needed to clarify whether presepsin-guided risk stratification can be integrated into precision-oriented ICU management pathways for sepsis and septic shock.

A112 Flow without congestion: combined levosimendan and angiotensin II for hemodynamic rescue in refractory cardiocirculatory failure

D. Fiumano’, E. Zendra, A. Capone, F. Celli, A. Bucaletti, S. Simoncini, I. Gatti, M. Michelini, C. Santorsola, R. Zanotti, G. Richini, A. Corona

ASST Valcamonica, Breno (BS), Italy

Correspondence: D. Fiumano’

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A112

Background

Refractory cardiocirculatory failure in the ICU often requires escalation beyond conventional catecholamines. In this setting, levosimendan may improve myocardial performance through calcium sensitization and vasodilatory effects, while angiotensin II (AT-II) may restore vascular tone in vasoplegic states and support perfusion pressure when high-dose adrenergic vasopressors are insufficient. Although both agents are increasingly used in rescue settings, real-world data on their combined use remain limited, especially when integrated with invasive hemodynamic monitoring and bedside echocardiography. We therefore evaluated the clinical, echocardiographic, and invasive hemodynamic profile of critically ill patients treated with levosimendan in our ICU, with a predefined exploratory focus on the subgroup also receiving adjunctive AT-II.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective single-center observational study in the ICU of ASST Valcamonica. All consecutive patients treated with levosimendan for refractory cardiocirculatory failure were reviewed. Demographic characteristics, ICU diagnosis, vasopressor requirements, advanced organ support, echocardiographic findings, and ICU outcomes were collected from the clinical dataset. A predefined subgroup analysis focused on patients receiving both levosimendan and AT-II. In this subgroup, available invasive or advanced hemodynamic variables at treatment start and end were analyzed, including cardiac index (CI), mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2), pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP), and systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI). Echocardiographic parameters were reviewed in parallel to assess whether ultrasound trends were consistent with invasive hemodynamic changes and clinically useful for bedside decision-making. Because paired measurements were incomplete and the cohort was small, the analysis was primarily descriptive and exploratory.

Results

A total of 14 patients received levosimendan during the study period. Of these, 6 also received adjunctive AT-II, identifying the highest-acuity subgroup. Mean (SD) age of the overall cohort was 75.4 (7.9) years, confirming an elderly and frail ICU population. Clinical presentations were heterogeneous and included cardiogenic shock, mixed cardiogenic-vasoplegic states, septic shock with myocardial dysfunction, severe respiratory failure, and post-resuscitation or perioperative instability. The overall picture was therefore one of advanced circulatory failure requiring escalation beyond conventional catecholamine support.

In the combined-treatment subgroup, invasive or advanced hemodynamic monitoring was available only in selected cases, yet a coherent rescue profile emerged. Exploratory paired analysis suggested an increase in cardiac index from 2.86 to 3.44 L/min/m², indicating improved forward flow after combined treatment. At the same time, SVRI increased from 1100 to 1510 dyn·s·cm^−5·m², suggesting recovery of vascular tone and improved vasoplegic control. Importantly, PAWP remained stable (13.5 vs 13.0 mmHg), supporting the interpretation that improved circulation occurred without a relevant increase in left-sided filling pressures or pulmonary congestion. By contrast, SvO2 showed no consistent directional change (70.7% vs 67.0%), probably reflecting the marked heterogeneity of the underlying shock phenotypes, oxygen extraction patterns, and degree of organ dysfunction.

Echocardiography was broadly synergistic with invasive hemodynamic trends and added clinically actionable bedside information. In practical terms, it supported treatment escalation, guided interpretation of invasive measurements, and helped distinguish patients with predominant pump failure from those in whom vasoplegia was the leading driver of instability. Ventricular recovery, however, remained heterogeneous: some patients showed improved function over time, whereas others displayed persistent or worsening dysfunction despite hemodynamic stabilization. This suggests that, in this setting, hemodynamic rescue and myocardial recovery cannot be considered synonymous. Rather, the combination appeared to provide circulatory stabilization even when structural or functional ventricular recovery was delayed or incomplete.

From a feasibility perspective, the levosimendan plus AT-II combination proved manageable in patients requiring advanced vasopressor escalation and multimodal support. No clear signal suggested worsening congestion, and the stability of wedge pressure supports the physiological plausibility of combining an inodilator with a vasoconstrictor in carefully selected patients. Although the number of paired observations was limited and no comparison achieved robust statistical significance, the directional consistency of CI, SVRI, PAWP, and echocardiographic bedside interpretation supports the clinical relevance of the observed trends.

Conclusions

In this exploratory single-center ICU series, the combination of levosimendan and AT-II was associated with a coherent hemodynamic rescue profile in refractory cardiocirculatory failure, characterized by improved forward flow and vascular tone without evidence of increased congestion. Bedside echocardiography paralleled invasive monitoring and supported real-time clinical decisions. These findings suggest that the combination may represent a pragmatic rescue strategy in selected high-risk ICU patients, but larger phenotype-driven studies are needed to define which cardiocirculatory profiles derive the greatest benefit.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A113 Angiotensin II in refractory septic shock: a prospective single-center experience from ASST Valcamonica

F. Celli, E. Zendra, A. Capone, D. Fiumano, A. Bucaletti, S. Simoncini, I. Gatti, M. Michelini, C. Santorsola, R. Zanotti, A. Corona

ASST Valcamonica, Breno (BS), Italy

Correspondence: F. Celli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A113

Background

Septic shock is a life-threatening condition characterized by persistent hypotension, circulatory failure, and progressive multiorgan dysfunction despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Mortality remains high, particularly in refractory cases requiring escalating vasopressor support. High-dose catecholamines are associated with arrhythmias, ischemic complications, and impaired microcirculatory perfusion, potentially worsening outcomes.

Angiotensin II (AT-II), a key component of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, has emerged as a non-catecholaminergic vasopressor capable of restoring vascular tone through activation of angiotensin type-1 receptors. Following the ATHOS-3 trial, AT-II is increasingly used as rescue therapy in refractory septic shock requiring high-dose vasopressors [1,2].

We report our prospective single-center experience with AT-II in patients with refractory septic shock requiring high-dose norepinephrine support.

Methods

We conducted a prospective observational study in the intensive care unit of ASST Valcamonica between February 2024 and April 2026. Adult patients with septic shock requiring norepinephrine >=0.75 mcg/kg/min despite adequate fluid resuscitation were eligible for AT-II treatment. Concomitant argipressin >=0.02 U/min was allowed.

AT-II infusion was initiated at 20–80 ng/kg/min and generally maintained around 40 ng/kg/min. Hemodynamic response was evaluated at 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 hours after initiation. Responders were defined as patients achieving mean arterial pressure (MAP) >=75 mmHg with stabilization or reduction of catecholamine requirements.

All patients received standard septic shock management including source control, antimicrobial therapy, invasive monitoring, mechanical ventilation when indicated, renal replacement therapy, corticosteroids, and metabolic optimization.

Demographic characteristics, infection source, severity scores, biomarkers, organ support requirements, vasopressor exposure, ICU length of stay, and mortality were prospectively collected. Mortality analysis included standardized mortality ratio (SMR) and variable life-adjusted display (VLAD).

Results

Thirty-two patients received AT-II during the study period. Twenty-six patients were male (81.2%). Mean age was 69.8 ± 12.4 years, while median Charlson Comorbidity Index was 5 (IQR 3–7).

Severity of illness was high, with median SAPS II of 52 (IQR 44–63) and SOFA score of 9 (IQR 7–12). All patients required norepinephrine >=0.75 mcg/kg/min before AT-II initiation. Concomitant argipressin was administered in 18 patients (56.2%), while methylene blue was used in 9 (28.1%) because of severe vasoplegia.

The most frequent infection sources were pneumonia (40.6%), bloodstream infections (21.9%), secondary peritonitis (18.7%), and complicated urinary tract infections (12.5%). Twenty patients (62.5%) required invasive mechanical ventilation, while 13 (40.6%) underwent continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT).

Median procalcitonin (PCT) at ICU admission was 9.2 ng/mL (IQR 4.1–18.6), while median presepsin was 2450 pg/mL (IQR 1870–3580).

Median duration of AT-II infusion was 22 hours (IQR 10–38). AT-II was administered with norepinephrine in all patients and with argipressin in 56.2%. Hemodynamic response rates were 78.1% at 1 hour, 84.3% at 3 hours, 87.5% at 6 hours, 84.3% at 12 hours, and 71.8% at 24 hours. In early responders, median time to MAP target achievement was 8 minutes (IQR 5–14).

Following AT-II initiation, norepinephrine requirements progressively decreased in most responders, with improved hemodynamic stability. Patients responding within the first hour showed lower lactate accumulation and reduced progression of organ dysfunction during the first 24 hours.

Median duration of invasive mechanical ventilation was 8 days (IQR 5–14), while ICU length of stay was 11 days (IQR 7–18). ICU mortality was 43.7% (14/32 patients).

Despite high illness severity, mortality analysis showed favorable findings. Mean SMR was 0.58 (95% CI 0.39–0.81), suggesting lower observed mortality than predicted. VLAD analysis remained positive during the study period, corresponding to approximately 2.6 more lives saved than expected.

No major ischemic complications directly attributable to AT-II were observed.

Conclusions

In this prospective single-center experience, AT-II demonstrated rapid and sustained hemodynamic efficacy in refractory septic shock requiring high-dose catecholamine support. Most patients achieved early MAP target restoration with progressive norepinephrine reduction and improved hemodynamic stabilization.

Despite high illness severity and frequent multiorgan dysfunction, observed mortality was lower than predicted by severity scores, with favorable SMR and VLAD performance. These findings support the potential role of AT-II as an adjunctive non-catecholaminergic vasopressor in refractory vasoplegic shock.

Larger prospective multicenter studies are needed to better define optimal timing, patient selection, and long-term clinical impact.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A114 Implementation of an integrated infection control and antimicrobial stewardship strategy in ICU: effects on HAIs, CRE colonization and carbapenem use

C.B. Bussemi, D. Scarano, A. Lucarelli, A. Piedepalumbo, D. Carbone

PO Umberto I, Nocera Inferiore, Italy

Correspondence: A. Piedepalumbo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A114

Background

Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs), antimicrobial overuse, and the emergence of multidrug-resistant organisms remain critical challenges in intensive care units (ICUs), contributing to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs [1,2]. Integrated infection control (IC) and antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) strategies have been proposed to mitigate these risks, but real-world evidence on their combined implementation is still limited [3,4]. Our goal was to evaluate the impact of a combined IC and AMS program on HAI incidence, antibiotic consumption, and new patient colonization rates in a tertiary ICU.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective before–after study comparing data from the first four months of 2025 (pre-implementation phase) with the same period in 2026 (post-implementation phase). The intervention included reinforcement of infection prevention measures, systematic collection of epidemiological surveillance data, active surveillance cultures, and staff education [3]. Preventive contact isolation was applied to patients at high risk of infection and/or colonization. In addition, rapid diagnostic tools were implemented to enable earlier targeted antimicrobial therapy [5]. Antimicrobial stewardship interventions included protocolized antibiotic prescribing and regular review of ongoing therapies according to current stewardship principles [4,6]. Outcomes assessed were: incidence of HAIs, antibiotic consumption expressed as defined daily doses (DDD) per 100 patient-days, and incidence of new colonization by multidrug-resistant organisms.

Results

Following implementation, a 23% reduction in HAI incidence was observed. Antibiotic consumption decreased overall, with a marked reduction in carbapenem use: DDD per 100 patient-days declined from 5.72 to 2.98, particularly reflecting reduced meropenem use. Moreover, new rectal colonization by carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) decreased by 74%, indicating a substantial impact on the control of multidrug-resistant organism spread within the ICU (Figs. 1 and 2)

Conclusions

The implementation of an integrated infection control and antimicrobial stewardship strategy in the ICU was associated with a significant reduction in healthcare-associated infections, carbapenem consumption, and new CRE rectal colonization. A multimodal approach based on epidemiological surveillance, early isolation measures, rapid diagnostics, and targeted antimicrobial therapy may represent an effective model to limit multidrug-resistant organism spread and optimize antibiotic use in critically ill patients [3–6].

A115 In vitro evaluation of immunoglobulin removal (Pentaglobin®) during hemoadsorption with CytoSorb®

G. Berlot1, M. Bixio2

1University of Trieste – Department of Medical, Surgical and Health Sciences, Trieste, Italy; 2San Martino Hospital of Genoa – Anesthesia and Intensive Care Unit, Italy

Correspondence: A. Piedepalumbo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A115

Background

Pentaglobin® is an intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) preparation enriched in IgM and IgA, with established immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory properties. It is used as adjunctive therapy in septic shock. CytoSorb® is an extracorporeal hemoadsorption device designed to remove hydrophobic circulating inflammatory mediators and other toxins with a molecular weight <55 kDa, including cytokines, pathogen-associated toxins, and other inflammatory mediators.

Given the high MW of immunoglobulins (approximately 150–900 kDa), their removal by adsorption-based extracorporeal therapies is theoretically unlikely. However, experimental data specifically addressing the interaction between IVIG preparations and hemoadsorption devices remain limited. Concerns regarding potential unintended clearance of therapeutic proteins during extracorporeal blood purification techniques warrant systematic evaluation.

The aim of this study was to investigate in vitro whether immunoglobulins contained in Pentaglobin® are removed during extracorporeal circulation incorporating CytoSorb®.

Material and methods

This was an in vitro experimental study conducted using a closed-loop hemoperfusion (HP) circuit simulating extracorporeal circulation at constant temperature. The system was operated at a constant blood flow rate (Qb) of 120 mL/min for a total duration of 210 minutes (reflecting the period during which sorbent adsorption is most active in the initial hours.). Two experimental models were evaluated.

Case A (bolus model, no CytoSorb®):

The circuit was primed with approximately 2,500 mL of isotonic saline. Pentaglobin® (50 mL; total dose 2,500 mg of immunoglobulins) was added as a single bolus injection into the system. This model was used to assess immunoglobulin stability and potential non-specific loss within the extracorporeal circuit. Serial systemic samples were collected at predefined time points (T-20: Pentaglobin infusion, T0: baseline, and T5–T210: samples; Tend: final concentration in the bag). The expected initial concentration was approximately 1.5–1.6 mg/mL.

Case B (continuous infusion model with CytoSorb®):

The circuit had a total priming volume of approximately 1,250 mL (including tubing and saline). Pentaglobin® (50 mL) was administered as a continuous infusion at 14 mL/h to mimic clinical administration, consistent with the manufacturer’s indications. CytoSorb® was integrated into the extracorporeal circuit. Paired pre- and post-cartridge blood samples were collected at defined intervals (T5–T210; Tend: final concentration in the bag). Baseline expected concentration was 1.5–1.6 mg/mL. Immunoglobulin concentrations were quantified at each time point using a validated quantitative immunoassay (bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein assays). Measurements were expressed as mg/mL. The presence of a concentration gradient between pre- and post-cartridge samples was used to assess potential adsorption.

Results (Figure 1)

Case A (bolus model, no CytoSorb®)

In the absence of CytoSorb®, immunoglobulin concentrations remained stable throughout the experimental period. Measured systemic concentrations ranged from 1.4 to 1.6 mg/mL over 210 minutes. No progressive decline or evidence of significant spontaneous degradation, adsorption to circuit components, or dilutional loss was observed. Also, the trend value (1.6 mg/mL) indicates that no degradation occurred.

Case B (with CytoSorb®)

In the presence of CytoSorb®, pre- and post-device immunoglobulin concentrations were consistently comparable across all time points. No relevant concentration gradients suggestive of adsorption were detected.

At the final time point (T210), values were 1.50 mg/mL pre-cartridge and 1.47 mg/mL post-cartridge, corresponding to a minimal and non-significant difference within assay variability. Similar findings were observed at all intermediate sampling points, with no trend toward progressive clearance over time. Also, the Trend value (1.47 mg/mL) indicates that no significant adsorption occurred

Overall, no evidence of significant immunoglobulin removal attributable to the hemoadsorption device was observed under steady-state or dynamic infusion conditions.

Conclusions

This in vitro study demonstrates that immunoglobulins contained in Pentaglobin® are not measurably removed during extracorporeal circulation incorporating CytoSorb®. These findings are consistent with the physicochemical characteristics of immunoglobulins, whose large molecular size (150–900 kDa) exceeds the adsorption capacity range of the device. Importantly, the absence of a measurable pre-post cartridge gradient suggests that neither direct adsorption nor secondary non-specific binding occurs to a clinically relevant extent. Furthermore, the stability observed in the bolus model confirms that the extracorporeal circuit itself does not induce significant immunoglobulin degradation or loss. These results provide experimental support for the concurrent use of IVIG therapy and CytoSorb® hemoadsorption in critically ill patients

In conclusion, under in vitro hemoperfusion conditions, CytoSorb® hemoadsorption does not result in measurable removal of immunoglobulins contained in Pentaglobin®. These findings support the physicochemical compatibility of IVIG therapy with CytoSorb® use and suggest that concomitant administration does not lead to clinically relevant immunoglobulin loss during extracorporeal blood purification.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

Immunoglobulin concentrations over treatment (case A and case B)

A116 Implementation of an evidence-based bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia in the intensive care unit

E. Balagna1, F. Moretto2, S. Giordano2, S. Lamberti2, A. Cardelli1, N. Gentile2, A.S. Costa Ferreira3, A. Chiodini1, A. Langella1, E. Bassi1,4,5, A. Dal Molin1,4,5, C. Gallione1,4,5, R. Vaschetto1,2,5

1Department of Translational Medicine, University of Eastern Piedmont, Novara, Italy; 2Anesthesia and Intensive Care, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy; 3Intensive Care, Hospital de Pedro Hispano, Matosinhos, Portugal; 4Directorate of Health Professions, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy; 5JBI University of Piemonte Orientale for Healthy Aging, Vercelli, Italy

Correspondence: E. Balagna

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A116

Background

Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is one of the most frequent healthcare-associated infections in critically ill patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation, with reported incidences ranging from 5% to 40%, negatively affecting patient outcomes [1]. This project aims to design an implementation plan for a bundle of evidence-based interventions for VAP prevention, based on the most recent recommendations [2–5], and its future application by nursing staff.

Materials and methods

The project is being conducted through the JBI Evidence Implementation methodology [6] in a mixed intensive care unit (ICU) of a tertiary university hospital in Italy. Informed consent was obtained from the nursing staff before the project started. During this pre-implementation phase, an anonymous 21-item multiple-choice questionnaire was administered. The questionnaire aimed to assess nurses’ professional characteristics, baseline knowledge, and current clinical practices related to VAP prevention, as well as their perceptions regarding the necessity and feasibility of implementation and their preferences for the subsequent training phase. Based on the questionnaire findings, a tailored educational intervention will be developed and implemented, followed by questionnaire re-administration and evaluation of adherence to the VAP prevention bundle (Figure 1).

Results

The pre-implementation assessment of 29 nurses revealed that 16 (55%) had never received specific training on VAP prevention guidelines, despite nearly half having 6–10 years of ICU experience. In the knowledge section, while approximately 80% identified micro-aspiration as the primary mechanism underlying VAP, as well as the appropriate frequency of oral hygiene and correct cuff pressure management, 20 participants (69%) were unable to identify the timeframe for early-onset VAP and no consensus emerged regarding ventilator circuit change or the use of saline solution for subglottic suctioning. Regarding clinical practice, most nurses identified regular oral hygiene, head-of-bed elevation 30° or more, subglottic suctioning, and cuff pressure monitoring as the most effective strategies for reducing VAP incidence. Twenty-three nurses (80%) reported barriers to guideline adherence, mainly due to excessive workload and lack of materials. Nevertheless, all participants agreed on the need to improve clinical practice, and 97% considered the implementation of a validated protocol feasible within their department. Regarding the training phase, the preferred educational methods included lectures, clinical case discussions, and practical sessions with specialists on device use (64%).

Conclusions

From the pre-implementation assessment, knowledge gaps, variability in clinical practice, and barriers to guideline adherence emerged, while the high level of staff acceptance confirmed the feasibility of implementing a VAP prevention bundle within the ICU setting.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A117 Innovative and easy to learn orotracheal intubation technique for high biocontainment transport: a civil military collaboration

M. Bixio1, A. Fiorini2, M. Lastilla3, M. Florio2, P. Boi2, C. Ferrari4, E. Garzia5, P. Perelli6, G. Berlot7

1IRCCS Metropolitan Hospital “San Martino” Polyclinic – Anesthesia and Intensive Care Unit, Genoa, Italy; 2Italian Air Force – Main Infirmary of Pratica di Mare, Rome, Italy; 3Italian Air Force – Aerospace Medicine Institute of Milan, Italy; 4IRCCS Metropolitan Hospital “San Martino” Polyclinic – Trauma Center and Emergency Unit, Genoa, Italy; 5Italian Air Force – Air Force Health Service (Servizio Sanitario A.M.), Rome, Italy; 6Italian Air Force – Aeronautical Medical Corps (Corpo Sanitario Aeronautico), Rome, Italy; 7Julian–Isonzo Integrated University Health Authority – Complex Operating Unit of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Therapy, Trieste, Italy

Correspondence: M. Bixio

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A117

Body

The management of airways in patients with highly transmissible respiratory infections is essential to prevent the spread of airborne pathogens and ensure the safe transport of mechanically ventilated patients. During the COVID 19 pandemic, the Stretcher Transit Isolator (STI) and the Aircraft Transit Isolator (ATI) were widely employed for this purpose; however, their structural configuration makes orotracheal intubation (TI) extremely challenging, prompting the need for an alternative technique. This study presents a novel device and procedure for TI developed in collaboration with the Italian Air Force (IAF). A wireless, disposable, compact video laryngoscope (WiLS) was designed to transmit real time images to an external screen, enabling the operator to intubate from the patient’s left side using a lateral approach. Initial tests on a dummy confirmed feasibility, followed by further assessment during an Air Force training activity. The procedure is performed by a four member team—including an anesthesiologist, an assistant, a nurse, and technical support—with the anesthesiologist conducting TI using a bougie guided lateral video assisted technique. Training sessions involving 20 non specialist providers demonstrated a remarkably rapid learning curve for the WiLS technique, with a first attempt mean intubation time of 88,6 ± 55,6 s (31,7 s for visualization of the vocal cords, 32,9 s for bougie insertion, and 24,1 s for tube insertion), and execution times progressively decreasing to approximately one minute in subsequent attempts. All participants rated the practicality of the device and the ease of execution as excellent. Although not intended as a standard approach, this technique represents a valuable life saving option should a patient’s condition deteriorate during transport in ATI-STI biocontainment stretchers and invasive airway management become necessary. This work also highlights the benefits of civil military collaboration in managing critical patients in austere environments, leveraging specialized skills and technological innovation for the broader community.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A118 Impact of nurse-led clinical reasoning on emergency medical dispatch accuracy and safety: a one-year retrospective analysis of 154,585 calls in the Florence–Prato ems system

L. Volpi1, R. Detti2, V. Bocciero1

1118 Florence–Prato – Emergency and Urgency Department, Central Tuscany Local Health Authority (AUSL Toscana Centro), Italy; 2112 Single Emergency Number, Central Tuscany Local Health Authority (AUSL Toscana Centro), Florence, Italy

Correspondence: L. Volpi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A118

Background

Increasing demand for emergency medical services and emergency department overcrowding require dispatch systems capable of ensuring both clinical safety and optimal resource allocation. Internationally, many systems rely on algorithm-based protocols managed by non-clinical personnel, prioritizing standardization over clinical interpretation. The Tuscany model, however, is based on nurse-led clinical decision-making supported by open-ended protocols, allowing integration of structured algorithms with professional clinical reasoning. This study aims to evaluate the impact of advanced nursing clinical judgement on diagnostic accuracy, patient safety, and resource utilization in emergency medical dispatch, and to contextualize these findings within the current international literature.

Materials and methods

A retrospective, observational, single-centre study was conducted on all emergency calls managed by the Florence–Prato Emergency Medical Dispatch Centre (Italy) during the 2025 calendar year. A total of 154,585 valid clinical events were analysed. Dispatch priority levels were compared with patient clinical outcomes using a confusion matrix approach. Performance indicators included sensitivity, predictive values, and Cohen’s kappa. Advanced statistical analyses included logistic regression (odds ratio) and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

To contextualize the findings, a structured literature review was performed, with relevant studies selected according to PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) methodology.

All data were anonymized and collected in accordance with institutional regulations; informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study.

Results

The nurse-led dispatch model demonstrated high clinical safety and diagnostic reliability, with a sensitivity of 92.01% and a negative predictive value of 87.31%. The overtriage rate was 51.5%, lower than values reported in algorithm-based systems (>60%), while clinically significant undertriage was rare (0.14%). Diagnostic performance measures are summarized in Table 1.

High-priority dispatch codes were strongly associated with actual critical conditions (OR 10.84; 95% CI 10.5–11.1), confirming the predictive validity of clinical prioritization. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis showed moderate discriminative performance (AUC 0.703), as shown in Figure 1.

Additionally, 8.3% of cases (n = 12,826) were managed without ambulance dispatch through telephone triage and referral pathways, underscoring the system’s gatekeeping role and its contribution to resource optimization.

Conclusions

Nurse-led clinical reasoning in emergency medical dispatch is associated with high levels of safety, diagnostic accuracy, and efficient resource utilization. Compared with purely algorithm-based systems, this approach reduces unnecessary resource activation while maintaining minimal undertriage rates.

The integration of clinical judgement with structured protocols represents a key element for the development of sustainable, patient-centred emergency care systems and reinforces the central role of advanced nursing competencies.

These findings have important implications for healthcare policy and emergency system organization, supporting the integration of advanced nursing roles in high-demand prehospital settings.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A119 Pre-hospital anesthesia training across borders: international evaluation of the parma-toronto exchange built on Italy’s 118 model

P. Panchal1, A. Lagrotteria1, G. Lorello1,2, M. Garavaglia1,2, B. Giammarioli1,3, R. Lanza4, M. Russo4, C. Madoni4, A. Volpi5, E.G. Bignami4, S. Schiavo1,2

1Department of Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine, University of Toronto, Canada; 2Department of Anesthesia and Pain Management, Toronto Western Hospital, University Health Network, Toronto, Canada; 3Department of Anesthesia, St. Michael s Hospital, Unity Health Toronto, Canada; 4Anesthesiology, Critical Care and Pain Medicine Division, Department of Medicine and Surgery, University of Parma, Italy; 5Emergenza Territoriale 118, Azienda USL di Parma, Italy

Correspondence: P. Panchal

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A119

Background

Italy is among the few healthcare systems in which pre-hospital emergency care is consistently led by anesthesiologists and intensivists, who provide advanced airway management, hemodynamic resuscitation and on-scene leadership through the Servizio di Emergenza Territoriale 118. This anesthesiologist-led model, built around physician-staffed “automedica” vehicles integrated within regional dispatch, represents a distinctive scope of practice largely absent from North America, and completely missing in its anesthesia residency curricula [1]. While the clinical performance of the Italian system is well established domestically, its value as an international educational asset has not been formally evaluated. The Parma-Toronto Global Health Exchange, formalized through a bilateral Memorandum of Understanding (2023) and Addendum (2025), was designed to test this question. The program is reciprocal: University of Toronto (UofT) residents complete a two-week pre-hospital rotation embedded within the Parma 118 service, while Parma residents undertake observerships across Toronto’s perioperative, intensive care, trauma and simulation environments (Fig. 1). We conducted a pilot mixed-methods evaluation of the Toronto-bound rotation to characterize residents’ perceived educational value, self-reported competency development, and priorities for refinement.

Materials and methods

Following Research Ethics Board approval (UofT, Protocol #63578), with electronic informed consent obtained at the start of the survey, we performed a retrospective mixed-methods program evaluation of University of Toronto anesthesia residents (PGY3-5) who completed the Parma rotation between 2023 and 2025. Residents worked in supervised pre-hospital clinical shifts within the Parma Emergency Medical System, with continuous on-scene supervision by anesthesiologists licensed in both jurisdictions and concurrent mentorship by the Parma anesthesia faculty. Anonymous post-elective surveys were administered via the Department’s secure online platform, independently of residency evaluation, to mitigate coercion and response bias. The instrument combined five-point Likert items across domains of program administration, learning objectives, supervision, learning environment, perceived competency development (mapped to selected CanMEDS roles: Medical Expert, Communicator, Collaborator, Leader), and overall satisfaction; together with open-ended reflective prompts. Quantitative responses were summarized with descriptive statistics; qualitative responses were analyzed using directed content analysis, with themes mapped against survey domains by two independent reviewers.

Results

Eight of eight eligible residents completed the survey (100% response rate). All rated overall satisfaction as “Very satisfied”. Across administration, learning environment and mentorship domains, all respondents selected “Agree” or “Strongly Agree”. Perceived competency development was endorsed across all four targeted CanMEDS roles, with strongest agreement for the Communicator and Collaborator domains. Directed content analysis identified three recurring themes: (1) enhanced rapid clinical decision-making in high-acuity, resource-limited environments, with residents describing the experience as a unique opportunity to practice managerial and prioritization skills not consistently taught in hospital-based residency; (2) increased adaptability and resource-conscious practice outside the operating room, including the cognitive shift from controlled in-hospital settings to time-pressured field encounters; and (3) strengthened leadership and interprofessional collaboration with paramedics, nurses and pre-hospital physicians within the integrated 118 team-based model. Residents reported improved procedural confidence and capacity for patient stabilization prior to hospital arrival. Suggested refinements clustered around two priorities: introduction of a formal post-call narrative debriefing protocol, and institutional financial support to broaden equitable accessibility.

Discussion

This evaluation provides preliminary evidence that structured exposure to Italy’s anesthesiologist-led pre-hospital system delivers educational gains aligned with several CanMEDS roles and Italy’s national Core Competency framework (DM 402/2017), central to modern anesthesia practice [2]. Convergence of quantitative and qualitative findings, such as high satisfaction, uniform endorsement across competency domains, and recurrent recognition of decision-making, adaptability and team leadership, supports the proposition that the Italian 118/EMS model carries educational value beyond its national borders, positioning pre-hospital training as a distinctive asset that can be deliberately offered to international anesthesia trainees within a formal bilateral framework. Limitations include small sample size, single-institution participation, voluntary self-selection bias, and reliance on self-reported outcomes. A prospective bidirectional study is underway, enrolling both cohorts and incorporating simulation-based assessment with longitudinal follow-up.

Conclusions

A structured, supervised elective embedded within Italy’s anesthesiologist-led pre-hospital system was associated with self-reported gains in decision-making, communication, leadership and interprofessional collaboration among Canadian residents. The bilateral Parma-Toronto framework demonstrates the feasibility and educational value of formalized international exchanges built on the Italian model, and supports recognition of Italian pre-hospital anesthesia as a transferable contribution to global anesthesia training and a template for reciprocal partnerships between European and North American programs [3].

Informed consent was obtained electronically from each participant at the start of the anonymous survey, in accordance with the REB-approved protocol.

A120 Trends in multimodal neurological prognostication in a hub center for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA)

M. Ombrosi1, A. Pieri2, V. Tabolli2, M.L. Migliaccio1, C. Lazzeri3, M. Scarpino4, A. Grippo4, A. Marabotti1, G. Cianchi1, M. Bonizzoli1

1Intensive Care Unit and Regional ECMO Referral Centre, Florence, Italy; 2University of Florence, Italy; 3Regional Organ and Tissue Allocation Center, Florence, Italy; 4Neurophysiopathology, Florence, Italy

Correspondence: V. Tabolli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A120

Background

Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a major clinical challenge, with survival rates of approximately 10% and a high risk of hypoxic–ischemic brain injury (HIBI). In patients achieving return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), neurological prognostication is essential for guiding therapeutic decisions and post-resuscitation care pathways [1,2,3]. The aim of this study was to evaluate the prognostic role and temporal evolution of a mul-timodal neurological assessment strategy in OHCA patients with ROSC admitted to a specialized hub intensive care unit. Two observational periods were analyzed (2022–2023 and 2024), corresponding to the progressive consolidation of a regional time-dependent OHCA network (Table 1).

Materials and methods

We retrospectively analyzed 113 patients admitted to the intensive care unit after OHCA with ROSC between January 2022 and December 2024. Neurological prognostication was performed using a multimodal approach integrating clinical parameters, blood gas analysis, brain computed tomography (CT) with Gray–White Matter Ratio (GWR) calcu-lation, Neuron-Specific Enolase (NSE) measurement, electroencephalography (EEG), and somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs). Neurological outcome at discharge was as-sessed using the Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) scale. The study was approved by the local Ethics Committee (Area Vasta Centro, protocol number 27241).

Results

Demographic characteristics remained stable over the study period. Coronary artery dis-ease was the leading cause of OHCA, accounting for approximately one-third of cases. Cardiac arrest was witnessed in 88.5% of patients, occurred in public places in 47.8% of cases and at home in 37%, while ventricular fibrillation was the presenting rhythm in 53%. Over time, resuscitation performed by healthcare professionals increased, whereas hospital arrival times remained unchanged. A progressive increase in the use of multi-modal neurological assessment tools, particularly NSE measurement, EEG, and CT, was observed between 2022 and 2024. High NSE values were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality. Similarly, GWR <1.21 and bilateral absence of the N20 response on SSEPs were confirmed as reliable predictors of poor neurological outcome. In-hospital mortality remained stable at approximately 31%, while favorable neurological recovery (CPC 1) was observed in 32% of patients, with no substantial variation across the three years.

Conclusions

The integration of intensive care evaluation with multimodal neurophysiological prognos-tication represents the main novelty of this study. Our findings support the increasing im-plementation of biochemical, neuroimaging, and neurophysiological tools in OHCA man-agement. The development of effective time-dependent networks and the centralization of OHCA patients to specialized hub centers may contribute to improved neurological out-comes after cardiac arrest.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A121 Ischemic stroke in the intensive care unit: evaluation of a regional time-dependent network in a tertiary hub center

M. Ombrosi1, L. Tanturli2, C. Lazzeri3, V. Tabolli2, P. Nencini4, L.A. Sorrentino1, M. Bonizzoli1

1Intensive Care Unit and Regional ECMO Referral Centre, Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria Careggi, Florence, Italy; 2University of Florence, Italy; 3Regional Organ and Tissue Allocation Center, Florence, Italy; 4Stroke Unit, Florence, Italy

Correspondence: V. Tabolli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A121

Background

Stroke requires rapid recognition, timely pre-hospital management, and efficient triage to appropriate facilities [1–3]. Intensive care unit (ICU) admission may be necessary because of the systemic consequences of acute cerebral injury [4,5]. This study aimed to identify organizational and clinical factors associated with morbidity and mortality throughout the care pathway within a time-dependent stroke network, focusing on ischemic stroke patients admitted to a tertiary hub ICU.

Materials and methods

All patients admitted to the Emergency and Trauma ICU of Careggi University Hospital between 2017 and 2024 were screened. Patients with ischemic stroke (ICD-11: 8B11), subarachnoid hemorrhage (8B01), and intracerebral hemorrhage (8B00) were initially identified, whereas traumatic brain injury and secondary cerebrovascular events were excluded.

Data were extracted from the GiViTI Prosafe database. According to Regional Decree (DGR Toscana n. 904/2017), formal Institutional Review Board approval was not required. After screening, only ischemic stroke cases were included in the final analysis. Additional clinical data were retrieved from the Archimed portal. Demographic, clinical, temporal, transfer pathway, treatment, and outcome variables were analyzed.

Results

A total of 102 patients were included, of whom 71 underwent primary centralization and 31 secondary centralization. Patients undergoing primary centralization presented with greater neurological severity at admission (median GCS 10 vs. 12; p = 0.03). Secondary centralization was associated with higher rates of intravenous thrombolysis (58.1% vs. 23.9%; p = 0.001) and mechanical thrombectomy (77.4% vs. 33.8%; p < 0.001), despite longer onset-to-needle times (230 vs. 109 minutes; p = 0.03) (Table 1).

Thirty-day mortality was 41.2%. After propensity score adjustment, no significant differences in mortality or neurological outcomes were observed between groups. In multivariate analysis, SAPS II was the only independent predictor of 30-day mortality (OR 1.130; 95% CI 1.071–1.215; p < 0.001) (Figure 1) and unfavorable neurological outcome, defined as Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) 3–5. In-hospital neurological complications independently increased mortality risk (OR 5.99; p = 0.020) (Figure 2). No differences in complication rates were observed between centralization models.

Conclusions

The regional time-dependent stroke network ensured comparable outcomes between primary and secondary centralization strategies in critically ill stroke patients. Despite longer treatment times, secondary centralization improved access to advanced neurointerventional therapies. SAPS II emerged as the main predictor of outcome, supporting the concept of stroke as a systemic disease in the intensive care setting. Neurological complications significantly affected prognosis, emphasizing the need for targeted monitoring and prevention strategies.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A122 Theoretical knowledge and decision readiness in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a survey of healthcare professionals and the general population

M. Madeo1, J. D Andria Ursoleo2, S. Fedele1, P.M. Wieruszewski3,4, V. Bellini1, E.G. Bignami1

1Anesthesiology, Critical Care and Pain Medicine Division, Department of Medicine and Surgery, University of Parma, Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milano, Italy; 3Department of Pharmacy, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, USA; 4Department of Anesthesiology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, USA

Correspondence: J. D Andria Ursoleo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A122

Background

Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide and is a time-critical emergency for which delays in early recognition and activation of emergency medical services contribute to poor patient outcomes [1–3]. Despite increasing public awareness and cardiopulmonary resuscitation training, delays in OHCA recognition persist – particularly when agonal breathing and other ambiguous clinical signs generate diagnostic uncertainty – and suggest a discrepancy between theoretical knowledge and real-world readiness to act during emergencies [4,5]. The objective of this study was to evaluate healthcare professional and general public’s theoretical knowledge and decision readiness to act when faced with OHCA, and the potential acceptability of artificial intelligence (AI)-embedded wearable monitoring technologies (Figure 1).

Materials and Methods

We performed a cross-sectional observational survey study designed to assess: 1) theoretical knowledge of OHCA recognition and early management; 2) perceived decision readiness in the event of OHCA; 3) psychological barriers to acting in OHCA; and 4) digital trust and acceptability of AI-supported wearable technologies. Participants were stratified into healthcare-related personnel and the general population. The recognition gap index (RGI) – a quantitative indicator of the difference between theoretical knowledge and perceived readiness – was calculated.

Results

Of the 182 survey responses, 106 were from healthcare-related personnel and 76 were from the general population. Both theoretical knowledge (82.1 vs. 63.5, p < 0.001) and decision readiness (72.1 vs. 59.7, p = 0.002) scores were significantly higher among healthcare-related participants compared to the general population. The mean RGI observed was positive in both groups, thus indicating a measurable discrepancy between OHCA knowledge and readiness to act. Additionally, the RGI was greater in the healthcare-related group (+10.0 vs. +6.4) than the general population, although this difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.24). Interestingly, participants expressed favourable attitudes toward wearable systems supporting OHCA recognition and emergency decision-making. Specifically, 84.2% of respondents believed that AI-supported wearable technologies could reduce critical delays in emergency response. Nonetheless, 96% considered human supervision essential within the decision-making process and 84.9% preferred human confirmation of automated alerts.

Conclusions

Decision vulnerability may represent an underrecognized contributor to delays in the early recognition and management of OHCA. The RGI provides an appealing conceptual framework for investigating the discrepancy between theoretical competence and real-world readiness to act during emergencies. Digital health technologies designed within a human-in-the-loop framework may provide supportive guidance prior to emergency medical services arrival, but require further validation.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

Conceptual Framework of the ‘Recognition Gap’ in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest. The ‘Recognition Gap’ quantifies the discrepancy between theoretical knowledge of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) management and readiness to initiate emergency response. Diagnostic uncertainty, psychological barriers, agonal breathing, and stress-related cognitive vulnerability may all collectively contribute to delayed recognition and activation of emergency medical services in this high-intensity clinical scenario. Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported wearable technologies may facilitate early recognition of OHCA while preserving human supervision within the decision-making continuum, thus ultimately potentially strengthening the earliest links in the chain of survival

A123 The invisible symptom: prehospital pain still lacks a voice

M. Frau2, L. Guddelmoni1, C. Marini1, A. Pinna1, R. Saba3, C. Casula1, L. Frau1, D. Barillari1

1CO118 Sud Sardegna, AREUS, Cagliari, Italy; 2Scuola specializzazione AR, UNICA, Cagliari, Italy; 3Scuola specializzazione MEU, UNISS, Sassari, Italy

Correspondence: M. Frau

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A123

Background

The clinical context of emergency and urgent care is characterized by the phenomenon of oligoanalgesia, defined as inadequate pain management. Factors contributing to this phenomenon include the lack of pain assessment, the absence of guidelines for its management, inadequate documentation investigating pain properly, and the failure to evaluate adequacy of treatment. Oligoanalgesia is a significant issue in Italy, but it is also reflected in Europe, with variations in pain management across different countries. Currently, there is no single standard for pain treatment in emergency settings, and practices vary based on local protocols, as highlighted by the European Society for Emergency Medicine (EUSEM).

Materials and Methods

The study conducted on a sample of 4760 adults treated by nurses and physicians of the Regional Emergency and Urgency Agency of Sardinia (AREUS) from 1 November 2024 to 30 April 2025. All individuals over the age of 18 with GCS > 8, GCSm > 6 if GCSv=T, and without neurocognitive disorders incompatible with pain assessment were included. Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) scores, administered drugs, and their effectiveness were recorded. Data analysis was performed using an Electronic Case Report Form compiled on the REDCap platform. Results Final data, conducted on 2,946 cases, show that only 187 cases (6.3%) include a pain assessment, while in 2,759 cases (93.7%), pain was not assessed. Despite the initial evaluation, 73 cases (39%) included a second assessment, pharmacological treatment was administered in 124 cases (4.2%), primarily consisting of opioids (63%), followed by paracetamol (18%) and ketamine (15%). Anaesthesiologists demonstrate greater sensitivity to the issue, assessing pain in 21% of cases, compared with 1.8% of cases evaluated by physicians from other specialties.

Conclusions

The presence and quantification of pain remain poorly considered parameters by pre-hospital healthcare personnel, who do not prioritize them or consider them as important as other vital signs. The lack of pain assessment makes its management impractical, both in terms of selecting the right analgesic and evaluating its effectiveness. Oligoanalgesia in emergency and urgent care represents a serious problem, directly affecting the quality of assistance, patient well-being, and even clinical outcomes. Inadequate pain management is not just a matter of immediate discomfort but can lead to far-reaching consequences, such as worsening prognosis and increased physiological and psychological stress. Addressing this issue requires a cultural and structural change in how pain is considered within emergency protocols. Healthcare professional training, the implementation of clear guidelines, and the use of easily accessible pain assessment tools can significantly help reduce oligoanalgesia.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A124 When reversible causes converge: prehospital management of multifactorial cardiac arrest in a young patient with panhypopituitarism

I. Porru3, L. Guddelmoni1, C. Marini1, A. Pinna1, R. Saba3, M. Frau2, C. Casula1, L. Frau1, D. Barillari1

1CO118 Sud Sardegna, AREUS, Cagliari, Italy; 2Scuola specializzazione AR, UNICA, Cagliari, Italy; 3Scuola specializzazione MEU, UNISS, Sassari, Italy

Correspondence: C. Marini

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A124

Background

This case report describes the prehospital management of a rare and highly complex cardiac arrest (CA) scenario in a young patient with multiple reversible causes of circulatory collapse. The case highlights the challenges of emergency medical management in the prehospital setting, where time, resources, and diagnostic tools are limited [1].

The patient presented with several concurrent reversible causes of cardiac arrest, including severe hypothermia, hypovolemia, electrolyte imbalance, respiratory failure, and endocrine dysfunction secondary to panhypopituitarism. The latter likely represented the primary predisposing condition, contributing—together with an underlying infectious process later confirmed in hospital—to the development of metabolic and hemodynamic instability.

Hypothermia is a well-recognized reversible cause of cardiac arrest and may present with bradyarrhythmias, atrioventricular blocks, QT prolongation, widened QRS complexes, pulseless electrical activity (PEA), and Osborne (J) waves on ECG. Panhypopituitarism is less frequently associated with cardiac arrest but may significantly increase cardiovascular morbidity and mortality through thyroid, corticosteroid, and hormonal deficiencies, predisposing patients to electrical instability, impaired myocardial contractility, hypotension, and malignant arrhythmias [3]. This case emphasizes the importance of early recognition of clinical deterioration in fragile endocrine patients and highlights the role of targeted prehospital treatment, including corticosteroid administration, thermal management, and correction of metabolic abnormalities. Case Report An advanced life support unit and physician-staffed rapid response vehicle were dispatched by the Cagliari Emergency Medical Dispatch Center for a neurological emergency involving a 19-year-old male presenting with altered mental status. On scene, the patient was conscious but severely slowed psychomotorically. Initial assessment revealed tachypnea (RR 35/min), cold and mottled skin, weak peripheral pulses, delayed capillary refill, and inability to obtain reliable blood pressure or oxygen saturation measurements [2]. Neurological examination showed a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 13 without focal deficits. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm at 83 bpm with diffuse Osborne waves and hyperacute anterior T waves. Medical history, obtained from relatives, revealed panhypopituitarism secondary to previous pituitary carcinoma surgery, treated with corticosteroid and thyroid hormone replacement therapy. The patient had experienced profuse diarrhea for approximately two weeks and had recently been evaluated in the emergency department for hypernatremia and hypercalcemia. Peripheral venous access was eventually obtained after multiple attempts, and intravenous saline infusion was initiated. Preparation for hydrocortisone and calcium administration was started while passive external warming measures were applied. During transport preparation, the patient rapidly deteriorated, developing progressive reduction in consciousness, bradypnea, and subsequently pulseless electrical activity. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was immediately initiated during transport, with basic airway management and early intravenous adrenaline administration. Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was achieved after the first adrenaline dose, followed by a second transient PEA arrest with ROSC obtained through CPR alone. Upon arrival at the emergency department, tympanic temperature was 28°C. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated severe mixed acidosis with elevated anion gap and lactate levels, acute hypercapnic respiratory failure, hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and hypercalcemia. Acute coronary pathology was excluded, and the patient underwent endotracheal intubation and intensive care admission for advanced treatment and diagnostic evaluation.

Conclusion

This case highlights the complexity of managing cardiac arrest caused by multiple simultaneous reversible factors in the prehospital environment [4]. It underscores the importance of early identification of endocrine emergencies, aggressive prevention of clinical deterioration, and prompt correction of reversible causes before cardiac arrest occurs. The case also demonstrates the importance of advanced prehospital diagnostic tools, including ECG interpretation and blood gas analysis, to guide targeted treatment strategies (Figs. 1 and 2) Severe hypothermia associated with altered consciousness and hemodynamic instability should prompt rapid transfer to a tertiary referral center capable of advanced extracorporeal life support (ECLS) when indicated. Finally, this report illustrates how prehospital decision-making often extends beyond standardized algorithms, requiring dynamic prioritization and clinical judgment under extreme time constraints in order to maximize patient survival.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A125 Psychomotor agitation in the prehospital setting comparison of two emergency management strategies

A. Corongiu2, L. Guddelmoni1, C. Marini1, A. Pinna1, R. Saba3, M. Frau2, F. Sanna3, C. Casula1, L. Frau1, D. Barillari1

1CO118 Sud Sardegna, AREUS, Cagliari, Italy; 2Postgraduate School in Anesthesia and Intensive Care (AR), University of Cagliari (UNICA), Italy; 3Postgraduate School in Emergency Medicine (MEU), University of Sassari (UNISS), Italy

Correspondence: A. Corongiu

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A125

Background

Prehospital management of psychomotor agitation represents a major clinical and organizational challenge in emergency medicine. Acute agitation may arise from psychiatric disorders, substance intoxication, neurological disease, or reversible medical conditions, requiring rapid assessment while simultaneously ensuring patient and provider safety. In the prehospital setting, healthcare professionals must manage potentially dangerous behaviors, evaluate underlying medical causes, and coordinate with psychiatric services and law enforcement agencies. Management strategies include verbal de-escalation, pharmacologic sedation, continuous reassessment, and, in selected cases, activation of compulsory health treatment (T.S.O.). These scenarios require rapid decision-making, multidisciplinary collaboration, and integration of both technical and non-technical skills. The aim is to describe two different models of prehospital psychomotor agitation management and highlight the advantages and limitations of integrated psychiatric collaboration compared with rapid pharmacologic sedation in high-risk scenarios.

Case report

Case1: A prehospital advanced life support unit was dispatched for a 24-year-old woman presenting with severe psychomotor agitation inside a supermarket. On arrival, the patient appeared markedly agitated and poorly cooperative, showing perseverative thoughts and repetitive verbalizations regarding allegedly spoiled food displayed on the shelves. Law enforcement personnel and psychiatrists from the Community Mental Health Center (CIM/CSM) were already present on scene. The patient had recently undergone psychiatric evaluation, and diagnostic assessment for suspected bipolar disorder was ongoing. According to the psychiatric team, she had progressively developed social withdrawal during the previous month and was now presenting with manic excitement associated with psychotic symptoms. Despite prolonged verbal de-escalation attempts, the patient remained severely agitated and intermittently uncooperative. Pharmacological sedation was initiated using delorazepam oral drops 5 mg combined with intramuscular aripiprazole 7.5 mg, administered by the psychiatric team because aripiprazole was not routinely available among medications carried by the advanced life support unit. A prolonged observation phase was required before the patient gradually became sufficiently cooperative to allow monitoring of vital parameters and safe transport. Once adequate calming was achieved, compulsory health treatment (T.S.O.) was activated and the patient was transferred to the psychiatric ward.

The main strength of this approach was the preservation of the patient’s ability to interact with the psychiatric team, allowing continuous psychiatric assessment and communication during the intervention. The integrated multidisciplinary collaboration also represented an important organizational advantage. However, the intervention required prolonged on-scene time compared with standard prehospital emergency operations. Case 2: A prehospital advanced life support unit was dispatched for severe psychomotor agitation in a 59-year-old woman with schizophrenia followed by territorial psychiatric services, which were not immediately available at the time of the event. Law enforcement personnel were already present because of aggressive behavior.

According to family members, the patient had been poorly compliant with psychiatric therapy for approximately one year. She lived with her mother, who suffered from severe dementia. On arrival, the patient appeared severely agitated and openly aggressive toward herself and family members, throwing objects and glass fragments inside the house, creating a high-risk environment. Attempts at verbal de-escalation were unsuccessful because of persistent agitation and escalating aggression. Given the immediate safety concerns, pharmacological sedation under a state of necessity was performed using intramuscular ketamine 50 mg combined with intramuscular midazolam 5 mg.

Approximately 10–15 minutes after drug administration, behavioral control was achieved, allowing safe transfer onto the ambulance stretcher and subsequent transport for further medical evaluation before psychiatric admission. The principal advantage of this strategy was the rapid onset of sedation, resulting in faster control of agitation and a shorter overall intervention time. However, deeper sedation prevented direct psychiatric assessment during the prehospital phase and required Emergency Department evaluation and monitoring before psychiatric transfer.

Conclusions

These cases demonstrate how prehospital psychomotor agitation management may require different operational strategies depending on clinical presentation, environmental conditions, and psychiatric service availability. The first case highlighted the benefits of integrated collaboration between emergency physicians and territorial psychiatric services, allowing maintenance of patient interaction and progressive behavioral control, although with prolonged operational times. The second case emphasized the role of rapid pharmacologic sedation in highly dangerous scenarios where immediate behavioral control and scene safety become priorities. This strategy enabled faster management but required deeper sedation and additional Emergency Department evaluation before psychiatric admission. Both cases underline the importance of individualized treatment strategies, multidisciplinary teamwork, communication, and integration of technical and non-technical skills in prehospital psychiatric emergencies. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A126 Beyond traditional cardiovascular risk factors hyperhomocysteinemia in a young stemi survivor

L. Guddelmoni1, R. Saba3, C. Marini1, A. Pinna1, M. Frau2, F. Sanna3, C. Casula1, L. Frau1, D. Barillari1

1CO118 Sud Sardegna, AREUS, Cagliari, Italy; 2Postgraduate School in Anesthesia and Intensive Care (AR), University of Cagliari (UNICA), Italy; 3Postgraduate School in Emergency Medicine (MEU), University of Sassari (UNISS), Italy

Correspondence: L. Guddelmoni

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A126

Background

Hyperhomocysteinemia is increasingly recognized as a proatherogenic and prothrombotic condition associated with endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, vascular inflammation, and premature atherosclerosis. Elevated homocysteine levels have been associated with an increased risk of arterial thrombotic events, including acute coronary syndromes and ischemic stroke, particularly in younger patients and in those with limited traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Several studies have suggested a correlation between hyperhomocysteinemia and greater severity of coronary artery disease in patients presenting with acute coronary syndromes. However, despite growing evidence supporting its pathophysiological role in arterial disease, current ESC and AHA guidelines do not recommend routine coronary artery disease screening solely on the basis of elevated homocysteine levels, as homocysteine-lowering therapies have not consistently demonstrated a reduction in major cardiovascular events. Nevertheless, hyperhomocysteinemia may represent an important cardiovascular risk modifier in selected patients with premature or unexplained coronary events, emphasizing the importance of individualized clinical assessment and broader cardiovascular risk evaluation.

Case report

A 34-year-old man was reported to the emergency dispatch center as unconscious and in presumed cardiac arrest. Family members referred a history of typical chest pain lasting several hours before collapse. Basic cardiopulmonary resuscitation had already been initiated by bystanders prior to the arrival of the advanced life support unit. On scene, advanced resuscitation maneuvers were continued according to ALS protocols. Cardiac monitoring revealed alternating rhythms, with repeated episodes of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) followed by recurrent ventricular fibrillation. During resuscitation, a total of 11 defibrillation attempts with escalating energy levels were delivered because of recurrent shockable rhythms. Naloxone was also administered because relatives reported a possible, although unspecified, opioid intake.

After definitive ROSC was achieved, endotracheal intubation was performed using a 7.5 mm endotracheal tube following ketamine administration for airway management and sedation. A 12-lead ECG obtained after stabilization demonstrated anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The patient was subsequently transported to the Emergency Department for urgent cardiological evaluation and advanced treatment.

Conclusion

Despite the prolonged resuscitation effort and multiple episodes of recurrent ventricular fibrillation, the patient achieved complete neurological recovery (restitutio ad integrum) following definitive treatment. Subsequent in-hospital investigations performed after the acute phase revealed hyperhomocysteinemia, later considered a possible contributing cardiovascular risk factor in the development of the acute coronary syndrome.This case highlights the complexity of managing cardiac arrest in young patients presenting with potentially overlapping toxicological and cardiovascular etiologies. Although initial information raised suspicion of opioid involvement, the persistence of malignant ventricular arrhythmias and post-ROSC ECG findings revealed an underlying acute coronary syndrome (Fig 1). The subsequent identification of hyperhomocysteinemia further emphasized the importance of broader etiological investigation in young patients presenting with severe coronary events and limited conventional cardiovascular risk factors.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.
