A127 Sedation in the intensive care unit: achieving optimal sedation balance through objective instrumental monitoring of sedation depth (PEEG) combined with traditional clinical assessment (RASS)

T.G. Zimotti1, L. Menzato1, L. Frigo1, F. Mazzon2, N. Todesco2, T. Pellis2, G. Di Gregorio1

1Hospital of Cittadella, (PD), Italy; 2AS FO Pordenone, (PN), Italy

Correspondence: T.G. Zimotti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A127

Background

Target Controlled Infusion (TCI) is widely adopted in operating rooms but remains underused in Intensive Care Units (ICU), where Total Intravenous Anesthesia (TIVA) is still more common. ICU sedation strategies are increasingly shifting from drug-centered approaches to monitoring-driven sedation. The Richmond Agitation–Sedation Scale (RASS) remains the clinical standard, but it is intermittent and subjective. Processed electroencephalography (pEEG), as Spectral Edge Frequency (SEF), may provide continuous objective assessment of sedation depth and help bridge this gap.

Objective

To compare TCI and TIVA for ICU sedation using both clinical (RASS) and instrumental monitoring (pEEG, SedLine®, Masimo) to guide propofol and remifentanil administration, and to evaluate the correlation between RASS and SEF.

Methods

Prospective randomized study conducted in two ICUs (Cittadella and Pordenone, Italy). Informed consent taken upon admission. Patients were randomized to TCI or TIVA. Sedation depth was evaluated using RASS and SEF. Continuous variables are presented as median [IQR] and compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test; categorical variables using Fisher’s exact or chi-square test. Correlation between mean RASS and SEF values was assessed using Spearman’s coefficient (alpha = 0.05).

Results

Forty-four patients were included (23 TCI, 21 TIVA); six were excluded prior to randomization. No significant differences were observed between groups in baseline characteristics, including age, BMI, and comorbidities. Weight-adjusted infusion rates were comparable for propofol (p = 0.7) and remifentanil (p = 0.6). Sedation duration was 64 [43–140] hours (TCI) versus 82 [43–192] hours (TIVA). ICU length of stay was 6 [3–11] days, and ICU mortality was 25%. A significant positive correlation was found between RASS and SEF (rho = 0.65; p < 0.001).

Conclusions

In this cohort, TCI and TIVA resulted in similar sedative and opioid consumption, with no significant differences in clinical outcomes. The lack of statistical significance may be related to the limited sample size. The significant correlation between RASS and SEF supports the integration of clinical assessment with EEG-derived indices, going towards a patient-tailored ICU sedation and suggesting that pEEG may improve precision beyond intermittent bedside clinical scoring. Larger multicentre studies are needed to validate SEF as a reliable adjunct in routine ICU sedation management.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A128 Italian multicenter prospective registry on blunt chest trauma: rationale, design and objectives of the IT-TRAUMA study

M. Leone1, I. Silvestri1, M.M. Cimino1, L. Cayre1, C. Martinet1, G. Ristagno2,3, G. Grasselli1,3

1Major Polyclinic Hospital of Milan, Italy; 2ASST Great Metropolitan Hospital Niguarda, Milan, Italy; 3University of Milan, Italy

Correspondence: I. Silvestri

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A128

Background

Blunt chest trauma (CBT) is a leading cause of trauma-related Emergency Department admissions and carries substantial morbidity, including respiratory failure, prolonged hospitalization, chronic pain, and progression to acute respiratory distress syndrome. CBT is an evolving condition: clinical deterioration frequently occurs hours to days after the initial assessment, and a systematic, timely approach is critical to prevent short- and medium-term complications. Several aspects of CBT management remain unresolved, including risk stratification, timely pain control, choice of respiratory support, optimal ward setting, and monitoring intensity. Current Italian practice is highly heterogeneous and national prospective data are lacking. The IT-TRAUMA registry was designed to address these gaps.

Materials and Methods

IT-TRAUMA is a prospective multicenter observational registry, promoted by the IT-TRAUMA Group, with a planned enrollment period of at least three years, including adults (+ or = 18 years) admitted to Italian Level I and II Trauma Centers with clinical or radiological CBT and at least one of: + or = 3 rib fractures, pleural involvement (pneumothorax/hemothorax), or pulmonary contusion. Patients with penetrating trauma, pediatric patients, and patients with concomitant traumatic brain injury will be excluded.

Data are collected via a GDPR/HIPAA-compliant REDCap® platform and include demographics, trauma mechanism, injury severity, thoracic injury patterns, physiological and laboratory parameters, respiratory support (HFNC, CPAP, NIV, invasive ventilation, ECMO), multimodal analgesia and locoregional techniques (epidural, erector spinae plane, serratus anterior plane, paravertebral blocks), chest drainage, ICU admission, and surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF). Patients are followed daily until discharge and reassessed at 1 and 6 months for chronic pain, respiratory symptoms, functional recovery, and quality of life.

Key descriptive measures include the prevalence of CBT-related complications, need for ventilatory support, rate of SSRF, ICU admission, in-hospital mortality, length of stay, failure of conservative management, and hospital readmissions. The registry will also describe the distribution of analgesic and ventilatory strategies across centers and their association with clinical course.

Expected Results

IT-TRAUMA is expected to provide the first nationwide prospective dataset on blunt chest trauma in Italy, characterizing epidemiology, treatment variability, and organizational differences across centers. The granularity of the dataset will support exploratory analyses to identify predictors of respiratory failure, ICU admission, prolonged hospitalization, chronic pain, and mortality, and to systematically evaluate management strategies — including SSRF — to identify factors associated with reduced complications. These analyses will generate hypotheses for future interventional trials.

Conclusions

IT-TRAUMA is the first Italian prospective multicenter registry dedicated to blunt chest trauma. By standardizing data collection and describing current clinical practice, it aims to strengthen multidisciplinary collaboration among Italian trauma centers, identify factors associated with adverse outcomes, and support the development of shared, evidence-based protocols to improve respiratory, functional, and survival outcomes in CBT patients.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A129 Metric: medical emergency team retrospective investigation of clinical activity at IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital

C.M. Scarsi Ardesi1, M. Maturo1, E. Costantini2, M. Mainetti2, M. Cecconi2, L. Carenzo2, A. Messina2

1Department of Biomedical Sciences, Humanitas University, Pieve Emanuele, Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Rozzano, Italy

Correspondence: C.M. Scarsi Ardesi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A129

Background

Clinical deterioration can be defined as an alteration in the patient’s homeostatic functions in the face of illness, leading to measurable changes in vital signs from baseline [1], and requiring prompt recognition and intervention to prevent adverse outcomes [1–3].

Medical emergency teams (METs), sometimes called rapid response teams, are dedicated teams that operate within hospitals to provide advanced interventions to patients experiencing clinical deterioration and to evaluate indications for intensive care unit (ICU) admission [3]. The MET represents the efferent arm of the rapid response system, and is activated by the afferent arm, which is generally composed of trained ward personnel [1, 3].

There is data that supports the role of METs in reducing in-hospital mortality [4, 5]. However, the current literature concerning the characteristics and effects of MET activity in clinical practice is heterogeneous [6], and the role of METs in defining patients’ prognosis remains less investigated. Furthermore, data is particularly lacking on implementation of these systems in Italian hospitals [7].

Materials and methods

We conducted a monocentric retrospective observational study on the activity of the MET at IRCCS Humanitas research hospital (ICH), which is composed of an ICU physician, often accompanied by a resident, and an ICU nurse.

All patients evaluated by the MET at ICH between 01/01/2025 and 31/12/2025 were considered eligible. The data was extracted from the electronic MET database of the hospital, in which interventions are routinely registered by the responding team. The study was approved by the local ethics committee (approval n° 06/25). We examined the frequency of each category of call, reason for the call and outcome of the intervention.

Results

Over the course of 2025, 959 MET interventions were recorded. The most frequent categories of intervention (Figure 1) were consultations (462; 48.2%), emergencies (283; 29.5%) and anaesthesiologic assistance for procedures when an anaesthesiologist wasn’t available (72; 7.5%). <FILE IMAGE=‘198_20260511200522.jpg’>

The reasons for intervention were collected (Table 1), with multiple reasons being allowed for each intervention. The most common concerns were desaturation/respiratory failure (281; 29.3%), hypotension (90; 9.4%) and sepsis/septic shock (90; 9.4%). A total of 194 interventions (20.2%) included the reason “other”.

The most common outcomes (Table 2) were treatment on site (391; 40.8%), consultation only/follow up (212; 22.1%), and general ICU admission (168; 17.5%). In case of consultation only/follow up the patient was evaluated but did not require treatment by the MET.

In 90 cases (9.4% of the total) the MET expressed a written no escalation consultation defining a formal ceiling of care for the patient. Within this subgroup, 79 interventions (87.7%) were categorised as consultations and 11 (12.2%) as emergencies. The most common problems in this population were desaturation/respiratory failure (42; 46.7%), sepsis/septic shock (21; 23.3%), hypotension (11; 12.2%) and other (11; 12.2%).

Conclusions

In one year, the MET of IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital responded to 959 calls, most of which were treatable on site, but a percentage of which required ICU admission. This represents a valuable dataset to investigate the variables associated to MET activation and intervention outcomes, which can broaden understanding of rapid response in our healthcare system.

Informed consent was waived under Italian Data Protection Code (Legislative Decree 196/2003, Art.110) for retrospective observational research performed by IRCCS institutions.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A130 ECMELLA support complicated by retroperitoneal bleeding and open abdominal treatment

P. Righetti, G.V. Chiacchio, C.A. Lanza, F. Ruotolo, C. Guida, A. Mastroianni, G. Di Giacomo, P. Bianchi

Department of Cardiovascular Anesthesia and Intensive Care A.O.R.N. Sant’Anna e San Sebastiano, Caserta, Italy

Correspondence: P. Righetti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A130

Background

Combined venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and Impella support (ECMELLA) may provide lifesaving circulatory support in refractory cardiogenic shock, but its use requires continuous balancing between antithrombotic therapy, bleeding risk, and end-organ perfusion. We report a complex case of postcardiac arrest myocardial infarction requiring ECMELLA, complicated by retroperitoneal hematoma, abdominal compartment syndrome, and open-abdomen management.

Case report

A 49-year-old man with hypertension was admitted after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with ongoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation. On arrival, he required advanced life support and immediate transfer to the catheterization laboratory. Coronary angiography showed acute myocardial infarction requiring percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent implantation. Because of refractory cardiogenic shock, mechanical circulatory support was escalated from intra-aortic balloon pump to Impella CP and venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMELLA). Early echocardiographic assessment documented severely depressed left ventricular function, with an ejection fraction of approximately 15%. During support, the patient developed progressive abdominal distension, hemodynamic instability, and multiorgan dysfunction. Intra-abdominal pressure increased up to 42 mmHg, consistent with abdominal compartment syndrome. Computed tomography demonstrated a large bilateral retroperitoneal hematoma without active arterial extravasation, associated with free serohematic intraperitoneal fluid. The patient underwent urgent decompressive laparotomy, hematoma evacuation, and open-abdomen management with negative-pressure ABTHERA VAC therapy. Persistent bleeding required surgical revision, packing, transfusion support, and careful modulation of antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapy. A further complication was the development of necrotizing hemorrhagic pancreatitis, likely secondary to local compression and inflammatory extension. Following multidisciplinary management involving intensive care, interventional cardiology, cardiac surgery, general surgery, and vascular surgery, abdominal conditions progressively improved. Cardiac function improved, allowing successful weaning from extracorporeal support (ECMO was removed on HD 9 and IMPELLA on HD 10). ABTHERA VAC was removed on hospital day (HD) 12, with no clinical or radiological evidence of intestinal ischemia. Despite a complicated course with neurologic and respiratory involvement, the patient was awake, cooperative, and breathing spontaneously via tracheostomy with low-flow oxygen support (2 L/min).

Conclusion

This case highlights the extreme complexity of ECMELLA rescue after cardiac arrest, where survival depends not only on circulatory stabilization but also on prompt recognition and treatment of extracardiac complications. Retroperitoneal bleeding and abdominal compartment syndrome should be actively considered in patients receiving temporary mechanical circulatory support who develop abdominal distension, elevated intra-abdominal pressure, worsening shock, or organ dysfunction.

Consent to publish

Written informed consent for publication of this case report was obtained from the patient.

A131 PH 6.63 and survival: early CVVHDF in severe metformin-associated lactic acidosis

F. Pulice, D. Battaglia, I. Pezzoli, T. Perricelli, C. Longo, F. Costantino, V. Alagna, L. Bocchino, F. Galeno, A. Monardo

Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Ospedale Lamezia Terme, Italy

Correspondence: F. Pulice

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A131

Background

Metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA) [1] is a rare but life-threatening condition (incidence <10 cases per 100,000 patient-years) resulting from impaired lactate clearance and metformin accumulation, typically triggered by acute renal impairment due to dehydration [2], diarrhea, sepsis, or hypoperfusion. Mortality approaches 50%, and renal replacement therapy remains the recommended treatment [3].

Case Report

An 84-year-old man with hypertension and metformin-treated type 2 diabetes presented to the emergency department with dyspnea, hypotension, and three days of diarrhea. Arterial blood gas revealed severe metabolic acidosis: pH 6.63, pCO2 13.9 mmHg, HCO3 1.5 mEq/L, lactate 21 mmol/L, anion gap 45. Due to respiratory failure and hemodynamic instability, the patient was admitted intubated to the ICU.

Initial management included lung-protective mechanical ventilation, balanced crystalloids administration, high-dose norepinephrine, and continuous sodium bicarbonate replacement. Laboratory findings confirmed acute kidney injury (creatinine 9.14 mg/dL, BUN 299 mg/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 100 × 10³/µL), hypofibrinogenemia (fibrinogen 98 mg/dL), and markedly elevated D-dimer (28,000 ng/mL), suggesting an underlying coagulopathy.

Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT) was initiated promptly. CRRT was delivered in CVVHDF mode using a high-surface ST150 hemofilter (PRISMAX platform), combining diffusion and convection to maximize early clearance of metformin and lactate while preserving hemodynamic stability. Blood flow was set at 120 ml/min with a total effluent dose of 39.3 ml/kg/h. Biphozyl, a phosphate- and bicarbonate-buffered, calcium-free solution, was used as both dialysate and replacement fluid to prevent hypophosphatemia and correct metabolic acidosis. Given the underlying coagulopathy, regional citrate anticoagulation (Regiocit, pre-filter) was preferred over systemic heparin, with systemic CaCl2 replacement targeting an ionized calcium of 1.1–1.25 mmol/L. Treatment was continued uninterrupted for 72 hours.

Within 6–12 hours (Fig. 1), arterial pH began to rise, lactate declined reflecting progressive hemodynamic stabilization. By 24–48 hours, pH had normalized, lactate returned to reference range, creatinine recovered to within normal limits (0.82 mg/dL), and norepinephrine was discontinued. Mechanical ventilation weaning was completed on day 5. The patient was transferred to a general ward on day 13 and discharged home on day 16.

Conclusion

MALA presenting with pH 6.63, an extreme condition associated with near-prohibitive mortality, can achieve complete resolution with early diagnosis and optimized CRRT. These findings support the integration of high-efficiency CRRT into standardized MALA protocols, even in cases of extreme acidemia traditionally considered non-survivable.

Written informed consent for publication of clinical data was obtained from the patient’s legal guardians prior to inclusion in this report

A132 From CT to LUS: assessing lung ultrasound as a low-radiation tool for monitoring the critically ill lung

A. Pigliacelli, A. Naccarato, A. Craba, L.J. Laricchia, L. Di Rezze, N. Spalletta, M. D’Ambrosio

San Giovanni Addolorata Hospital, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: A. Pigliacelli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A132

Background

Computed tomography (CT) and chest X-ray (CXR) remain the reference imaging modalities for critically ill patients with acute respiratory failure, but their repeated use is associated with significant exposure to ionizing radiation and logistical challenges in unstable patients. Lung ultrasound (LUS) has emerged as a bedside, radiation-free, repeatable imaging technique, enabling real-time assessment of lung aeration and potentially reducing reliance on conventional imaging.

Objectives

To evaluate the feasibility and clinical impact of a LUS-centered monitoring strategy in critically ill patients, focusing on its ability to reduce cumulative radiation exposure and to reliably track the evolution of lung pathology compared with standard imaging approaches.

Materials and Methods

We conducted a retrospective, single-center observational study in a polyvalent intensive care unit. Adult patients admitted for acute or acute-on-chronic respiratory failure and managed with a structured LUS protocol (LUS group, n=8) were compared with a cohort treated using standard imaging (control group, n=6).

The LUS protocol consisted of 12 thoracic regions (six per hemithorax), each scored from 0 to 3 according to aeration patterns (A-lines, isolated or multiple B-lines, coalescent B-lines, and subpleural or parenchymal consolidations), yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 36. Daily bedside LUS examinations were performed until clinical resolution or ICU discharge.

Collected variables included demographic and clinical data, diagnosis, need for mechanical ventilation, number and type of imaging studies (CT, CXR), cumulative radiation dose (mSv), and serial LUS values. Descriptive statistical analysis was performed. Inter-cohort comparison of radiation exposure was conducted using the Mann–Whitney U test, given the small sample size and non-normal distribution.

Results

Implementation of the LUS protocol resulted in a marked shift in imaging strategy. In the LUS cohort, the mean number of CT scans per patient was 1.125 (all patients underwent baseline CT, with only one requiring a repeat scan), compared with a higher and less standardized use in the control cohort. Patients underwent a mean of 2.75 CXRs and 8.25 LUS examinations, confirming LUS as the dominant tool for longitudinal monitoring (Figs. 1 and 2). With the introduction of LUS, the average number of radiological examinations per patient decreased.

The mean cumulative radiation dose per patient in the LUS group was 8.18 ± 2.56 mSv (median 9.04 mSv; range 3.95–10.83), remaining below the clinically relevant threshold of 10 mSv for prolonged ICU stays. In contrast, the control group showed a mean dose of 17.17 ± 11.08 mSv (median 13.95 mSv; IQR 8.46–25.07). This corresponds to a 52.4% reduction in mean radiation exposure and a 35.1% reduction in median values. Although the difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.345), effect size analysis suggested a trend toward lower exposure in the LUS group.

Mean cumulative radiation dose: LUS protocol: 8.18 ± 2.56 mSv per patient (median 9.04 mSv), below the 10 mSv threshold considered clinically relevant for patients with prolonged hospitalization. Standard protocol: 17.17 ± 11.08 mSv (median 13.95 mSv). Mean dose reduction: 52.4%.

Serial LUS assessment demonstrated consistent agreement with clinical evolution and therapeutic response, particularly in patients receiving targeted antibiotic therapy. LUS trends effectively captured improvement, stability, or deterioration of lung aeration, supporting clinical decision-making.

Feasibility was excellent, with a 100% protocol completion rate and a mean of 8.25 examinations per patient (range 7–9). Each examination required approximately 10–15 minutes and provided high-quality diagnostic information, allowing early detection of complications such as atelectasis and pleural effusions, and enabling real-time optimization of ventilatory strategies.

Discussion

This study highlights a paradigm shift from a CT-dependent approach toward a LUS-centered monitoring model in critical care. The integration of LUS into daily practice significantly reduced reliance on ionizing imaging while maintaining high diagnostic performance and clinical safety. The ability to perform frequent, bedside, radiation-free assessments represents a major advantage, particularly in patients who are difficult to transport or clinically unstable.

From a radioprotection perspective, the observed reduction in cumulative dose is clinically relevant and aligns with current recommendations emphasizing minimization of unnecessary radiation exposure. Importantly, this reduction was achieved without compromising patient monitoring or outcomes.

Limitations include the small sample size, retrospective design, and potential temporal bias between cohorts, which may reflect evolving clinical practices beyond the introduction of LUS. Therefore, findings should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating, warranting confirmation in larger prospective studies.

Conclusions

A LUS-centered monitoring strategy is feasible, safe, and highly effective in the management of critically ill patients with respiratory failure. Its implementation may substantially reduce radiation exposure while preserving, and potentially enhancing, the quality of clinical assessment. These findings support the adoption of LUS as a primary tool for lung monitoring in intensive care, promoting a shift toward a more sustainable and patient-centered imaging paradigm.

Ethics Statement

This retrospective study was conducted on anonymized data collected during routine clinical practice, in accordance with current data protection regulations. No additional interventions were performed.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A133 Emergency department boarding as a distinct post-admission risk phase: a scoping review of clinical outcomes

M. Patanè1, S. Fresilli2, M. Madeo3, M. Barillaro1, M. Federica1, C. Giovanna4, F. Santo4, M. Mariagrazia4, P. Renata1, G. Mazza1

1Intensive Care Unit, Department of Medical and Surgical Sciences, University Hospital Mater Domini, Catanzaro, Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milano, Italy; 3Anesthesiology, Critical Care and Pain Medicine Division, Department of Medicine and Surgery, University of Parma, Italy; 4Intensive Care and Anesthesiology, Annunziata Hospital, Cosenza, Italy

Correspondence: M. Patanè

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A133

Background

Emergency department (ED) boarding, defined as the interval between the decision to admit and physical transfer to an inpatient unit, has emerged as an important marker of hospital system strain and has been associated with adverse clinical outcomes [1–3]. However, many studies conflate boarding with total ED length of stay, limiting interpretation of its independent clinical impact. We conducted a scoping review to characterize the association between ED boarding as a distinct post-admission exposure and patient outcomes.

Materials and methods

We performed a scoping review according to PRISMA-ScR guidance [4]. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 21 March 2026. Eligible studies included adult or mixed ED populations, explicitly defined boarding as the interval between admission decision and inpatient transfer, and reported clinical outcomes stratified by boarding duration. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Due to methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. The study selection process and conceptual framework of boarding-related harm are summarized in Figure 1.

Results

Sixteen studies including 473,392 patients were analyzed. Prolonged boarding was consistently associated with increased in-hospital mortality, particularly among critically ill patients awaiting intensive care unit admission, with adjusted odds ratios reaching 2.6 in high-acuity cohorts [2,5]. Boarding was also associated with prolonged hospital length of stay, increased intensive care resource utilization, and delays in time-sensitive care, including medication administration and order completion. Process-of-care failures, including missed or delayed orders, were frequently reported [6]. In older adults, prolonged boarding was additionally associated with delirium and severe agitation [7]. Although some mortality associations attenuated after adjustment for illness severity, process-level harms remained consistently evident across settings.

Conclusions

ED boarding, when defined as the post-admission interval, represents a clinically meaningful exposure rather than a neutral operational delay. Adverse effects appear to accumulate through fragmented care delivery and are most pronounced among critically ill and high-risk patients. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether targeted system-level interventions can reduce boarding-related harm and improve patient outcomes.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A134 Heterogeneity of definitions of peri-intubation cardiovascular instability in critically ill patients: a narrative synthesis

L. Leuci1, A. Protti1,2, A. Messina1,2, V. Russotto3,4, M. Cecconi1,2, L. Carenzo2

1Department of Biomedical Sciences, Humanitas University, Pieve Emanuele, Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine, IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Rozzano, Italy; 3Department of Oncology, University of Turin, Italy; 4Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, San Luigi Gonzaga University Hospital, Orbassano, Italy

Correspondence: L. Leuci

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A134

Background

Peri-intubation cardiovascular instability is a common, potentially fatal complication of emergency tracheal intubation in critically ill patients, with reported incidences of 17–42.6% [1–3]. It encompasses severe hypotension, vasopressor requirement, cardiac arrest, and death in the peri-intubation period [1–5]. Despite its relevance, no consensus definition exists. We aimed to characterize the extent and sources of definitional heterogeneity across published studies and its implications for evidence synthesis and clinical practice.

Methods

A narrative review was conducted, focusing on studies that defined, measured, or reported peri-intubation cardiovascular instability in critically ill adults undergoing intubation in Intensive Care Units (ICUs), emergency departments (EDs), or acute care settings. Case reports, pediatric studies, and elective surgical intubation in non-critically ill patients were excluded. Ten studies published between 2012 and 2023 were identified and analyzed. No individual patient data were collected and no informed consent was required.

Results

The ten studies varied in design (two RCTs, six observational, one systematic review, one secondary analysis), setting (ICU, ED, mixed), and size (105 to 34357 intubations). Profound heterogeneity was identified across four domains (Figure 1).

Blood pressure thresholds ranged from SBP<65 mmHg – in the INTUBE cohort [1] and two RCTs [4,5] – to SBP <90 mmHg in five studies [1,2,6–8]. One study incorporated a relative threshold (decrease >20% from baseline) [6]. MAP<65 mmHg was included by three studies [2,6,7]. No two studies used identical criteria.

Temporal windows varied from 2 minutes after intubation [4,5] to 2 hours [8], with 30 minutes being the most common. One study used ‘immediately after the procedure’ without definition [9].

Composite components were inconsistently assembled. Vasopressor initiation or escalation was included in five studies [1,4–6,9] within windows of 2–30 minutes or unspecified. Cardiac arrest was a component in five studies [4,5,7–9], with timing from 30 minutes to 2 hours. Death within one hour was included in three [4,5,9], fluid bolus in two [1,2], and bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm within 2 hours) uniquely in one [8].

Terminology was equally heterogeneous: ‘cardiovascular collapse’ [4,5,9], ‘severe cardiovascular collapse’ [2], ‘cardiovascular instability’ [1,8,10], ‘postintubation hemodynamic instability’ [6], ‘hemodynamic derangement’ [7], and ‘peri-intubation major adverse events’ [3]. Two studies used multiple terms interchangeably [3,10].

Eight of ten studies provided no justification for their definitional choices. Only Green et al. developed their definition through formal expert consensus [6], Perbet et al. noted that event rates depend on the definition applied [2]. Blood pressure monitoring methods were reported in only two studies [2,6].

Event rates varied widely: severe cardiovascular collapse in 29.8% of hemodynamically stable patients [2], cardiovascular instability in 42.6% in the INTUBE cohort [1], and an overall major adverse event rate of 30.5% pooled across 44 studies [3], differences that may partly reflect definitional rather than true clinical variation. The two large RCTs testing prophylactic fluid boluses [4,5] found no benefit using restrictive definitions (SBP <65 mmHg, 2-minute window); more permissive criteria might have yielded different results.

Conclusions

Definitions of peri-intubation cardiovascular instability are profoundly heterogeneous across thresholds, temporal windows, components, and terminology, with minimal justification. This limits cross-study comparability, complicates evidence synthesis, and may obscure intervention efficacy. A formal consensus process to establish standardized, physiologically grounded definitions is urgently needed.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A135 Beyond the gums: hemorrhagic shock in a postpartum woman treated with arterial embolization

A. Iannuzzi, M. De Furio, L. Ciappa, F. Corvino, F. Liccardi

A.O.R.N. Antonio Cardarelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: A. Iannuzzi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A135

Background

Hemorrhage originating from the oral cavity is an uncommon occurrence, yet it frequently constitutes a genuine medical emergency, particularly among patients receiving anticoagulant therapy, those with congenital arteriovenous malformations, or with coagulation disorders. The differential diagnosis is often challenging, owing both to the difficulty in reconstructing a precise medical history and to the complexity of distinguishing true oral cavity bleeding from other hemorrhagic events, such as epistaxis, hemoptysis or hematemesis. This case report presents an episode of oral cavity bleeding as a complication following a dental procedure in a postpartum patient, in the absence of underlying pathology.

Description

A 33-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with active oral cavity bleeding. Ten days prior to admission, she had undergone extraction of tooth 48, which was complicated by gingival hemorrhage and managed with suturing. Three days before her arrival at the emergency department, she had delivered a child through mechanically induced labor without complications. Her medical history was unremarkable. Upon arrival in the shock room, she was alert, cooperative, and fully oriented. Her airways were patent, SpO2 was 96% on room air, and her respiratory rate was mildly increased. Hemodynamic parameters were initially stable, with a blood pressure of 170/80 mmHg and a heart rate of 104 bpm. Urine output was reported as satisfactory. Due to persistent oral bleeding, gauze soaked in tranexamic acid was applied to the gingival area, though this intervention failed to achieve adequate hemostasis. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed the following values: pH 7.26, pO2 190 on FiO2 40%, pCO2 28.4, hemoglobin 9.4 g/dl, HCO3 12.1, lactate 4.5. Her blood tests were normal and no coagulation abnormalities were detected. Subsequently, 500 ml of Ringer’s lactate and 1 g of tranexamic acid were administered intravenously.

A few minutes after admission to the shock room, the patient became confused, blood pressure decreased to 70/50 mmHg, and heart rate increased to 120 bpm. Two units of 0-negative packed red blood cells were requested, 2 g of fibrinogen were administered intravenously, and the patient was intubated orotracheally and connected to mechanical ventilation in IPPV mode. Noradrenaline therapy was initiated at 0.1 mcg/kg/min to maintain a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg. After hemodynamic stabilization, facial CT scan with contrast medium was performed, revealing a focal area of contrast accumulation in the arterial phase at the site of tooth 48, with maximum dimensions of approximately 7 x 6 mm and progressive density reduction in the venous phase.

The patient was transferred to the angiography suite, where angiographic examination confirmed the CT findings, demonstrating a prominent area of hypervascularization along the right inferior maxillary branch adjacent to the distal teeth, supplied by alveolar branches of the maxillary artery. Superselective catheterization of the feeder vessel was performed, with subsequent occlusion using metal coils. Follow-up selective arteriography from the external carotid artery revealed no further areas of active bleeding.

Upon return to the intensive care unit and following transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells, SpO2 was 98% on FiO2 40%, blood pressure was 125/60 mmHg, and heart rate was 74 bpm. Repeat arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.40, pO2 200 on FiO2 40%, pCO2 38.4, hemoglobin 10.7 g/dl, HCO3 24.1, lactate 1.5. The patient was extubated five hours after arrival in the emergency department and discharged after four days of hospitalization in good clinical condition.

At the outpatient follow-up after seven days, the patient denied any further hemorrhagic events and oral examination revealed no signs of active bleeding.

Conclusions

This case underscores the critical importance of prompt recognition and intervention in oral hemorrhages, which, though rare, may be life-threatening, particularly in postpartum patients without underlying coagulopathies. The multidisciplinary approach—including immediate resuscitation, advanced imaging, and targeted arterial embolization—was essential for achieving hemostasis and facilitating a positive clinical outcome. For clinicians, maintaining a high index of suspicion for atypical sources of bleeding and considering endovascular treatment when conventional measures prove insufficient is imperative; timely management can substantially improve patient prognosis in similar clinical scenarios.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A136 Severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis with normal lactate levels in a patient treated with dapagliflozin: a case report

M. De Caro, G. Benigni, P. Internicola, G. Petroni, G. Castellano

Asl Avellino PO Ariano Irpino, Italy

Correspondence: M. De Caro

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A136

Body

Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are increasingly used in the treatment of diabetes mellitus and heart failure because of their significant metabolic and cardiovascular benefits. However, these agents may rarely precipitate severe euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA), particularly in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus or during acute illness. We report the case of a 35-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus treated with dapagliflozin who developed severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis with normal lactate levels following a brief gastrointestinal illness and emergency surgery. Prompt recognition of the condition and aggressive intensive care management resulted in rapid clinical recovery. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis and awareness of SGLT2i-associated euDKA in critically ill patients.

Introduction

SGLT2 inhibitors have become widely used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease because of their favorable effects on glycemic control, body weight, and cardiovascular outcomes. Nevertheless, the use of these drugs has been associated with rare but potentially life-threatening adverse events, including euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis. The diagnosis may be challenging because patients often present with severe metabolic acidosis despite near-normal blood glucose levels. We describe a case of severe metabolic acidosis associated with dapagliflozin therapy in a patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus admitted to the intensive care unit.

Case Presentation

A 35-year-old woman with longstanding type 1 diabetes mellitus, regularly followed at a specialized diabetes center and treated with stable insulin therapy, presented with diarrhea, fever, abdominal pain, and vomiting. She was overweight but otherwise clinically stable prior to admission. After surgical evaluation at a peripheral hospital, she underwent appendectomy for suspected acute appendicitis.

In the hours following surgery, the patient progressively deteriorated, developing dyspnea and worsening metabolic acidosis. Laboratory investigations revealed severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis (anion gap >20), hypocapnia, and normal lactate levels. Whole-body computed tomography and CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism and other acute pathologies. Her clinical condition rapidly worsened, with oliguria, tachypnea, and progressive impairment of consciousness. She required endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and vasopressor support. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated profound acidosis with a pH of 6.87.

The patient was subsequently transferred to our intensive care unit. Bedside echocardiography showed preserved cardiac function and a collapsible inferior vena cava, suggesting severe dehydration. The combination of severe metabolic acidosis, elevated anion gap, normoglycemia, and normal lactate levels prompted suspicion of SGLT2i-associated euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis. Urinalysis confirmed marked glycosuria.

Treatment consisted of aggressive intravenous hydration, sodium bicarbonate administration, insulin infusion, glucose supplementation, electrolyte correction, and hemodynamic support. Following discussions with the family, it emerged that the patient had recently been prescribed dapagliflozin for weight control by her diabetologist. Clinical and laboratory parameters progressively improved within hours, with restoration of urine output, normalization of acid-base balance, and discontinuation of vasopressor therapy. The patient was extubated after approximately 12 hours and continued to improve with ongoing insulin therapy and hydration. Glycosuria resolved within 48 hours. She was discharged from the intensive care unit on day 5 and subsequently returned home in good clinical condition.

Discussion

Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis is a recognized but uncommon complication of SGLT2 inhibitor therapy. The mechanism involves increased urinary glucose excretion, reduction in circulating insulin levels, enhanced glucagon secretion, and increased ketogenesis. Precipitating factors include infection, dehydration, fasting, surgery, and reduced insulin administration.

The diagnosis may be delayed because hyperglycemia is often absent or mild. In critically ill patients, severe metabolic acidosis with elevated anion gap and normal lactate levels should prompt consideration of euDKA, particularly when SGLT2 inhibitor therapy is suspected. Early urinalysis and ketone testing are essential diagnostic tools.

This case underlines the importance of multidisciplinary awareness regarding the off-label use of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus. Although these drugs provide important metabolic benefits, clinicians should carefully evaluate risks and contraindications before prescription. Prompt recognition and appropriate intensive care management can be lifesaving.

Conclusion

SGLT2 inhibitor-associated euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis is a potentially fatal condition that may present with profound metabolic acidosis despite normal glucose and lactate levels. Critical care physicians and anesthesiologists should maintain a high index of suspicion in patients receiving SGLT2 inhibitors who develop unexplained metabolic acidosis during acute illness or the perioperative period. Rapid diagnosis and timely initiation of supportive therapy are crucial to improving outcomes.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A137 When pneumonia is not pneumonia: anti-PL12 antisynthetase syndrome presenting as isolated life-threatening ild

S. Pilloni1, M. Deplano1, D. Schiliro’2, A. Cossu2, F.M. Loddo1

1Complex Unit of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, ASL Ogliastra, Lanusei, Italy; 2Complex Unit of Internal Medicine, ASL Ogliastra, Lanusei, Italy

Correspondence: S. Pilloni

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A137

Background

Antisynthetase syndrome (ASS) is a rare disease, with a reported annual incidence of two new cases per one million adults. ASS is associated with autoantibodies directed against the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase complex and is characterized by a multifaceted clinical picture, in which fever, myositis, dysphagia, arthritis, Raynaud’s phenomenon, mechanic’s hands and interstitial lung disease (ILD) coexist in different combinations [1]. ILD can be the first or only manifestation of ASS. Diagnosis is typically made by combining HRCT, anti-ASS serology, physical examination and symptoms, while lung biopsy is discouraged according to current guidelines [2]. ILD is the most life-threatening complication of ASS and strongly affects its prognosis. Anti-PL12 and anti-PL7 antibodies are associated with a rapidly progressive and severe ILD.

We report the case of a 73-year-old woman, diagnosed with anti-PL12 and anti-Ro52 positive ASS with isolated pulmonary involvement.

Case report

The patient presented with a 3-week history of cough and dyspnea, initially treated with oral antibiotics at home. On admission, she was afebrile with severe respiratory failure. Laboratory tests showed leucocytosis (20,000/uL, 70% neutrophils), elevated C-reactive protein (209 mg/L), and negative procalcitonin. Chest CT revealed bilateral interstitial thickening with a predominantly subpleural distribution and extensive ground-glass opacities, consistent with acute interstitial lung disease (Figure 1).

Initial management included blood cultures, empiric antibiotic therapy (piperacillin-tazobactam and levofloxacin), and non-invasive ventilation. Within a few hours, however, the patient’s condition deteriorated, requiring orotracheal intubation, invasive mechanical ventilation, and ICU transfer. Vasopressor support with norepinephrine (0.15 ug/kg/min) was started; neuromuscular blockade and prone positioning were required to optimize ventilation.

Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed for FilmArray and galactomannan testing, alongside a nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory pathogen panel and serological testing for Mycoplasma and Chlamydia. An extensive immunological workup - including ANA, ENA, ANCA, anti-DNA, rheumatoid factor and myositis-specific autoantibodies immunoblot - was also performed. Galactomannan tested positive on BAL, leading to empiric antifungal therapy with voriconazole; all other microbiological results returned negative.

As cultures became available and confirmed the absence of mould infection, voriconazole was discontinued. The myositis panel then revealed marked positivity for anti-PL12 and anti-Ro52 antibodies, establishing the diagnosis of ASS and guiding the initiation of immunosuppressive therapy. A chest CT at this time showed worsening interstitial involvement, consolidation of dependent areas, and pleural effusion (Figure 2), consistent with the aggressive natural history of anti-PL12-associated ILD.

Notably, thorough evaluation revealed no extra-pulmonary manifestations of ASS: no muscle (skeletal nor cardiac), esophageal, cutaneous, microvascular, or articular involvement was observed at presentation or during follow-up, defining an ‘amyopathic presentation’ - a rare subset of ASS.

Treatment consisted of two cycles of high-dose methylprednisolone pulses (500 mg/day for three consecutive days each), followed by tapering from 1 mg/kg/day to 20 mg/day over several weeks, in association with cyclophosphamide infusions (500 mg every 15 days, 6 g total) and monthly intravenous immunoglobulins (immunomodulatory regimen: 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 consecutive days monthly).

Antimicrobial prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ganciclovir was administered throughout; serial CMV and EBV DNA monitoring were performed.

The clinical course remained complex despite treatment initiation: pneumothorax developed as an additional complication, and persistent respiratory failure necessitated tracheostomy on day 30.

After four weeks of treatment, the patient started showing clinical improvement, with progressive reduction in CRP and ferritin. Ventilatory weaning was gradually achieved, with discontinuation of mechanical ventilation on day 60 and decannulation on day 120. Radiological resolution was considerably delayed, with meaningful CT improvement only at 90 days (Figure 3), underscoring the protracted course of ASS-associated ILD even when therapy is initiated promptly.

Conclusion

This case highlights the challenges posed by rapidly progressive ILD as the sole manifestation of ASS, particularly when classic extra-pulmonary features are absent. Early serological evaluation for ASS-specific autoantibodies is a key diagnostic step in all cases of idiopathic, rapidly progressive ILD. A multidisciplinary approach - with close collaboration between intensivists and rheumatologists - was pivotal in reaching a timely diagnosis and guiding treatment. Even when therapy is initiated promptly, clinicians should anticipate a prolonged course, with radiological recovery and ventilatory weaning potentially requiring several months.

Written informed consent for the publication was obtained from the patient.

A138 Feasibility of femoral superficial vein for central vascular access devices (CVADS) in pediatric population: a prospective observational study

E. La Rosa1, V. Bartolucci2, C. Vecchio3, M. Pagano2, C. Greco1, D. Colosimo1, Z. Ricci1

1Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Meyer Children’s Hospital IRCCS, Florence, Italy; 2University of Florence, Italy; 3University of Messina, Italy

Correspondence: V. Bartolucci

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A138

Background

According to the ISAC-Ped Bundle (GAVeCeLT, 2016), a specific protocol for pediatric patients, the selection of the optimal vessel must be guided by six fundamental criteria to minimize complications. Ultrasound-based vascular assessment protocols improve the safety of catheter placement by enabling systematic evaluation of venous anatomy. In the femoral district, the Rapid Femoral Vein Assessment (RaFeVA) protocol allows structured ultrasound exploration of the femoral venous system. While the common femoral vein is a well known option for access site, cannulation of the superficial femoral vein may offer several theoretical advantages, however evidence regarding the feasibility of this approach in pediatric populations is extremely limited.

Objective

The aim of this study was to evaluate the anatomical characteristics of the superficial femoral vein in pediatric patients using the RaFeVA ultrasound protocol and to assess its anatomical feasibility as a potential target for central venous catheterization.

Methods

This prospective observational study included pediatric patients (<10 years) undergoing ultrasound evaluation of the femoral venous district using the RaFeVA protocol. Vessel diameter, depth, and anatomical relationships were recorded. The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients with superficial femoral vein (SFV) diameter ≥ 3 mm. A composite feasibility endpoint combined vein diameter ≥3 mm with depth between 2 and 3 cm. Secondary endpoints included anatomical characteristics such as proximity to arteries and ultrasound visibility of femoral nerves. Correlations between characteristics and antropometric data were investigated via multivariate logistic regression models.

The study protocol was approved by the local Ethics Committee. Written informed consent for participation in the study and for the publication of anonymized clinical data was obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all enrolled patients prior to enrollment.

Results

Forty-six pediatric patients were included (median age 2.92 years [1.00–6.75]; median weight 13.75 kg [10.25–22.00]). A SFV diameter > 3 mm was observed in 61.7% of patients on the right side and 59.6% on the left. Venous diameters showed strong positive correlations with weight, height and age, while prematurity was associated (p<0,05) with smaller vessel size.

Regarding the composite feasibility endpoint (diameter >3 mm associated with a depth of 2–3 mm), this was achieved in approximately one-third of the sample (31.9% bilaterally). The highest prevalence of this optimal anatomical profile was observed in the intermediate weight categories (10–30 kg).

Depth analysis showed a narrow range of only a few millimeters, confirming the anatomical stability of the vessel, although preterm patients exhibited a significantly more superficial localization (< 0.05) and smaller vessel calibers.

In terms of safety criteria, the femoral nerve was visible in only a minority of cases. The multivariate logistic regression model indicated that nerve visibility does not depend on local morphological variables or prematurity; instead, it is significantly associated with clinical complexity. An increase in ASA physical status was the only relevant predictor of nerve visibility (OR > 1; p < 0.05).

Conclusions

More than 60% of the children screened presented an SFV caliber adequate for the insertion of 3 French CVADS. However, when applying stricter feasibility criteria (the diameter-depth composite endpoint), the proportion of ideal candidates falls to approximately one-third of the population, with the 10–30 kg weight group showing the best anatomical match. Furthermore, femoral nerve visibility appears to be linked more to global clinical status (ASA) than to local anatomy. In conclusion, the SFV represents a viable and safe anatomical target in a significant portion of the pediatric population, provided that selection is guided by systematic pre-procedural ultrasound assessment.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A139 Pain and delirium assessment in pediatric patients undergoing enzymatic debridement with NexoBrid®: a prospective observational study

E. La Rosa1, C. Vecchio2, M. Pagano3, F. Becci4, A. Cipolletti3, M. Certini5, F. Facchini5, D. Colosimo1, Z. Ricci1

1Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Meyer Children’s Hospital IRCCS, Florence, Italy; 2University of Messina, Italy; 3University of Florence, Italy; 4University of Milan, Italy; 5Department of Pediatric Plastic Surgery and Burn Center, Florence, Italy

Correspondence: C. Vecchio

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A139

Background

Enzymatic debridement (ED) with NexoBrid® has revolutionized the management of deep partial- and full-thickness burns by offering a selective, non-surgical alternative. Nevertheless, the procedure involves a critical 4-hour exposure period characterized by significant nociceptive stimulation. Retrospective data acquired in the adult population indicate that pain peaks during application and persists over time, representing a challenge despite the use of multimodal analgesia. This prospective study aims to assess the progression of pain intensity during this contact time and the incidence of emergence delirium.

Materials and Methods

This prospective, single-center, observational study included pediatric patients (<16 years) with scald burns undergoing ED at a tertiary burn center in 2025. In addition to clinical monitoring, systematic assessments using validated scales for pain (VAS or FLACC) and delirium (PAED) were conducted hourly at five specific time points: application (T0), every hour during the maintenance phase (T1, T2, T3), and after removal (T4). Analgesic protocols and pharmacological interventions were also recorded. The study protocol was approved by the local Ethics Committee. Written informed consent for participation in the study and for the publication of anonymized clinical data was obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all enrolled patients prior to enrollment.

Results and Discussion

The study population was composed of 40 patients, mostly males, with a median age of 30 months [14,8–82]. After application, the drug was left in place for an average of 4 hours and 40 minutes (±36 minutes). The median pain score at T0 was 6 [3–8]; this increased significantly during NexoBrid® application, reaching a peak value at T1 (8 [7–8]), remaining sustained through T2 (7 [5–7]), and eventually reducing at T3 (4 [3–7]). Notably, 15% of patients reported a pain score of 9; 80% of patients required additional analgesic doses during the observation period, 60% of whom received additional opioids.

Of the overall population, 15% were excluded from PAED evaluation due to the need for ICU admission or neurological disorders, while 52.5% were excluded due to incomplete charts. The resulting 32.5% with complete PAED scale data showed a significant incidence of emergence delirium (defined as a PAED score >10), especially in the first hours of observation (median value 11 [7–17]), which progressively reduced to basal levels in the subsequent hours (T0: 2 [0–3]; T2: 5 [3.5–11]; T3: 3.5 [3–7.5]; T4: 4 [0–6]). Overall, 15.4% of the analyzed sample in the Overall, 15.4% of the analyzed sample in the cohort analyzed showed a sustained PAED score >10 during the 4-hour observation. Regarding the treatment of delirium, most patients received midazolam (23% at T1, 30% at T2, and 30% at T4); as secondary treatment, less than 20% received low-dose ketamine (15.4% at T1 and T2, 7.7% at T3); 25% received an off-label infusion of dexmedetomidine during the entire 4-hour period, resulting in a stable reduction of the PAED score. Younger patients with limited burns showed higher delirium rates.

Conclusions

Despite the use of general anesthesia with opioids, most patients experienced worsening pain during the contact period, requiring additional treatments. Standardizing the monitoring of pain and delirium through validated scales is essential to refining pediatric-specific analgesic protocols for NexoBrid®. Understanding the temporal dynamics of distress during the 4-hour treatment period is crucial to preventing long-term neuropsychological sequelae and ensuring the safe, effective application of enzymatic debridement in the pediatric population.

A140 Impact of enzymatic debridement on hospital care burden and pain management in pediatric burns: a retrospective cohort study

E. La Rosa1, M. Pagano2, C. Vecchio3, F. Becci4, V. Bartolucci2, M. Certini5, F. Facchini5, Z. Ricci1

1Department of Anesthesia and Critical Care Meyer Children s Hospital, Florence, Italy; 2University of Florence, Florence, Italy; 3University of Messina, Messina, Italy; 4University of Milan, Milan, Italy; 5Pediatric Plastic Surgery and Burn Centre Division Meyer Children s Hospital, Florence, Italy

Correspondence: M. Pagano

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A140

Background

The management of pediatric burns entails a significant healthcare burden, as the complexity of the condition is compounded by the inherent vulnerability, psychological impact, and family circumstances of this population.

Pediatric burn care necessitates a dedicated multidisciplinary team and involves frequent surgical procedures, complex dressing changes, repeated sedation, and high analgesic requirements, demanding a tailored, integrated, and multimodal approach. The advent of enzymatic debridement (ED) vith NexoBrid™ potentially alleviates this healthcare burden compared to the standard of care (SOC), thereby optimizing clinical outcomes, hospital organizational efficiency and cost-effectiveness.

Objective

To evaluate the hospital impact (length of stay, dressing necessity, and sedation requirements) of enzymatic debridement with NexoBrid™ compared to conventional surgical treatment in pediatric burn patients.

Materials and Methods

We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of pediatric burn patients (<16 years) admitted to Meyer Children’s Hospital with deep dermal thermal or deep partial-thickness burns. Patients treated with standard of care (SOC) were included from September 2022 to June 2024, while those treated with NexoBrid™ were included from July 2024—following its official approval in Europe—to April 2026. Burns caused by chemicals, electricity and radiation were excluded. Data regarding demographics, burn characteristics (TBSA, depth, location), pre- and post-procedural management, and clinical outcomes were systematically collected. Primary endpoint was to collect the total number of post-treatment dressings, the number of dressings performed under sedation, the length of hospital stay (LOS) and analgesic need requirements. Secondary endpoints encompassed surgical outcomes as time to re-epithelialization, skin grafting requirements, and other procedural variables.

To reduce selection bias, a 1:1 propensity score matching was applied, accounting for age, TBSA, burn depth, location, and time to treatment.

Results

The SOC cohort comprised 26 patients (17 males, 9 females) with a median age of 46 months (16–96) at burn injury and a median weight of 17 kg (11.8–33). Twenty-five patients presented with second-degree burns (10 of whom had concomitant third-degree areas), while one patient presented exclusively with third-degree burns; the median calculated TBSA was 10% (7.5–13.5).

The ED cohort of patients included 39 patients (23 males, 16 females) with a median age of 30 months (15.55–81.92) and a median weight of 14 kg (12–25). In this group, 38 patients presented with second-degree burns (including 10 with concomitant third-degree areas), and one patient presented with isolated third-degree burns; the median TBSA was 9% (5–18).

Comparative analysis showed that the NexoBrid™ group required fewer post-dermabrasion dressings compared to the surgical group (2 vs. 3), with lower skin grafting rates (38.5% vs. 46.2%, respectively). While the injury-to-treatment mean interval was similar between groups (3.2±4.8 vs. 3.61±3.1 days), blood transfusions were more frequent in the NexoBrid™ cohort (5 vs. 1). Although perioperative complication rates were comparable (17% vs. 15.4%), the NexoBrid™ group was associated with a longer mean hospital stay (18.2±10.6 vs. 14.9±16.7 days).

These preliminary findings suggest that NexoBrid™ correlates with reduced postoperative care complexity, particularly regarding the reduction in dressings performed under sedation, indicating less traumatic wound management and decreased demand for anesthesiology services. Length of stay is not an indicator yet, but further studies are needed. Skin grafting and scarring outcomes were considered as secondary clinical control variables.

Conclusions

In pediatric burn care, the debridement strategy could influence hospital care burden. Enzymatic debridement represents a viable therapeutic option to reduce clinical and organizational complexity; it provides tangible benefits for patients, families, and the healthcare system by optimizing resource allocation and minimizing procedural trauma.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A141 Intraoperative anesthetic management in selective dorsal rhizotomy: experience of the bambino gesù children’s hospital

S. Marchetta1, A. Savioli2, E. Malara3, F. Randi3, G. Esposito3, P. Palma3, A. Carai3, S. Reali2

1Hôpital Necker Enfants-Malades, Paris, France; 2Intensive Care Unit, Department of Emergency, Bambino Gesù Children s Hospital, IRCCS, Rome, Italy; 3Neurosurgery Unit, Department of Neuroscience and Neurorehabilitation, Bambino Gesù Children s Hospital, IRCCS, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: S. Marchetta

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A141

Background

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a non-progressive neurological disorder characterized by abnormalities in muscle tone, posture, and movement, often associated with spasticity and significant motor impairment. Selective dorsal rhizotomy (SDR) is an effective surgical option for reducing spasticity. Perioperative anesthetic and analgesic management plays a crucial role in optimizing clinical outcomes and promoting postoperative functional recovery.

Objectives

To evaluate the effectiveness of intra- and postoperative analgesic strategies, as well as anesthetic complications and adverse events, in order to develop a standardized anesthetic protocol for the Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital (OPBG).

Methods

A retrospective observational study was conducted on 46 pediatric patients (26 males, 20 females; mean age 11.2 years) who underwent SDR between 2019 and 2025. Postoperative pain (VAS on days 1–4), time to mobilization, length of hospital stay, and need for intensive care admission were analyzed. Patients were grouped according to the analgesic technique used, with particular focus on the erector spinae plane (ESP) block.

Results

The erector spinae plane (ESP) block showed a significant reduction in postoperative pain compared to morphine on postoperative days 2 and 3 (p < 0.05) (Figure 1; Table 1), with a favorable trend already evident from day 1. The combination of ESP with continuous opioid infusion also resulted in significantly lower visual analogue scale (VAS) scores compared to morphine alone.

ESP use was associated with earlier mobilization compared to other analgesic strategies (2.91 vs 3.50 days; p =0.076). No significant differences were observed in length of hospital stay, which ranged from 5 to 7 days. The addition of adjuvant agents, such as magnesium and clonidine, did not provide significant clinical benefits.

Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital protocol involves total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) with propofol and remifentanil, an ultrasound-guided bilateral ESP block with 0.2% ropivacaine, and an opioid-sparing approach.

Conclusions

The adoption of a standardized multimodal anesthetic protocol represents a key factor in improving outcomes in pediatric patients with cerebral palsy undergoing selective dorsal rhizotomy.

The ESP block is confirmed to be an effective and safe technique for postoperative pain control, allowing reduced opioid consumption and earlier mobilization, with potential benefits for rehabilitation. It also contributes to minimizing the use of systemic opioids and their associated side effects.

The study has been approved by the competent Ethics Committee.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A142 Digitalization of the paediatric perioperative pathway: translation and Italian validation of PreOpApp™ Kids

T. Domenichetti1, V. Bellini1, L. Welsh2, A. Simonini3, L.J. Dahrour1, E.G. Bignami1

1Anesthesiology, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine Division, Department of Medicine and Surgery, University of Parma, Italy; 2Pediatric Anesthesiology, Prisma Health Children s Hospital, Columbia, USA; 3Pediatric Anesthesia and Intensive Care Unit, Salesi Children s Hospital, Ancona, Italy

Correspondence: T. Domenichetti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A142

Background

Digitalization is transforming perioperative medicine through innovative tools that support integrated surgical pathway management, personalized care, and multidisciplinary coordination [1, 2]. Recent evidence shows that digital health interventions,like telemonitoring and mobile applications, improve patient safety while reducing readmissions and unplanned healthcare visits [3].

In paediatric care, PreOpApp™ Kids was developed as a digital educational platform to prepare children and caregivers for surgery through interactive, age-appropriate experiences. The app includes educational content, fasting guidance and reminders, breathing and relaxation games, familiarization with the hospital environment and equipment, and immersive storytelling aimed at reducing anxiety. Biofeedback and digital engagement tools further support communication, preparation, and emotional well-being in paediatric surgical care [4].

This project aims to translate and culturally adapt PreOpApp™ Kids into Italian, promoting its integration within the national healthcare system and improving accessibility for children undergoing surgery and their caregivers.

Materials and Methods

The project involves the translation and cultural adaptation of PreOpApp™ Kids into Italian aiming to making it usable towards the greatest number of people. Then, the app will undergo validation by the SIAARTI-AIIC-SIHTA Committee, a multidisciplinary expert group including the Società Italiana di Anestesia, Analgesia, Rianimazione e Terapia Intensiva (SIAARTI), its Paediatric Anaesthesia Study Group, the Associazione Italiana Ingegneri Clinici (AIIC) and the Società Italiana di Health Technology Assessment (SIHTA).

Following technical and scientific validation, the application will be tested in a controlled cohort of children and caregivers to assess usability, accessibility, user satisfaction, and potential clinical and organizational benefits.

Results

The project aims to expand the dissemination of digital perioperative tools by improving engagement of children and caregivers through interactive educational pathways designed to enhance preparation, adherence to clinical instructions, and anxiety reduction.

Preoperative anxiety is associated with surgical delays and cancellations, with a rate of up to 20% in UK [5], increased postoperative pain, delirium, maladaptive behaviours, and greater perioperative stress. Digital technologies may help reduce anxiety and improve perioperative outcomes while optimizing healthcare resource utilization [6,7].

PreOpApp™ Kids has been specifically designed to help children become familiar with the hospital environment, procedures, and equipment encountered on the day of surgery. It also provides clear fasting instructions, reducing the risk of excessive or insufficient fasting, which may result in dehydration, irritability, electrolyte imbalance, hypotension, or aspiration. Interactive games and narrative tools promote engagement, distraction, and stress reduction. A multimodal digital communication strategy associated with the platform achieved a caregiver satisfaction rate of 91% [4].

The application may also improve sustainability of paediatric perioperative pathways by reducing the need for in-person educational visits, optimizing organizational time, and increasing adherence to standardized preoperative instructions through accessible digital content.

Moreover, the project may facilitate real-world implementation of digital perioperative tools. Many promising technologies fail to progress beyond pilot phases because of limited validation, insufficient multidisciplinary involvement, poor integration within healthcare pathways, or inadequate adaptation to local cultural and organizational contexts. Through structured translation, cultural adaptation, multidisciplinary validation, and direct feedback from children and caregivers, this project aims to bridge the gap between research and routine clinical practice (Fig. 1).

Conclusions

These findings support the integration of digital platforms into perioperative medicine, highlighting their clinical and organizational benefits. The Italian translation and validation of PreOpApp™ Kids may contribute to the digitalization of paediatric anaesthesia care by providing caregivers with clear, accessible, and standardized information, reducing preoperative stress and uncertainty, and offering children effective emotional support and distraction up to anaesthetic induction.

Consent to publish

Not applicable.

A143 Perioperative perfusion index trends in children undergoing general anesthesia: a prospective observational study

A. Cipolletti1, A. Vecchione2, V. Gatti2, E. La Rosa1, D. Colosimo1, Z. Ricci1,2

1Department of Anesthesia and Critical Care, Meyer Children’s Hospital, IRCCS,, Florence, Italy; 2Department of Health Sciences, Section of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, University of Florence, Italy

Correspondence: A. Cipolletti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A143

Background

The Perfusion Index (PI), derived from photoplethysmography, is a non-invasive marker of peripheral perfusion that may complement standard haemodynamic monitoring. This study aimed to describe perioperative PI trends and reference values in standard general anesthesia.

Methods

We conducted a prospective observational study in pediatric patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia. The study was conducted in a tertiary care pediatric institution, between september 2025 and december 2025. PI values were prospectively recorded by pulse oximetry at five predefined time points: baseline (before induction), maintenance (three measurements during the surgical phase) and recovery (at emergence from anesthesia). Furthermore, correlation analyses were performed between PI values and demographic, clinical, and haemodynamic variables. The study protocol was approved by the local Ethics Committee.

Results

Ninety-nine children were analysed. PI values increased significantly after induction and during maintenance, from 1.98 (1.08–3.68) at baseline to 6.47 (4.86–8.44) during early maintenance, then decreased at emergence to 4.79 (2.39–6.51), without returning to baseline (p<0.01). Demographic variables showed weak associations with PI. Conversely, PI was inversely associated with haemodynamic variables. Multivariable models identified heart rate during maintenance (beta = −0.042; 95% CI, −0.070 to −0.013; p=0.004) and mean arterial pressure at recovery (beta = −0.121; 95% CI, −0.215 to −0.026; p=0.012) as independent predictors.

Conclusions

PI is a dynamic perioperative marker in pediatric general anesthesia, reflecting peripheral vasomotor changes beyond conventional macro-hemodynamic parameters.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A144 Divergent treatment strategies in oral antidiabetic–related metabolic emergencies in intensive care unit: when insulin prevails over extracorporeal therapy

M. Pazzi, T. Meconi, R. Papa, C. Pantanelli, P. Ruggiano, D. Conti

Emergency Department and Critical Care Area, Anesthesia and Intensive Care Unit, Santa Maria Annunziata Hospital, Firenze, Italy

Correspondence: M. Pazzi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A144

Background

Fixed-dose combinations of metformin and sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are widely used in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) due to their complementary mechanisms and favorable glycemic profiles [1,2]. However, both drug classes carry rare but distinct risks of life-threatening metabolic complications. Indeed, metformin is associated with metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA), while SGLT2 inhibitors predispose to Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis (EDKA), a high–anion gap metabolic acidosis with near-normal blood glucose and excessive ketogenesis [3]. Although contrasting pathophysiological mechanisms, predisposing factors, and diagnostic criteria of both conditions (Figure 1), the atypical presentation of EDKA can delay diagnosis and lead to inappropriate management in the intensive care unit (ICU).

Case Report

We report a 65-year-old man with T2DM on dapagliflozin (10 mg/day) and metformin (500 mg twice daily), who provided written informed consent for publication, admitted to the ICU with dyspnea, nausea, confusion, and severe dehydration after five days of vomiting and diarrhea. He presented with hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressor support (norepinephrine 0.08 µg/kg/min) and a Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of 6.

Arterial blood gas revealed severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.05, HCO3- 2 mmol/L), markedly elevated anion gap (36 mmol/L), serum glucose 9.0 mmol/L, lactate 5.2 mmol/L, and positive urinary ketones. MALA was initially suspected, and continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) was initiated. Despite 24 hours of dialysis, bicarbonate administration, and hemodynamic stabilization, acidosis persisted with ongoing ketonuria, prompting reassessment toward SGLT2 inhibitor–associated EDKA.

Intravenous insulin (0.1 U/kg/h) with 10% dextrose (1 mL/kg/h) was started alongside continuation of continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Within 24 hours, acid–base status improved markedly (pH 7.34, HCO3- 18 mmol/L), vasopressors were discontinued, and CRRT was stopped 12 hours after insulin initiation.

Conclusion

This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of overlapping metabolic complications in critically ill patients on combination antidiabetic therapy [1,4]. In this context, extracorporeal treatment alone does not address ketone overproduction driving EDKA, whereas high–anion gap metabolic acidosis with near-normal glycemia in patients on SGLT2 inhibitors warrants prompt recognition of EDKA with early insulin therapy and glucose supplementation.

The clinician should quickly identify the pathophysiological differences between the two complications so as not to delay appropriate treatment to prevent prolonged organ dysfunction and worse outcomes.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.
