A145 Nutritional adequacy in patients receiving non-invasive ventilation: preliminary findings from the pro-nutriniv study

O.A. Koku1, F. Moretto1,2, T. Esposito1,2, F. Minelli2, S. Riso3, C.A.M. Castorina1, F. Baroffio1, I. Scannella4, E. Massara5, A. Iorio6, A. Manieri7, M. Pirisi1,4, M. Campanini5, M. Bellan1,6, G. Patti1,7, R. Vaschetto1,2

1Department of Translational Medicine, University of Eastern Piedmont, Novara, Italy; 2Anesthesia and Intensive Care, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy; 3Dietetics and Clinical Nutrition, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy; 4Internal Medicine 1, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy; 5Internal Medicine 2, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy; 6Emergency and Admission Medicine and Surgery, “Maggiore della Carità” University Hospital, Novara, Italy; 7Cardiologia Azienda Ospedaliero Universitaria Maggiore della Carità, Novara, Italy

Correspondence: O.A. Koku

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A145

Background

Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) may impair adequate nutritional intake, increasing the risk of malnutrition, while recommendations on nutritional targets and management in this population remain limited [1]. This study aimed to quantify calorie and protein intake and adequacy - defined as intake relative to target - in patients undergoing NIV across different levels of care.

Materials and Methods

This preliminary analysis of a prospective observational study included adult patients who signed informed consent, started NIV within 24 hours of admission for ARF and received oral nutrition in the intensive care unit (ICU), intermediate care units, or ordinary wards of a tertiary university hospital in Italy between December 2024 and October 2025. Caloric and protein intake were assessed by a hospital dietitian using a daily food diary collected for five days from NIV initiation. Due to the lack of specific recommendations in this population, nutritional targets were calculated according to the ESPEN guidelines for critically ill patients [2,3]: 25 kcal/kg/day and 1.3 g/kg/day of protein, using a stepwise approach (25% of target on day 1, 50% on day 2, and 70% on day 3–5).

Results

Seventy-one patients were included: 2 in the ICU, 30 in intermediate care units, and 39 in ordinary wards. Forty-four (62%) were male, with a median age of 77 years [IQR 70–85], admitted for pulmonary oedema (45%), pneumonia (20%), obstructive disease exacerbation (31%). Median Nutritional Risk Screening (NRS) 2002 score was 2 [IQR 1–3], and calf circumference was 34 cm [IQR 32–39]. NIV was initiated in pressure support mode in 44 patients (62%), with a median duration of 21 hours [IQR 15–23] on day 1; 33 patients (46%) remained on NIV by day 5. On day 1, 18 patients (25%) were fasting, mainly due to NIV dependency or medical indication. Median caloric intake increased from 5.5 kcal/kg [IQR 1.2–11.6] on day 1 to 15.6 kcal/kg [IQR 11.5–20.4] on day 5 (Figs 1, 2 and 3). Caloric adequacy was highest on day 2 (108% [IQR 66–139]) and reached 85% [IQR 62–115] on day 5. Median

protein intake ranged from 0.2 g/kg [IQR 0–0.4] on day 1 to 0.7 g/kg [IQR 0.4–0.8] on day 5, with a mean (SD) protein adequacy of 66% (6). Caloric intake was higher in intermediate care and wards than in ICU patients.

Conclusion

Patients receiving NIV were started on early oral feeding. Caloric intake was generally adequate, whereas protein intake remained substantially insufficient, with marked inter- individual variability.

A146 A systematic review of enteral nutrition interruptions in hospitalized adults

F. Di Vezza1, F. Carbone2, A. Montalbano1, I. Giuliano1, A. Piazza1, V. Vano1, F. Bilotta1

1Tor Vergata Polyclinic, Rome, Italy; 2Sapienza, University of Rome, Italy

Correspondence: F. Di Vezza

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A146

Background

Many hospitalized adult patients require enteral nutrition (EN) because they cannot meet their nutritional needs safely or adequately by mouth, yet hospitalized patients experience frequent interruptions that may contribute to clinically meaningful nutrition deficits. Guidelines recommend minimizing avoidable cessation of EN to reduce cumulative nutritional loss (1,2), but contemporary studies suggest that a significant proportion of feeding interruptions may still be preventable (3,4). Although EN interruptions are well described in ICU settings, far less is known about patterns on general wards. To date, no review has synthesized evidence across ICU and non-ICU settings or categorized interruption reasons using a unified framework. We conducted a systematic review to describe the types, frequency, and drivers of unplanned EN interruptions in hospitalized adults.

Methods

A systematic review was conducted using PRISMA-2020 methodology and registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251067529). We used Covidence systematic review software (Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) to organize the search results, remove duplicates, perform independent title/abstract screening, adjudicate conflicts, and extract data using structured forms. MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and Cochrane databases were searched from inception through September 2025. Studies were eligible if they included adults receiving EN and reported unplanned interruptions, regardless of ICU or ward location. Pediatric, outpatient, and intentionally intermittent feeding protocols were excluded. Study selection was performed by three independent reviewers, with a minimum of two reviewers screening each title/abstract and full text, and disagreements resolved by consensus.

Interruption drivers were categorized as clinical (e.g., intolerance, instability), procedural (imaging, surgery, airway), or organizational/system-level (staffing, NPO orders, restart delays). Meta-analysis was not feasible due to heterogeneity; narrative synthesis was prespecified.

Results

We screened 2848 studies by abstract, and we identified 209 for full text review. Finally, 76 studies were extracted for further review (ICU: 75, non-ICU: 1; Figure 1). Table 1 summarizes included studies, which represented >20 countries. Because nearly all extractable data were derived from ICU-based cohorts, the following results reflect ICU studies unless otherwise noted. Study designs were predominantly prospective observational (53%), with fewer retrospective cohorts (25%) and randomized trials (10%). Median ICU sample size was 415 (range 18–15,918). Gastric feeding predominated (55%), 7% used post-pyloric routes, and 35% reported mixed access. Most cohorts involved mixed medical-surgical ICUs (70%). Risk of bias varied across included studies (low 45%, high 39%, unclear 16%). Clinical causes were the most frequently reported interruptions (100% of ICU studies; primary in 58.6%), followed by procedural factors (89.3%; primary in 38.6%) and organizational contributors (72%; primary in only 2.6%) (Table 2).

Interruption burden was high: 55% of ICU patients experienced more than 1 EN stoppage, with a median 2.5 interruptions per patient (1.65–3.5) or ~1.5 interruptions/day. Thirty percent of feeding days were interrupted (13–49%), equating to approximately 5 hours/day withheld and a cumulative ~56 hours lost per admission (Table 3).

Conclusion

Unplanned EN interruptions occur frequently and are reported almost exclusively in ICUs. Guideline recommendations to minimize avoidable cessation stand in contrast to the high burden of withheld nutrition observed across studies. The absence of meaningful ward-based data limits our understanding of interruption burden beyond the ICU. Future work should include multicenter, prospective studies on general wards that measure interruption frequency and identify reasons for avoidable fasting. Next steps should also include evaluating effects on nutritional adequacy and clinical outcomes in both ICU and non-ICU patients, including recovery after hospitalization. Sustainable improvements will require coordinated efforts among nursing, respiratory therapy, dietitians, bedside providers, and operational leadership to develop protocolized approaches that reduce unnecessary fasting. Automatic restart pathways and standardized peri-procedural fasting protocols may reduce interruption burden and support nutrition delivery.

A147 A systematic review of nutrition delivery and clinical outcomes associated with enteral nutrition interruptions in hospitalized adults

F. Di Vezza1, F. Carbone2, F. Lucci1, M. Falcone1, G. Storti1, F. Bilotta1

1Tor Vergata Polyclinic, Rome, Italy; 2Sapienza, University of Rome, Italy

Correspondence: F. Di Vezza

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A147

Background

Many hospitalized adult patients require enteral nutrition (EN) because they cannot meet their nutritional needs safely or adequately by mouth, yet hospitalized patients many experience frequent interruptions that may contribute to clinically meaningful nutrition deficits. Guidelines recommend minimizing avoidable cessation of EN to reduce cumulative nutritional loss (1,2), but contemporary studies suggest that a significant proportion of feeding interruptions may still be preventable (3,4). Although EN interruptions are well described in ICU settings, far less is known about incidence patterns on general wards. To date, no review has synthesized evidence across ICU and non-ICU settings or examined how feeding interruptions influence caloric/protein adequacy and clinical outcomes such as infection, length of stay, and mortality. We conducted a systematic review to quantify nutrition deficits delivery during interrupted EN and evaluate associated outcomes in hospitalized adults.

Methods

A systematic review was conducted using PRISMA-2020 methodology and registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251067529). We used Covidence systematic review software (Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) to perform independent title/abstract screening, remove duplicates, adjudicate conflicts, extract data, and organize the search results using structured forms. MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and Cochrane databases were searched from inception through September 2025. Studies were eligible if they included Inclusion criteria were adults receiving EN and reported unplanned interruptions, regardless of ICU or ward location. Exclusion criteria were Pediatric, outpatient, and scheduled intermittent feeding protocols were excluded. Study selection was performed by three independent reviewers, with a minimum of two reviewers screening each title/abstract and full text, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Meta- analysis was not feasible due to heterogeneity; narrative synthesis was prespecified. For this analysis, studies were further assessed for caloric/protein adequacy and reported clinical outcomes.

Results

We screened 2848 studies by abstract, and we identified 209 for full text review. (Fig. 1) 76 studies were chosen for further review (ICU: 75, non-ICU: 1). Table 1 summarizes included studies, which represented over 20 countries. Because nearly all extractable data were derived from ICU-based cohorts, the following results reflect ICU studies unless otherwise noted.

Study designs were mainly prospective observational (53%), with fewer retrospective cohorts (25%) and randomized trials (10%). Median ICU sample size was 415 (ranging from 18 to15,918). Gastric feeding predominated (55%), 7% used post-pyloric routes, and 35% reported mixed access. Most cohorts involved mixed medical–surgical ICUs (70%). Risk of bias varied across included studies (low risk 45%, high risk 39%, unclear 16%). Nutrition delivery fell well below prescribed targets. Median caloric delivery was about 69% of prescription (range 6.4–96%) and protein delivery was about 63% (33–89%).

Reported deficits averaged around 846 kcal/day and around 42 g of protein/day, and median time to goal rate was 3.3 days. Volumetric adequacy averaged 74%, with a median volume deficit of around 365 mL/day (Table 2). No non-ICU studies reported caloric or protein adequacy. Across studies reporting outcomes, greater interruption burden was generally associated with higher infection rates, longer ICU length of stay, and increased mortality risk, while associations with aspiration, ventilator-free days, and hospital length of stay were inconsistent or sparsely reported (Table 3).

Conclusions

EN delivery in hospitalized adults falls consistently below prescribed caloric and protein targets, with substantial daily deficits.

Evidence linking

Interruptions to outcomes is generally directionally consistent, but limited by heterogeneity and the near absence of ward-based data. Future work should include multicenter, prospective studies that evaluate nutrition adequacy and outcomes in both ICU and non-ICU patients. Sustainable improvements will require coordinated efforts among nursing, respiratory therapy, dietitians, bedside providers, and operational leadership to develop protocols that reduce unnecessary fasting. Automatic restart pathways and standardized peri-procedural EN protocols represent potential strategies that could be tested prospectively for their effect on nutrition delivery.

A148 Critical care management in a patient with a rare metabolic disease in a complex clinical scenario

F. De Vivo1, A. Diana1, I. Casaburo1, C. Morrone1, M. Piccolo1, G. Sagristani1, G. Cosenza2, V. Santoro2, M. Fiore1, F. Coppolino1, P. Sansone1, M.B. Passavanti1, V. Pota1, M.C. Pace1

1Department of Women, Child, General and Specialized Surgery, University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Naples, Italy; 2Complex Unit of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Vanvitelli University Hospital (AOU Vanvitelli), Naples, Italy

Correspondence: F. De Vivo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A148

Background

Glycogen storage disease type I (GSD I) is a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder characterized by impaired endogenous glucose production due to defects in glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, resulting in hypoglycemia and severe lactic acidosis. During acute stress conditions, such as surgery, pregnancy, or hemorrhage, patients are at particularly high risk of severe metabolic decompensation. Lactic acidosis may result from both intrinsic metabolic mechanisms (type B) and tissue hypoperfusion (type A), which frequently coexist [1,2].

Case Report

We report the case of a 33-year-old primiparous woman affected by GSD type Ib who underwent emergency cesarean section complicated by postoperative uterine atony with massive blood loss and acute anemia (Hb 6.6 g/dL). In the early postoperative period, she rapidly developed severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.2; pCO2 28 mmHg; BE −12 mmol/L; lactate 9.2 mmol/L), despite the absence of clinically significant hypoglycemia and with preserved blood glucose levels (glycemia 85 mg/dL).The clinical picture was likely related to increased lactate production caused by metabolic shunting of glucose-6-phosphate toward glycolysis, exacerbated by surgical stress and possible tissue hypoperfusion [2]. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit, sedated, and intubated because of hemorrhagic shock. Monitoring included invasive hemodynamic assessment, serial arterial blood gas analyses, and continuous metabolic evaluation.Treatment consisted of ventilatory support, transfusion therapy with packed red blood cells and plasma, intravenous crystalloids, and glucose infusion to maintain euglycemia. Intensification of 10% dextrose infusion (1500 mL at 63 mL/h) was required, together with hemodynamic support and correction of severe acidosis using bicarbonate therapy. Prompt treatment and close monitoring allowed progressive normalization of metabolic and clinical parameters, leading to successful extubation (arterial blood gas analysis at ICU discharge: pH 7.4; pCO2 35 mmHg; BE 5 mmol/L; lactate 4 mmol/L; glycemia 83 mg/dL).

Conclusions

This case highlights how acute stress in patients with GSD type Ib may precipitate severe metabolic crises characterized by lactic acidosis even in the absence of hypoglycemia, emphasizing the complex pathophysiology of the disease [1]. The anesthetic and intensive care management of patients with rare metabolic diseases remains particularly challenging and requires an individualized approach.

Current evidence confirms that prompt glucose administration represents the cornerstone of treatment, helping to reduce lactate production and prevent metabolic decompensation [2]. In the perioperative setting, it is essential to prevent fasting-related complications, ensure adequate carbohydrate supplementation, and promptly recognize metabolic acidosis in order to treat its multifactorial causes. A multidisciplinary approach and targeted management are crucial to improving clinical outcomes.

Declaration

Informed consent for data collection and pubblication has been collected.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A149 Incidence of secondary sarcopenia in emergency surgery

R. Foreste, S. Cotena, R. Annunziata, M. Mariani, E. Santoriello, F. Gison, C. Iavarone, M. Vicedomini, O. Volino, S. Alfieri, R. Villani

A.O.R.N. A. Cardarelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: R. Foreste

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A149

Background

Patients with an acute abdominal pathology, who undergo to emergency laparotomy, often develop a loss of skeletal muscle mass and function in postoperative period, caused by hypercatabolism, immobilization and nutritional deficits [1]. This condition is potentially reversible end its early recognition allow clinicians to optimize nutritional therapies to counteract the loss of muscle mass and its long-term consequences [2,3]. Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA) is a non-invasive method to estimate body composition, including muscle mass, but because of its high dependence on patient hydtratation status and inflammatory response, this analysis could be difficult to interpret in emergency surgery, thus an integration with other diagnostic tool, like ultrasound, is necessary [4,5].

Materials and methods

A retrospective observational study was conducted in the emergency surgery and trauma department of Cardarelli Hospital in Naples from September 2025 to December 2025.

All patients older than 18 years, who underwent to emergency laparotomy and hospitalized for at least 7 days, were included in the study. BIA, hand grip strenght and rectus femoris ultrasound were performed on admission (T0) and on the seventh postoperative day (T7). Primary outcome was the body composition variation, evaluated by BIA and rectus femoris ultrasound, from T0 to T7. Secondary outcome were the incidence of sarcopenia in the postoperative period and the comparison between BIA and ultrasound derived parameters. The Wilcoxon signed rank, wilcoxon rank sum and Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) tests were used for the statistical analysis. P < 0,05 was considered statistically significant. Informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Results

16 patients who undergone emergency laparotomy were included. Of these, 69% were women. The median age was 64 years (IQR 53–74), with a median BMI of 26.15 (IQR 23.67–27.95). SARC-F values were found to be less than 2. The indications for surgery were: Perforation(50%), intestinal occlusion (38%), Ischemic/hemorrhage (12%). Comorbidities are reported in Figure 1. BIA showed a statistically significant reduction of the Total Body Water (TBW), of the Body Cell Mass (BCM) and of the Lean Body Mass (LBM) between T0 and T7 (p = 0,039; p = 0,021; p = 0,023), while no statistically significant change was observed in phase angle, Appendicular Muscle Mass (ASMM), Skeletal Muskle Index (SMI) and in handgrip. Muscle ultrasound showed a statistically significant reduction of the quadriceps layer thickness, of the pennation angle and of Quantitative Value (QV) from T0 to T7 (p = 0,030; p = 0,006; p = 0,021), while no statistically significant change was observed for rectus femoris cross-sectional area (Table 1). Only 2 patients out of 16 (12,5%) had a confirmed sarcopenia on day 7, while 3 patients (18,75%) had a probable sarcopenia. A reduction of ASMM occurred in 4 patients (25%), while a low handgrip occurred in 5 patients (31,25%,). In lower ASMM group, a trend of reduction of ultrasound values was observed. The reliability of ultrasound measurements was assessed through the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC), showing good/excellent reliability for Rectus femoris Area and Quadriceps Thickness, while the Pennation angle presented moderate reliability (Figure 2).

Conclusions

Our results show an early functional alteration of muscle mass that may be still reversible. The diagnosis of sarcopenia is multidimensional: BIA and Ultrasound have a complementary role and their combined use may enhance diagnostic accuracy and risk stratification, particularly in clinically complex and nutritionally vulnerable patients.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A150 Impact of using a hemodynamic monitoring system on anesthetic consumption during abdominal surgery: a randomised controlled trial

T. Torce, A. Russo, T. Iacobucci, F. Scialanga, G. Romano, S.S. Melcore, A. Ingrosso, P. Aceto

Agostino Gemelli University Polyclinic Foundation IRCCS, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: T. Torce

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A150

Background

Volatile anesthetics are known to induce dose-dependent myocardial depression and systemic vasodilation, frequently leading to intraoperative hypotension. Given the correlation between hypotensive events and adverse postoperative outcomes, advanced hemodynamic monitoring may offer a dual benefit: improving blood pressure stability and facilitating more precise anesthetic titration.

Objectives

To evaluate whether continuous noninvasive hemodynamic monitoring reduces sevoflurane consumption and mitigates intraoperative hypotension compared to standard intermittent monitoring in patients undergoing laparoscopic colorectal surgery.

Design and methods

Following the acquisition of written informed consent, 84 patients at a tertiary-care center were randomized 1:1 into two groups. In the control group (n=42), blood pressure was measured using standard intermittent oscillometry at 5-minute intervals. In the intervention group (n=42), continuous noninvasive blood pressure was monitored via the Acumen IQ-Cuff sensor on the HemoSphere platform (Edwards Lifesciences, Irvine, CA, USA). Bispectral Index (BIS) monitoring was utilized in all patients to standardize anesthetic depth.

Results

Total sevoflurane consumption was significantly lower in the intervention group compared to the control group (43.0 [32.2–52.0] mL vs. 55.0 [45.2–63.7] mL; p = 0.0002). Furthermore, patients managed with continuous monitoring experienced a significantly lower burden of hypotension, with a reduced Time-Weighted Average (TWA) of MAP <65 mmHg (0.10 vs. 0.29 mmHg; p = 0.01). Continuous monitoring was also associated with a shorter cumulative duration of hypotension (p = 0.017) and a lower percentage of intraoperative time spent in a hypotensive state (p = 0.016). Multivariable analysis, adjusting for mean BIS and total sevoflurane dose, confirmed that group allocation remained an independent predictor of lower TWA-MAP (p = 0.0025).

Conclusions

The integration of continuous noninvasive hemodynamic monitoring within a goal-directed protocol significantly reduces both volatile anesthetic consumption and the burden of intraoperative hypotension. The persistence of these benefits after adjusting for anesthetic depth suggests that continuous feedback enables superior hemodynamic stability beyond simple anesthetic titration. These findings support the role of advanced monitoring in enhancing patient safety and promoting green anesthesia practices.

Clinicaltrials.gov identifier: NCT06439732

Keywords: hypotension; halogenate; hemodynamic monitoring; green anaesthesia; patient safety.

A151 Contraflurantm anaesthetic gas capture system in clinical practice: analysis of desflurane consumption and estimation of avoided environmental impact in an anaesthesia department

M. Covotta1, M. Di Folco1, V. Ceccarelli2, G. Gazzè1, S. Orlando1, J. Salvato1, D. Sammartini1, E. Scalia2

1Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Therapy, IRCSS Regina Elena National Cancer Institute, Rome, Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Therapy, Policlinico Umberto I, Sapienza, Univerity of Rome, Italy

Correspondence: M. Di Folco

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A151

Keywords

CONTRAfluranTM, volatile anaesthetics, environmental sustainability, anaesthetic gas capture, green anaesthesia

Introduction

The environmental impact of halogenated anaesthetic agents is an increasing issue within the anaesthesiology community1–4. Sevoflurane and desflurane have a 100-year global warming potential (GWP100) approximately 130 and 2,540 times greater than CO2, respectively, contributing substantially to the carbon footprint of operating theatres4,5.

The CONTRAfluranTM system (Figure 1), an activated charcoal adsorption technology originally developed in the 1990 s, has recently regained attention owing to its effectiveness in capturing exhaled volatile anaesthetic vapours and the possibility of recycling recovered agents6–8.

The aim of this single-centre, retrospective observational study was to quantify desflurane consumption and estimate the amount of CO2 equivalent emissions (CO2eq) potentially avoided through the use of the CONTRAfluranTM gas capture system.

Materials and Methods

Consumption data automatically recorded by the mechanical ventilator were collected over the period from 17th of March to 4th of May 2025 (49 days), during 110 general anaesthesia procedures performed with desflurane (total anaesthesia time: 11,335 min; mean duration: 103 min/case).

The ventilator recorded both the total amount of anaesthetic agent delivered and the uptake (fraction absorbed by the patient). The difference between these two values was assumed to represent the amount of exhaled vapour potentially capturable by the CONTRAfluranTM system.

Conversion to mass was performed using the conventional vapour density of desflurane (0.143 g/mL). CO2 equivalent emissions were calculated by multiplying the estimated mass by the GWP100 of desflurane (2,540; IPCC AR6)9.

Results

During the observation period, 110 inhalation-based anaesthesia procedures were performed, corresponding to a cumulative anaesthesia time of 11,327 minutes. Total Desflurane consumption was 7,547.5 mL, with a measured uptake of 2,174.3 mL (28.8% of the delivered dose). Estimated exhaled vapour amounted to 5,373.2 mL, corresponding to approximately 768 g of gaseous desflurane (Figure 2).

When extrapolated to an annual workload (approximately 270 working days), the estimated amount of exhaled desflurane would reach approximately 4,230 g/year, equivalent to nearly 10,744 kg CO2eq/year for a single operating theatre.

Over the study period, use of the CONTRAfluranTM system would have potentially prevented the emission of approximately 1,952 kg CO2eq, equivalent to the average emissions generated by a passenger vehicle travelling approximately 11,500 km (EEA reference value: 170 g CO2/km, European fleet average).

An additional relevant finding was that the entire study period was managed using a single CONTRAfluranTM canister, which remains in use.

Conclusions

The collected data demonstrate that a substantial proportion of delivered Desflurane (approximately 71%) is exhaled unmetabolised by the patient, representing a potentially preventable source of greenhouse gas emissions.

The CONTRAfluranTM system appears to be a sustainable and cost-effective strategy for reducing the environmental impact of inhalational anaesthesia. In a context where the healthcare sector contributes approximately 4–5% of global greenhouse gas emissions (GGE), capture of exhaled anaesthetic vapours represents a high-impact intervention with relatively low operational complexity10.

The documented capture capacity, together with the prolonged lifespan of a single canister, supports the routine implementation of this technology in operating theatres. Multicentre studies including direct measurement of captured mass are warranted to validate the real-world capture efficiency of the device.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A152 Continuous deep serratus anterior plane block as a respiratory support adjunct in severe blunt chest trauma

E. Bertoli, L. Ottombrini, M. Cascielli, M. Vissani, F. Quaranta, G. Brunelli, S. Paciotti, G. Nicoletta

Complex Unit of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Foligno Hospital, Perugia, Italy

Correspondence: E. Bertoli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A152

Background

Blunt chest trauma is a major cause of respiratory morbidity in polytrauma patients, particularly in the presence of multiple rib fractures. Pain-induced thoracic splinting may severely impair inspiratory effort, respiratory drive, cough effectiveness, and secretion clearance, ultimately leading to hypoventilation, atelectasis, worsening gas exchange, pneumonia, and respiratory failure [1].

Thoracic epidural analgesia has traditionally represented the gold standard for chest wall analgesia. However, neuraxial techniques are not always feasible in critically ill trauma patients because of positioning difficulties, anticoagulation, hemodynamic instability, or associated injuries. Ultrasound-guided fascial plane blocks, such as the serratus anterior plane block (SAPB), have recently emerged as effective and minimally invasive alternatives capable of improving both pain control and respiratory function [2].

Adequate analgesia may represent a key determinant of successful respiratory support de-escalation in severe chest trauma.

Case report

A 48-year-old male was admitted to the Emergency Department following a high-impact road traffic accident. Initial total-body CT scan demonstrated severe blunt chest trauma characterized by bilateral pneumothorax with significant loss of pulmonary volume, pneumomediastinum, extensive subcutaneous emphysema extending to the cervical region, multiple displaced fractures of the left hemithorax involving ribs I–VI, and associated fractures of the left clavicle and scapula (Fig 1.1- 1.2).

After initial stabilization with oxygen therapy, the patient was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), where bilateral chest drains were positioned under sedation because of massive bilateral pneumothorax.

During the first days of ICU stay, the patient required multimodal respiratory support with high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) and intermittent non-invasive ventilation (NIV) because of progressive respiratory impairment.

Despite systemic multimodal analgesia with intravenous paracetamol and opioids, severe thoracic pain progressively resulted in thoracic splinting, ineffective cough, impaired secretion clearance, and reduced respiratory drive. Persistent pain significantly limited thoracic expansion, coughing attempts, and mobilization.

On ICU Day 3, worsening respiratory mechanics and persistent impairment in oxygenation were documented, with PaO2/FiO2 values ranging between 195 and 220. Pain intensity was rated as Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) 8, particularly during coughing attempts and physiotherapy sessions.

Considering the progressive pain-driven respiratory failure, an ultrasound-guided continuous deep serratus anterior plane block (Deep SAPB) was performed at the level of the fifth intercostal space, with insertion of a perineural catheter approximately 2 cm beyond the needle tip (Figure 1.3).

A 30 mL bolus of ropivacaine 0.2% (60 mg) was administered, followed by intermittent boluses of ropivacaine 0.2%, 20 mL every 6 hours through the catheter.

Initial analgesic efficacy was partially reduced because of secondary catheter displacement, resulting again in inadequate analgesia and worsening respiratory limitation. Catheter repositioning was therefore performed.

Following optimization of catheter positioning, significant pain reduction was achieved (NRS 8 to 2), associated with restoration of respiratory drive, improved thoracic expansion, enhanced cough effectiveness and improved secretion clearance. Optimization of regional analgesia also contributed to opioid sparing and improved patient mobilization.

A progressive improvement in respiratory mechanics and gas exchange subsequently occurred, with PaO2/FiO2 values increasing above 300, allowing gradual de-escalation from HFNC/NIV to low-flow oxygen therapy.

No procedure-related complications were observed.

Conclusion

In severe blunt chest trauma, pain itself may become a reversible cause of respiratory failure.

Continuous Deep SAPB may represent a valuable minimally invasive strategy capable of improving not only analgesia but also respiratory drive, cough effectiveness, secretion clearance, respiratory mechanics, and gas exchange, altering respiratory trajectory and reducing the need for invasive ventilatory support.

Regional anesthesia should therefore be considered not only as an analgesic strategy, but also as a respiratory support adjunct in critically ill chest trauma patients.

Early optimization of regional analgesia may significantly influence respiratory trajectory in severe chest trauma patients. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A153 The R.E.S.P.I.R.O. project: emission reduction and sustainability through target-controlled infusion (TCI) pumps and operational reorganization

S. Santarelli1, A. Bassani1, J. Scardua1, E. Trapè1, G. Baldi2, C. Baraldi1, G. Casalis3, D. Candido3, A. Riccheo1

1Local Health Authority of Bologna (AUSL Bologna), Maggiore Hospital – Complex Unit of Operating Theatre Management and Southern Anesthesia, Bologna, Italy; 2Local Health Authority of Bologna (AUSL Bologna), Maggiore Hospital – Operative Block Platform Unit (UA), Bologna, Italy; 3Postgraduate School in Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Alma Mater Studiorum – University of Bologna, Italy

Correspondence: J. Scardua

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A153

Background

International policies and guidelines, including the Paris Agreement [1] and the European Green Deal [2], have mandated a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. Public awareness on this issue is now widespread and has led international and national anesthesia societies to issue consensus documents emphasizing the high global warming potential (GWP) of desflurane (GWP100 = 2540) and the ozone-depleting impact of nitrous oxide, as well as advocating for their restriction to highly specific and clinically indicated scenarios. Current recommendations strongly support a transition toward total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) or loco-regional anesthesia, where clinically appropriate.

In response, the UOC Governo Blocchi Operatori at Ospedale Maggiore, AUSL Bologna, developed the R.E.S.P.I.R.O. project (Reduction of Emissions and Sustainability through TCI pumps and Operational Reorganization) to implement ‘Green Anesthesia’ protocols.

Materials and methods

In early 2025, a multidisciplinary ‘Green Team’ was established, comprising the Director of Anesthesia, the Operating Block Nursing Coordinator, the Head of Pharmacy, and a dedicated Green Anesthesia lead. After an initial audit, which reviewed consumption patterns and identified organizational and technological barriers, a set of targeted interventions were deployed, namely: systematic reduction of volatile agents, decommissioning of desflurane vaporizers from all ORs, procurement of TCI pumps, standardization of TIVA protocols, and expansion of loco-regional anesthesia techniques. Besides the measures above, personnel training programs and the implementation of anesthetic gas scavenging and recycling systems are also in the pipeline.

Two clinical flowcharts have been developed to guide eco-sustainable decision-making in general and loco-regional anesthesia (Figs. 1 and 2).

Performance was monitored using three key performance indicators (KPIs):

< 5% desflurane use in total general anesthesia (GA) cases;

< 5% desflurane use in total general anesthesia (GA) cases;

> 60% reduction in sevoflurane use on total GA;

> 60% reduction in sevoflurane use on total GA;

> 40% rate of loco-regional anesthesia in orthopedic and vascular surgery.

> 40% rate of loco-regional anesthesia in orthopedic and vascular surgery.

Results

Preliminary data from late 2025 indicated a decrease in sevoflurane use for GA and a concomitant increase in loco-regional anesthesia. While the established sevoflurane reduction targets have not been reached yet - primarily due to limited TCI pump availability - the target for desflurane elimination was fully met by the first quarter of 2026.

Conclusions

Adopting eco-sustainable anesthesia strategies significantly mitigates the environmental footprint of operating theaters as well as improving clinical safety and efficiency. This project serves as a replicable model for integrating environmental sustainability with high-quality perioperative care. Continuous staff education and sensitization remain essential for the long-term success of such initiatives.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A154 Wearable-derived HRV before spinal anesthesia: a pilot investigation

C. Chiumiento1, G.M. Cancello1, C. Grandis1, A. Calabrese1, A. Fruncillo1, L. Baccari1, P. Russo1, G. Micieli1, M. Busana2, F. Chiumiento1

1Anesthesia and Intensive Care Unit, Maria SS. Addolorata Hospital, Eboli, Italy; 2Department of Anesthesiology, University Medical Center of Göttingen, Göttingen, Germany

Correspondence: C. Chiumiento

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A154

Body

Rationale

Spinal anesthesia acutely modifies autonomic cardiovascular control, but the clinical response varies among patients. Heart rate variability (HRV), derived from beat-to-beat heart rate fluctuations, may provide a non-invasive description of the preoperative autonomic profile. In short recordings, time-domain indices (SDNN, RMSSD) and Poincaré plot-derived indices (SD1, SD2) describe RR-interval variability, while frequency-domain indices (LF, HF, LF/HF) describe cardiovascular oscillations influenced by respiration, vascular tone, and baroreflex regulation. LF/HF was therefore considered a context-dependent descriptor of autonomic state, not a direct measure of sympathetic-vagal balance. We explored whether pre-spinal wearable-derived HRV could describe autonomic profiles associated with different clinical responses to spinal anesthesia.

Materials and methods

Patients undergoing surgery below the umbilicus under spinal anesthesia were monitored with a Polar H10 chest strap, used as a pragmatic RR-interval recording tool in the preoperative setting. Three-minute supine recordings were obtained immediately before spinal anesthesia. HRV analysis included time-domain indices (SDNN, RMSSD), Poincaré plot-derived indices (SD1, SD2), frequency-domain indices (LF, HF, LF/HF), and stress index. Hypotension was defined as a?20% decrease in mean arterial pressure after dural puncture. According to the post-spinal clinical course, patients were classified as normotensive, hypotensive, or drug-treated for symptomatic hypotension. In patients with an additional HRV recording at preoperative consultation, absolute agreement with immediate pre-spinal measurements was explored.

Results

Twenty patients were included in the group analysis: 9 were classified as normotensive, 7 as hypotensive, and 4 as drug-treated for symptomatic hypotension. Baseline characteristics, including age, weight, height, preoperative heart rate, preoperative mean arterial pressure, beta-blocker use, and local anesthetic dose indexed to height, did not differ significantly among groups (Table 1). Pre-spinal LF/HF differed among groups (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.005). LF/HF was lowest in hypotensive patients compared with normotensive and drug-treated patients: 1.26 [1.21–1.38] versus 2.98 [2.17–4.71] and 4.53 [3.62–5.73], respectively; adjusted p = 0.032 for both pairwise comparisons (Figure 1). Among patients with both consultation and immediate pre-spinal recordings (n = 16), absolute agreement varied across the HRV panel and was most consistent for heart rate (p = 0.754), RMSSD (p = 0.712), and SD1 (p = 0.706).

Conclusions

In this pilot investigation, pre-spinal wearable-derived HRV described different autonomic profiles across clinical responses to spinal anesthesia. The main signal was observed for LF/HF, with lower values in patients who developed hypotension and higher values in those requiring rescue treatment for symptomatic hypotension. Since baseline clinical and anesthetic variables did not significantly differ among groups, LF/HF may have captured information not evident from standard preoperative assessment. Given the small sample size, the drug-treated subgroup, and the pragmatic 3-minute recording protocol, these findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. However, they raise a clinically relevant possibility: post-spinal hypotension and symptomatic hypotension requiring treatment may not simply represent increasing severity of the same response, but potentially different pre-spinal autonomic profiles. The absolute agreement of heart rate, RMSSD, and SD1 between consultation and immediate pre-spinal recordings suggests that selected HRV components may be measurable before the day of surgery.

A155 Intravenous and intra-arterial milrinone for vasospasm management in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: a single-center retrospective case series

E. Ricci1, C.A. Castioni2, V. Ferrucci2, M. Moneti2, R. Aspide2

1Alma Mater Studiorum di Bologna, Italy; 2IRCCS Bellaria, Bologna, Italy

Correspondence: E. Ricci

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A155

Background

In subarachnoid hemorrhage from aneurysm rupture (aSAH), one of the most feared complications remains Delayed Cerebral Ischemia (DCI). Among the causes of DCI, vasospasm remains diagnosable. When vasospasm is diagnosed, associated with neuroworsening or focal neurological deficits, the primary treatment, in addition to mean arterial pressure (MAP) augmentation, is interventional neuroradiology. In addition to balloons, angioplasty, stents, and intra-arterial administration of nimodipine, a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor, Milrinone, an inodilator, has been used in the last decade.

In the following single-center retrospective case series, the authors describe the use of Milrinone administered intravenously and intra-arterially and the neurological outcome at discharge from the Intensive Care Unit (ICU).

Materials and methods

This study is a retrospective, single-center case series; patients were collected from September 2024 to April 2026 at the Intensive Care Unit of Bellaria IRCCS in Bologna.

The study has been conducted according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and it did not alter the Good Clinical Practice guidelines.

The variables recorded through the computerized file were: mean patient age, gender, Body Mass Index (BMI), Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) at onset, the World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) grading score, placement or absence of an external ventricular shunt, presence or absence of intraparenchymal hemorrhage, presence or absence of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), days of ICU stay, number of days during which intravenous Milrinone was administered, administration or absence of intra-arterial Milrinone, total intra-arterial administrations, and onset of new ischemic lesions.

Outcome variables were expressed using the modified Rankin Scale score (mRS) at ICU discharge.

The statistics are purely descriptive and used median and standard deviation for continuous variables and percentages for dichotomous variables.

Results

Eight patients were enrolled in this study, all with subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) [Table 1]. The mean age was 57 years, the standard deviation was 9.56, and 100% of patients were female; the mean BMI was 26.06.

The GCS at presentation was 10.4/15, the mean WFSN score was 3.4, with 5 out of 8 cases resulting in “poor grade” from onset; 62.5% of patients had no evidence of intraparenchymal hemorrhage, while 100% of patients had IVH.

All patients underwent external ventricular drain (EVD) placement, and the mean length of stay (LOS) was 22.9. The average number of days of continuous intravenous milrinone administration was 7.5. Intra-arterial bolus administration of milrinone was performed in the angiography room in 75% of cases, with an average number of intra-arterial administrations of 2.83.

New ischemic events were observed in 87.5% of the analyzed cases. One patient did not survive intensive care. The average mRS score at ICU discharge for all seven other patients was 3.14.

Conclusions

The use of intravenous/intra-arterial Milrinone for the treatment of vasospasm in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, although not included in current guidelines, appears to be a operable treatment in an environment with high levels of clinical and instrumental neuromonitoring.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A156 Perioperative management of prone thoracic spinal surgery during third-trimester pregnancy: a case report

A. Palmese1, M.M. Spanò1, F. Sbaraglia1, G. Cinquegrana1, D. Posa1, E. Console1, C. Cuomo1, L. Baiocchi1, M. Rossi1

Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli, Roma, Italy

Correspondence: A. Palmese

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A156

Background

Non-obstetric surgery during pregnancy is not common and should be delayed until delivery to reduce risk for child and mother. The mantain of adequate hemodynamic hemostasis and placental perfusion should be the goal during all perioperative care. In addition, the need of prone position during surgery could be furtherly challenging mostly in the third trimester, because compression on the gravid uterus can cause aortocaval compression resulting in reduced venous return, decreased cardiac output, and compromised uteroplacental perfusion, which may lead to maternal hypotension and fetal hypoxia [1].

Case presentation

We report the case of a 40-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 31 weeks of gestation, who presented a two-months history of progressive worsening of low arms sensibility and to difficulty maintaining an upright position. When a MRI demonstrated a thoracic expansile lesion, likely epidural origin, causing marked compression of the spinal cord, an urgent decompressive laminectomy was scheduled.

Preoperative assessment included a multidisciplinary evaluation involving anesthesiologists, neurosurgeons, obstetrician and hematologists.

In the days preceding the procedure the patient received corticosteroid prophylaxis to promote fetal lung maturation.

Upon arrival in the operating room, standard monitoring and invasive arterial blood pressure monitoring were established. General anesthesia was induced with propofol and sufentanil, and tracheal intubation was achieved without complications. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane and remifentanil in TCI, guaranteeing hemodynamic stability based on HemoSphere monitoring.

The patient was then placed on prone position on an Allen orthopedic table (Figure 1) and the fetal well-being was intermittently assessed at key perioperative time points, including before induction, after positioning, and at the end of surgery.

The patient underwent D6-D8 laminectomy with complete resection of the lesion. Intraoperative blood loss was moderate and did not require transfusion. No episodes of significant hypotension, hypoxia, or fetal compromise occurred during surgery.

At the end of the procedure, the patient was repositioned supine and emerged uneventfully from anesthesia. In the follow-up neurological symptoms progressively improved.

Conclusions

Our experience highlighted the challenges of such uncommon procedure. Non obstetric surgery during pregnancy requires specifical attention in the perioperative management.

The primary aim was to balance urgent maternal neurosurgical treatment with fetal well-being, as progressive neurological deficits and the risk of irreversible spinal cord injury justified urgent decompression. Anesthetic management focused on maintaining uteroplacental perfusion through hemodynamic and respiratory stability, anticipating pregnancy-related airway challenges, and ensuring safe prone positioning.

Hemodynamic stability was mandatory and maintained throughout the procedure, with arterial pressure kept close to baseline values and no need for vasopressor support, because uteroplacental blood flow is closely dependent on maternal hemodynamic and respiratory conditions. Ventilatory management was tailored to pregnancy-related physiological changes, and serial arterial blood gas analyses confirmed adequate respiratory parameters throughout the procedure because hypoxia leads to a reduction in uterine perfusion through an increase in vascular resistance, while hypercapnia contributes to the development of acidosis and further vasoconstriction of the uteroplacental circulation. Continuous advanced hemodynamic assessment through the HemoSphere platform allowed real-time evaluation of cardiac output, stroke volume variation, and dynamic preload parameters, guiding fluid therapy and vasoactive support throughout the procedure. This multimodal monitoring contributed to prompt optimization of tissue perfusion and cardiovascular stability during surgery.

However, in our case the prone position could have contributed to aortocaval compression, with all the related consequences; therefore, the patient was carefully placed prone on an Allen orthopedic table using dedicated thoracic and pelvic supports to allow the abdomen to remain freely suspended, thereby minimizing intra-abdominal pressure and reducing aortocaval compression while preserving venous return and uteroplacental perfusion. The radiolucent open-frame design of the Allen table also facilitated optimal positioning and pressure distribution, limiting venous congestion and respiratory impairment during surgery. The use of dedicated supports and meticulous positioning allowed adequate abdominal decompression and maintenance of maternal hemodynamic stability throughout the procedure.

Continuous fetal monitoring was desirable but impractical because of prone positioning and limited abdominal access. Therefore, intermittent fetal heart rate assessments were performed at key surgical stages when feasible.

Although intraoperative radiation was required, fetal exposure was minimized with lead shielding and considered low due to scatter radiation only [2].

This case highlights how individualized anesthetic management can safely support urgent non-obstetric surgery during advanced pregnancy.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A157 Unexpected neurological complications in the postoperative period: identifying serotonin syndrome

S. Paciotti, S. Maccherani, G. Nicoletta, M. Vissani, M. Cascelli, G. Brunelli, E. Bertoli, R. Pannacci, A. Tarquini

Anesthesia and Intensive Care Unit (SC), Foligno–Spoleto, Italy

Correspondence: S. Paciotti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A157

Body

Serotonin syndrome (SS) is a potentially life-threatening toxic reaction caused by excessive serotonergic receptor activation, most commonly resulting from drug interactions. In the perioperative setting, diagnosis may be particularly challenging because of clinical overlap with conditions such as Malignant Hyperthermia, status epilepticus, and postoperative delirium. Several anesthetic and perioperative agents, including synthetic opioids and ondansetron, may precipitate SS. Diagnosis is primarily based on the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria. We report a case of early-onset SS occurring shortly after extubation, highlighting perioperative triggers, differential diagnosis, and management strategies.

Case Report

A 63-year-old man (60 kg) with a medical history of hypertension, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, and anxiety-depressive disorder, chronically treated with Venlafaxine, Levosulpiride, Alprazolam, and Triazolam, underwent robot-assisted nephrectomy, cholecystectomy, and inguinal hernioplasty. SNRI therapy was continued throughout the perioperative period.

General anesthesia was induced with propofol 120 mg, Fentanyl 100 mcg, and rocuronium 40 mg. Intraoperative analgesia included paracetamol 1 g, ketorolac 30 mg, fentanyl 100mcg and intravenous morphine 5 mg. Ondansetron 4 mg and desametasone 4 mg was administered for postoperative nausea and vomiting prophylaxis. The intraoperative course was uneventful. At the end of the procedure, following pharmacological reversal of neuromuscular blockade and evidence of a TOF ratio > 0.9 and a BIS value of 90, the patient was extubated. Spontaneous ventilation was restored, with recovery of airway protective reflexes and responsiveness to painful stimuli. Due to incomplete recovery of consciousness, 0.2 mg of flumazenil was administered. The patient was subsequently transferred to the recovery room.

Approximately five minutes after extubation, the patient developed rapid neurological deterioration characterized by reduced responsiveness, muscle rigidity, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Vital signs revealed hyperthermia (38.4°C) and tachycardia, while blood pressure remained stable (120/70 mmHg). Following transient improvement after intravenous midazolam 3 mg, the patient required re-intubation and transfer to the intensive care unit (ICU).

Laboratory investigations on ICU admission demonstrated mixed acidosis and hyperlactatemia. Brain imaging findings were unremarkable. Persistent seizures and epileptiform activity on electroencephalography required optimization of antiepileptic therapy. Differential diagnosis included Malignant Hyperthermia, which was considered unlikely because of the absence of intraoperative signs, and infectious encephalitis, excluded by negative cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Considering the patient’s chronic SNRI therapy and perioperative exposure to Fentanyl and Ondansetron, a diagnosis of Serotonin syndrome was established according to the Hunter Criteria (Fig. 1).

Treatment with Cyproheptadine was initiated with a loading dose of 12 mg, followed by 2 mg every 2 hours (total dose: 16 mg). Sedation was optimized with Dexmedetomidine. Clinical improvement was rapid, with resolution of hyperthermia, cessation of seizures, and progressive normalization of neurological status. The patient was extubated after 48 hours and discharged on postoperative day 15.

Conclusion

Serotonin syndrome should be considered in cases of postoperative neurological deterioration, particularly in patients receiving chronic serotonergic therapy. Interactions between home medications and perioperative agents, especially synthetic opioids and ondansetron, may play a critical role in triggering the syndrome. Early recognition based on the Hunter Criteria and prompt initiation of targeted treatment are essential to ensure favorable clinical outcomes.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A158 Vasospastic hemispheric ischemia in schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia. A case report

A. Mantovani, G. Crescini, A.M. Giannini

Children’s Hospital – ASST Spedali Civili, Brescia, Italy

Correspondence: A. Mantovani

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A158

Background

Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia (SIOD) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the SMARCAL1 gene. It is characterized by multisystem involvement, including immunodeficiency, nephrotic syndrome, and progressive arteriopathy, with a high risk of cerebral ischemia and stroke. Prognosis is variable, with early mortality often related to vascular and infectious complications. Only about 100 cases has been reported since 1971.

We describe here the case of a seven year old child who had cerebral ischemia, and subsequent multiple episodes of headache, likely due to vasospasm associated to minors ystemic infections, who was studied with Transcranial Doppler (TCD) and treated with nimodipine.

Case Report

The proband was a seven year old male, second child of healthy consanguineous parents. He was then diagnosed with SIOD by genetic test.

Patient had normal intellectual development. He was admitted to hospital after he had a sudden onset of right temporo-parietal headache, followed by vomit, loss of consciousness and gaze deviation to the left side. An initial brain CT scan performed upon arrival was unremarkable. The patient neurological status was alternating from wakefulness to unresponsiveness with gaze deviation to the left, without frank clonic movements. CSF was clear with 1 cell, protein 108 mg/ml, glucose 77 mg/dl. PCR for virus and bacteria on CSF resulted negative. Molecular biology analysis of nasopharyngeal aspirate resulted positive for metapneumovirus and mildly positive for adenovirus. Urine and blood cultures were negative. MRI of the brain performed at 24 hours from the acute event showed an excitotoxic lesion in the fronto-temporo-parietal cortex, interpreted in first hypothesis as a consequence of seizures. Phenobarbital therapy was started to prevent further epileptic activity and an EEG showed diffuse slow waves in the right hemisphere. The patient was neurologically stuporous, he reported right headache with severe systemic hypertension (200/100 mmHg). Blood infection markers (CRP and PCT) were negative. After a negative echocardiography an anti-hypertensive therapy was started with amlodipine and transdermic clonidine with poor response, so therapy was potentiated with captopril and nimodipine in the suspect of a vasospastic mechanism for the headache (as suggested by the results of TCD performed at the bedside, Fig. 1), with a good response of blood pressure and reduction of head pain (and TCD velocities).

Eight days after the onset of the symptoms the patient was still drowsy, with a reduced strength in the left arm, so MRA was repeated which showed edema and ischemic lesions of the right hemisphere without macrovascular occlusions (Fig. 2).

Anti aggregating therapy with ASA was instituted. Subsequently the patient neurologic conditions improved with only some impairment in the left arm, blood pressure was under control, headache almost disappeared and seventeen days after the acute event the patient was discharged from PICU. A body angio-CT scan was performed which ruled out anomalies of great vessels.

Conclusion

Our seven year old child was admitted for an alteration of neurological status probably due to a seizure, which is not a direct complication of SIOD, on the other side SIOD is associated with stroke and cerebral vasospasm which in turn can cause seizures [1]. We ruled out brain structural anomalies, tumors and infections. The MRA showed ischemic lesions of the right hemisphere without macrovascular occlusions and since it has been proposed that the mechanism for neurological complications in SIOD could be Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) [2], we started treatment with nimodipine, even without clear evidence of efficacy, and decided to monitor the evolution of vasospasm with TCD, which to our knowledge was not used before in studying vasospasm in SIOD.

In the following years the patient was readmitted multiple times for headaches associated with minor infections. Knowing his tendency to vasospasm with the potential for cerebral ischemia, the patient was always studied with TCD and when an increase in MCA peak velocities was demonstrated (Table 1), therapy with nimodipine was promptly instituted. The dose of nimodipine used was 1 mg/kg dose every 4 hours [3].

Follow up was clinical and TCD was used to guide nimodipne tapering down and suspension.

Informed consent was obtained from the patient’s parents for the publication of this case report and the accompanying images.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A159 Reverse Takotsubo in aneurysmal hemorrhage: successful cardiac recovery, unfavorable neurological outcome

V. Lomonaco, D. Gaetano, E. Coppa, G. Caputo, M. Del Prete, A. Castaldi, F. Rocereto, V. Colucci, A. Merola, P. De Negri

Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, A.O.R.N Sant’Anna e San Sebastiano, Caserta, Italy

Correspondence: V. Lomonaco

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A159

Background

Subarachnoid hemorrhage can trigger neurogenic myocardial dysfunction, including stress-induced cardiomyopathy. The clinical course may be characterized by a dissociation between cardiac and neurological outcomes. We describe a case of reverse Takotsubo syndrome complicating aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Case report

A 43-year-old patient was admitted to the emergency department in a coma (Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3) after subarachnoid hemorrhage, likely due to aneurysm rupture. Toxicology screening was positive for cocaine. At admission, the patient required mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support (norepinephrine 0.3 mcg/kg/min), with a lactate level of 3 mmol/L.

Early cardiologic evaluation showed severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction 25%) with a non-coronary pattern of basal and mid-ventricular akinesia and apical hyperkinesia, consistent with reverse Takotsubo syndrome. High-sensitivity troponin levels were markedly elevated (up to 5358 pg/mL). In the intensive care unit, levosimendan infusion was initiated on day 1 (0.1 mcg/kg/min for 24 hours), alongside vasopressor support. Vasopressin (1.8 IU/h) was added.

Endovascular embolization of the aneurysm was successfully performed on day 2. Despite initial hemodynamic stabilization and lactate clearance (0.8 mmol/L at 24 hours), neurological status progressively worsened. Serial neuroimaging demonstrated persistent subarachnoid hemorrhage with progressive diffuse cerebral edema and loss of cortico-subcortical differentiation, evolving to transtentorial herniation. Clinical examination showed fixed bilateral mydriasis.

Cardiac function improved over time, with recovery of left ventricular ejection fraction to 57% and absence of coronary artery disease on subsequent angiography. However, despite cardiovascular recovery, the patient developed irreversible neurological injury and progressed to brain death after 9 days of hospitalization.

Conclusion

This case highlights a marked dissociation between successful cardiac recovery and unfavorable neurological outcome in neurogenic stress cardiomyopathy following aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage. Despite timely neurocritical and interventional management, including aneurysm embolization and intensive supportive care, the patient developed progressive and irreversible brain injury. In parallel, targeted cardiovascular therapy with levosimendan and vasopressors led to rapid hemodynamic stabilization and full recovery of cardiac function. These findings emphasize that, even when both neurocritical and cardiocirculatory strategies are appropriately applied, cardiac improvement does not necessarily translate into neurological recovery. This underscores the complex and potentially uncoupled evolution of brain and heart injury, reinforcing the need for integrated neuro-cardiac assessment in critically ill patients.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A160 Incidence and prognostic significance of rhythmic and periodic EEG patterns in a cohort of patients with acute brain injury

E. Micalizzi1, F. Tarantino3, C. Robba3, A. Ferrari1, A. Berardino3, C. Giordano2, M. Biringhelli2, F. Della Torre Piccinelli2, G. Carboni2, A. Pittaluga2, M. Simionato2, L.T. Barberis2

1IRCCS San Martino, Neurophysiology Unit, Genoa, Italy; 2University of Genoa, Italy; 3IRCCS San Martino, Neurointensive Care Unit, Genoa, Italy

Correspondence: C. Giordano

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A160

Body

Purpose: Rhythmic and periodic EEG patterns (RPPs) lying in the ictal–interictal continuum (IIC) are frequently observed in patients with acute brain injury of different etiologies. Their short- and long-term prognostic significance remains uncertain. The aim of this study was to evaluate the incidence of RPPs and their association with clinical variables.

Methods

We retrospectively collected clinical and EEG data from patients older than 18 years who were admitted to the Neurointensive Care Unit (NICU) at our hospital between January and July 2023. Patients with primary or secondary acute brain injury of various etiologies (vascular, traumatic, infectious, metabolic, autoimmune) who underwent at least one EEG during their ICU stay were included. Patients with a previous diagnosis of epilepsy were excluded.

Results: A total of 71 patients were included and subdivided into two groups: 14 patients with RPPs and 57 without RPPs (noRPP). The two groups differed significantly in age [median 66.5 years (58.5–70.5) vs 61 years (53–74), p = 0.03], but not in sex distribution (Pearson’s chi-square test, p = 0.27). The most frequently reported RPPs were generalized periodic discharges (GPDs; 35.7%), lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs; 21.4%), and generalized rhythmic delta activity (GRDA; 14.3%). Regarding etiology, RPPs were most frequently observed in patients with traumatic brain injury (4/14, 28.6%) and ischemic stroke (4/14, 28.6%). No significant differences were found between the two groups in terms of length of hospitalization, seizure recurrence, mRS (modified Rankin Scale) at last follow up or ICU mortality.

Conclusion

EEG monitoring in neurocritical care patients is crucial not only for seizure detection but also for identifying RPPs, which may play a role in the assessment of short- and long-term neurological prognosis.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A161 Multimodal non-invasive approach for predicting risk of intracranial hypertension in the intensive care unit: an observational study

R. Frontera, R.V. Liouras, L. Agostinone, R. Zocaro, A. Frattari

Santo Spirito Civil Hospital, Pescara, Italy

Correspondence: R. Frontera

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A161

Background

Intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring represents a crucial component in the management of neurocritical care patients affected by traumatic brain injury, stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, subarachnoid hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, post-anoxic brain injury, and other acute neurological conditions. Elevated ICP is associated with reduced cerebral perfusion pressure, secondary ischemic injury and increased mortality. Invasive monitoring techniques such as external ventricular drainage (EVD) and intraparenchymal probes represent the gold standard for ICP measurement, but their use is not always feasible or indicated because of procedural risks, contraindications, or logistical limitations. In this context, non-invasive techniques are emerging as useful complementary tools for indirect assessment of intracranial hypertension. These methods do not provide an absolute ICP value but reflect physiological and hemodynamic correlates of intracranial hypertension. The integration of multiple non-invasive modalities may further improve diagnostic performance and clinical interpretation in neurocritical patients. The aim of this study was to evaluate the correlation between different non-invasive ICP monitoring techniques and to assess their ability to predict intracranial hypertension in critically ill patients admitted to a neuro-intensive care unit.

Methods

This prospective observational ICU study (Jan–Dec 2025) was conducted in the Intensive Care Unit of Santo Spirito Civil Hospital in Pescara, Italy. Twenty-five adult patients with suspected ICP alterations were serially monitored using quantitative pupillometry (NPi), TCD, and ONSD ultrasound. Non-invasive parameters were correlated with clinical data (Glasgow Coma Scale, GCS), physiological variables (pCO2, body temperature), neuroradiological imaging findings (brain CT scan), and, when available, invasive ICP measurements. Statistical analysis included correlation, multivariate regression, and ROC analysis for ICP >20 mmHg.

A total of 225 patients were screened; 25 were included in the final analysis after exclusions (incomplete clinical data, severe ocular disease preventing pupillometric or ultrasonographic assessment, technical impossibility to perform TCD, and expected survival <24–48 hours). All patients underwent serial multimodal monitoring including pupillometry (Neuroptics NPi-200), TCD (middle cerebral artery evaluation), and ONSD ultrasound (3 mm posterior to the globe). Measurements were performed at predefined intervals during ICU stay. Clinical variables included GCS, temperature, arterial pCO2, SOFA and SAPS II scores, and brain CT findings. When available, invasive ICP measurements were used as reference. Statistical analysis included correlation analysis, multivariate regression models, and ROC curve analysis for prediction of ICP >20 mmHg.

Informed consent was obtained from patients or legal representatives.

Results

The study population had a mean age of 59.4 ± 19.3 years. Among the 25 enrolled subjects, 19 patients survived ICU hospitalization (76%), while 5 patients died during ICU stay (24%). Episodes of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP >20 mmHg), identified through non-invasive monitoring and/or radiological-clinical correlation, were observed in approximately 21.5% of the total monitoring assessments performed during the study period. Overall correlations between non-invasive parameters and ICP were modest but statistically significant, reflecting the complexity of neurocritical physiology. No single parameter demonstrated strong standalone predictive value. ROC curve analysis showed limited discriminative ability of individual non-invasive variables (Figure 1). Mean flow velocity (MFV) demonstrated the highest AUC (0.57), followed by ONSD (0.54), while NPi and pulsatility index (PI) showed lower predictive performance (0.46 and 0.41 respectively). In contrast, arterial pCO2 demonstrated the highest overall predictive accuracy for ICP elevation (AUC 0.753), highlighting the strong physiological influence of carbon dioxide on cerebral hemodynamics.

GCS showed good predictive ability for CT-confirmed intracranial hypertension (AUC 0.782), followed by ONSD (AUC 0.622). The multimodal approach combining TCD, pupillometry, ONSD, and physiological variables demonstrated improved clinical interpretability compared with isolated parameters. Multivariate regression analysis confirmed that no single non-invasive parameter independently predicted neurological outcome or ICP elevation, whereas combined physiological assessment provided stronger predictive trends.

Conclusion

In this prospective cohort of critically ill neurocritical patients, single non-invasive parameters showed limited ability to independently predict intracranial hypertension. However, the integration of multiple non-invasive modalities, combined with clinical and physiological variables, improved overall diagnostic interpretation.

Non-invasive ICP monitoring techniques such as TCD, ONSD ultrasound, and automated pupillometry should not be considered replacements for invasive monitoring in severe cases, but rather complementary tools for screening, trend analysis, and bedside decision making. Future research should focus on larger multicenter cohorts and the development of multimodal predictive models potentially enhanced by artificial intelligence to improve early detection of intracranial hypertension in neurocritical care settings.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A162 Association between ventilatory mode and eeg- derived sedation levels in critically ill patients: a qCON/qNOX-based analysis

E. Verrigni, A. Stagnoli, L. Pertegato, F. Cinquegrana, M. Riccardo, C.A. Volta, S. Spadaro, G. Scaramuzzo

Department of Translational Medicine, University of Ferrara, Italy

Correspondence: E. Verrigni

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A162

Background

Monitoring sedation depth in critically ill mechanically ventilated patients remains a major challenge in intensive care practice, particularly during assisted ventilation modes. Clinical sedation scales may be difficult to apply in deeply sedated or ventilated patients, while electroencephalogram (EEG)-derived indices such as qCON may provide a more objective assessment of hypnotic state [1]. qCON is an EEG-derived index ranging from 0 to 99, with values between 40 and 60 generally considered indicative of adequate sedation or anesthesia, whereas lower values may reflect excessive hypnotic depth [2]. The relationship between ventilatory mode and qCON/qNOX values, however, has not yet been fully clarified.

Methods

As of April 7, 2026, 200 intensive care unit patients admitted within the previous 24 hours for respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation were screened for inclusion. All patients were receiving continuous analgosedation and were aged between 18 and 90 years. qCON values were analyzed according to ventilatory mode, comparing Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV) and Controlled Ventilation (CV) including both volume controlled and pressure controlled modes. Data were expressed as mean, median, and interquartile range (IQR) and count (percentage) according to data distribution and entity. Statistical analysis was performed using the Chi-square test. Two different qCON cut-off values were evaluated: 60 and 40. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

Results

A total of 127 patients were excluded according to predefined exclusion criteria. The final study population consisted of 73 patients, including 23 women (31.5%) and 50 men (68.5%). The analysis included 219 PSV and 84 CV recordings. Among PSV measures, 135 (61.6%) presented qCON values >60, while 84 (38.4%) showed qCON values <60. In the CV group, 37 recordings (44%) had qCON values >60 and 47 (56%) had qCON values <60 (p = 0.02).

A second analysis was performed using a qCON cut-off value of 40. Among PSV measures, 206 out of 219 (94.1%) showed qCON values >40 and 13 (5.9%) showed qCON values <40. In the CV group, 75 out of 84 measures (89.3%) had qCON values >40 and 9 (10.7%) had qCON values <40. No statistically significant difference was observed between the two groups in this analysis (p = 0.315). No significant differences were found in the RASS values (3±1.2 vs 3.3±1.07, p=0.07) or in sedatives drugs dosages among groups.

Conclusions

Patients ventilated in Controlled mode (CV) showed a higher prevalence of qCON values <60 compared with patients ventilated in Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV), suggesting deeper hypnotic levels during controlled ventilation, despite similar RASS levels and drugs administered. Since lower qCON values may reflect excessive sedation and may be associated with an increased risk of EEG suppression patterns, these findings could indicate a greater predisposition to burst suppression in patients ventilated with CV. Ventilatory mode should be carefully considered when personalizing level of sedation monitoring in critically ill mechanically ventilated patients.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.
