A163 Usability and clinical acceptance of surgiguide: healthcare professionals’ evaluation of a rule-based perioperative digital assistant

V. Bellini1, L.J. Darhour1, M. Cavicchioli2, M. Perna2, E. Bignami1

1Anesthesiology, Critical Care and Pain Medicine Division, Department of Medicine and Surgery, University of Parma, Vial, Italy; 2Department of Medicine and Surgery, University of Parma, Viale Gramsci 14, 43126, Parma, Italy

Correspondence: L.J. Darhour

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A163

Background

Digital agents are increasingly integrated into perioperative care to improve patient education, engagement, and continuity of care. Their implementation depends not only on technological performance but also on acceptance by healthcare professionals, who remain central to clinical decision-making and patient communication [1]. SurgiGuide is a rule-based digital assistant developed to provide structured perioperative information for patients undergoing elective colorectal surgery. Based on predefined and clinically validated pathways, the system aims to ensure transparency, consistency, and control over delivered content while supporting patients throughout the surgical journey without replacing clinician–patient interaction [2]. This approach reflects the concept of extended perioperative medicine, in which digital technologies contribute to continuity of care beyond hospital settings [3]. This study evaluated healthcare professionals’ perceptions of SurgiGuide, focusing on usability, reliability, accuracy, and patient-oriented comprehensibility.

Materials and methods

A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 10 healthcare professionals involved in perioperative care (3 surgeons and 7 anesthesiologists). After providing written informed consent, participants self-assessed digital competence on a 7-point Likert scale. Usability was evaluated through a 10-item questionnaire inspired by the System Usability Scale [4] using a 5-point Likert scale, assessing complexity, ease of use, integration, learnability, and user confidence. Participants also rated perceived reliability (1–6 scale), accuracy, and patient-oriented comprehensibility (1–3 scale).

Results

Participants reported a relatively high level of digital competence (mean 5.1/7). Overall usability of SurgiGuide was highly rated. Participants expressed willingness to use the system (mean 4.6/5) and perceived it as easy to use (mean 4.7/5), well integrated (mean 4.7/5), learnable (mean 4.6/5), and comfortable to use (mean 4.8/5). Negative usability indicators were consistently low: the system was not considered unnecessarily complex (mean 1.6/5), difficult to use (mean 1.2/5), or inconsistent (mean 1.2/5). The perceived need for external support (mean 1.4/5) and prior learning effort (mean 1.2/5) was minimal. Perceived reliability was high (mean 5.7/6), while accuracy achieved a mean score of 2.8/3. Patient-oriented comprehensibility achieved the maximum score (3.0/3), indicating that the information was considered clear and accessible with minimal technical terminology (Figure 1).

Discussion and conclusions

The findings demonstrate high acceptance of SurgiGuide among healthcare professionals, particularly regarding usability, reliability, and clinical appropriateness. High positive usability scores and low negative scores suggest a system that is intuitive and efficient. The high ratings for reliability and accuracy also support the potential value of rule-based architectures in clinical settings, where transparency, consistency, and validated content are essential. Compared with generative AI systems, rule-based approaches may provide greater control over informational outputs while reducing variability and the risk of non-validated responses [5]. High comprehensibility scores further support the role of SurgiGuide as a patient-centered educational tool capable of translating perioperative information into accessible language [6], particularly within extended perioperative care models where patient understanding and adherence may influence outcomes [3]. Although participants reported relatively high digital competence, the low perceived need for training suggests potential applicability even in less digitally experienced populations, supporting scalability and broader implementation. Perceived reliability and coherence may also reflect the ability of rule-based systems to maintain clinical validation and governance over informational content [5]. Limitations include the small sample size, single-center design, and reliance on subjective perceptions rather than objective clinical outcomes. Future studies should evaluate the impact of SurgiGuide on patient behavior, adherence, and perioperative outcomes in larger populations. Overall, SurgiGuide was perceived as a usable, reliable, and clinically appropriate tool for perioperative patient education, supporting the potential integration of rule-based digital agents into extended perioperative care.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A164 Comparison between intermittent oscillometric method vs. clearsight in hemodynamic monitoring in patients undergoing enhanced recovery cesarean section (ERAC): a prospective observational study

C. Pantanelli1, M. Pazzi1, F. Marchi1, V. Manetti1, F. Perelli1, P. Ballo1, D. Conti1

1Emergency Department and Critical Care Area, Anaesthesia and Intensive Care Unit, Santa Maria Annunziata Hospital, Bagno a Ripoli, Firenze, Italy; 2Azienda USL Toscana Centro, Gynecology and Obstetric Department, Santa Maria Annunziata Hospital, Bagno a Ripoli, Firenze, Italy; 3Department of Cardiology Unit, Santa Maria Annunziata Hospital, Bagno a Ripoli, Firenze, Italy

Correspondence: C. Pantanelli

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A164

Background

Intraoperative hypotension during cesarean section (CS) is associated with multiple maternal and fetal complications [1]. This study aimed to compare the oscillometric technique with the ClearSight system for blood pressure monitoring and to evaluate patient acceptance of both methods.

Materials and Methods

We enrolled patients undergoing elective enhanced recovery after cesarean section (ERAC). The study was approved by the local Ethics Committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all patients [2]. Systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and mean arterial pressure (MAP) were measured simultaneously using both techniques. Measurements were recorded before subarachnoid anesthesia, every 3 minutes during the first 10 minutes after anesthesia, and subsequently every 5 minutes thereafter. In the postoperative period, patients’ opinions were assessed using a dedicated questionnaire evaluating discomfort and preference.

Results

Seventeen patients were included, yielding a total of 404 paired measurements. A moderate correlation was observed between the two techniques for SBP (R = 0.67; p < 0.01), DBP (R = 0.63; p < 0.01), and MAP (R = 0.70; p < 0.01). (Figure 1) Bland–Altman analysis demonstrated good agreement between methods, with a slight overestimation of DBP by the ClearSight system (mean difference 5.63 mmHg). (Figure 2) No significant differences were found in patient discomfort (Figure 3, Table 1), perceived comfort (Figure 4, Table 2), and expressed preferences (Figure 5, Table 3) among the methods (p = 0.95, 0.93, and 0.92, respectively).

Conclusion

Our study demonstrates good agreement between blood pressure values obtained with the ClearSight system and the oscillometric technique [3]. Patient acceptance of the ClearSight system was comparable to that of the standard oscillometric method. Therefore, ClearSight monitoring may represent a valuable noninvasive tool in selected patients undergoing ERAC to help detect and prevent hypotensive episodes.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A165 Anesthetic management of cesarean section in a patient with congenital bladder exstrophy and multiple reconstructive procedures: a multidisciplinary case report

S. Marchino, A. Maltoni, P. Antonazzo, A. Martinelli, F. Fracassi

Infermi Hospital, Rimini, Italy

Correspondence: S. Marchino

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A165

Background

Bladder exstrophy [1] is a rare congenital malformation involving the abdominal wall and genitourinary tract, frequently requiring multiple reconstructive surgeries [2] throughout life. Pregnancy [3] in affected women is associated with increased [4] maternal and fetal risks, including distorted pelvic anatomy, dense adhesions, urinary tract abnormalities, and major hemorrhage, making anesthetic and surgical management particularly challenging [5].

Case report

We describe a 19-year-old pregnant woman with congenital bladder exstrophy previously treated with multiple reconstructive procedures and neo-bladder creation. Pregnancy occurred spontaneously and remained uncomplicated until admission at 33+4 weeks for preterm premature rupture of membranes.

Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging showed severely altered abdominopelvic anatomy, with a large neo-bladder occupying the right hemiabdomen, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, and displacement of pelvic structures (Fig. 1). After multidisciplinary evaluation, cesarean delivery at 34 weeks was planned following fetal lung maturation with betamethasone.

Considering the high hemorrhagic risk, prophylactic bilateral hypogastric artery balloon catheters were positioned in the interventional radiology suite under epidural anesthesia. The same epidural catheter positionated at the L1-L2 level was then used for cesarean delivery, allowing anesthetic continuity across two procedures performed in different settings while avoiding general anesthesia and limiting fetal exposure to anesthetic agents.

Cesarean section was performed through a left paramedian longitudinal laparotomy with pediatric surgeons present intraoperatively. Extensive adhesions between the neo-bladder, uterus, abdominal wall, and bowel loops were identified. Ultrasound-guided placental localization was performed before hysterotomy to identify the safest uterine incision site, enabling delivery of a live breech fetus.

Estimated blood loss was approximately 600 mL. No transfusion, vasopressor support, conversion to general anesthesia, or inflation of the arterial occlusion balloons was required. Postoperative analgesia was provided with epidural PCA(patient controlled analgesia) with levobupivacaine. Two weeks later, the patient developed left iliac arterial thrombosis, likely related to the endovascular procedure.

Conclusions

Pregnancy after surgical correction of bladder exstrophy [6] requires highly individualized [7] multidisciplinary [8] management [9]. In this case, epidural anesthesia enabled successful management of both interventional radiology and complex cesarean delivery despite severely altered anatomy and nonconventional surgical access, while avoiding general anesthesia and minimizing fetal exposure to anesthetic agents. Prophylactic endovascular strategies may help reduce hemorrhagic risk, although vascular complications remain possible.

Patient Consent

Written informed consent from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying.

A166 Multidisciplinary management of pregnant patients with mechanical heart valves

M. Maio1, E. Menaldo1, L. Magnano1, N. Montali2, F.M. Comoglio3

1University Hospital “City of Health and Science” – Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Emergency, Turin, Italy; 2University Hospital “City of Health and Science” – Department of Cardiology, Turin, Italy; 3University Hospital “City of Health and Science” – Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics, Turin, Italy

Correspondence: M. Maio

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A166

Background

Pregnancy in patients with mechanical heart valve is a challenge for the cardio-obstetric team [1].

Materials and methods

We retrospectively evaluated 20 pregnancies in 15 patients with a prosthetic mechanical heart valve referred to the tertiary Sant’Anna Hospital (Italy) between 2007 and 2025. Demographic, obstetric and cardiological data were collected (Table 1). A written informed consent was acquired at admission.

Results

Of the 20 pregnancies, 6 were miscarriages and 1 was a therapeutical interruption.

As for the anticoagulation management, in 3 cases low-dose warfarin was continued until 36 gestational weeks (GW), while in the remaining 17 cases we performed a switch to low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) in the first trimester and then a second switch in the third trimester back to warfarin until 36 GW. Of the 13 pregnancies at term, in 5 cases we switched to unfractioned heparin (UFH) 36 hours prior to delivery, which was re-started 4–6 hours after; the other 8 had LMWH until labour and in the post-partum.

We performed Cesarean Section in 46,1% cases. They all required general anesthesia, because of emergency or non-reassuring coagulation labs. We adopted an endovenous analgesia protocol with remifentanil in most cases (71%) of vaginal deliveries. We didn’t perform neuraxial analgesia to avoid longer interruption of anticoagulation (Table 2).

Data has changed since the institution of Cardio-Obstetric team in 2015, composed by an Ob/Gyn specialist, a Cardiologist and an Anesthesiologist. According to the new guidelines, vaginal deliveries increased under analgesia, and caesarean sections were mainly performed for obstetric or fetal indications (Table 3). According to literature [2], we noted that C-section is associated to hemorragic events, which required blood transfusions, artery embolization or re-laparotomy.

Conclusion

Vaginal delivery under endovenous analgesia is preferrable. UFH 36 hours prior to delivery is associated with less hemorragic complications. Post-operative anticoagulation is the most critical trigger for hemorragic complications. Neonatal data are reassuring.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A167 Gastric ultrasound in pregnant patients: the end of an old superstition?

L. Tettamanzi, A. Di Sauro, L. Rota, G. Russo

Maggiore Hospital of Lodi, Italy

Correspondence: L. Tettamanzi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A167

Background

Pregnant patients have traditionally been considered at increased risk of pulmonary aspiration during anesthetic procedures, even after adequate preoperative fasting. This assumption has reinforced the longstanding dogma that every pregnant woman should be regarded as having a “full stomach”. Gastric ultrasound is a rapid, non-invasive and repeatable bedside technique that enables objective assessment of gastric content and aspiration risk.

Materials and methods

A prospective observational study was conducted at Ospedale Maggiore di Lodi in 2025. Twenty pregnant women undergoing elective cesarean section were enrolled after providing informed consent. Inclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria were age >=18 years, hemodynamic stability and appropriate preoperative fasting of at least 6 h for solid food. Patients undergoing urgent or emergency surgery, with previous gastric surgery, or unable to tolerate supine or right lateral decubitus positioning were excluded. Gastric ultrasound assessment was performed in both supine and right lateral decubitus positions using the Perlas Grading Scale. Gastric volume was estimated through measurement of the gastric antral cross-sectional area (CSA). A gastric volume >1.5 mL/kg was considered indicative of high aspiration risk.

Results

Median fasting time was 10 h. Most patients demonstrated a Perlas grade 1 pattern, corresponding to minimal clear fluid content and low aspiration risk. Mean estimated gastric volume was 38.75 mL. Analysis indexed to actual body weight (ABW) identified no patients at high risk, whereas analysis indexed to ideal body weight (IBW) identified one potentially high-risk patient. A positive correlation between body mass index (BMI) and gastric volume was also observed (Figure 1).

Conclusions

Gastric ultrasound appears to be an effective and reliable tool for objective evaluation of gastric content in pregnant patients. The findings suggest that adequately fasted pregnant women do not demonstrate significantly increased gastric volumes and therefore should not automatically be considered at high risk of pulmonary aspiration. Larger studies are required to confirm these preliminary findings.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A168 Immersive virtual reality during early labor: a prospective single-center pilot feasibility study (Real-V study)

V. Corritore, T. Palladino, F. Santoro, P. Vaira

Department of Obstetric Anesthesia, IRCCS Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza, San Giovanni Rotondo, Italy

Correspondence: V. Corritore

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A168

Background

Labor pain is a multidimensional experience involving both sensory and affective-cognitive components. During early labor, anxiety activation may influence pain perception and maternal autonomic response. Immersive virtual reality (VR) may modulate cortical and limbic circuits involved in the emotional-affective component of pain through attentional distraction and multisensory immersion mechanisms.

Objective

To evaluate the feasibility of implementing an immersive virtual reality system during early labor and to assess its impact on anxiety, pain, and hemodynamic parameters.

Methods

Prospective single-center, investigator-initiated pilot feasibility study conducted at the Obstetric Analgo-Anesthesia Unit of IRCCS Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza (San Giovanni Rotondo, Italy) over a 12-month period. Forty patients in early labor were enrolled (20 VR group; 20 pharmacological labor analgesia group). Allocation was based on patient preference after informed counseling. The intervention consisted of the administration of a standardized, non-interactive immersive audiovisual content (“Magnificient”, duration: 20 minutes) delivered through an Oculus headset. The content, identical for all participants, provided a highly immersive multisensory visual and auditory experience without gamification or active interaction, representing a passive immersive experience.

The primary outcome was feasibility and acceptability of the intervention in a real-world clinical setting. Secondary endpoints included changes in anxiety (STAI-Y1), pain (NRS), mean arterial pressure (MAP), and heart rate (HR), assessed before and after the intervention. Statistical analysis was performed using non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired data; Mann–Whitney U test for between-group comparisons). Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. The study was approved by the local Ethics Committee, and written informed consent for participation and scientific publication was obtained from all participants.

Results

The two groups were comparable at baseline for anxiety (p=0.574) and pain (p=0.432). Anxiety significantly decreased in both groups (VR group p<0.001; pharmacological labor analgesia group p=0.025), with a significantly greater reduction observed in the VR group (p=0.001). Pain significantly decreased in both groups (p<0.001); however, pain reduction was greater in the pharmacological labor analgesia group (p<0.001 for between-group comparison). MAP and HR showed significant intra-group reductions (p<0.01) in both groups, without significant between-group differences in changes from baseline.

Conclusions

Immersive VR during early labor appears feasible, safe, and well tolerated. Although less effective than pharmacological labor analgesia in reducing nociceptive pain, VR significantly reduced anxiety, supporting its role as a complementary non-pharmacological intervention targeting emotional-cognitive and stress-related components of labor. Larger randomized controlled trials are needed to better define the role of VR within a multimodal labor management strategy.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A169 Clinical safety profile of atogepant and tirzepatide combination therapy in patients with migraine and obesity: a case series

S. Sorrenti1, M. Ciuffreda1, E. Pisello1, C. Pellegrino2, A. Monacelli2, G. Cucè3, C. Piangatelli1, D. Galante4

1Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, AST Ancona, Fabriano (AN), Italy; 2Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, UNIVPM, Ancona, Italy; 3Department of Public Health, University of Messina, Italy; 4Department of Anesthesia, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, AST Ancona, Cerignola (FG), Italy

Correspondence: S. Sorrenti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A169

Background

Tirzepatide, in combination with a hypocaloric diet and physical activity, is indicated for the treatment of obesity (BMI >30) and overweight (BMI 27–30 in the presence of comorbidities). It is a long-acting dual agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptors.

Atogepant is indicated for migraine prophylaxis in adults experiencing at least four migraine days per month and acts as an antagonist of the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP).

Currently, data regarding the concomitant use of tirzepatide and atogepant are extremely limited. The aim of this study was to evaluate the clinical safety and preliminary efficacy profile of this pharmacological association in patients affected by migraine without aura and obesity.

Materials and Methods

Five female patients aged between 35 and 45 years, diagnosed with migraine without aura and obesity, were included in the study. All patients were receiving prophylactic therapy with atogepant 60 mg once daily. After at least one month of treatment with atogepant alone, tirzepatide therapy was initiated at a dosage of 2.5 mg administered subcutaneously every seven days, subsequently increased after four weeks to 5 mg every seven days. None of the patients had diabetes mellitus.

Patients were simultaneously followed by our Headache Center and by a dietologist. Tirzepatide administration was associated with a hypocaloric diet and regular physical activity.

Clinical safety and therapeutic efficacy were evaluated during follow-up. Migraine outcomes were assessed using the MIDAS (Migraine Disability Assessment) questionnaire, while tolerability and possible adverse events related to pharmacological interaction were systematically monitored.

The baseline BMI ranged from 30 to 32 kg/m². Before treatment, four patients presented a MIDAS Grade 4 disability score, while one patient presented a MIDAS Grade 3 score.

Results

No clinically significant pharmacological interactions were observed during combined treatment with atogepant and tirzepatide. Both therapies demonstrated clinical efficacy and were well tolerated by all patients.

A progressive and linear reduction in body weight was observed in all subjects throughout the follow-up period. In parallel, a reduction in migraine intensity and frequency was documented, with improvement in MIDAS scores after initiation of combined therapy.

After one month of treatment with atogepant alone, most patients improved from MIDAS Grade 4 to Grades 2–3. Following the addition of tirzepatide, clinical benefit was maintained or further improved over the subsequent two months. At the end of follow-up, most patients achieved MIDAS Grade 2 disability levels, suggesting better migraine control and reduced functional impairment.

No adverse events attributable to possible pharmacological interference between tirzepatide and atogepant were reported. In particular, no severe gastrointestinal, neurological, cardiovascular, or metabolic complications occurred during observation.

Conclusions

Available literature regarding the concomitant use of tirzepatide and atogepant is currently scarce. In our limited case series, the association demonstrated a favorable safety profile, without evidence of clinically relevant pharmacological interactions.

Both medications showed clinical efficacy, with improvement in migraine-related disability and progressive reduction in body weight. Although limited by the small sample size and short follow-up, these preliminary findings suggest that combined therapy with tirzepatide and atogepant may represent a safe and potentially effective therapeutic option in selected patients with migraine and obesity. Further studies involving larger populations are needed to confirm these observations.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A170 Role of PlateletMapping® tromboelastography in periprocedural antitrombotic management in a patient with myelofibrosis on dual antiplatelet therapy

C. Morrone, A. Diana, F. De Vivo, G. Sagristani, G. Cosenza, F. Coppolino, V. Pota, S. Pasquale, M.B. Passavanti, M.C. Pace

University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: C. Morrone

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A170

Background

Myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm. Approximately 90% of patients harbor mutations in the JAK2 gene, associated with increased production of reactive oxygen species. This link between inflammation and elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels is responsible for the prothrombotic risk [1]. Periprocedural management of antithrombotic therapy represents a clinical challenge, especially following acute coronary events.

Case Report

We describe this case about a 45-year-old woman with myelofibrosis, already receiving anticoagulant therapy and a JAK2 inhibitor. The patient after about a week of atypical chest pain developed an anterolateral ST elevation myocardial Infarction (STEMI) complicated by cardiac arrest. After return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), the patient underwent percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA) and was subsequently admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Dual antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation were initiated. After 10 days of mechanical ventilation, percutaneous thacheostomy became necessary. In preparation for the procedure, aspirin was discontinued 5 days prior and heparin was temporarily withheld, while clopidogrel was maintained. Given the marked interindividual variability in response to clopidogrel, with substantial differences in clinical outcomes, upon aspirin discontinuation we performed thromboelastography [2]. Informed consent to publish had been obtained. Thromboelastography (TEG), particularly in its PlateletMapping® variant, allows identification of patients with a suboptimal response to clopidopgrel. In non-responders, tromboelastography demonstrates parameters such as increased platelet aggregation, enhanced clot strength, and reduced clot lysis.

Conclusion

Our patient didn’t exhibit resistance to clopidogrel; therefore, tracheostomy was performed as planned on the fifth day of aspirin discontinuation. The procedure was completed without complications or bleeding. Once hemostasis had been achieved, aspirin and therapeutic-dose heparin were reintroduced.

This case highlights how tromboelastography with PlateledMapping® may represent a useful tool to guide the management of antithrombotic therapy in high risk patients, reducing, as in this one, the risk of stent thrombosis without increasing hemorrhagic complications.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A171 Sustainability and efficiency in the operating room: implementation of prefilled syringes for emergency drugs (safedose green project)

G. Bernardi1, A. Ingrosso1, L. Bray1, D. De Padova1, D. Crupi1, A. Fiore2, R. Campopiano3, L. Parroni3, M. Sanguigni1, A. Vergari1

1Department of Emergency, Anesthesiology and Resuscitation Sciences, IRCCS A. Gemelli University Polyclinic Foundation, Roma, Italy; 2Quality and Accreditation Unit, IRCCS A. Gemelli University Polyclinic Foundation, Roma, Italy; 3Hospital Pharmacy Unit, IRCCS A. Gemelli University Polyclinic Foundation, Roma, Italy

Correspondence: A. Ingrosso

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A171

Background

The global healthcare sector currently faces what can be defined as the healthcare carbon paradox. While the primary goal of medicine is to preserve human health, healthcare activities themselves contribute significantly to climate change, fueling a vicious cycle where environmental degradation increases the demand for care. It is estimated that healthcare facilities are responsible for 4.4% - 5.2% of global CO2 emissions [1]. Within hospitals, Operating Rooms (OR) represent one of the highest-impact departments, alone producing between 20% and 33% of total hospital waste [2].

This study is part of a structured project promoted by our University Hospital’s Management on institutional environmental sustainability. This initiative aims to integrate a Green Health culture into daily clinical practice, starting with a critical analysis of production and logistics chains, which account for 50% of the sector’s total emissions. In anaesthesiology, the management of emergency drugs (atropine, ephedrine, and phenylephrine) represents an elective criticality: traditional manual preparation from glass ampoules results in an average overall waste of 38% in the OR, with peaks of 92.4% for suxamethonium [3]. Notably, our internal audits reveal that over 97% of prepared atropine and 84% of prepared ephedrine vials are routinely discarded unused at the end of the shift. The current status quo requires the mandatory disposal of unused prepared drugs, resulting in an unsustainable drain of economic, temporal, and material resources.

Objectives

The SafeDose Green project evaluates the clinical, economic, and environmental impact of transitioning from traditional manual preparation to Ready-To-Administer (RTA) Prefilled Syringes (PFS) for emergency drugs. The goal is to demonstrate how this institutional choice allows for the reduction of the carbon footprint, optimization of management costs, and maximization of patient safety, in line with the University Hospital’s sustainability goals.

Materials and Methods

The study compares the traditional workflow (ampoule preparation) with the closed system offered by PFS. The evaluated parameters include:

Ecological impact: Estimation of the Carbon Footprint and waste generation based on literature evidence [1,4].

Ecological impact: Estimation of the Carbon Footprint and waste generation based on literature evidence [1,4].

Economic impact: An 11-month analysis of real-world usage volumes, evaluating the cost-savings from unused disposable materials (syringes and needles), the value of drugs no longer wasted, and staff labor-time.

Economic impact: An 11-month analysis of real-world usage volumes, evaluating the cost-savings from unused disposable materials (syringes and needles), the value of drugs no longer wasted, and staff labor-time.

Safety: Assessment of compliance with Joint Commission International (JCI) standards and ESAIC/EAHP guidelines [5,6].

Safety: Assessment of compliance with Joint Commission International (JCI) standards and ESAIC/EAHP guidelines [5,6].

Results

Environmental Impact: The use of PFS reduces the carbon footprint from 0.515 kgCO2eq (manual preparation) to a range of 0.340 - 0.430 kgCO2eq. The institutional model allows unused syringes to remain intact and be returned to storage, leading to an 84% reduction in materials used for emergencies. The elimination of systematic waste avoids the production of tons of additional healthcare waste annually.

Economic Impact

The economic analysis shows that the efficiency gained from avoided waste more than offsets the purchase cost of PFS. For atropine, the transition to PFS eliminated the wastage of 1,970 vials over 11 months (reducing the total units prepared from 2,030 down to just 60 PFS utilized). This directly resulted in an estimated 39.3% cost reduction compared with traditional manual preparation. For ephedrine, higher acquisition costs were offset by reduced drug waste, lower disposal burden, and significant staff time savings, supporting overall ecological and operational sustainability. Additionally, more than 1,512 staff labor-hours per year were recovered from low-value-added preparation tasks.

Clinical Safety: The PFS closed system eliminates the risk of glass micro-fragment contamination and sharps injuries to staff. Compliance with JCI Medication Management criteria is ensured by pre-applied ISO-standard color-coded labeling, which drastically reduces cognitive load and the risk of human error (e. g., syringe swap) in critical situations, while guaranteeing standardized drug concentration and high-precision industrial production.

Conclusions

The adoption of PFS, promoted as a pillar of our University Hospital’s environmental policy, represents a concrete step toward a modern and safe healthcare system. The SafeDose Green project proves that it is possible to combine clinical excellence with ecological responsibility, transforming emergency drug management into a model of efficiency for national healthcare.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A172 Second-degree atrioventricular block following thoracic spinal anesthesia: a case report

M. Fiore1, C. Porfidia1, V. Improta1, T. Formisano2, M. Ciaravola1, A. Allaria3, F. Ferraro1

1Departement of Women, Child and General and Specialized Surgery, University of Campania Luigi Vanvitelli, Naples, Italy; 2Cardiology Unit, University Hospital Luigi Vanvitelli, Naples, Italy; 3Department of Integrated Activities in Surgery, Orthopedy anHepato-Gastroenterology, Universitary Policlinico Vanvitelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: V. Improta

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A172

Background

Thoracic Spinal Anesthesia (TSA) is neuraxial technique indicated for high-risk patients to preserve hemodynamic stability and reduce opioid consumption [1]. However, the cranial spread of local anesthetic toward the T1–T4 segments can lead to the blockade of cardioaccelerator sympathetic fibers. This results in vagal predominance over the atrioventricular (AV) nodes [2–3], a phenomenon that becomes particularly evident in patients with pre existing conduction abnormalities [4–5].

Case Presentation

A 64-year-old hypertensive woman on chronic beta-blocker therapy (Nebivolol) underwent supra-umbilical repair under TSA. The preoperative electrocardiogram (ECG) showed a first-degree AV block associated with a right bundle branch block. The TSA was performed at the T7–T8 level using isobaric ropivacaine (12 mg) and morphine (80 micrograms). Following the induction of deep sedation with propofol and desflurane, the patient remained hemodynamically stable throughout the 75-minute procedure. However, upon arrival in the recovery room, monitoring revealed an anomaly in the plethysmographic wave. A 12-lead ECG documented a second-degree Mobitz Type I AV block (Wenckebach phenomenon), with a QTc interval of 498 ms (Figure 1). Despite the arrhythmia, the patient remained asymptomatic and well-perfused, with electrolytes and lactate levels within normal limits. After 23 hours of intensive monitoring, the heart rhythm spontaneously returned to baseline (Figure 2).

Conclusion

The incidence of arrhythmias during spinal anesthesia is directly correlated with the height of the block, exceeding 30% when the sensory level rises above T4 [6]. Post-TSA bradycardia has a reported incidence of approximately 20% and is usually self-limiting [7]. Notably, the sympathetic block can extend up to two segments higher than the sensory block identified by pinprick test [8]. In this case, the sympathetic blockade likely involved the T1–T4 segments, exacerbating a pre-existing conduction disorder that with the beta-blocker therapy further reduced the patient’s dromotropic reserve, facilitating the progression of the AV block. While TSA offers significant clinical advantages, pre-existing conduction disorders represent a critical risk factor for severe arrhythmias. Rigorous preoperative evaluation and prolonged postoperative monitoring are essential to ensure patient safety in contexts of electrophysiological fragility.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A173 A smartphone-based labeling system for anesthesia drug safety: design and concept of a compact, user-centered solution for operating room workflows

G. Dian

University of Brescia, Italy

Correspondence: G. Dian

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A173

Body

Medication errors in anesthesia remain a well-recognized and clinically relevant safety issue. In this context, drug preparation and administration are particularly vulnerable steps, with errors often arising not from a lack of knowledge but from human factors such as distraction, similar drug names and packaging, and inconsistent labeling practices. Evidence from the literature suggests that medication errors in anesthesia, while often underreported, occur with non-negligible frequency and may lead to significant morbidity, especially when involving high-risk drugs such as opioids, neuromuscular blockers, or vasoactive agents. Among the contributing factors, inadequate or absent labeling of syringes has been consistently identified as a key and preventable cause. Accordingly, multiple international safety initiatives have emphasized the importance of standardized labeling systems and color coding to improve drug identification and reduce the risk of substitution errors.

We present the concept and design of a compact, flexible, and user-centered drug labeling system specifically tailored for anesthesiology practice. The proposed solution integrates a smartphone-based application with a portable, customized thermal printer, aiming to deliver a rapid, intuitive, and scalable approach to medication labeling in the operating room environment.

The application is designed to support different clinical scenarios through a set of streamlined functionalities integrated into a unified interface (Figure 1).

A rapid access mode allows immediate printing of preconfigured labels for the most commonly used drugs and standard dilutions with minimal user interaction, making it suitable for time-critical situations. A guided creation pathway enables the user to select a drug, either from a predefined database or via barcode scanning, define the number of vials and dilution volume, and automatically obtain the final concentration, which is then printed on the label. In parallel, users can define and store customizable presets consisting of multiple drugs and standard preparations, allowing batch printing during routine setup of the anesthesia workstation and functioning as an implicit safety checklist. Additional flexibility is provided through a free labeling option for non-standard scenarios and the possibility of generating labels for infusion bags, larger containers, and intravenous lines.

The system adopts color coding and label formatting consistent with established international standards in anesthesiology to enhance readability and reduce the risk of misidentification.

From a practical standpoint, the system is conceived to be compact, portable, and economically sustainable. Small, rechargeable thermal printers can be positioned directly on anesthesia carts, ensuring proximity to the point of care and facilitating consistent use. Compared to existing commercial solutions, which are often relatively bulky and costly, this approach supports broader distribution, potentially enabling each operating room to be equipped with its own device.

Importantly, the overall design philosophy emphasizes the reduction of cognitive load and the elimination of unnecessary steps. Default automation, such as automatic time stamping and user identification, reduces the need for manual data entry, which is particularly critical in emergency situations.

In conclusion, the proposed system is intended to support safer medication practices by improving the standardization, readability, and immediacy of drug labeling, while remaining economically sustainable and fully compatible with the dynamic and often unpredictable nature of the operating room environment. Future developments will include usability testing, simulation-based validation, and prospective evaluation of medication error reduction.

A174 Variability in adherence to regional anesthesia guidelines: results of a single-center survey among anesthesia providers

E. Cialdella, D.M. Abbott, D. Esposito, F. Piccioni, M. Greco, R. Monzani, S. Brusa

IRCSS Humanitas Research Hospital, Rozzano, Italy

Correspondence: E. Cialdella

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A174

Background

Regional anesthesia (RA), encompassing both neuraxial and peripheral nerve blocks, is a cornerstone of modern perioperative medicine due to its proven efficacy in optimizing analgesia, reducing systemic opioid consumption, and facilitating accelerated functional recovery. To ensure patient safety and procedural success, international and national scientific societies, including SIAARTI and ESRA, have established evidence-based guidelines regarding aseptic techniques, anticoagulant management, and hemodynamic monitoring. Despite the availability of these standards, the degree of translation from clinical recommendations into daily bedside practice - the so-called knowledge-to-action gap - remains a critical area of investigation in the pursuit of clinical excellence.

Objectives

To assess adherence to guideline-based recommendations for regional anesthesia within the anesthesia department of an Italian IRCCS hospital, with a specific focus on characterizing the variability in anticoagulant management, aseptic precautions, monitoring standards, and procedural techniques among anesthesia professionals.

Methods

An anonymous web-based survey was distributed to anesthesia providers within an IRCCS Hospital Anesthesiology Department. Eighty-eight complete responses were collected from hospital-based physicians. Respondents included specialists (53.4%, n=47) and residents (46.6%, n=41). The survey instrument investigated several domains: professional profile, weekly RA activity, perioperative management of antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy (including Direct Oral Anticoagulants - DOACs), use of ultrasound and nerve stimulation, sterile precautions, monitoring standards, and postoperative management after neuraxial anesthesia. Descriptive statistics were used for data analysis.

A175 Risk factors for perioperative cardiac rhythm disturbances during adult spinal anesthesia: a protocol-concordant evidence synthesis

M. Fiore1, V. Arpenti1, G. Cosenza1, V. Improta1, V. Simeon2, P. Chiodini2

1Department of Women, Child and General and Specialized Surgery, University of Campania Luigi Vanvitelli, Naples, Italy; 2Statistics Unit, Department of Public, Clinical and Preventive Medicine, University of Campania Luigi Vanvitelli, Naples, Italy

Correspondence: V. Arpenti

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A175

Background

Cardiac rhythm disturbances during spinal/subarachnoid anesthesia — including bradycardia, atrioventricular block, and cardiac arrest — are recognized perioperative complications whose incidence and predisposing factors remain incompletely characterized. Despite the widespread global use of spinal anesthesia, no recent systematic review has comprehensively synthesized patient-related, anesthetic-related, and surgical risk factors for perioperative arrhythmias in adults.

Objectives

This systematic review aims to identify and synthesize the patient-related, anesthetic-related, and surgical factors associated with perioperative cardiac rhythm disturbances in adults undergoing spinal/subarachnoid anesthesia, with specific attention to the anatomical level selected for subarachnoid puncture and the resulting block height.

Methods

A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (1) and registered prospectively in PROSPERO (CRD420261389457). MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL were searched for studies of adult patients undergoing spinal anesthesia reporting cardiac arrhythmias. Eligible studies included randomized trials and observational cohorts. Data were extracted on patient age, ASA class, baseline heart rate, medications, puncture level, sensory block height, sedatives, and intraoperative factors.

Results

A total of 2217 papers were retrieved, 1260 after the duplicate remotion. Of these, only 15 were assessed for eligibility and only 5 were included (Table1) in the qualitative synthesis (Figure 1). Cardiac rhythm disturbances were consistently more frequent than clinically anticipated across all settings. Low baseline heart rate was the strongest independent predictor of intraoperative bradycardia across studies. High sensory block level (>T5) produced profound sympathectomy and significantly increased arrhythmia risk. In a prospective obstetric cohort (n=254) (2), first- and second-degree atrioventricular block each occurred in 3.5% and severe bradycardia in 6.7%, with advanced age as independent risk factor. In a large retrospective series (3), sinus bradycardia was associated with continuous subarachnoid technique, age >61 years, and female sex. Among older adults receiving dexmedetomidine sedation (n=102) (4), bradycardia requiring treatment occurred in 27.3% of untreated controls, significantly reduced by prophylactic atropine or ephedrine. In a retrospective cohort (n=91), low baseline heart rate and prolonged tourniquet time were independent predictors of bradycardia on logistic regression analysis. An incident reporting study (5) across 51 hospitals identified bradycardia as the dominant adverse event (74.4%), with high sensory block and inadequate prehydration as main contributing factors.

Conclusions

Consistently identified risk factors include low baseline heart rate, high sensory block level, advanced age, female sex, dexmedetomidine sedation, and prolonged tourniquet time. Spinal anesthesia should be managed as a monitored hemodynamic intervention. Preoperative identification of high-risk patients allows targeted prophylaxis including preload optimization, vasopressors, and anticholinergics.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A176 Pericapsular nerve block pulsed radiofrequency for hip arthrosis chronic pain: a case series

A.U. de Siena1, G. Giugliano1, S. Nappi1, D. Mancino1, S. Sodano2, P. Buonanno2

1A.O.U. Federico II Hospital, Naples, Italy; 2Department of Neurosciences, Reproductive and Odontostomatological Sciences, University of Naples Federico II, Italy

Correspondence: S. Sodano

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A176

Background

Chronic hip pain is a debilitating condition that significantly impairs mobility and reduces quality of life; traditional management involves a multimodal approach, including NSAIDs and intra-articular injections [1]. However, these strategies often provide only short-term or partial relief. Recent anatomical studies have identified the articular branches of the femoral, obturator, and accessory obturator nerves as the primary nociceptive pathways for the anterior hip capsule [2]. The Pericapsular Nerve Group (PENG) block has emerged as a landmark-based regional technique to target these branches [3,4]. This case series evaluates the efficacy of Ultrasound (US)-guided Pulsed Radiofrequency (PRF) of the PENG nerves as a long-term, mechanistic-based therapy for chronic hip pain.

Case Report

We report the cases of two male patients (78 and 81 years old) presenting with chronic hip pain associated with low back pain (Table 1). Both patients shared similar comorbidities, including Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, obesity, and systemic hypertension. Radiographic imaging confirmed advanced hip osteoarthritis in one patient and acetabular sclerosis in the second. Physical examination demonstrated positive FABER (Flexion, Abduction, External Rotation) and FADDIR (Flexion, Adduction, Internal Rotation) tests, indicating intra-articular pathology, without evidence of neuropathic deficits. Prior to intervention, both patients were managed with Tapentadol (100 mg/day) and Paracetamol 1 g on-demand, reporting baseline Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) scores of 9 and 8, respectively.

After obtaining informed consent to the procedure and publication of the cases, a diagnostic PENG block was performed using 6 mL of 0.5% Lidocaine under US guidance. Following a positive response (total pain relief within 30 minutes), the patients proceeded to PRF. Using a high-frequency US convex probe, the iliopsoas tendon and the ileoo-pubic eminence were identified. A radiofrequency needle was advanced in-plane toward the plane between the psoas tendon and the pubic bone. Sensory stimulation (2–100 Hz, 0.5 V) evoked a concordant deep pressure sensation in the hip, while motor stimulation (2 Hz, 1 V) confirmed the absence of a motor response. PRF was subsequently performed at three distinct points—beneath the center of the iliopsoas tendon, and 1 cm medially and laterally—to ensure a comprehensive coverage of the articular branches. The parameters were set at 42 °C and 70 V for a duration of 90 seconds per point. Follow-up assessments were conducted at 2 and 6 weeks’ post-procedure. The first patient reported a 100% reduction in pain (NRS 0), while the second patient reported an 87.5% reduction (NRS 1). Both patients experienced a significant improvement in walking comfort and overall mobility. No procedural complications or neurological deficits were observed. Notably, the analgesic effect allowed for a reduction in daily opioid consumption.

Conclusion

US-guided PENG PRF appears to be a safe, effective, and minimally invasive technique for the management of chronic hip pain due to osteoarthrosis. By targeting the sensory innervation of the anterior capsule without affecting motor function, this technique offers a promising alternative for patients who are poor candidates for surgery or those refractory to conservative management. While these results are encouraging, further randomized controlled trials with larger cohorts and longer follow-up periods are necessary to establish the duration of the analgesic effect and to standardize the PRF targets and parameters.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A177 Combined ultrasound suprascapular nerve and supraclavicular plexus pulsed radiofrequency for chronic arm pain in a patient with a history of choroid plexus papilloma: a case report

A.U. de Siena1, G. Giugliano1, S. Nappi1, D. Mancino1, F. Tesone2, P. Buonanno2

1A.O.U. Federico II Hospital, Naples, Italy; 2Department of Neurosciences, Reproductive and Odontostomatological Sciences, University of Naples Federico II, Italy

Correspondence: F. Tesone

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A177

Background

Choroid plexus papilloma (CPP) is a rare central nervous system tumor. It is typically located in the infratentorial compartment in adults and in the supratentorial compartment in children [1]. Most patients often present with signs and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure secondary to cerebrospinal fluid overproduction, seizures, and focal neurologic sensory deficits, hemiparesis, or cerebellar signs [1]. The first-line treatment is surgical resection [1].

Case report

We present the case of a 57-year-old male with a history of childhood surgical resection of a left ventricular CPP, which resulted in chronic right hemiparesis with asymmetrical gait and postural instability. Additionally, the patient reported severe functional limitation of the left shoulder due to ultrasound (US)-documented lesions of the supraspinatus and subscapularis tendons. Physical exam showed preserved range of motion in the hand, elbow, and wrist, but a total loss of shoulder mobility. The patients referred also positive neuropathic symptoms and hypoesthesia on the ventral face of the forearm and in the dorsal face of the hand; only positive neuropathic symptoms on the dorsal face of the arm, with a numerical rating scale (NRS) of 9 at rest and 10 at movement. The initial pharmacological treatment included tapentadol 100 mg per day, paracetamol 2000 mg per day, etoricoxib 60 mg for 7 days and muscle relaxant, resulting in a slight clinical improvement (pain relief of 20%). After signing informed consent to the procedure and article publication, the patient was a candidate for pulse radiofrequency (PRF) of left suprascapular nerve and supraclavicular plexus. Under US guidance and aseptic conditions, the suprascapular nerve (at the spinoglenoid notch) and the left supraclavicular brachial plexus (over the first rib) were identified [2,3]. PRF needles were then advanced under US guidance with in-plane approaches near the two targets. Sensory stimulation was performed with 10–200 Hz, pulse width up to 0.5 V reporting paresthesia in the shoulder joint for the suprascapular nerve and on the whole arm and forearm for the supraclavicular plexus. After motor stimulation (2 Hz,1 V), contractions of the infra- and supraspinatus, biceps, and triceps muscles were observed. PRF was then performed for 300 seconds (50 V, temperature 40 °C) for each point. Analyzing the change in static and dynamic NRS between baseline and after 15 days (Table 1), the patient presented a clinically significant reduction in static pain of 100% (NRS =0) and dynamic NRS of 80% (NRS=2); these led to improved abduction (0° up to 60°) and flexion (0° up to 45°) of the left shoulder (Table 1). The patient stopped all the medication except rescue analgesia with Paracetamol 1000 mg PRN. After three months, the values of NRS remained stable (Table 1).

Conclusion

Combined US-guided suprascapular nerve and supraclavicular plexus PRF could be a safe and effective technique for treating chronic shoulder and arm pain, providing significant reduction in NRS, improvement of motor function, and higher levels of satisfaction in patients with a history suggestive of rare cerebral tumors.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

Transfusion, hemostasis, and thrombosis

A178 Double hit hemorrhage: trauma and gastrointestinal bleeding in von willebrand disease

D. Gaetano, V. Lomonaco, C. Evangelista, G. Climaco, I. Orsini, M.G. Di Domenico, P. Di Monaco, A. Merola, P. De Negri

Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, A.O.R.N. Sant’Anna e San Sebastiano, Caserta, ITALY

Correspondence: C. Evangelista

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A178

Background

Patients with von Willebrand disease (vWD) are at increased risk of bleeding in the setting of trauma and surgery. Additional triggers such as severe colitis may create a “double-hit” hemorrhagic scenario, significantly increasing morbidity.

Case report

A 61-year-old man with known type I vWD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and obstructive sleep apnea sustained a severe crush injury of the left upper limb caused by a motorized agricultural device, resulting in extensive soft tissue damage requiring urgent orthopedic surgery with external fixation. Perioperative hemostatic prophylaxis with plasma-derived FVIII/vWF concentrate (Haemate) was administered. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit on postoperative day 2 (hospital day [HD] 2) for acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. His ICU course was complicated by prolonged ventilation, tracheostomy, and polymicrobial wound infection. During hospitalization, a progressive decline in vWF levels was observed, requiring repeated replacement therapy guided by laboratory monitoring and clinical bleeding. The first hemorrhagic “hit” was related to the initial traumatic and surgical event. On HD 24, the patient developed melena followed by massive hematochezia with progressive anemia (hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL), representing the second hemorrhagic “hit.” Stool testing was positive for Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli. Endoscopic evaluation revealed multiple ulcerative lesions of the sigmoid and descending colon, consistent with severe colitis of likely mixed etiology (infectious and ischemic). Despite aggressive medical management, including antifibrinolytics, targeted antimicrobial therapy, repeated FVIII/vWF supplementation, and massive transfusion support (>13 units of packed red blood cells), bleeding persisted. Computed tomography demonstrated colonic dilation without active contrast extravasation, supporting an initial conservative approach and excluding endovascular treatment. Due to ongoing hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability, the patient underwent left hemicolectomy with open abdomen management (HD 33), under perioperative FVIII/vWF prophylaxis. A second-look procedure (HD 37) included transverse colostomy and abdominal closure, again with factor replacement prophylaxis. Postoperatively, the patient progressively improved, was weaned from mechanical ventilation, decannulated, and transferred to a rehabilitation facility on HD 54.

Conclusion

This case highlights sequential hemorrhagic events in vWD: initial trauma-related bleeding followed by severe gastrointestinal hemorrhage due to colitis of mixed etiology. Management required repeated, clinically guided FVIII/vWF replacement, massive transfusion support, and escalation from conservative therapy to damage control surgery. Early recognition of multifactorial bleeding and multidisciplinary management are crucial in critically ill patients with vWD.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A179 Timing, team, and transfusion: a multidisciplinary rescue in postpartum hemorrhage

D. Gaetano, V. Lomonaco, A. D’Amico, M.G. Di Domenico, A. Mastropietro, P. Di Monaco, P. Di Monaco, R. Orlando, A. Merola, P. De Negri

Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, A.O.R.N. Sant’Anna e San Sebastiano, Caserta, Italy

Correspondence: D. Gaetano

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A179

Background

Postpartum hemorrhage remains a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, with outcomes strongly influenced by rapid recognition, coordinated multidisciplinary management, and timely activation of massive transfusion strategies. We report a case highlighting the impact of a system-based response and lactate-guided resuscitation.

Case report

A 33-year-old primiparous woman was transferred from a private clinic after postpartum hemorrhagic shock following a cesarean section complicated by uterine atony and subtotal hysterectomy. On arrival at the emergency department (22:51), she was in extremis, with non-measurable blood pressure, lactate >17 mmol/L, and ongoing high-dose vasopressor support (norepinephrine 0.6 mcg/kg/min). Focused assessment with sonography for trauma revealed massive hemoperitoneum, prompting immediate activation of a multidisciplinary pathway involving anesthesiologists, radiologists, general surgeons, and obstetricians. A thromboelastogram was performed. Massive transfusion was initiated using a balanced 1:1:1 strategy. The patient had already received 4 units of red blood cells prior to transfer; additional resuscitation included at least 4 units of red blood cells and 4 units of plasma intraoperatively, along with platelets, fibrinogen (3 g total), and tranexamic acid (2 g total, bolus plus infusion over 8 hours). She was transferred to the operating room within 30 minutes (23:20), where a two-step surgical approach was performed: emergency exploratory laparotomy followed by gynecologic hemostatic revision with cervical stump resection. Surgery concluded at 02:00, and the patient was admitted to the intensive care unit at 02:45. In the intensive care unit, vasopressor support included norepinephrine and vasopressin (1.8 IU/h), with progressive weaning (norepinephrine discontinued on day 6 and vasopressin on day 7). Mechanical ventilation was required for 6 days, with a total intensive care unit stay of 9 days. Lactate levels showed progressive normalization (13.1 mmol/L to 3.3 mmol/L to 0.8 mmol/L), paralleling recovery from multi-organ hypoperfusion. The patient was subsequently transferred to the obstetric ward with full functional recovery and no residual deficits.

Conclusion

This case illustrates how early activation of a coordinated multidisciplinary response, combined with structured massive transfusion, can reverse extreme hemorrhagic shock. Lactate trajectory provided a dynamic marker of resuscitation effectiveness and system performance, emphasizing the critical role of timing, team integration, and protocol-driven care in severe postpartum hemorrhage.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A180 Patients comfort during highflow oxygen therapy with asymmetrical prongs: the comfoxy-1 trial

A. Zanaga1, I. Paiusco1, M. Toniolo1, E. Vidal1, T. Pettenuzzo1,2, N. Sella1,2, F. Zarantonello1,2, P. Navalesi1,2, A. Boscolo Bozza 1,2

1Department of Medicine - DIMED, Section of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, University of Padova, Italy; 2Institute of Anesthesia and Intensive Care - Padova University Hospital, Italy

Correspondence: A. Zanaga

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A180

Background

High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) is a promising respiratory support modality that improves oxygenation, alveolar recruitment and comfort, while reducing dead space compared to conventional oxygen therapy [1]. Recently, a novel asymmetrical HFNC interface (Optiflow® Duet system; Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, New Zealand) has been introduced, but its physiological effects are not clear [2]. This study aimed to investigate whether different configurations of the asymmetrical HFNC interface—specifically, fully versus partially occlusive nasal prong—affect patient comfort, dyspnea, lung aeration, ventilatory efficiency, gas exchange, and hemodynamic parameters.

Methods

This was a randomized crossover physiological pilot study (ClinicalTrial.gov registration number NCT06778291) including 40 adults admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) of Padua University Hospital for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Each patient received oxygen therapy with fully and partially occlusive nasal configurations in randomized order (60 minutes each, with a 10-minute washout between phases). Nostril cross-sectional area was measured using a dedicated software, allowing standardized assignment of each nasal cannula configurations (Figure 1). Primary outcomes included comfort (Numeric Rating Scale, NRS) and dyspnea (Borg scale); secondary outcomes were lung aeration (assessed by electrical impedance tomography [EIT]), ventilatory efficiency (measured by corrected minute ventilation [MV] and ventilatory ratio), gas exchange, and hemodynamic variables. Comparisons between the two configurations were conducted both in the overall population and in predefined subgroups, according to baseline respiratory rates (< 24 or at least 24 breaths per minute).

Results

No significant differences were observed between fully and partially occlusive nostril setups in terms of comfort, dyspnea, EIT-derived measurements, gas exchange, or hemodynamic parameters, both in the overall population and in the subgroups. However, in patients with a baseline respiratory rate < 24 breaths/min, the fully occlusive nasal prong setup was associated with a modest increase in corrected minute ventilation (13 [10–16] vs. 11 [8–12], p = 0.02) and ventilatory ratio (0.0023 [0.0017–0.0027] vs. 0.0018 [0.0015–0.0020], p = 0.04) (Figure 2).

Conclusions

The degree of nasal occlusion in asymmetrical HFNCs did not significantly influence comfort, dyspnea, lung aeration, gas exchange, or hemodynamic parameters. A slight increase in ventilatory load was observed with the fully occlusive configuration in ICU patients with lower baseline respiratory rates, although the clinical relevance of this finding remains uncertain.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A181 A bench evaluation of work of breathing during non-invasive ventilation

I. Piccione, M. Bianco, A. Giannattasio, A. Credendino, M. Maiuri, S. Volpe, P. Giugliano, I. Clemente, L. Nunziata, G. Servillo, M. Vargas

University of Naples Federico II, Italy

Correspondence: M. Bianco

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A181

Background

Patient effort during non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is strongly influenced by ventilator triggering performance and pressurization capability [1]. Poor patient–ventilator interaction may increase inspiratory workload and negatively affect NIV tolerance and clinical efficacy [2]. Pressure–time product during triggering (PTPt) represents a reliable surrogate of the work required to activate ventilatory support. This bench study aimed to compare the triggering performance of different mechanical ventilators (MV) used for NIV under simulated respiratory conditions [3, 4].

Materials and Methods

This experimental bench study was conducted in the Intensive Care Department of the University of Naples Federico II. As no human subjects were involved, ethical committee approval was not required. Ten mechanical ventilators were evaluated, including eight ICU ventilators tested in NIV mode: Infinity V800, Infinity C500, Evita XL, and Evita 2 (Dräger, Lübeck, Germany); Bellavista 100 (IMT Medical, Buchs, Switzerland); SV600 (Mindray, Shenzhen, China); Servo-I (Getinge AB, Göteborg, Sweden); and Astral-150 (ResMed, San Diego, CA, USA). Two devices were dedicated NIV ventilators: V60 (Philips Respironics, Murrysville, PA, USA) and VIC8 (Awakzon, Shanghai, China) (Table 1). Ventilators were connected t o a manikin head linked to an artificial lung simulator (Figure 1) reproducing three respiratory mechanics profiles: restrictive (compliance 20 mL/cmH2O; resistance 5 cmH2O/L/s), normal (compliance 50 mL/cmH2O; resistance 5 cmH2O/L/s), and obstructive (compliance 50 mL/cmH2O; resistance 20 cmH2O/L/s). All ventilators were tested in pressure support ventilation or equivalent mode with inspiratory pressure support levels of 10, 14, and 18 cmH2O and PEEP set at 5 cmH2O. The inspiratory trigger was set at 1 L/min, the inspiratory time (Ti) was 2 seconds, the FiO2 was 21%. The primary endpoint was PTPt, expressed in cmH2O·s.

Results

Substantial differences in triggering performance were observed among ventilators across all simulated respiratory patterns. The VIC8 ventilator consistently demonstrated the lowest PTPt values, indicating reduced inspiratory effort required to trigger ventilatory assistance. In the restrictive pattern, VIC8 achieved significantly lower PTPt values compared with SV600, Evita 2 Dura, V60, Bellavista 100, Infinity C500, and Evita V800 (p < 0.001), while showing comparable performance to Servo-I and Astral 150 (Table 2). In the normal respiratory pattern, VIC8 exhibited the lowest PTPt value (1.39 ± 0.56 cmH2O·s), whereas Bellavista 100 and Evita 2 Dura showed the highest inspiratory workload (Table 3). Similar findings were observed in the obstructive pattern, where VIC8 maintained the best overall triggering performance with markedly reduced PTPt values compared with all other tested ventilators (Table 4).

Conclusions

This bench study demonstrated marked variability in work of breathing among MV used for NIV. Advanced triggering algorithms and improved MV responsiveness may substantially reduce patient inspiratory effort. Among the tested devices, VIC8 provided the most favorable triggering performance across restrictive, normal, and obstructive respiratory mechanics, suggesting a potential advantage in optimizing patient–ventilator interaction during NIV.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A182 Non-invasive assessment of inspiratory effort predicts extubation failure across three spontaneous breathing trial modalities: a multicenter observational study

F. Murgolo1, C.A. Bellissimo3, I.S. Morris1,4, G.M. Plens3, G. Roman-Sarita3, D.L. Grieco4,5, S. Spadaro6, V.M. Ranieri2, S. Grasso2, E.C. Goligher1,3, L. Del Sorbo1

1Toronto General Research Institute, University Health Network, Canada; 2Department of Precision-Regenerative Medicine and Jonic Area (DiMePRe-J), Section of Anaesthesiology and ICM, University of Bari, Italy; 3Department of Medicine, Division of Respirology, University Health Network, Toronto, Canada; 4Nepean Clinical School, Sydney Medical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, University of Sydney, Australia; 5Department of Anaesthesia, Intensive Care and Emergency, Fondazione Policlinico A. Gemelli IRCCS, Rome, Italy; 6Department of Anaesthesiology and ICM, Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, Rome, Italy

Correspondence: F. Murgolo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A182

Background

Airway occlusion pressure (Pocc) measured at the end of a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) is a promising predictor of extubation failure, but its predictive value has been demonstrated only during SBT performed with PEEP 5 cmH2O and pressure support (PS) 7 cmH2O [1]. Whether this relationship holds across other SBT modalities remains unknown.

Objective

To assess the predictive accuracy of end-SBT Pocc across three SBT modalities.

Methods

Three prospective multicenter cohorts were analysed: PEEP 5+PS 7 cmH2O (n=238; published cohort [1]), PEEP 0+PS 7 cmH2O (n=208; Bari University Hospital, ethics committee approval 0019587), and PEEP 0+PS 0 (n=69; ongoing multicenter study, NCT05857774). Pocc was measured at the end of the successful SBT before extubation. The primary endpoint was reintubation within 7 days. ROC analysis identified optimal thresholds using the Youden index. Informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Results

Among 515 patients, 100 (19.4%) required reintubation within 7 days after extubation. Pocc discriminated reintubation risk across all SBT modalities (AUC 0.908, 0.916, and 0.829 for PEEP5+PS7, PEEP0+PS7, and PEEP0+PS0, respectively; overall AUC 0.886; Figure 1). The median Youden-optimal threshold of Pocc across groups was −15 cmH2O. At this cutoff, sensitivity/specificity were 80.4%/90.1% for PEEP5+PS7, 87.5%/89.3% for PEEP0+PS7, and 100.0%/45.5% for PEEP0+PS0. Notably, the odds ratio associated with progressively more negative Pocc values beyond −15 cmH2O decreases as ventilatory support during SBT decreases: from 1.8 in PEEP5+PS7 to 1.6 in PEEP0+PS7 and 1.2 in PEEP0+PS0 (Fig. 2- Table 1).

Conclusions

A threshold of −15 cmH2O of Pocc measured at the end of the successful SBT before extubation predicts extubation failure across different SBT modalities.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A183 Physiological phenotypes of response to non-invasive respiratory support after extubation

F. Murgolo1, L.S. Menga3, D.L. Grieco4,5, G.M. Plens6, S. Spadaro7, E.C. Goligher1,6, M. Antonelli4,5, L. del Sorbo1, S. Grasso2

1Interdepartmental Division of Critical Care Medicine, University Health Network, Toronto General Research Institute, Canada; 2Department of Precision-Regenerative Medicine and Jonic Area (DiMePRe-J), Section of Anaesthesiology and ICM, University of Bari, Italy; 3Keenan Research Centre, Li Ka Shing Knowledge Institute, St Michael’s Hospital, Unity Health Toronto, Canada; 4Department of Anaesthesia, Intensive Care and Emergency, Fondazione Policlinico A. Gemelli IRCCS, Rome, Italy; 5Department of Anaesthesiology and ICM, Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, Rome, Italy; 6Department of Medicine, Division of Respirology, University Health Network, Toronto, Canada; 7Department of Translational Medicine, Section of Anaesthesiology and ICM, University of Ferrara, Italy

Correspondence: F. Murgolo

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A183

Background

NIV is recommended over HFNC after extubation in high-risk patients, yet response heterogeneity is substantial [1,2]. Occlusion pressure (Pocc) and dynamic lung compliance (CL,dyn) from a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) may improve phenotyping [3].

Objectives

To assess whether end-SBT Pocc and CL,dyn identify differential responses to NIV versus HFNC on inspiratory effort (δPes), respiratory rate (RR) and transpulmonary driving pressure (δPL,dyn).

Methods

Crossover study in 55 high-risk adults ventilated >=48 h. Pocc and CL,dyn/PBW were measured at end-SBT. Patients received alternating NIV and HFNC (12 h each). δPes, RR and δPL,dyn were analyzed with non-linear interaction models.

Results

There is a statistically significant interaction between the post-extubation strategies of respiratory support and the end-SBT Pocc or CL,dyn/PBW for all three target physiologic parameters (Figure 1). The change in δPes was significantly higher during HFNC than during NIV at intermediate values of end-SBT Pocc (−8 to −15 cmH2O) and end-SBT CL,dyn/PBW (0.43 to 0.62 mL/cmH2O·kg-1), with the largest between-treatment difference of δPes change of 2.9 cmH2O (95% CI 2.4–3.5) at Pocc of −12 and 2.5 cmH2O (95% CI 2.0–2.9) at CL,dyn/PBW of 0.51 mL/cmH2O·kg-1. The change in RR was higher during HFNC, for values of end-SBT Pocc <−15 cmH2O or CL,dyn/PBW < 0.43 mL/cmH2O·kg-1, with maximum differences of 9 breaths/min (95% CI 8–10) at Pocc of −18 cmH2O and 8 breaths/min (95% CI 7–9) at CL,dyn/PBW of 0.35 mL/cmH2O·kg-1. In contrast, δPL,dyn was consistently higher during NIV, with the between-treatment difference attenuated at intermediate values of end-SBT Pocc (−8 to −15 cmH2O) and end-SBT CL,dyn/PBW (0.43 to 0.62 mL/cmH2O·kg-1) and maximal at the extremes, reaching 5.5 cmH2O (95% CI 4.7–6.3) at a Pocc of −21 cmH2O and 5.9 cmH2O (95% CI 5.2–6.6) at a CL,dyn/PBW of 0.79 mL/cmH2O·kg-1.

Conclusions

NIV versus HFNC effects on effort, respiratory rate and lung stress depend on end-SBT Pocc and CL,dyn, supporting individualized post-extubation support.

A184 Mortality outcomes of VV-ECMO in adult ards: a systematic review and meta-analysis

A. D’Onofrio, E.R. Ginghina

Sapienza University of Rome, Italy

Correspondence: A. D’Onofrio

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A184

Background

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) remains associated with high mortality despite advances in mechanical ventilation and intensive care management. Veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) has been increasingly used as rescue therapy in severe ARDS, although evidence regarding its impact on mortality remains heterogeneous. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate mortality outcomes associated with VV-ECMO in adult ARDS patients compared with conventional management.

Methods

A systematic literature search was performed using PubMed and Scopus databases. Studies including adult patients with ARDS treated with VV-ECMO and compared with conventional mechanical ventilation were included. Randomized controlled trials and observational cohort studies reporting mortality outcomes were eligible. The primary outcome was mortality. Secondary analyses included subgroup analysis according to study design, etiology, and COVID versus pre-COVID period. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed using odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic. Publication bias was evaluated using Egger test.

Results

A total of 16 studies including 1104 patients treated with VV-ECMO and 5463 controls were included in the primary mortality analysis. VV-ECMO was not associated with a statistically significant reduction in mortality compared with conventional management (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.56–1.16; p=0.250). Substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed (I2=73.1%). Funnel plot asymmetry was not statistically significant according to Egger test (p=0.346). Subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent results across observational studies, COVID-related ARDS, and pre-COVID cohorts without statistically significant mortality differences. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses showed no individual study exerted disproportionate influence on pooled estimates (Figure 1).

Conclusions

VV-ECMO showed a non-significant trend toward lower mortality in adult ARDS patients compared with conventional management. Interpretation of results is limited by substantial heterogeneity and predominance of observational data. Further high-quality randomized studies are required to better define the role of VV-ECMO in severe ARDS management.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.
