A185 A bench evaluation of asynchronies during non-invasive ventilation

A. Giannattasio, P. Giugliano, L. Nunziata, S. Volpe, I. Piccione, M. Bianco, A. Credendino, I. Clemente, M. Maiuri, G. Servillo, M. Vargas

University of Naples Federico II, Italy

Correspondence: A. Giannattasio

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A185

Background

Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) has been used as first-line therapy in intensive care unit (ICU) patients with acute respiratory failure [1]. Therefore, selecting the mechanical ventilator (MV) that best fits each patient’s needs is crucial [2]. Accordingly, we perfomed a bench study specifically evaluating patient-ventilator asynchronies in ten ventilators during non-invasive ventilation.

Materials and methods

This experimental bench study was conducted in the Intensive Care Department of the University of Naples Federico II. No patient was involved and neither the approval from ethical committee was required.

Ten MV were tested. Eight out of ten were ICU ventilators set in NIV mode: Infinity V800, Infinity C 500, Evita XL, Evita 2 (Dräger, Lübeck, Germany), Bellavista 100 (IMT medical,Buchs, Switzerland) SV 600 (Mindray, Shenzhen, China), Servo-I (Getinge AB, Göteborg, Sweden), Astral¬150 (Resmed, San Diego, CA, USA). Among the ten ventilators tested, two were exclusively intended for NIV use: V60 (Philips Respironics, Murrysville, PA, USA) and VIC8 (Awakzon, Shanghai, China). The circuit of each ventilator was calibrated before the tests as set by the ventilator software. A 5-minutes trial was perfomed on each ventilator using pressure support ventilation (PSV) or an equivalent mode. Three PSV levels (10, 14 and 18 cm H2O) were applied to each ventilators, whereas PEEP level was maintained at 5 cm H2O in all conditions. The inspiratory trigger was set at 1 L/min, the inspiratory time (Ti) was 2 seconds, the FiO2 was 21%.

Three respiratory patterns were simulated by a lung simulator:

Restrictive pattern (RS) with a respiratory system compliance (RSC) of 20 mL/cmH2O and an airway resistance (AR) of 5 cmH2O L/s;

Restrictive pattern (RS) with a respiratory system compliance (RSC) of 20 mL/cmH2O and an airway resistance (AR) of 5 cmH2O L/s;

Normal pattern (NP) with a RSC of 50 mL/cmH2O and an AR of 5 cmH2O L/s;

Normal pattern (NP) with a RSC of 50 mL/cmH2O and an AR of 5 cmH2O L/s;

Obstructive pattern (OP) with a RSC of 50 mL/cmH2O and an AR of 20 cmH2O L/s.

Obstructive pattern (OP) with a RSC of 50 mL/cmH2O and an AR of 20 cmH2O L/s.

The primary endpoint was the patient-ventilator Asynchrony Index (AI), calculated as follows: AI=Number of asynchronies/global respiratory rate (ventilatory cycles + ineffective efforts) × 100 (%) [3]. The secondary endpoints were the type of asynchrony: flow asynchrony (FA), reverse triggering (RT), premature cycling (PC), double triggering (DT), delayed cycling (DC), ineffective effort (IE), auto-triggering (AT) [4,5]. Inter-ventilator comparison tests were performed with analysis of variance.

Results

In the RS, double triggering was the predominant asynchrony and seven ventilators have 100% of AI (Table 2). In the NP, double triggering and auto triggering were the predominant asynchrony and six ventilators have 100% of AI (Table 3). In the OP, auto triggering was the predominant asynchrony and six ventilators have 100% of AI (Table 4).

Conclusions

In this bench study evaluating mechanical ventilators during non-invasive ventilation (NIV), differences in ventilatory performance may explain the variability in the Asynchrony Index observed among devices. Notably, most ventilators failed to achieve adequate patient–ventilator synchronization even under normal respiratory conditions. Among the devices tested, the VIC 8—being the most recently developed ventilator—may benefit from more advanced and sensitive inspiratory and expiratory triggering systems, resulting in improved synchronization across all tested settings. The VIC 8 is a non-invasive ventilator designed to provide continuous respiratory support to adult patients with respiratory insufficiency who retain spontaneous breathing and require mechanical ventilation. These findings may support further investigation in future peer-reviewed studies.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A186 Use and limitations of transpleural pressure measurements in patients receiving non-invasive ventilation

A. D’Amore, I. Calamai, M. Ursitti, M. Luchini, R. Spina

Central Tuscany Local Health Authority (AUSL Toscana Centro), Empoli, Italy

Correspondence: A. D’Amore

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A186

Background

Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is widely used in acute respiratory failure, both hypoxemic and hypercapnic, but its failure remains frequent, particularly in patients with high respiratory drive and risk of patient self-inflicted lung injury (P-SILI). Transpulmonary (transpleural) pressure (PL) and its surrogate measurement via esophageal pressure (Pes) may provide a more physiologic assessment of lung stress during spontaneous breathing. However, their role in NIV remains poorly defined.

Methods

We conducted a prospective observational study in 20 adult patients admitted to the intensive care unit of San Giuseppe Hospital (Empoli) with acute hypoxemic and/or hypercapnic respiratory failure requiring high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) and/or NIV. Inclusion criteria were age >18 years, acute respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 <200 and/or pH <7.35 with PaCO2 >50 mmHg), and informed consent for participation. Exclusion criteria included contraindications to esophageal catheter placement and need for immediate invasive mechanical ventilation. Esophageal pressure was measured using a NutriVent catheter, positioned according to standard protocols. D-Pes (Delta-Pes) was recorded repeatedly during NIV/HFNC sessions and integrated with clinical and gas exchange parameters. Sedation with dexmedetomidine was used when necessary to improve patient-ventilator synchrony. Clinical severity and NIV failure were assessed using ROX index and HACOR score. Outcomes included need for intubation and relationship between D-Pes and ventilatory failure.

Written informed consent was obtained from all patients or legal representatives prior to enrollment.

Results

Twenty patients were enrolled, predominantly affected by pneumonia or acute exacerbation of chronic respiratory disease. Higher inspiratory effort, expressed as D-Pes >12 cmH2O, was associated with increased likelihood of NIV failure and intubation. Although statistical analysis using Fisher’s exact test did not reach significance (p=0.0623,), a clear trend toward higher failure rates in patients with elevated D-Pes was observed.

Case analyses demonstrated that D-Pes identified clinical deterioration earlier than conventional indices (ROX and HACOR). In several cases, persistently elevated D-Pes guided earlier escalation to invasive mechanical ventilation despite stable conventional scores.

Discussion

This study suggests that esophageal pressure-derived indices may provide additional physiologic insight into NIV performance beyond conventional clinical scores. Elevated inspiratory effort reflects increased pleural pressure swings and may contribute to P-SILI even during non-invasive support. While ROX and HACOR scores remain useful, they may underestimate early ventilatory failure in patients with high respiratory drive. D-Pes may therefore represent a more sensitive marker of impending NIV failure and lung stress. However, routine use of esophageal pressure monitoring is limited by technical complexity, need for expertise, and lack of validated thresholds in NIV settings.

Conclusions

Transpulmonary pressure estimation via esophageal pressure monitoring offers a promising tool for personalized management of NIV in acute respiratory failure. It may help identify patients at risk of NIV failure earlier than conventional indices and guide escalation of respiratory support. Further larger studies are required to validate clinical thresholds and impact on outcomes.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A187 Personalization of positive end-expiratory pressure using electrical impedance tomography and transpulmonary pressure monitoring during pressure support ventilation in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: the pepsi study

M. Bassi1, T. Pettenuzzo1,2, F. Zarantonello1, G. Pacchiarini1, F. Monteleone1, P. Dissegna1, F. Geraldini1, A. De Cassai1,2, A. Boscolo Bozza1,2, N. Sella1,2

1Department of Medicine (DIMED) – Section of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, University of Padua, Italy; 2Institute of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care – Padua University Hospital, Italy

Correspondence: M. Bassi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A187

Introduction

Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) is employed to prevent end-expiratory alveolar collapse and improve oxygenation. The best strategy to select PEEP during pressure support ventilation (PSV) in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) has not been extensively studied: PEEP is frequently selected empirically. A recently proposed strategy to set PEEP combines electrical impedance tomography (EIT) and transpulmonary pressure monitoring to balance alveolar collapse and overdistension [1]. Another approach may identify the optimal PEEP during PSV based on the ability to maintain stable end-expiratory lung impedance (EELI), reflecting sustained alveolar recruitment, similarly to what happens in controlled ventilation [2]. An alternative strategy may aim to optimize ventilation/perfusion matching. With this study we aimed to compare different strategies for PEEP selection during PSV and evaluate their agreement.

Methods

Patients with AHRF in PSV, monitored with esophageal manometry and EIT, underwent an incremental PEEP trial with each PEEP level maintained for 10 minutes. The ideal PEEP according to the following four criteria was identified: clinical PEEP, the PEEP offering the best compromise between EIT-based overdistension and collapse, the PEEP associated with the most stable EELI, and the PEEP associated with minimal EIT-based ventilation/perfusion mismatch. PEEP levels, as well as the corresponding physiologic variables, were compared. Agreement among PEEP-selection methods was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) based on a two-way absolute-agreement model. Pairwise agreement between methods was further evaluated using Bland–Altman analysis.

Results

Fourteen patients (median age 60 years, 10 men) were studied. In the subgroup of 8 patients with full data, the ideal PEEP levels did not differ significantly among the four PEEP-selection strategies (Friedman test, p = 0.147) (Figure 1, Table 1). The single-measure ICC for absolute agreement was 0.208 (95% CI, −0.072 to 0.666), whereas the average-measure ICC was 0.513 (95% CI, −0.359 to 0.888). Bland–Altman analysis showed small mean biases between methods, but relatively wide limits of agreement (Figure 2). When physiologic variables measured at the PEEP selected by each criterion were compared, no significant differences were observed.

Conclusions

Median selected PEEP levels were similar despite poor individual agreement among the four PEEP-selection strategies, suggesting limited interchangeability at the individual-patient level. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size and the limited number of complete cases available for some analysis.

Acknowledgements

The authors are indebted to all the colleagues, nurses and healthcare assistants who made this work possible.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying data.

A188 Awake intubation and the brixia airscoop scale to assess the analgo-sedative state

E. Cagnazzi1, M. Carlessi2, M. Adamo De Rossi2, G. Santacatterina2, F.A. Rasulo2, V. Torrano1

1Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care with an Anesthesiology Focus, Spedali Civili of Brescia, Italy; 2University of Brescia, Italy

Correspondence: M. Carlessi

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A188

Background

Awake intubation under analgo-sedation requires balancing patient comfort with preservation of cooperation.

Traditional sedation scales, including RASS and Ramsay, are not designed to assess dynamic responses during invasive airway maneuvers.

The Brixia Sedation Cooperative Scale, termed the Airscoop Scale (Airway Sedation Cooperative Scale), was introduced in 2023 at Spedali Civili Brescia (University-affiliated hospital) to evaluate procedural tolerance.

Aim

The primary outcome of the study was the occurrence of an Airscoop score >= 5 during awake intubation. In addition, the study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of using the Airscoop Scale for intraprocedural assessment of patient comfort and cooperation during awake intubation, as well as to describe its association with sedation management.

Methods

This prospective observational study was approved by the Ethics Committee on 18/01/2023, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. We enrolled 16 adult patients scheduled for elective or urgent surgery requiring awake intubation; this represents a preliminary report of a planned sample of 93 patients.

A six-step protocol was implemented, spanning from the initiation of sedation and topical anesthesia (T0) to the verification of the end-tidal CO2 curve (T5) (Table 1).

The AIRSCOOP scale evaluates five domains: gag reflex, cough, verbalization, limb movement, and cooperation. The first four domains are graded as: (A) fully compatible with the procedure; (B) compatible but with difficulty; or (C) incompatible with procedure completion unless sedation or patient comfort is optimized. Cooperation is graded as COOP or NCOOP (Table 2). Total score ranges 0–10; scores >= 5 indicate inadequate preparation (Table 3).

Sedation regimens included dexmedetomidine, ketamine, fentanyl, midazolam, remifentanil and low-dose propofol.

Depth of sedation was also assessed with RASS and Ramsay scales. Topical anesthesia: lidocaine 1% (or oxybuprocaine 0.5%) for the oral cavity; lidocaine 2% (or oxybuprocaine 1%) for the vocal cords/trachea.

Results

Awake intubation was successful in all cases (16/16), utilizing video laryngoscopy in 56.3% (9/16) and fiberoptic bronchoscopy in 43.8% (7/16) (Figure 1). The median AIRSCOOP score was 1.

Three patients (18.8%) presented an AIRSCOOP score >= 5, necessitating rescue topical anesthesia before successful intubation.

At T0, sedation was initiated with dexmedetomidine (87.5%) or ketamine (12.5%).

By T2, pharmacological management included fentanyl (87.5%), midazolam (62.5%), propofol (37.5%), and ketamine (37.5%) (Table 4)

No patient received monotherapy: 18.8% received two drugs, 37.5% three drugs, and 43.8% four drugs.

Topical anesthesia was achieved using lidocaine (81.3%) or oxybuprocaine (18.75%) (Table 5).

Median RASS and Ramsay scores are –1 and 3, respectively.

The primary clinical indications for awake intubation were achalasia/hiatal hernia (56.3%) and restricted temporomandibular joint (TMJ) opening (25%).

Conclusions

The preliminary report suggests that an AIRSCOOP score >= 5 identifies insufficiently prepared patients. In such cases, the procedure should be interrupted for corrective actions before intubation to ensure patient comfort. Overall, the AIRSCOOP scale provides a reliable and multidimensional way to evaluate patient tolerance during awake intubation.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.

A189 Management of difficult airways and closed-loop communication

G. Benigni, M. De Caro, K. Siconolfi, G. Castellano

ASL Avellino, Ariano Irpino, Italy

Correspondence: G. Benigni

Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care 2026, 6(1):A189

Background and Objectives

Managing difficult airways represents a critical clinical challenge requiring advanced technical skills and impeccable team coordination. This study aims to evaluate nursing knowledge in this field, their perception of preparedness, and their role within the multidisciplinary team. Particular focus is placed on closed-loop communication, an essential tool for patient safety whose effectiveness depends on training and clarity of roles.

Materials and Methods

A cross-sectional observational study was conducted through an anonymous questionnaire administered to 108 nurses working in various clinical settings, including emergency services, emergency departments, and intensive care. The survey explored theoretical knowledge, clinical experience, perceived competence, and the presence of operational protocols.

Results

Knowledge: Approximately 70% of participants possess an adequate, though non-uniform, theoretical basis.

Organization: Only 43% reported the presence of shared protocols; 31% signaled their absence, and 26% were unaware of their existence. Perception and Training: While the perception of personal preparedness is moderate, over 90% of the sample considers joint doctor-nurse multidisciplinary training to be fundamental.

Discussion and Conclusions

The data highlight organizational criticalities, particularly the limited dissemination of structured protocols, which can compromise the management of high-complexity situations. It is evident that the issue is not merely technical but involves the entire systemic and educational framework.

In conclusion, the management of difficult airways requires a multidisciplinary approach based on shared skills and structured protocols. Closed-loop communication must be integrated into a comprehensive educational system. There is a clear need to implement structured multidisciplinary training paths, starting from university education, to improve patient safety and teamwork effectiveness.

Informed consent was obtained for the publication of this scientific article.
